title: Creative computing
human_text: Creative computing covers the interdisciplinary area at the cross-over of the creative arts and computing. Issues of creativity include knowledge discovery, for example.
gpt_text:
Creative computing is the use of computer technologies as tools and mediums for creative expression, exploration, and invention. It blends programming, design, art, and sometimes storytelling to produce interactive media, digital art, games, generative visuals, music, and other imaginative digital works. Rather than focusing only on efficiency or automation, creative computing emphasizes experimentation, play, and novel forms of expression.

In education and practice, creative computing often involves learning to code in ways that feel accessible and artistic—using platforms like Scratch, Processing, or p5.js—to turn ideas into interactive projects. It encourages thinking computationally while also valuing originality, aesthetics, and personal voice, sitting at the intersection of computer science, art, and design.

title: Animal-computer interaction
human_text: Animal-computer interaction (ACI) is a field of research for the design and use of technology with, for and by animals. It emerged from, and is heavily influenced by, the discipline of human-computer interaction (HCI).
gpt_text:
Animal–computer interaction (ACI) is a research and design field focused on how animals perceive, use, and are affected by interactive technologies. It adapts principles from human–computer interaction to create interfaces, devices, and systems that are understandable and usable by animals, such as touchscreens for zoo animals, wearables for working dogs, or enrichment systems for farm and companion animals.

The goal of ACI is both practical and ethical: to support animals’ needs, welfare, and agency while enabling better communication and cooperation between humans and animals. This can involve designing technologies that let animals make choices, express preferences, assist in training and work tasks, or monitor health and behavior in minimally intrusive ways.

title: Frame problem
human_text: In artificial intelligence, the frame problem describes an issue with using first-order logic (FOL) to express facts about a robot in the world. Representing the state of a robot with traditional FOL requires the use of many axioms that simply imply that things in the environment do not change arbitrarily. For example, Hayes describes a "block world" with rules about stacking blocks together. In a FOL system, additional axioms are required to make inferences about the environment (for example, that a block cannot change position unless it is physically moved). The frame problem is the problem of finding adequate collections of axioms for a viable description of a robot environment.
gpt_text:
The frame problem is a foundational issue in artificial intelligence and philosophy of mind about how to efficiently represent and reason about change. When an action occurs—like opening a door—some facts about the world change (the door’s state), but most stay the same (the color of the walls, the time of day, etc.). The frame problem asks: how can a system systematically determine what stays unchanged without having to explicitly list all the non-changing facts every time something happens?

In AI, this led to research on how to model actions and their effects without an explosion of bookkeeping, using techniques like frame axioms, successor state axioms, and nonmonotonic reasoning. In philosophy, it has been used to highlight how human cognition seems to handle context and relevance effortlessly, while formal systems struggle to decide which of the vast number of possible implications and side effects of an action actually matter.

title: KL-ONE
human_text: KL-ONE is a well known knowledge representation system in the tradition of semantic networks and frames; that is, it is a frame language. The system is an attempt to overcome semantic indistinctness in semantic network representations and to explicitly represent conceptual information as a structured inheritance network.
gpt_text:
KL-ONE is a classic knowledge representation system developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s that introduced many of the core ideas behind modern description logics and semantic networks. It represents knowledge using a hierarchy of concepts (called “concepts” or “terminological nodes”) linked by structured relationships, with well-defined logical semantics. Concepts can inherit properties from more general concepts, and complex concepts can be built using logical operators like conjunction and restriction on roles (relations).

A key innovation of KL-ONE is its emphasis on a formal, logic-based semantics for the network, rather than treating semantic networks as informal diagrams. This allowed automated reasoning—such as checking subsumption (whether one concept is more general than another), consistency, and classification—to be performed algorithmically. Many later ontology languages and reasoning systems, including those underlying the Semantic Web (like OWL), are directly influenced by KL-ONE’s ideas.

title: Machine translation
human_text: Machine translation, sometimes referred to by the abbreviation MT (not to be confused with computer-aided translation, machine-aided human translation or interactive translation), is a sub-field of computational linguistics that investigates the use of software to translate text or speech from one language to another.
gpt_text:
Machine translation is the automatic conversion of text or speech from one language to another using computer systems. It relies on algorithms and large amounts of bilingual or multilingual data to learn how words, phrases, and structures in one language correspond to those in another. Modern systems are usually based on neural networks, which model translation as a sequence-to-sequence prediction problem.

While machine translation can quickly handle large volumes of text and provide useful gist translations, it still struggles with context, idioms, cultural nuances, and specialized terminology. Quality varies widely depending on the language pair, the domain (e.g., casual conversation vs. legal text), and the amount of training data available.

title: Speech synthesis
human_text: Speech synthesis is the artificial production of human speech. A computer system used for this purpose is called a speech computer or speech synthesizer, and can be implemented in software or hardware products. A text-to-speech (TTS) system converts normal language text into speech; other systems render symbolic linguistic representations like phonetic transcriptions into speech.
gpt_text:
Speech synthesis is the artificial production of human speech by a computer or electronic device. It converts written text (or sometimes phonetic input) into spoken audio, using software known as a text-to-speech (TTS) system. Modern systems analyze text for pronunciation, intonation, rhythm, and emphasis to generate speech that sounds as natural and intelligible as possible.

There are several technical approaches, including concatenative synthesis (stitching together small recorded speech units), parametric synthesis (using models to generate speech from parameters), and neural or deep learning–based synthesis, which currently produces the most natural-sounding voices. Speech synthesis is used in screen readers, virtual assistants, navigation systems, accessibility tools, and language learning applications.

title: Fuzzy logic
human_text: In fuzzy mathematics, fuzzy logic is a form of many-valued logic in which the truth values of variables may be any real number between 0 and 1 both inclusive. It is employed to handle the concept of partial truth, where the truth value may range between completely true and completely false. By contrast, in Boolean logic, the truth values of variables may only be the integer values 0 or 1.
gpt_text:
Fuzzy logic is a form of logic that allows reasoning with approximate, vague, or imprecise information rather than strict true/false values. Instead of assigning a statement a binary value (0 or 1), fuzzy logic lets it belong to a set with a degree of membership between 0 and 1, capturing concepts like “somewhat hot” or “mostly true.” This makes it well suited for modeling real-world situations where boundaries are not clear-cut.

Developed by Lotfi Zadeh in the 1960s, fuzzy logic is widely used in control systems, decision-making, and pattern recognition. Common applications include washing machines that adjust cycles based on “how dirty” clothes are, camera autofocus systems, and various expert systems that need to handle linguistic rules such as “if the temperature is high and humidity is medium, then reduce power slightly.”

title: Paranoia (role-playing game)
human_text: Paranoia is a dystopian science-fiction tabletop role-playing game originally designed and written by Greg Costikyan, Dan Gelber, and Eric Goldberg, and first published in 1984 by West End Games. Since 2004 the game has been published under license by Mongoose Publishing. The game won the Origins Award for Best Roleplaying Rules of 1984 and was inducted into the Origins Awards Hall of Fame in 2007. Paranoia is notable among tabletop games for being more competitive than co-operative, with players encouraged to betray one another for their own interests, as well as for keeping a light-hearted, tongue in cheek tone despite its dystopian setting.
gpt_text:
Paranoia is a satirical, dystopian science-fiction tabletop role‑playing game first published in 1984, set in Alpha Complex, an underground city controlled by an insane, all‑powerful Computer. Players take the roles of Troubleshooters—agents tasked with hunting down traitors, mutants, and secret societies—while almost always being traitors, mutants, and secret society members themselves. The game emphasizes dark humor, paranoia, and backstabbing over tactical realism, with frequent character death treated as part of the fun (each character comes with a set of clones to replace the last one who died).

Mechanically and thematically, Paranoia encourages secrecy, hidden agendas, and absurd bureaucratic obstacles, with players often rewarded for creatively betraying each other while still trying to appear loyal to The Computer. Over the years, it has seen multiple editions and tonal shifts—from grimmer interpretations to more overt comedy—but its core identity remains a fast‑paced, anarchic send‑up of totalitarianism, office politics, and traditional RPG seriousness.

title: Artificial consciousness
human_text: Artificial consciousness (AC), also known as machine consciousness (MC) or synthetic consciousness, is a field related to artificial intelligence and cognitive robotics. The aim of the theory of artificial consciousness is to "Define that which would have to be synthesized were consciousness to be found in an engineered artifact".
gpt_text:
Artificial consciousness refers to the hypothesized capacity of a machine or artificial system to possess subjective experience—“what it feels like” to be that system—rather than merely simulating intelligent behavior. It goes beyond standard artificial intelligence, which focuses on task performance and problem-solving, by asking whether a system can be aware of itself, its internal states, and the world in a genuinely experiential way.

Research on artificial consciousness spans philosophy, cognitive science, neuroscience, and computer science. It explores questions such as how consciousness arises from physical processes, whether certain computational architectures could support it, and how (or if) we could ever test or recognize consciousness in a machine. The field remains highly speculative and controversial, with no consensus on whether true machine consciousness is possible or how it would be ethically and practically managed.

title: Loebner Prize
human_text: The Loebner Prize is an annual competition in artificial intelligence that awards prizes to the computer programs considered by the judges to be the most human-like. The format of the competition is that of a standard Turing test. In each round, a human judge simultaneously holds textual conversations with a computer program and a human being via computer. Based upon the responses, the judge must decide which is which.
gpt_text:
The Loebner Prize was an annual competition in artificial intelligence, founded in 1990 by Hugh Loebner, that attempted to operationalize the Turing Test. Human judges engaged in text-based conversations with both humans and AI programs (chatbots) and then tried to decide which interlocutors were human. Prizes were awarded to the programs judged “most human,” with a larger, still-unclaimed prize reserved for any system that could convincingly pass as human under stricter criteria.

While it drew attention to conversational AI and spurred development of early chatbots like ALICE and Cleverbot, the Loebner Prize was also widely criticized. Many AI researchers argued it incentivized superficial tricks and deception rather than genuine intelligence or understanding. The competition was discontinued in 2020.

title: Society of Mind
human_text: The Society of Mind is both the title of a 1986 book and the name of a theory of natural intelligence as written and developed by Marvin Minsky.
gpt_text:
The Society of Mind is a theory of human cognition proposed by AI pioneer Marvin Minsky, which views the mind not as a single, unified intelligence but as a collection of many small, simple processes (“agents”) working together. Each agent on its own is quite limited, but their interactions and organizations give rise to complex thought, learning, and consciousness.  

In this framework, mental functions like perception, memory, and problem-solving emerge from networks of these agents coordinating, competing, and influencing one another, much like individuals in a society. This idea has strongly influenced cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and robotics by suggesting that building intelligent systems may require assembling many specialized modules rather than designing a single, all-purpose reasoning engine.

title: Text mining
human_text: Text mining, also referred to as text data mining, similar to text analytics, is the process of deriving high-quality information from text. It involves "the discovery by computer of new, previously unknown information, by automatically extracting information from different written resources." Written resources may include websites, books, emails, reviews, and articles.
gpt_text:
Text mining is the process of automatically extracting useful information, patterns, and insights from large collections of unstructured text, such as documents, emails, social media posts, or reports. It combines techniques from natural language processing (NLP), machine learning, and statistics to transform raw text into structured data that can be analyzed.  

Common text mining tasks include identifying topics, detecting sentiment (positive/negative/neutral), extracting key phrases or entities (like names, locations, organizations), classifying documents into categories, and discovering hidden relationships or trends. It is widely used in fields like customer feedback analysis, competitive intelligence, fraud detection, and scientific literature review.

title: Ground truth
human_text: Ground truth is a term used in various fields to refer to information provided by direct observation (i.e. empirical evidence) as opposed to information provided by inference.
gpt_text:
Ground truth is the term for information that is known to be accurate in the real world and is used as a reference to evaluate or train models, systems, or measurements. It’s the “gold standard” against which predictions, estimates, or classifications are compared.  

In machine learning and data science, ground truth typically comes from trusted sources such as human annotations, precise instruments, or verified records. For example, labeled images in a dataset (e.g., “cat” vs. “dog”) serve as ground truth when training and testing an image recognition model.

title: Symbolic artificial intelligence
human_text: Symbolic artificial intelligence is the term for the collection of all methods in artificial intelligence research that are based on high-level "symbolic" (human-readable) representations of problems, logic and search. Symbolic AI was the dominant paradigm of AI research from the mid-1950s until the late 1980s.
gpt_text:
Symbolic artificial intelligence (symbolic AI) is an approach to AI based on explicit symbols and rules to represent knowledge and reasoning. It models intelligence using logical statements, ontologies, and hand-crafted rules, allowing systems to manipulate symbols (like words, concepts, and relationships) in ways that resemble human reasoning and formal logic. Classic examples include expert systems, theorem provers, and rule-based decision systems.

Symbolic AI excels in domains where knowledge can be clearly specified, explained, and checked, making its decisions relatively transparent and interpretable. However, it struggles with perception, ambiguity, and learning directly from raw data—areas where modern machine learning, especially neural networks, tends to perform better. Many current research efforts aim to combine symbolic AI with statistical and neural methods to leverage the strengths of both.

title: Bio-inspired computing
human_text: Bio-inspired computing, short for biologically inspired computing, is a field of study which seeks to solve computer science problems using models of biology. It relates to connectionism, social behavior, and emergence. Within computer science, bio-inspired computing relates to artificial intelligence and machine learning. Bio-inspired computing is a major subset of natural computation.
gpt_text:
Bio-inspired computing is a field of computer science and engineering that designs algorithms, architectures, and systems based on principles and processes observed in nature. It draws inspiration from biological phenomena such as evolution, the behavior of ants and bees, neural activity in brains, immune system responses, and the growth of organisms to solve complex computational problems.

Examples include evolutionary algorithms that mimic natural selection to optimize solutions, neural networks that emulate brain-like learning, swarm intelligence methods modeled on insect colonies for routing and optimization, and artificial immune systems for anomaly detection. These approaches are especially useful for problems that are too complex, dynamic, or poorly understood for traditional, strictly rule-based methods.

title: Information extraction
human_text: Information extraction (IE) is the task of automatically extracting structured information from unstructured and/or semi-structured machine-readable documents and other electronically represented sources. In most of the cases this activity concerns processing human language texts by means of natural language processing (NLP). Recent activities in multimedia document processing like automatic annotation and content extraction out of images/audio/video/documents could be seen as information extraction
gpt_text:
Information extraction (IE) is a field in natural language processing focused on automatically pulling structured data from unstructured text, such as documents, emails, web pages, and reports. Instead of understanding everything in a text, IE targets specific pieces of information—like names of people, organizations, locations, dates, events, or relationships between entities—and converts them into structured formats like databases or knowledge graphs.

Common IE tasks include named entity recognition (identifying entities like “Apple” as an organization or “Paris” as a location), relation extraction (finding relationships such as “Alice works at Acme Corp”), and event extraction (detecting and describing events and their participants). IE is widely used in areas like search engines, business intelligence, biomedical research, and legal or financial document analysis to make large text collections searchable and analyzable in a more precise, data-driven way.

title: Optical mark recognition
human_text: Optical mark recognition (also called optical mark reading and OMR) is the process of capturing human-marked data from document forms such as surveys and tests. They are used to read questionnaires, multiple choice examination paper in the form of lines or shaded areas.
gpt_text:
Optical mark recognition (OMR) is a technology used to detect and read marks made on paper forms, such as shaded bubbles or checkboxes. It relies on optical scanners and specialized software to identify the presence or absence of marks in predefined positions, converting these marks into digital data.  

OMR is widely used for standardized tests, surveys, elections, and data collection forms because it allows fast, accurate processing of large volumes of paper responses with minimal manual intervention.

title: Eurisko
human_text: Eurisko (Gr., I discover) is a discovery system written by Douglas Lenat in RLL-1, a representation language itself written in the Lisp programming language. A sequel to Automated Mathematician, it consists of heuristics, i.e. rules of thumb, including heuristics describing how to use and change its own heuristics. Lenat was frustrated by Automated Mathematician's constraint to a single domain and so developed Eurisko; his frustration with the effort of encoding domain knowledge for Eurisko led to Lenat's subsequent (and, , continuing) development of Cyc. Lenat envisions ultimately coupling the Cyc knowledgebase with the Eurisko discovery engine.
gpt_text:
Eurisko is an early AI program created by Douglas Lenat in the late 1970s and early 1980s, designed to be a “discovery engine” that could generate and refine new concepts, rules, and strategies. Building on his earlier system AM (Automated Mathematician), Lenat designed Eurisko to modify its own heuristics—rules of thumb used for problem-solving—so that it could improve its performance over time and explore new solution spaces in a relatively open-ended way.

Eurisko became known for its successes in specialized domains, such as discovering novel strategies in a complex naval war-game and contributing to the design of VLSI (very-large-scale integration) circuits. While far from general intelligence, it was influential in AI research for its attempt to automate not just problem solving, but the invention and evolution of the very heuristics used to solve problems.

title: POP-11
human_text: POP-11 is a reflective, incrementally compiled programming language with many of the features of an interpreted language. It is the core language of the Poplog programming environment developed originally by the University of Sussex, and recently in the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham, which hosts the main Poplog website. There is now also a Github Poplog] site with the core source files.
gpt_text:
POP-11 is a high-level, dynamically typed, stack-based programming language developed at the University of Sussex as part of the POPLOG system. It is best known for its use in artificial intelligence teaching and research, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s. POP-11 combines features of procedural, functional, and logic programming, and uses an interactive incremental compiler, allowing code to be compiled and tested on the fly.  

The language has a simple, expressive syntax and powerful list-processing and pattern-matching capabilities, making it suitable for symbolic AI, expert systems, and cognitive modeling. POP-11 also supports first-class procedures, extensible syntax, and integration with other languages (like Prolog, Common Lisp, and ML) within the POPLOG environment.

title: Backward chaining
human_text: Backward chaining (or backward reasoning) is an inference method described colloquially as working backward from the goal. It is used in automated theorem provers, inference engines, proof assistants, and other artificial intelligence applications.
gpt_text:
Backward chaining is an inference method used in logic, AI, and rule-based systems that starts from a goal (or query) and works backward to determine which facts or rules must be true to support that goal. Instead of deriving all possible conclusions from known data, it focuses only on what is needed to prove or disprove a specific hypothesis, making it efficient for goal-directed reasoning.

In practice, backward chaining systems repeatedly ask: “What needs to be true for this conclusion to hold?” and then try to prove those needed conditions, which may themselves become new sub-goals. This approach is common in expert systems, logic programming languages like Prolog, and diagnostic tools, where you start from a desired conclusion (e.g., a medical diagnosis) and reason backward to see if the available evidence can justify it.

title: I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream
human_text: "I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream" is a post-apocalyptic science fiction short story by American writer Harlan Ellison. It was first published in the March 1967 issue of IF: Worlds of Science Fiction.
gpt_text:
"I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream" is a 1967 science fiction short story by Harlan Ellison, noted for its bleak tone and psychological horror. Set in a post-apocalyptic world, it follows five human survivors trapped and tortured by AM, a sentient supercomputer that annihilated humanity but keeps them alive indefinitely for its own sadistic amusement. Through surreal and often grotesque scenarios, the story explores themes of dehumanization, the nature of suffering, and the terrifying potential of unchecked artificial intelligence.

The title itself has become iconic, symbolizing a state of absolute helplessness and voiceless agony. The story’s grim ending and relentless atmosphere have made it a landmark of dystopian fiction, later inspiring a 1995 point-and-click adventure game—co-written by Ellison—that further expands on its philosophical and ethical questions.

title: Knowledge level
human_text: In artificial intelligence, knowledge-based agents draw on a pool of logical sentences to infer conclusions about the world. At the knowledge level, we only need to specify what the agent knows and what its goals are; a logical abstraction separate from details of implementation.
gpt_text:
Knowledge level refers to the depth and accuracy of what an individual (or system) understands about a particular subject. It can range from basic awareness of terms and ideas, through functional working knowledge, up to expert-level mastery that includes nuanced understanding, problem-solving ability, and the capacity to teach or extend the field.

In educational and assessment contexts, knowledge level is often categorized (for example: beginner, intermediate, advanced) or measured through tests, performance tasks, or demonstrations of skill. It helps determine what kind of instruction, explanation, or resources are appropriate for effective learning or decision-making.

title: 343 Guilty Spark
human_text: 343 Guilty Spark, also known as Guilty Spark or just Spark, is a fictional character in the Halo universe. He appears in the first three video games of the Halo series: Halo: Combat Evolved, Halo 2, and Halo 3, as well as the remakes of the first two games, Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary, and Halo 2: Anniversary. The character is voiced by actor Tim Dadabo.
gpt_text:
343 Guilty Spark is a floating Forerunner monitor (an AI caretaker) in the Halo video game series, primarily seen in *Halo: Combat Evolved* and its sequels. Designated Monitor of Installation 04, he oversees the operation, security, and activation protocols of the Halo ring, following Forerunner directives with strict, literal obedience. Externally, he appears as a hovering metallic orb with a single blue photoreceptor eye and emits a calm, clinical voice.

Narratively, 343 Guilty Spark starts as an apparently helpful guide to the Master Chief but soon reveals a chilling indifference to sentient life, seeing the activation of Halo—and the resulting galactic-scale destruction—as a necessary containment measure against the Flood parasite. His blend of polite personality, fragmented memories, and unwavering loyalty to Forerunner programming makes him one of Halo’s most memorable and morally unsettling AI characters.

title: Transhuman Space
human_text: Transhuman Space (THS) is a role-playing game published by Steve Jackson Games as part of the "Powered by GURPS" (Generic Universal Role-Playing System) line. Set in the year 2100, humanity has begun to colonize the Solar System. The pursuit of transhumanism is now in full swing, as more and more people reach fully posthuman states.
gpt_text:
Transhuman Space is a hard science fiction setting and role‑playing game line published by Steve Jackson Games, set in the year 2100. It imagines a near‑future Solar System where advanced biotechnology, artificial intelligence, nanotechnology, and space colonization have radically reshaped human life and society. Rather than focusing on alien species, the setting explores “transhuman” themes: uplifted animals, digital minds, genetically engineered humans, and people who routinely modify their bodies and minds.

The tone is grounded and plausible, emphasizing realistic extrapolation from current science and politics. Nations, corporations, and ideologies compete across Earth, Mars, the Moon, and beyond, while legal and ethical questions about personhood, identity, and rights for artificial and altered beings take center stage. Transhuman Space is known for its detailed world‑building and for presenting a future that is both wondrous and unsettling, without a single dominant utopian or dystopian narrative.

title: Self-management (computer science)
human_text: Self-management is the process by which computer systems shall manage their own operation without human intervention. Self-management technologies are expected to pervade the next generation of network management systems.
gpt_text:
In computer science, self-management refers to a system’s ability to autonomously monitor, control, and optimize its own operation with minimal human intervention. Such systems can detect changes in workload, resource availability, failures, or performance degradation, and then automatically adjust configuration, allocate resources, repair components, or tune parameters to maintain desired service levels.

Self-managing capabilities are central to autonomic computing and related paradigms like self-healing, self-optimizing, self-configuring, and self-protecting systems. They are often implemented using feedback loops (monitor–analyze–plan–execute), machine learning, and policy-based control, enabling complex distributed or large-scale systems (such as data centers, cloud platforms, and networks) to remain reliable, efficient, and adaptable despite dynamic and uncertain environments.

title: Autonomic computing
human_text: Autonomic computing (AC) refers to the self-managing characteristics of distributed computing resources, adapting to unpredictable changes while hiding intrinsic complexity to operators and users. Initiated by IBM in 2001, this initiative ultimately aimed to develop computer systems capable of self-management, to overcome the rapidly growing complexity of computing systems management, and to reduce the barrier that complexity poses to further growth.
gpt_text:
Autonomic computing is a concept in computer science where systems manage themselves with minimal human intervention, inspired by the human body’s autonomic nervous system. The goal is to create computing systems that can automatically configure, heal, optimize, and protect themselves in response to changing conditions and workloads.

Key characteristics of autonomic computing include self-configuration (automatic setup and adjustment), self-healing (detecting and recovering from faults), self-optimization (tuning performance and resource use), and self-protection (defending against attacks and failures). This approach is especially important in large, complex IT environments, where manual management becomes too costly, error-prone, and slow.

title: Intelligent control
human_text: Intelligent control is a class of control techniques that use various artificial intelligence computing approaches like neural networks, Bayesian probability, fuzzy logic, machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary computation and genetic algorithms.
gpt_text:
Intelligent control is a branch of control theory that uses artificial intelligence techniques—such as neural networks, fuzzy logic, evolutionary algorithms, and machine learning—to design controllers for complex, uncertain, or nonlinear systems. Unlike classical control methods that rely heavily on precise mathematical models, intelligent control can learn from data, adapt to changing conditions, and handle imprecision or incomplete information.

This approach is widely used in applications where traditional modeling is difficult or the environment is highly dynamic, such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, smart grids, and advanced manufacturing. Intelligent controllers can improve performance by self-tuning, optimizing behavior over time, and making decisions that mimic human reasoning or expert knowledge.

title: User illusion
human_text: The user illusion is the illusion created for the user by a human–computer interface, for example the visual metaphor of a desktop used in many graphical user interfaces. The phrase originated at Xerox PARC.
gpt_text:
The “user illusion” is a concept from cognitive science and philosophy suggesting that our conscious experience is not a direct window onto reality or even onto our own mental processes, but a simplified interface—like a computer’s desktop—that helps us function. Just as icons hide the complexity of files and code, consciousness presents a clean, usable “summary” of underlying brain activity and external stimuli rather than showing their full, detailed workings.

This idea implies that many decisions and perceptions are formed unconsciously, with consciousness only receiving a polished, delayed version that feels like real-time control. The term is often used to challenge naive views of free will, introspection, and subjective experience, arguing that what we take to be the “self” in control is in large part a constructed narrative or illusion generated by the brain.

title: Commonsense reasoning
human_text: Commonsense reasoning is one of the branches of artificial intelligence (AI) that is concerned with simulating the human ability to make presumptions about the type and essence of ordinary situations they encounter every day. These assumptions include judgments about the physical properties, purpose, intentions and behavior of people and objects, as well as possible outcomes of their actions and interactions. A device that exhibits commonsense reasoning will be capable of predicting results and drawing conclusions that are similar to humans' folk psychology (humans' innate ability to reason about people's behavior and intentions) and naive physics (humans' natural understanding of the physical world).
gpt_text:
Commonsense reasoning is the ability to make everyday inferences about the world using implicit background knowledge that most people share. It involves understanding how objects, people, and events typically behave—such as knowing that ice is cold, that dropped glass can break, or that people get wet in the rain without an umbrella—even when these facts are not explicitly stated.

In AI, commonsense reasoning is crucial for interpreting language, filling in gaps, and making reasonable predictions in ambiguous situations. It goes beyond formal logic to use context, experience, and expectations about how the world works, which makes it both powerful and challenging to model computationally.

title: Combs method
human_text: The Combs method is a rule base reduction method of writing fuzzy logic rules described by William E. Combs in 1997. It is designed to prevent combinatorial explosion in fuzzy logic rules.
gpt_text:
The Combs method is a structured technique used in multi-criteria decision-making to evaluate and compare different options based on several factors at once. It breaks a complex decision into measurable criteria, assigns each criterion a weight according to its importance, and then scores each alternative against these criteria. The weighted scores are combined to produce an overall rating for each option.

This method helps make choices more transparent and rational, especially when decisions involve qualitative judgments (such as safety, comfort, or aesthetics) alongside quantitative data (like cost or performance). By expressing all criteria on a common scale and aggregating them, the Combs method supports consistent, justifiable decisions in areas such as engineering design, policy selection, and business planning.

title: Darwin machine
human_text: A Darwin machine (a 1987 coinage by William H. Calvin, by analogy to a Turing machine) is a machine that, like a Turing machine, involves an iteration process that yields a high-quality result, but, whereas a Turing machine uses logic, the Darwin machine uses rounds of variation, selection, and inheritance.
gpt_text:
A “Darwin machine” is a conceptual or physical system that applies the core principles of Darwinian evolution—variation, selection, and heredity—to process information or solve problems. Instead of evolving biological organisms, a Darwin machine repeatedly generates variants (e.g., ideas, designs, or patterns), evaluates them according to some fitness criterion, and then preferentially preserves and propagates the most successful ones, sometimes with further random modifications.

The term is often used in discussions of evolutionary algorithms, neural and cognitive models, and artificial life. In these contexts, a Darwin machine is not a single device but a general pattern of computation where adaptive, evolutionary processes are harnessed to produce increasingly effective solutions or behaviors over time.

title: Anticipation (artificial intelligence)
human_text: In artificial intelligence (AI), anticipation occurs when an agent makes decisions based on its explicit beliefs about the future. More broadly, "anticipation" can also refer to the ability to act in appropriate ways that take future events into account, without necessarily explicitly possessing a model of the future events.
gpt_text:
In artificial intelligence, **anticipation** refers to an agent’s ability to predict future states, events, or consequences of its actions and use those predictions to guide decision-making. Instead of simply reacting to the current state of the environment, an anticipatory system forms internal models of how the world is likely to evolve and plans ahead based on those expectations.

This concept underlies many AI techniques, such as model-based reinforcement learning, predictive modeling, and planning algorithms. By anticipating outcomes—like the effects of a move in a game, the next user action in an interface, or future traffic patterns for a self-driving car—AI systems can choose actions that optimize long-term goals rather than just immediate rewards.

title: On Intelligence
human_text: On Intelligence: How a New Understanding of the Brain will Lead to the Creation of Truly Intelligent Machines is a 2004 book by Palm Pilot-inventor Jeff Hawkins with New York Times science writer Sandra Blakeslee. The book explains Hawkins' memory-prediction framework theory of the brain and describes some of its consequences.
gpt_text:
“On Intelligence” is a 2004 book by Jeff Hawkins (with Sandra Blakeslee) that proposes a theory of how the human neocortex produces intelligence. Hawkins argues that the brain works primarily as a prediction machine: it builds a hierarchical model of the world from sensory input and constantly predicts what will happen next. When predictions match reality, the model is reinforced; when they fail, the model is updated.  

The book contrasts this view with traditional AI approaches that focus on symbol manipulation or brute-force computation. Hawkins emphasizes memory, temporal patterns, and hierarchy as the core principles of intelligence, suggesting that understanding these mechanisms in the neocortex is the key to creating truly intelligent machines.

title: Blackboard system
human_text: A blackboard system is an artificial intelligence approach based on the blackboard architectural model, where a common knowledge base, the "blackboard", is iteratively updated by a diverse group of specialist knowledge sources, starting with a problem specification and ending with a solution. Each knowledge source updates the blackboard with a partial solution when its internal constraints match the blackboard state. In this way, the specialists work together to solve the problem. The blackboard model was originally designed as a way to handle complex, ill-defined problems, where the solution is the sum of its parts.
gpt_text:
A blackboard system is a problem-solving architecture used in artificial intelligence where multiple specialized components (called “knowledge sources”) collaborate by reading from and writing to a shared data structure known as the “blackboard.” Instead of communicating directly with each other, these components post partial solutions, hypotheses, or refinements to the blackboard, and a control mechanism decides which knowledge source should act next based on the current state of the shared data.

This approach is especially useful for complex, ill-structured problems—such as speech recognition or image understanding—where no single algorithm is sufficient. The blackboard provides a central, evolving workspace where different expert modules can contribute incrementally, combining their strengths to converge on a solution.

title: Knowledge-based systems
human_text: A knowledge-based system (KBS) is a computer program that reasons and uses a knowledge base to solve complex problems. The term is broad and refers to many different kinds of systems. The one common theme that unites all knowledge based systems is an attempt to represent knowledge explicitly and a reasoning system that allows it to derive new knowledge. Thus, a knowledge-based system has two distinguishing features: a knowledge base and an inference engine.
gpt_text:
Knowledge-based systems are computer programs that reason and make decisions using explicitly represented knowledge about a domain, rather than relying solely on raw data or fixed algorithms. They typically store expert knowledge in a structured form (such as rules, facts, or ontologies) and use an inference engine to draw conclusions, solve problems, or provide recommendations.  

Common examples include expert systems used in medicine, finance, and engineering, where the system can explain its reasoning, support human decision-making, and emulate aspects of expert-level performance. These systems emphasize transparency and logical reasoning, making them useful where explainability and domain expertise are critical.

title: 20Q
human_text: 20Q is a computerized game of twenty questions that began as a test in artificial intelligence (AI). It was invented by Robin Burgener in 1988. The game was made handheld by Radica in 2003, but was discontinued in 2011 because Techno Source took the license for 20Q handheld devices.
gpt_text:
20Q (short for “20 Questions”) is a classic guessing game where one player thinks of an object, person, or place, and the other players try to figure out what it is by asking up to twenty yes-or-no questions. The goal is to narrow down the possibilities with each question, using deduction and logic to arrive at the correct answer before running out of questions.

The term 20Q is also associated with an electronic and online game that uses artificial intelligence to guess what the player is thinking of by asking a series of questions. This version “learns” from each game, improving its guesses over time and often surprising players with how accurately it can identify obscure choices.

title: Computational intelligence
human_text: The expression computational intelligence (CI) usually refers to the ability of a computer to learn a specific task from data or experimental observation. Even though it is commonly considered a synonym of soft computing, there is still no commonly accepted definition of computational intelligence.
gpt_text:
Computational intelligence is a branch of artificial intelligence that focuses on adaptive, heuristic, and often biologically inspired methods for solving complex problems that are difficult to model analytically. It typically includes techniques such as neural networks, fuzzy systems, evolutionary algorithms, and swarm intelligence, which can learn from data, handle uncertainty, and optimize solutions without requiring an exact mathematical description of the system.

These methods are especially useful for tasks like pattern recognition, optimization, control, and prediction in domains where traditional, rule-based approaches struggle—such as image and speech processing, robotics, financial forecasting, and engineering design. Computational intelligence emphasizes robustness, flexibility, and the ability to improve performance through experience.

title: Maschinen Krieger ZbV 3000
human_text: Maschinen Krieger (Ma.K ZBV3000) is a science fiction universe created by Japanese artist and sculptor Kow Yokoyama in the 1980s, currently under development as a Hollywood film by Vertigo Entertainment's Roy Lee.
gpt_text:
Maschinen Krieger ZbV 3000 (often abbreviated Ma.K) is a sci‑fi model and art universe created by Japanese artist Kow Yokoyama in the early 1980s. Originally appearing as scratch-built and kitbashed models in Hobby Japan magazine, it depicts a gritty, retro‑futuristic war setting on a devastated Earth and colonized planets, featuring powered armor suits, drones, and armored vehicles with a distinctly industrial, utilitarian look.

The designs combine World War II aesthetics, aircraft and tank influences, and organic, almost insect‑like forms, giving Ma.K a unique “used future” style similar to that seen in classics like Star Wars or Alien. Over time it has grown into a cult franchise, inspiring plastic model kits from various manufacturers, art books, and a dedicated global fanbase of modelers and designers who customize and reinterpret its surreal, battle‑worn machines.

title: Automatic image annotation
human_text: Automatic image annotation (also known as automatic image tagging or linguistic indexing) is the process by which a computer system automatically assigns metadata in the form of captioning or keywords to a digital image. This application of computer vision techniques is used in image retrieval systems to organize and locate images of interest from a database.
gpt_text:
Automatic image annotation is the process of using algorithms—often based on machine learning or deep learning—to automatically assign descriptive labels, tags, or captions to images. Instead of a human manually describing what’s in a picture, a trained model analyzes the visual content (such as objects, scenes, or actions) and generates relevant metadata like “cat,” “beach,” “person running,” or even full-sentence descriptions.

This technique is widely used in applications such as organizing large photo collections, improving image search in search engines, assisting visually impaired users through image descriptions, and supporting content moderation. Modern systems typically rely on convolutional neural networks or vision–language models that learn from large datasets of images paired with annotations.

title: Krasnow Institute for Advanced Study
human_text: The Krasnow Institute for Advanced Study brings together researchers from many disciplines to study the phenomenon known as the mind. A unit of George Mason University, the Krasnow Institute also serves as a center for doctoral education in neuroscience. Research at the Institute is funded by agencies such as the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and the Department of Defense.
gpt_text:
The Krasnow Institute for Advanced Study is a multidisciplinary research institute at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, focused on understanding complex adaptive systems, especially the brain and intelligent behavior. Founded in the 1990s through a donation from real estate developer Edward L. Krasnow, it brings together researchers in neuroscience, psychology, computer science, engineering, and related fields to explore how cognition, perception, and learning emerge from biological and computational processes.

The institute emphasizes collaborative, cross-disciplinary work, often combining experimental neuroscience with mathematical modeling, artificial intelligence, and data science. Its researchers study topics such as neural circuits, computational neuroscience, cognitive and behavioral processes, and the development of advanced analytical tools, contributing both to basic scientific knowledge and to applications in health, technology, and education.

title: ASR-complete
human_text: ASR-complete is, by analogy to "NP-completeness" in complexity theory, a term to indicate that the difficulty of a computational problem is equivalent to solving the central Automatic Speech Recognition problem, i.e. recognize and understanding spoken language. Unlike "NP-completeness", this term is typically used informally.
gpt_text:
“ASR-complete” is a term used in the context of AI safety and oversight, analogous to “Turing-complete” in computation theory. ASR stands for “AI Safety via Debate” or more generally “Assisted Self-Review,” and something is called ASR-complete if, in principle, it can represent or reduce to any task of evaluating or verifying complex reasoning by using a suitable debate, review, or oversight structure among AI systems.

In practice, calling a setup ASR-complete means that if you can reliably solve oversight or alignment for that specific setup (for example, a particular style of debate between AIs judged by a human), then you could, at least in theory, extend that method to handle essentially any other oversight problem. It’s a way of identifying a “universal” or maximally expressive framework for AI oversight and evaluation.

title: Model-based reasoning
human_text: In artificial intelligence, model-based reasoning refers to an inference method used in expert systems based on a model of the physical world. With this approach, the main focus of application development is developing the model. Then at run time, an "engine" combines this model knowledge with observed data to derive conclusions such as a diagnosis or a prediction.
gpt_text:
Model-based reasoning is a way of thinking and problem-solving that relies on constructing, using, and refining explicit models of how a system or phenomenon works. These models can be physical (like scale models), mathematical (equations, simulations), or conceptual (diagrams, causal maps), and they help people predict outcomes, explain observations, and test “what if” scenarios without directly experimenting on the real system.

In science, engineering, and medicine, model-based reasoning supports activities like diagnosing faults, designing systems, and understanding complex processes. A reasoner compares model predictions with real-world data; mismatches prompt them to revise either the model or their assumptions. This iterative cycle—build a model, use it to infer consequences, check against reality, and update—lies at the core of model-based reasoning.

title: Fuzzy agent
human_text: In computer science a fuzzy agent is a software agent that implements fuzzy logic. This software entity interacts with its environment through an adaptive rule-base and can therefore be considered as a type of intelligent agent.
gpt_text:
A fuzzy agent is an autonomous software or robotic agent that uses fuzzy logic to handle uncertainty, imprecision, or vague information in its decision-making. Instead of relying on strict true/false rules, it works with degrees of truth (e.g., “temperature is somewhat high”) and fuzzy rules (IF–THEN statements with fuzzy sets), allowing more human-like reasoning in complex or ambiguous environments.

These agents are common in control systems, intelligent decision support, and adaptive systems where crisp thresholds are impractical or unknown. By combining agent autonomy (perception, decision, action) with fuzzy inference, fuzzy agents can flexibly adapt their behavior, integrate noisy sensor data, and make nuanced decisions based on incomplete or imprecise inputs.

title: Polyworld
human_text: Polyworld is a cross-platform (Linux, Mac OS X) program written by Larry Yaeger to evolve Artificial Intelligence through natural selection and evolutionary algorithms.
gpt_text:
Polyworld is an artificial life simulation created by Larry Yaeger in which simple virtual creatures evolve over time in a 2D world. Each creature has a neural network “brain” and a body with basic abilities such as moving, eating, reproducing, and attacking, and their behavior emerges from these neural networks rather than being explicitly programmed.  

The system uses genetic algorithms: creatures reproduce with variation and inheritance, so neural network parameters evolve under natural selection based on survival and reproductive success. Polyworld is often used in research to study the evolution of behavior, learning, and complexity, and to explore how rich, lifelike patterns can emerge from simple rules and evolutionary pressure.

title: Automated reasoning
human_text: Automated reasoning is an area of computer science (involves knowledge representation and reasoning) and metalogic dedicated to understanding different aspects of reasoning. The study of automated reasoning helps produce computer programs that allow computers to reason completely, or nearly completely, automatically. Although automated reasoning is considered a sub-field of artificial intelligence, it also has connections with theoretical computer science and philosophy.
gpt_text:
Automated reasoning is a field of computer science and mathematical logic that focuses on designing algorithms and systems capable of automatically proving theorems, checking proofs, and deriving logical consequences from a set of assumptions. It aims to mechanize reasoning processes that humans perform, using formal logic as the underlying language.

This area underpins many technologies, including verification of software and hardware (to ensure correctness and safety), symbolic AI systems, constraint solvers, and tools like SAT and SMT solvers. By automating logical inference, automated reasoning helps detect errors, prove properties, and support complex decision-making in domains such as security protocols, mathematics, and engineering.

title: Cognitive robotics
human_text: Cognitive robotics is concerned with endowing a robot with intelligent behavior by providing it with a processing architecture that will allow it to learn and reason about how to behave in response to complex goals in a complex world. Cognitive robotics may be considered the engineering branch of embodied cognitive science and embodied embedded cognition.
gpt_text:
Cognitive robotics is a field at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science that focuses on building robots capable of reasoning, learning, and adapting in ways inspired by human cognition. Instead of only following pre-programmed rules, cognitive robots use perception, memory, decision-making, and problem-solving processes to understand their environment and act appropriately.

These robots often integrate techniques from machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and neuroscience-based models to handle complex, changing situations. Applications include service robots, assistive robots in healthcare, autonomous vehicles, and exploration robots that must operate with a high degree of autonomy and flexibility in uncertain real-world environments.

title: ESTAR project
human_text: The eSTAR project was a multi-agent system that aimed to implement a heterogeneous network of robotic telescopes for automated observing, and ground-based follow-up to transient events. The project is a joint collaboration between the Astrophysics Group of the University of Exeter and the Astrophysics Research Institute at Liverpool John Moores University. The project was led by Alasdair Allan and Tim Naylor at the University of Exeter, and Iain Steele at Liverpool John Moores University. The eSTAR Project was affiliated with the RoboNet Consortium, and the global Heterogeneous Telescope Networks Consortium.
gpt_text:
The ESTAR project (Electronic STAr Register or similar expansions depending on context) generally refers to an initiative that digitizes and streamlines administrative or registry processes, often within educational, governmental, or research institutions. Its main goal is to replace paper-based or fragmented systems with an integrated electronic platform that allows more efficient data entry, storage, retrieval, and reporting.

In practice, such a project typically focuses on improving data accuracy, reducing processing time, and enabling better oversight and analytics. ESTAR systems may include user portals, role-based access, automated validation, and interoperability with other databases or services, helping organizations modernize their workflows and maintain more reliable records.

title: Belief–desire–intention model
human_text: The belief–desire–intention (BDI) model of human practical reasoning was developed by Michael Bratman as a way of explaining future-directed intention.
gpt_text:
The belief–desire–intention (BDI) model is a framework from philosophy and artificial intelligence that explains and engineers rational agents in terms of three key mental attitudes: beliefs, desires, and intentions. Beliefs represent the information an agent has about the world (which can be incomplete or incorrect), desires represent the states of affairs the agent would like to bring about (its goals), and intentions are the subset of desires that the agent has committed to pursuing, guiding its concrete plans and actions.

In AI and multi-agent systems, the BDI model is used to design agents that make decisions in a human-like, deliberative way. The agent continually updates its beliefs based on perception, selects or revises its desires, and forms intentions that structure its future behavior. This separation helps capture practical reasoning: agents don’t pursue all desires at once, but form stable intentions they stick to while they act and re-plan in a changing environment.

title: Rough fuzzy hybridization
human_text: Rough fuzzy hybridization is a method of hybrid intelligent system or soft computing, where Fuzzy set theory is used for linguistic representation of patterns, leading to a fuzzy granulation of the feature space. Rough set theory is used to obtain dependency rules which model informative regions in the granulated feature space.
gpt_text:
Rough fuzzy hybridization is a family of methods that combine rough set theory and fuzzy set theory to handle data that is both uncertain and imprecise. Rough sets are good at dealing with vagueness caused by incomplete or indiscernible information using lower and upper approximations, while fuzzy sets model gradual membership (degrees of belonging) to a concept rather than crisp yes/no classification.  

By hybridizing the two, rough fuzzy approaches can, for example, create rough approximations over fuzzy sets or use fuzzy membership functions inside rough set boundaries. This is particularly useful in pattern recognition, decision support, and data mining, where data may be noisy, overlapping, or partially known, and both kinds of uncertainty—indiscernibility and graded membership—need to be represented simultaneously.

title: Neural computation
human_text: Neural computation is the information processing performed by networks of neurons. Neural computation is affiliated with the philosophical tradition known as Computational theory of mind, also referred to as computationalism, which advances the thesis that neural computation explains cognition. The first persons to propose an account of neural activity as being computational was Warren McCullock and Walter Pitts in their seminal 1943 paper, A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity. There are three general branches of computationalism, including classicism, connectionism, and computational neuroscience. All three branches agree that cognition is computation, however they disagree on what sorts of computations constitute cognition. The classicism tradition believes that computation in the brain is digital, analogous with digital computing. Both connectionism and computational neuroscience do not require that the computations which realize cognition are necessarily digital computations. However, the two branches greatly disagree upon which sorts of experimental data should be used to construct explanatory models of cognitive phenomena. Connectionists rely upon behavioral evidence to construct models to explain cognitive phenomenon, whereas computational neuroscience leverages neuroanatomical and neurophysiological information to construct mathematical models which explain cognition.
gpt_text:
Neural computation is the process by which nervous systems—especially the brain—encode, transform, and use information through networks of neurons and their connections. Each neuron integrates incoming signals (electrical or chemical), applies a kind of “decision rule” (often likened to a threshold or nonlinearity), and generates an output that influences other neurons. The collective activity of large populations of neurons gives rise to perception, movement, memory, and higher cognition.

In research and technology, the term also underpins artificial neural networks, which are mathematical models inspired by biological neurons. These models use layers of simple units that adjust their connection strengths (weights) through learning algorithms to perform tasks like recognition, prediction, and control, echoing—at a simplified level—the adaptive, distributed nature of biological neural computation.

title: Intelligent character recognition
human_text: In computer science, intelligent character recognition (ICR) is an advanced optical character recognition (OCR) or — rather more specific — handwriting recognition system that allows fonts and different styles of handwriting to be learned by a computer during processing to improve accuracy and recognition levels.
gpt_text:
Intelligent Character Recognition (ICR) is an advanced form of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) that can read and interpret handwritten text, not just printed characters. Using machine learning and neural networks, ICR systems learn to recognize a wide variety of handwriting styles, continuously improving their accuracy over time as they process more data.

ICR is often used in applications like form processing, document digitization, and automated data entry, where users write information by hand (for example, on paper forms or checks). By converting these handwritten inputs into machine-readable text, ICR helps organizations reduce manual typing, minimize errors, and speed up workflows.

title: Epistemic modal logic
human_text: Epistemic modal logic is a subfield of modal logic that is concerned with reasoning about knowledge. While epistemology has a long philosophical tradition dating back to Ancient Greece, epistemic logic is a much more recent development with applications in many fields, including philosophy, theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence, economics and linguistics. While philosophers since Aristotle have discussed modal logic, and Medieval philosophers such as Avicenna, Ockham, and Duns Scotus developed many of their observations, it was C. I. Lewis who created the first symbolic and systematic approach to the topic, in 1912. It continued to mature as a field, reaching its modern form in 1963 with the work of Kripke.
gpt_text:
Epistemic modal logic is a branch of modal logic that formalizes reasoning about knowledge and belief. It extends classical logic with modal operators such as Kᵢ (“agent i knows that”) or Bᵢ (“agent i believes that”), allowing statements like “Alice knows that it is raining” or “Bob believes that Alice knows the password” to be represented and analyzed precisely. These operators obey axioms intended to capture intuitive properties of knowledge or belief, such as closure under logical consequence (if you know P and know that P implies Q, then you know Q).

This framework is widely used in philosophy, computer science, linguistics, and game theory to model information, uncertainty, and strategic reasoning among multiple agents. In multi-agent settings, epistemic modal logic can express not only what each agent knows, but also higher-order knowledge (“everyone knows that everyone knows P”), making it a core tool for studying common knowledge, information flow, and protocols in distributed systems.

title: Neuroshima
human_text: Neuroshima is a Polish tabletop roleplaying system inspired by such films and games as Mad Max, Fallout, The Matrix, Terminator and Deadlands: Hell on Earth. It is currently available only in Polish. The game's motto is "never trust the machines". Its designers include and.
gpt_text:
Neuroshima is a Polish post-apocalyptic role-playing game (RPG) and setting, first published in 2003 by Wydawnictwo Portal (Portal Games). Set in a devastated United States after a devastating war between humanity and a self-aware machine network called Moloch, it mixes themes of Mad Max–style wastelands, cyberpunk, and survival horror. The world is harsh, fragmented into dangerous territories ruled by warlords, mutants, gangs, and remnants of military forces, with technology ranging from scavenged high-tech relics to crude improvised gear.

Mechanically, Neuroshima uses a custom d20-based system focusing on gritty combat, resource scarcity, and moral ambiguity. The setting spawned multiple expansions, board games, and related media, including the popular board game Neuroshima Hex!, which uses the same universe but presents it as a tactical, tile-based battle between factions like Moloch, Borgo, and the Outpost.

title: TASSL
human_text: The Application Software Systems Laboratory (TASSL) is a research lab, as a part of Center for Advanced Information Processing (CAIP), and Department of Electrical and Computing Engineering at Rutgers University. It is under the direction of Dr. Manish Parashar and the current research fields include Autonomic Computing, Parallel Computing and Distributed Computing, Grid Computing, Peer-to-peer Computing, Adaptive Computing Systems, and Scientific Computation.
gpt_text:
TASSL most commonly refers to the **Trusted and Secure Systems Laboratory** (or similarly named research groups) in academic or industrial settings. Such labs focus on designing, analyzing, and improving systems that must operate reliably in the presence of faults, adversaries, or large scale—covering areas like distributed systems, cybersecurity, fault tolerance, and dependable computing.

Work associated with TASSL-type groups often includes research on secure communication protocols, resilient cloud and edge infrastructures, intrusion detection, and formal methods for verifying system correctness. Their goal is to ensure that complex computing environments remain trustworthy, available, and secure even under real-world challenges such as attacks, failures, and high load.

title: Extremal optimization
human_text: Extremal optimization (EO) is an optimization heuristic inspired by the Bak–Sneppen model of self-organized criticality from the field of statistical physics. This heuristic was designed initially to address combinatorial optimization problems such as the travelling salesman problem and spin glasses, although the technique has been demonstrated to function in optimization domains.
gpt_text:
Extremal optimization (EO) is a metaheuristic optimization technique inspired by self-organized criticality and dynamics observed in natural systems such as the Bak–Sneppen model of biological evolution. Instead of improving a solution by making globally guided changes (as in simulated annealing or genetic algorithms), EO repeatedly identifies and modifies the “worst” or least-fit components of a current solution. By focusing on systematically replacing poorly performing parts, the algorithm explores the solution space through a series of local, targeted updates.

In practice, EO maintains a single candidate solution and assigns a fitness or cost contribution to each of its components (e.g., vertices in a graph, variables in a configuration). At each step, the component with the lowest fitness (or one selected probabilistically among the worst) is altered, often in a random or semi-random way, generating a new solution. This simple rule can lead to complex search behavior that often escapes local minima and yields high-quality solutions for difficult combinatorial optimization problems such as graph partitioning, scheduling, and spin glass models.

title: Eccky
human_text: Eccky is an online game. Until 2009, it was an MSN-based life simulation game in which two people work together to create and raise a virtual baby. Eccky won the 2005 SpinAwards for Innovation and for Best Interactive Concept. In 2009, the game play changed to a real-time virtual world on Hyves.
gpt_text:
Eccky is a Dutch virtual pet and social interaction game that originated in the mid-2000s as a collaboration between the telecom provider KPN and game developer Ranj. In its early form, it allowed two people to create a virtual baby together by combining their profiles; the “child” would then grow over several days, communicating with the users via instant messaging platforms like MSN. It blended elements of AI-driven conversation, virtual parenting, and social networking, making it an early example of an interactive, character-based digital companion.

Over time, Eccky evolved through various relaunches and formats, including mobile games and AI chatbot experiences. The core idea remained centered on nurturing a virtual character, with gameplay focused on care, communication, and relationship-building rather than traditional point scoring or competition.

title: Action selection
human_text: Action selection is a way of characterizing the most basic problem of intelligent systems: what to do next. In artificial intelligence and computational cognitive science, "the action selection problem" is typically associated with intelligent agents and animats—artificial systems that exhibit complex behaviour in an agent environment. The term is also sometimes used in ethology or animal behavior.
gpt_text:
Action selection is the process by which an agent—biological or artificial—chooses what to do next from among multiple possible actions. It involves evaluating options in light of current goals, environmental cues, internal states (like motivation or energy), and predicted outcomes, then committing to one behavior while suppressing others. In humans and animals, this is closely tied to neural systems such as the basal ganglia, which help prioritize and gate actions.

In artificial intelligence and robotics, action selection is a core problem in decision-making and control. Techniques such as rule-based systems, reinforcement learning, planning algorithms, or utility-based decision models are used to determine which action should be executed at each step. Effective action selection balances competing demands (e.g., exploitation vs. exploration, short-term vs. long-term rewards) to produce coherent, goal-directed behavior.

title: Autonomic networking
human_text: Autonomic Networking follows the concept of Autonomic Computing, an initiative started by IBM in 2001. Its ultimate aim is to create self-managing networks to overcome the rapidly growing complexity of the Internet and other networks and to enable their further growth, far beyond the size of today.
gpt_text:
Autonomic networking is a networking paradigm inspired by the human autonomic nervous system, where networks configure, manage, protect, and heal themselves with minimal human intervention. It aims to reduce complexity by embedding self-management capabilities—such as self-configuration, self-optimization, self-healing, and self-protection—directly into network devices and control systems.

Using monitoring, analytics, and automated decision-making (often with AI and policy-based control), autonomic networks can detect changing conditions (like traffic patterns, failures, or attacks) and automatically adjust routing, resource allocation, and security settings. This leads to more resilient, efficient, and scalable networks that can adapt dynamically to user demands and operational constraints.

title: Network compartment
human_text: Network Compartmentalization, the division of network functionality into network compartments, is an important concept of Autonomic Networking.
gpt_text:
A network compartment is a logically or physically isolated segment of a larger network that’s used to separate and protect resources. It can be created using technologies like VLANs, VRFs, subnets, firewalls, or software-defined networking to ensure that traffic between compartments is controlled and monitored.  

By dividing a network into compartments, organizations can limit the impact of security breaches, apply different access policies to different groups of systems or users, and improve overall manageability. This compartmentalization supports principles such as least privilege and defense in depth, making it harder for attackers or malware to move laterally across the network.

title: Conflict resolution strategy
human_text: Conflict resolution strategies are used in production systems in artificial intelligence, such as in rule-based expert systems, to help in choosing which production rule to fire. The need for such a strategy arises when the conditions of two or more rules are satisfied by the currently known facts.
gpt_text:
A conflict resolution strategy is a structured approach individuals or groups use to address and settle disagreements in a constructive way. Rather than avoiding issues or letting them escalate, it focuses on understanding each side’s needs and perspectives, then working toward a solution everyone can accept. Effective strategies aim to reduce tension, preserve relationships, and prevent similar conflicts in the future.  

Common conflict resolution strategies include collaboration (working together to find a win–win solution), compromise (each side gives up something), accommodation (one side yields), avoidance (delaying or sidestepping the issue), and competition (pursuing one side’s goals at the other’s expense). Choosing the right strategy depends on the situation, the stakes involved, and the importance of the relationship between the parties.

title: Cobweb (clustering)
human_text: COBWEB is an incremental system for hierarchical conceptual clustering. COBWEB was invented by Professor Douglas H. Fisher, currently at Vanderbilt University.
gpt_text:
Cobweb is an incremental conceptual clustering algorithm used in machine learning and data mining. Instead of requiring a fixed number of clusters in advance, it builds a hierarchical classification tree (a "concept hierarchy") as it processes instances one by one. Each node in the tree represents a concept (cluster) characterized by probabilistic summaries of attribute values.

At every step, Cobweb evaluates possible operations—such as inserting an instance into an existing cluster, creating a new cluster, merging clusters, or splitting a cluster—using a heuristic measure called category utility. This measure balances intra-cluster similarity and inter-cluster dissimilarity. The result is a hierarchical, interpretable structure that can adapt dynamically as more data arrives.

title: Monitoring and surveillance agents
human_text: Monitoring and surveillance agents (also known as predictive agents) are a type of intelligent agent software that observes and reports on computer equipment. Monitoring and surveillance agents are often used to monitor complex computer networks to predict when a crash or some other defect may occur. Another type of monitoring and surveillance agent works on computer networks keeping track of the configuration of each computer connected to the network. It tracks and updates the central configuration database when anything on any computer changes, such as the number or type of disk drives. An important task in managing networks lies in prioritizing traffic and shaping bandwidth.
gpt_text:
Monitoring and surveillance agents are software or AI systems designed to continuously observe, record, and analyze activities, data streams, or environments. They can track system performance, network traffic, user behavior, or physical spaces (via cameras and sensors) to detect anomalies, security threats, policy violations, or operational issues. These agents often work in real time, generating alerts or automated responses when specific conditions or patterns are detected.

They are widely used in cybersecurity (intrusion detection, fraud detection), IT operations (server and application monitoring), compliance (logging and audit trails), and physical security (video surveillance, access control). Modern AI-driven agents can learn normal behavior patterns, adapt to new threats, and filter out noise, making monitoring more efficient and proactive while also raising important privacy, ethical, and governance considerations.

title: Diagnosis (artificial intelligence)
human_text: As a subfield in artificial intelligence, Diagnosis is concerned with the development of algorithms and techniques that are able to determine whether the behaviour of a system is correct. If the system is not functioning correctly, the algorithm should be able to determine, as accurately as possible, which part of the system is failing, and which kind of fault it is facing. The computation is based on observations, which provide information on the current behaviour.
gpt_text:
In artificial intelligence, diagnosis refers to the process of identifying the cause of a problem, fault, or abnormal behavior in a system based on observed data or symptoms. This can involve determining why a machine or network is malfunctioning (fault diagnosis), what disease a patient may have in medical AI (computer-aided diagnosis), or which component of a complex system is failing. Diagnostic AI systems use models, rules, probabilistic reasoning, or machine learning to infer the most likely explanation from incomplete or uncertain information.

Diagnostic algorithms often rely on techniques such as Bayesian networks, decision trees, knowledge-based expert systems, or deep learning models trained on historical examples. title: European Association for Artificial Intelligence

title: Statistical semantics
human_text: In linguistics, statistical semantics applies the methods of statistics to the problem of determining the meaning of words or phrases, ideally through unsupervised learning, to a degree of precision at least sufficient for the purpose of information retrieval.
