This idea underlies many modern natural language processing techniques, including word embeddings (e.g., word2vec, GloVe) and large language models. In statistical semantics, the core assumption is that “you shall know a word by the company it keeps”: words that appear in similar contexts tend to have related meanings, and these relationships can be captured and manipulated mathematically.

title: For a Breath I Tarry

title: Artificial intelligence systems integration

title: Sinewave synthesis
human_text: Sinewave synthesis, or sine wave speech, is a technique for synthesizing speech by replacing the formants (main bands of energy) with pure tone whistles. The first sinewave synthesis program (SWS) for the automatic creation of stimuli for perceptual experiments was developed by Philip Rubin at Haskins Laboratories in the 1970s. This program was subsequently used by Robert Remez, Philip Rubin, David Pisoni, and other colleagues to show that listeners can perceive continuous speech without traditional speech cues, i.e., pitch, stress, and intonation. This work paved the way for a view of speech as a dynamic pattern of trajectories through articulatory-acoustic space.
gpt_text:
Sinewave synthesis is the process of constructing complex sounds or signals by adding together multiple sine waves of different frequencies, amplitudes, and phases. Because any periodic signal can be decomposed into a sum of sine and cosine components (by Fourier theory), sinewave synthesis can, in principle, recreate almost any tone, timbre, or waveform by carefully choosing and combining these pure tones.

In audio and music technology, sinewave (or additive) synthesis is used to design sounds from the ground up, such as organ-like tones, evolving pads, or precise test signals. By controlling each sine component—often called a partial or harmonic—sound designers can shape the spectrum and time-varying character of a sound with very fine detail, resulting in highly controllable and often very clean or “pure” audio.

title: Language identification
human_text: In natural language processing, language identification or language guessing is the problem of determining which natural language given content is in. Computational approaches to this problem view it as a special case of text categorization, solved with various statistical methods.

Technically, language identification systems use features like character sequences, word patterns, and statistical models trained on labeled examples to distinguish among languages. title: Fred (chatterbot)

title: Anytime algorithm
human_text: In computer science, an anytime algorithm is an algorithm that can return a valid solution to a problem even if it is interrupted before it ends. The algorithm is expected to find better and better solutions the longer it keeps running.
gpt_text:
An anytime algorithm is an algorithm that can return a valid (though possibly suboptimal) solution even if it is interrupted before it finishes its full computation. The longer it is allowed to run, the better or more refined the solution becomes, ideally approaching optimality over time. This makes anytime algorithms especially useful in real-time or resource-constrained settings where the available computation time is uncertain or can change dynamically.

Key properties of anytime algorithms include interruptibility (they can be stopped at almost any time), monotonicity (solution quality does not decrease as time increases), and measurable progress (they provide a way to estimate how good the current solution is). Examples appear in areas like heuristic search, planning, and optimization, where having a “good enough now” answer is often more valuable than waiting for a perfect one.

title: Cognitive philology
human_text: Cognitive philology is the science that studies written and oral texts as the product of human mental processes. Studies in cognitive philology compare documentary evidence emerging from textual investigations with results of experimental research, especially in the fields of cognitive and ecological psychology, neurosciences and artificial intelligence. "The point is not the text, but the mind that made it". Cognitive Philology aims to foster communication between literary, textual, philological disciplines on the one hand and researches across the whole range of the cognitive, evolutionary, ecological and human sciences on the other.
gpt_text:

It combines methods and theories from cognitive science, linguistics, literary studies, and traditional philology to understand not just what texts say, but how human minds shape and are shaped by them.

This approach examines phenomena like how stories are remembered and altered in oral traditions, how readers mentally construct meaning from written texts, and how cognitive constraints affect language change and textual variation. By foregrounding the role of human cognition, cognitive philology seeks to explain patterns in textual history, reception, and interpretation that classical philological methods alone might leave unexplained.

title: Zeuthen strategy
human_text: The Zeuthen strategy is a negotiation strategy used by some artificial agents. Its purpose is to measure the willingness to risk conflict. An agent will be more willing to risk conflict if it does not have much to lose in case that the negotiation fails. In contrast, an agent is less willing to risk conflict when it has more to lose. The value of a deal is expressed in its utility. An agent has much to lose when the difference between the utility of its current proposal and the conflict deal is high.
gpt_text:
The Zeuthen strategy is a bargaining approach from game theory that describes how rational negotiators decide whether to stand firm or concede during a conflict of interests. Each side assesses its own “risk of breakdown” (the chance that insisting on its current demand will cause negotiations to fail) relative to the other side’s risk. The party with the lower relative risk is predicted to concede first, moving its offer closer to the opponent’s position.

Formally introduced by Frederik Zeuthen and later developed by John Nash and others, the strategy assumes both parties are rational, informed about each other’s payoffs, and motivated to reach agreement. Under these conditions, alternating concessions according to the Zeuthen rule can lead to a stable and efficient bargaining outcome, often matching the Nash bargaining solution.

title: Computer audition
human_text: Computer audition (CA) or machine listening is general field of study of algorithms and systems for audio understanding by machine. Since the notion of what it means for a machine to "hear" is very broad and somewhat vague, computer audition attempts to bring together several disciplines that originally dealt with specific problems or had a concrete application in mind. The engineer Paris Smaragdis, interviewed in Technology Review, talks about these systems --"software that uses sound to locate people moving through rooms, monitor machinery for impending breakdowns, or activate traffic cameras to record accidents."Paris Smaragdis taught computers how to play more life-like music
gpt_text:

Applications include speech recognition and enhancement, music information retrieval (e.g., genre classification, beat tracking, transcription), sound event detection (like recognizing alarms, footsteps, or machinery faults), and audio-based surveillance or monitoring. Computer audition underpins many modern technologies, from virtual assistants and hearing aids to smart home devices and multimedia search systems.

title: Ontology learning
human_text: Ontology learning (ontology extraction, ontology generation, or ontology acquisition) is the automatic or semi-automatic creation of ontologies, including extracting the corresponding domain's terms and the relationships between the concepts that these terms represent from a corpus of natural language text, and encoding them with an ontology language for easy retrieval. As building ontologies manually is extremely labor-intensive and time-consuming, there is great motivation to automate the process.
gpt_text:

This process typically includes tasks like term extraction, concept clustering, taxonomy induction (“is-a” hierarchies), relation extraction (“part-of”, “works-for”, etc.), and ontology refinement. Ontology learning helps reduce the manual effort required to build knowledge graphs or domain ontologies, supporting applications such as semantic search, information integration, and intelligent assistants.

title: Autognostics

title: Nouvelle AI
human_text: Nouvelle artificial intelligence (AI) is an approach to artificial intelligence pioneered in the 1980s by Rodney Brooks, who was then part of MIT artificial intelligence laboratory. Nouvelle AI differs from classical AI by aiming to produce robots with intelligence levels similar to insects. Researchers believe that intelligence can emerge organically from simple behaviors as these intelligences interacted with the "real world," instead of using the constructed worlds which symbolic AIs typically needed to have programmed into them.

It is closely associated with researchers like Rodney Brooks and approaches such as behavior-based robotics and subsumption architectures.

Core ideas of nouvelle AI include building intelligence from the bottom up, using simple behaviors layered together rather than a central symbolic model, and exploiting direct sensor–motor couplings to navigate and act. This led to robots and systems that could robustly handle dynamic, noisy environments without needing detailed world models, influencing later work in embodied cognition, autonomous robotics, and some strands of modern reinforcement learning and swarm intelligence.

title: Admissible heuristic
human_text: In computer science, specifically in algorithms related to pathfinding, a heuristic function is said to be admissible if it never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal, i.e. the cost it estimates to reach the goal is not higher than the lowest possible cost from the current point in the path.
gpt_text:
An admissible heuristic is a heuristic function used in search algorithms (like A*) that never overestimates the true cost of reaching a goal from any given state. Formally, for every state n, the heuristic estimate h(n) is always less than or equal to the actual minimal cost h\*(n) from n to a goal. This “optimistic” property ensures that the heuristic is safe in the sense that it will not mislead the search into discarding the optimal path.

Because it never overestimates, an admissible heuristic guarantees that algorithms such as A* will find an optimal solution, provided other conditions (like consistent cost functions) are met. In practice, admissible heuristics are often derived from simplified or relaxed versions of the original problem, where solving the relaxed problem gives a lower bound on the true cost.

title: Personoid

title: And–or tree
human_text: An and–or tree is a graphical representation of the reduction of problems (or goals) to conjunctions and disjunctions of subproblems (or subgoals).

Leaves typically represent basic conditions, facts, or atomic subproblems.

And–or trees are widely used in artificial intelligence, automated theorem proving, game playing, and planning. They provide a clear way to decompose complex tasks or logical formulas into combinations of simpler components, making it easier to analyze solvability, compute strategies, or evaluate logical expressions by traversing and propagating truth or success values up the tree.

title: Adaptive autonomy

title: Neurorobotics
human_text: Neurorobotics, a combined study of neuroscience, robotics, and artificial intelligence, is the science and technology of embodied autonomous neural systems. Neural systems include brain-inspired algorithms (e.g. connectionist networks), computational models of biological neural networks (e.g. artificial spiking neural networks, large-scale simulations of neural microcircuits) and actual biological systems (e.g. in vivo and in vitro neural nets). Such neural systems can be embodied in machines with mechanic or any other forms of physical actuation. This includes robots, prosthetic or wearable systems but also, at smaller scale, micro-machines and, at the larger scales, furniture and infrastructures.

This area supports both better robots and better brain science: robots gain more adaptive, flexible, and biologically plausible control, while neuroscientists can test hypotheses about brain function in embodied systems. Applications range from neuro-inspired autonomous robots and prosthetics to rehabilitation devices and brain–machine interfaces that link neural activity directly to robotic control.

title: CALO

title: Attributional calculus
human_text: Attributional calculus is a logic and representation system defined by Ryszard S. Michalski. It combines elements of predicate logic, propositional calculus, and multi-valued logic. Attributional calculus provides a formal language for natural induction, an inductive learning process whose results are in forms natural to people.

It sits between propositional and first-order logic in expressiveness: objects are represented by attribute–value pairs, and rules (often called attributional rules) relate combinations of these attributes to conclusions such as class labels or decisions.

In machine learning, attributional calculus underlies methods that produce human-readable, tabular or rule-based models. It supports operations like generalization, specialization, and abstraction over attribute values, enabling algorithms to learn compact, interpretable rule sets from data while remaining more structured than simple propositional rules but less complex than full predicate logic.

title: The Emotion Machine

title: Artificial imagination

Unlike simple automation or rule-based generation, artificial imagination aims at producing content that is not just random or repetitive, but coherent, context-aware, and sometimes original enough to inspire humans or solve complex problems. title: Ordered weighted averaging aggregation operator
human_text: In applied mathematics – specifically in fuzzy logic – the ordered weighted averaging (OWA) operators provide a parameterized class of mean type aggregation operators. They were introduced by Ronald R. Yager. Many notable mean operators such as the max, arithmetic average, median and min, are members of this class. They have been widely used in computational intelligence because of their ability to model linguistically expressed aggregation instructions.

The final aggregated value is the weighted sum of these ordered inputs, where the weights are nonnegative and sum to 1.

OWA operators are useful because they allow a continuum between different aggregation behaviors, such as “and” (similar to taking the minimum), “or” (similar to taking the maximum), and the arithmetic mean. By choosing different weight vectors, one can model various decision attitudes, from highly optimistic (emphasizing larger values) to highly pessimistic (emphasizing smaller values), making OWAs especially important in decision making, risk analysis, and information fusion.

title: Hierarchical control system

It is typically portrayed as a large, biomechanical brain housed in a glass container, wired into the systems of the Space Pirates’ base on planet Zebes. Mother Brain functions as both a supercomputer and a living organism, controlling defenses, coordinating pirate activity, and managing biological experiments—most notably those involving the parasitic Metroids.

Narratively, Mother Brain represents cold, calculating intelligence fused with organic horror, standing in contrast to the lone, human bounty hunter Samus Aran. As a recurring final boss, it often symbolizes the core of the Space Pirate threat: if Mother Brain is destroyed, their operations collapse. Across games and adaptations (like the Super Metroid redesign and various manga/animated portrayals), its imagery and role have evolved, but it consistently remains a mastermind villain and a key symbol of the Metroid franchise.

title: Activity recognition
human_text: Activity recognition aims to recognize the actions and goals of one or more agents from a series of observations on the agents' actions and the environmental conditions. Since the 1980s, this research field has captured the attention of several computer science communities due to its strength in providing personalized support for many different applications and its connection to many different fields of study such as medicine, human-computer interaction, or sociology.
gpt_text:
Activity recognition is the process of automatically identifying what a person (or sometimes an object) is doing based on data from sensors. These sensors can include smartphone accelerometers and gyroscopes, smartwatches, cameras, GPS, or ambient sensors in a smart home. Using patterns in this data, algorithms infer activities such as walking, running, sitting, driving, cooking, or exercising.

This field combines signal processing and machine learning or deep learning to classify sequences of sensor readings into specific activities. Activity recognition is widely used in fitness tracking, health monitoring (e.g., detecting falls in the elderly), human-computer interaction, surveillance, context-aware mobile apps, and industrial safety systems.

title: Competitions and prizes in artificial intelligence
human_text: There are a number of competitions and prizes to promote research in artificial intelligence.
gpt_text:
Competitions and prizes in artificial intelligence are organized challenges that invite researchers, companies, and hobbyists to build AI systems that solve specific tasks, such as image recognition, game playing, natural language understanding, or robotics. They often provide standardized datasets, clear evaluation metrics, and leaderboards so that different approaches can be fairly compared. Famous examples include the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, Kaggle machine learning competitions, and robotics contests like RoboCup.  

These events drive progress by focusing attention on concrete problems, encouraging innovation, and lowering barriers for newcomers through shared benchmarks and open-source solutions. High-profile prizes—such as the Loebner Prize for chatbot conversations or XPRIZE challenges—also raise public awareness and investment in AI. At the same time, competitions can shape research priorities, sometimes emphasizing benchmark performance over broader issues like robustness, fairness, or long-term societal impact.

title: Artificial Intelligence System
human_text: Artificial Intelligence System (AIS) was a distributed computing project undertaken by Intelligence Realm, Inc. with the long-term goal of simulating the human brain in real time, complete with artificial consciousness and artificial general intelligence. They claimed to have found, in research, the "mechanisms of knowledge representation in the brain which is equivalent to finding artificial intelligence", before moving into the developmental phase.
gpt_text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) system is a software- or hardware-based system designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as recognizing patterns, understanding language, making decisions, or learning from data. These systems use algorithms and models—often based on machine learning or deep learning—to process inputs (like text, images, or sensor data), infer patterns, and produce outputs or actions.

AI systems can be narrowly focused on a specific task (such as recommending products, detecting fraud, or driving a car) or aim for broader, more general capabilities. They are increasingly embedded in everyday technologies—from search engines and virtual assistants to medical diagnostics and industrial automation—where they augment or automate human decision-making and problem-solving.

title: Smart object
human_text: A smart object is an object that enhances the interaction with not only people but also with other smart objects. Also known as smart connected products or smart connected things (SCoT), they are products, assets and other things embedded with processors, sensors, software and connectivity that allow data to be exchanged between the product and its environment, manufacturer, operator/user, and other products and systems. Connectivity also enables some capabilities of the product to exist outside the physical device, in what is known as the product cloud. The data collected from these products can be then analyzed to inform decision-making, enable operational efficiencies and continuously improve the performance of the product.
gpt_text:
A smart object is a layer type in Adobe Photoshop that preserves an image’s original data so it can be edited non-destructively. Instead of directly altering the pixels, Photoshop applies transformations, filters, and adjustments to the smart object as instructions, meaning you can resize, rotate, warp, or apply effects repeatedly without degrading image quality.

Smart objects can contain raster images, vector artwork (such as from Adobe Illustrator), or even multiple layers. They’re especially useful for maintaining flexibility in complex designs, working with templates, or updating repeated elements: when you edit the contents of one smart object, all its linked instances update automatically.

title: Knowledge compilation
human_text: Knowledge compilation is a family of approaches for addressing the intractability of
gpt_text:
Knowledge compilation is a family of techniques in artificial intelligence and logic where complex, often intractable knowledge bases (such as propositional formulas) are transformed into alternative representations that support fast, repeated querying. The idea is to perform a potentially expensive one-time “compilation” step—turning the original logical description into a structured form like decision diagrams, decomposable negation normal form (DNNF), or related circuits—so that many different queries (e.g., satisfiability, counting models, conditioning on evidence) can then be answered efficiently.

This approach is especially useful when the knowledge base is relatively static but queries are frequent or time-sensitive, as in planning, diagnosis, verification, and probabilistic reasoning. Knowledge compilation balances a trade-off between the size of the compiled representation and the range and speed of tractable queries it enables.

title: Artificial psychology
human_text: Artificial psychology (AP) has had multiple meanings dating back to 19th century, with recent usage related to artificial intelligence (AI).
gpt_text:
Artificial psychology is the study and design of psychological processes in artificial systems, especially in robots and advanced AI. It explores how machines can model, simulate, or approximate human-like mental states such as beliefs, intentions, emotions, learning, and personality, and how those internal states influence behavior.  

The field sits at the intersection of psychology, cognitive science, and AI, aiming both to better understand human minds by recreating aspects of them in machines, and to build more adaptive, socially aware, and trustworthy artificial agents. This can include designing artificial emotions to guide decision-making, modeling motivation or curiosity in learning systems, and creating frameworks for AI that can understand and respond to human psychological cues.

title: Context-sensitive user interface
human_text: A context-sensitive user interface offers the user options based on the state of the active program.Webopedia : context sensitive Context sensitivity is ubiquitous in current graphical user interfaces, often in context menus.
gpt_text:
A context-sensitive user interface is a UI that adapts what it shows and what actions it offers based on the user’s current situation—such as what they’re doing, what they’ve selected, or where they are in an application. Instead of presenting every possible command all the time, it dynamically reveals only the most relevant options, controls, and information for that moment.

Common examples include right‑click context menus that change based on the selected object, toolbars that update when you switch modes (e.g., from drawing to text editing), or mobile apps that show different buttons depending on the screen or user state. This approach reduces clutter, streamlines workflows, and can make complex systems easier and faster to use by aligning the interface with user intent.

title: Natural-language user interface
human_text: Natural-language user interface (LUI or NLUI) is a type of computer human interface where linguistic phenomena such as verbs, phrases and clauses act as UI controls for creating, selecting and modifying data in software applications.
gpt_text:
A natural-language user interface (NUI or NLUI) is a way of interacting with computers using everyday human language—spoken or written—instead of formal commands, menus, or graphical controls. It relies on natural language processing (NLP) to interpret what a user says or types, map that to an intention, and then trigger the appropriate action or response from the system.

These interfaces appear in chatbots, virtual assistants (like voice-activated helpers), search engines that accept questions in plain language, and applications that let users control software or devices by talking or typing naturally. The goal is to make technology more intuitive by reducing the need to learn specific commands or technical terminology.

title: Decision list
human_text: Decision lists are a representation for Boolean functions which can be easily learnable from examples. Single term decision lists are more expressive than disjunctions and conjunctions; however, 1-term decision lists are less expressive than the general disjunctive normal form and the conjunctive normal form.
gpt_text:
A decision list is a simple, interpretable model for making classifications or decisions by following an ordered sequence of if-then rules. Each rule checks a specific condition; if the condition is satisfied, the associated decision (such as a class label or action) is taken and the process stops. If not, the system moves on to the next rule in the list, and if no rule applies, a default decision is used.

In machine learning, decision lists are valued for their transparency and ease of understanding: they resemble the way humans often describe procedures (“if condition A, then do X; else if condition B, then do Y…”). They can be learned from data and are particularly useful when interpretability and simplicity are more important than achieving the absolute highest predictive accuracy.

title: Radiant AI
human_text: The Radiant AI is a technology developed by Bethesda Softworks for The Elder Scrolls video games. It allows non-player characters (NPCs) to make choices and engage in behaviors more complex than in past titles. The technology was developed for The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and expanded in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim; it is also used in Fallout 3, Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 4, also published by Bethesda.
gpt_text:
Radiant AI is the dynamic artificial intelligence system used in Bethesda’s games, most notably in *The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion* and later refined in *Skyrim*. Instead of scripting every character’s behavior by hand, Radiant AI gives non-player characters (NPCs) general goals (like eating, working, sleeping, or socializing) and a set of rules for how to achieve them. NPCs then choose actions on their own based on needs, environment, and time of day, leading to more lifelike and unpredictable behavior.

In *Skyrim*, Bethesda expanded this approach with “Radiant Story,” which can generate quests and events tailored to the player’s location, progress, and choices. Together, Radiant AI and Radiant Story aim to make the game world feel more reactive and alive, reducing repetition and making each playthrough feel slightly different.

title: Rule-based system
human_text: In computer science, a rule-based system is used to store and manipulate knowledge to interpret information in a useful way. It is often used in artificial intelligence applications and research.
gpt_text:
A rule-based system is an artificial intelligence approach that uses explicit “if-then” rules to represent knowledge and make decisions or inferences. Each rule specifies a condition (the “if” part) and an action or conclusion (the “then” part). When the system’s input data matches a rule’s conditions, that rule “fires,” producing an output, recommendation, or new fact that can trigger further rules.

These systems are common in expert systems, decision support tools, and simple automation. Their main advantages are transparency and ease of explanation—humans can inspect and understand the rules directly. However, they can become hard to manage as the number of rules grows, and they struggle with ambiguity or noisy data compared with statistical or machine learning–based methods.

title: Concurrent MetateM
human_text: Concurrent MetateM is a multi-agent language in which each agent is programmed using a set of (augmented) temporal logic specifications of the behaviour it should exhibit. These specifications are executed directly to generate the behaviour of the agent. As a result, there is no risk of invalidating the logic as with systems where logical specification must first be translated to a lower-level implementation.
gpt_text:
Concurrent MetateM is a logic-based framework for specifying and executing concurrent systems directly from their formal specifications. Instead of writing programs in an imperative language, system behavior is described using temporal logic rules of the form “past ⇒ future,” which express how the system should react over time given its history. These rules are then executed by a specialized engine that interprets them, effectively turning temporal specifications into running code.

In Concurrent MetateM, multiple agents (or components) each have their own sets of temporal rules and run in parallel, communicating via messages or shared events. This makes it well-suited for modeling and implementing distributed, reactive, or multi-agent systems where correctness properties and time-dependent behavior are important, such as protocol verification, coordination in distributed systems, and high-level agent programming.

title: Pop music automation
human_text: Pop music automation is a field of study among musicians and computer scientists with a goal of producing successful pop music algorithmically. It is often based on the premise that pop music is especially formulaic, unchanging, and easy to compose. The idea of automating pop music composition is related to many ideas in algorithmic music, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and computational creativity.
gpt_text:
Pop music automation refers to the use of software, algorithms, and digital tools to streamline or even partially replace human tasks in creating, producing, and promoting pop music. This includes AI-assisted songwriting, automated beat and melody generation, vocal tuning, mixing and mastering presets, and algorithmic recommendations that help decide which songs get pushed to listeners on streaming platforms.

Beyond the studio, automation shapes how pop music is distributed and marketed: recommendation engines suggest tracks to users, automated playlist curation influences what becomes a “hit,” and data-driven systems help labels and artists decide release strategies. Together, these tools can increase efficiency and accessibility in music production, while also raising questions about originality, artistic control, and the homogenization of mainstream pop sound.

title: Mobile translation
human_text: Mobile translation is any electronic device or software application that provides audio translation. The concept includes any handheld electronic device that is specifically designed for audio translation. It also includes any machine translation service or software application for hand-held devices, including mobile telephones, Pocket PCs, and PDAs. Mobile translation provides hand-held device users with the advantage of instantaneous and non-mediated translation from one human language to another, usually against a service fee that is, nevertheless, significantly smaller than a human translator charges.
gpt_text:
Mobile translation refers to the use of smartphones and tablets to translate text, speech, or images between languages in real time. It typically relies on mobile apps or built‑in phone features that use online or offline language models to convert words, sentences, signs, menus, or conversations into another language.

Common features include text input, camera-based translation (pointing the camera at printed text), voice translation for spoken conversations, and sometimes handwriting recognition. Mobile translation is widely used for travel, business, and communication between people who do not share a common language.

title: Grammar systems theory
human_text: Grammar systems theory is a field of theoretical computer science that studies systems of finite collections of formal grammars generating a formal language. Each grammar works on a string, a so-called sequential form that represents an environment. Grammar systems can thus be used as a formalization of decentralized or distributed systems of agents in artificial intelligence.
gpt_text:
Grammar systems theory is a branch of formal language theory that studies collections of grammars working together cooperatively to generate strings or languages. Instead of a single grammar producing a language, a *grammar system* consists of several component grammars that take turns rewriting a common sentential form according to specified “modes” or rules of cooperation (for example, each component might apply a certain number of steps before control passes to another component).

This framework models distributed and cooperative aspects of computation and language generation, and it generalizes classical grammars such as context-free or phrase-structure grammars. Grammar systems theory explores how the interaction patterns between components affect generative power, complexity, and relationships to other models of computation, making it relevant both in theoretical computer science and in understanding modular or distributed language-processing mechanisms.

title: Allen (robot)
human_text: Allen was a robot introduced by Rodney Brooks and his team in the late 1980s, and was their first robot based on subsumption architecture. It had sonar distance and odometry on board, and used an offboard lisp machine to simulate subsumption architecture. It resembled a footstool on wheels.
gpt_text:
Allen is an autonomous robot developed by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the 1980s, led by Rodney Brooks. It is notable as an early embodiment of the “subsumption architecture,” a robotics control philosophy that rejects detailed internal world models in favor of layered, behavior-based control systems. Instead of planning complex actions in advance, Allen responds directly to sensor inputs through simple, interacting behaviors.

Physically, Allen was a mobile robot equipped with sensors such as sonars to perceive its environment and navigate around obstacles. Its control system was organized in layers, where lower layers handled basic tasks like avoiding collisions, and higher layers added more complex behaviors like wandering or exploring, all built incrementally. Allen’s success demonstrated that relatively simple, reactive rules could produce robust, intelligent-seeming behavior in the real world, influencing later generations of mobile robots and the broader field of behavior-based AI.

title: Seth (Street Fighter)
human_text: is a fictional character in Capcom's Street Fighter fighting game series. First introduced in Street Fighter IV, heAlthough the character is an artificial intelligence lifeform with no defined gender, multiple primary and secondary sources cited in this article have referred to Seth by the masculine pronoun. is the final boss of the game and its subsequent updates. He is the chief executive officer of the Shadaloo Intimidation Network (S.I.N.), the weapons division of the Shadaloo terrorist organization in the game's narrative. His body has been heavily modified using advanced technology, with a device installed in his abdomen called the "Tanden Engine". Other appearances by Seth include Project X Zone and Street Fighter V. Seth is voiced by Akio Ōtsuka in Japanese, and Michael McConnohie in English.

Seth is a character from Capcom’s Street Fighter series, first introduced as the final boss of Street Fighter IV. Designed as a synthetic being and the “King of Chaos,” Seth serves as the head of the S.I.N. organization, a weapons division spun off from M. Bison’s Shadaloo. Equipped with the Tanden Engine in his chest, Seth can analyze and mimic the special techniques of other fighters, making him an adaptive, highly versatile opponent. His fighting style, therefore, incorporates a mix of moves resembling those of Ryu, Chun-Li, Zangief, and others.

In Street Fighter V, Seth returns in a new, more androgynous body, having transferred consciousness into a spare Doll unit after the original body’s destruction. This version emphasizes the character’s artificial, experimental nature and continues the theme of copying and repurposing other fighters’ moves. Across appearances, Seth represents the fusion of cutting-edge technology, stolen martial arts data, and ruthless ambition, embodying the dangerous legacy of Shadaloo’s experiments.

title: Web intelligence
human_text: Web intelligence is the area of scientific research and development that explores the roles and makes use of artificial intelligence and information technology for new products, services and frameworks that are empowered by the World Wide Web.
gpt_text:
Web intelligence is the field that studies and develops methods to understand, analyze, and make intelligent use of data and behavior on the web. It combines techniques from artificial intelligence, data mining, machine learning, information retrieval, and social network analysis to extract meaningful patterns and insights from web content, web usage, and online social interactions.

Applications of web intelligence include personalized recommendations, search engine optimization, sentiment analysis, fraud detection, trend prediction, and user profiling. By leveraging large-scale web data, it helps organizations and systems make smarter decisions, improve user experiences, and better understand how people and information move and interact online.

title: Stanford University centers and institutes
human_text: Stanford University has many centers and institutes dedicated to the study of various specific topics. These centers and institutes may be within a department, within a school but across departments, an independent laboratory, institute or center reporting directly to the Dean of Research and outside any school, or semi-independent of the University itself.
gpt_text:
Stanford University’s centers and institutes are specialized organizations that bring together faculty, students, and external partners to focus on particular themes, problems, or disciplines. They often cut across traditional departmental boundaries, supporting interdisciplinary research, teaching, and outreach in areas such as medicine, engineering, the environment, public policy, the humanities, and entrepreneurship.

These entities provide resources like research funding, collaborative workspaces, seminars, fellowships, and industry or community partnerships. Examples include the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI), the Hoover Institution, the Precourt Institute for Energy, and the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment. Collectively, they help drive innovation at Stanford by enabling large-scale projects and collaborations that individual departments might not be able to support on their own.

title: Document capture software
human_text: Document Capture Software refers to applications that provide the ability and feature set to automate the process of scanning paper documents or importing electronic documents, often for the purposes of feeding advanced document classification and data collection processes. Most scanning hardware, both scanners and copiers, provides the basic ability to scan to any number of image file formats, including: PDF, TIFF, JPG, BMP, etc. This basic functionality is augmented by document capture software, which can add efficiency and standardization to the process.
gpt_text:
Document capture software is a tool that converts physical or digital documents (such as paper, PDFs, images, and emails) into structured, usable electronic data. It typically handles scanning, importing, and automatically classifying documents, then extracting key information (like names, dates, invoice numbers) using technologies such as OCR (optical character recognition) and sometimes AI/ML.

These systems streamline workflows by reducing manual data entry, improving accuracy, and enabling faster search and retrieval in downstream systems like document management, ERP, or CRM platforms. They are commonly used for invoices, forms, contracts, mailrooms, and compliance-related records in sectors such as finance, healthcare, government, and manufacturing.

title: Australian Artificial Intelligence Institute
human_text: In Australia, the Australian Artificial Intelligence Institute (Australian AI Institute, AAII, or A2I2) was a government-funded research and development laboratory for investigating and commercializing Artificial Intelligence, specifically Intelligent Software Agents.
gpt_text:
The Australian Artificial Intelligence Institute (AAII) is a research-focused organization dedicated to advancing artificial intelligence technologies and their real-world applications. Based at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), it brings together experts in machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, robotics, and related fields to tackle complex challenges across industry and society.

AAII works closely with government, industry, and community partners to develop AI solutions in areas such as healthcare, smart cities, finance, manufacturing, and environmental monitoring. Alongside cutting-edge research, the institute also emphasizes ethics, safety, and responsible AI, aiming to ensure that AI systems are transparent, fair, and beneficial to people and society.

title: Language Acquisition Device (computer)
human_text: The Language Acquisition Device is a computer program developed by Lobal Technologies, a computer company in the United Kingdom, and scientists from King's College. It emulates the functions of the brain's frontal lobes where humans process language and emotion.Games to take on a life of their own: Copying the brain's neural networks By Alfred Hermida, BBC News Online 11 February 2002.
gpt_text:
A *Language Acquisition Device* (LAD) in the context of computers is a conceptual or implemented system designed to mimic the human capacity for acquiring language. Inspired by Noam Chomsky’s original linguistic theory, a computational LAD refers to algorithms, models, or architectures that enable machines to learn grammar, vocabulary, and linguistic structure from input data, often with minimal explicit instruction.  

In practice, this can include machine learning and deep learning systems (such as neural networks) trained on large text corpora to infer rules of syntax, semantics, and usage. These systems aim to capture some of the generalization power humans show in language learning—using limited examples to understand and generate novel, grammatically coherent sentences—though current implementations are data-driven approximations rather than true cognitive equivalents of the human LAD.

title: SmartAction
human_text: SmartAction is a US company based in El Segundo, Ca. that provides artificial intelligence-based services to businesses across diverse industries including financial services, healthcare, insurance, retail, travel and hospitality and utilities. Originally founded in 2002 as a research project, SmartAction's Intelligent Voice Automation (IVA) is a hosted IVR platform that uses natural language speech recognition and is based on an object-oriented coding framework. SmartAction was founded by inventor and entrepreneur Peter Voss.
gpt_text:
SmartAction is a customer service automation platform that uses AI-driven virtual agents to handle voice and digital interactions such as phone calls, chats, and texts. It is designed to understand natural language, manage routine inquiries, and complete common tasks—like password resets, appointment scheduling, order status checks, and payments—without needing a human agent for most of the interaction.

Typically integrated with existing contact center systems and CRMs, SmartAction aims to reduce call volumes for live agents while improving response times and consistency. When an issue is too complex, it can transfer the customer to a human representative, often passing along context from the automated conversation so the customer doesn’t need to repeat information.

title: AI Memo
human_text: The AI Memos are a series of influential memorandums and technical reports published by the MIT AI Lab, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, United States. They cover Artificial Intelligence, a field of computer science.
gpt_text:
An “AI memo” is a written document, often internal to an organization, that explains, analyzes, or recommends actions related to artificial intelligence. It can cover topics such as adopting new AI tools, assessing risks and opportunities, setting ethical guidelines, or outlining technical architectures and implementation plans.

These memos are commonly used by leadership, technical teams, and policy-makers to align stakeholders on how AI will be used, governed, and integrated into products or workflows. They typically summarize key facts, potential impacts, trade-offs, and next steps, enabling informed decisions about AI strategy and deployment.

title: WebCrow
human_text: The WebCrow is a research project carried out at the Information Engineering Department of the University of Siena with the purpose of automatically solving crosswords.
gpt_text:
WebCrow is an automated crossword puzzle–solving system developed in the field of artificial intelligence. It combines techniques from natural language processing, information retrieval, and constraint satisfaction to interpret crossword clues, search large text corpora (like the web) for candidate answers, and fit those answers into the crossword grid while respecting crossing constraints.

Unlike traditional rule-based puzzle solvers, WebCrow leverages web search and statistical methods to handle the ambiguity and variety of natural-language clues. It became notable for competing against human solvers in crossword competitions, demonstrating how AI can tackle tasks that require both linguistic understanding and combinatorial reasoning.

title: Eclipse Phase
human_text: Eclipse Phase is a science fiction horror role-playing game with transhumanist themes. Originally published by Catalyst Game Labs, Eclipse Phase is now published by the game's creators, Posthuman Studios, and is released under a Creative Commons license.
gpt_text:
Eclipse Phase is a science-fiction tabletop role-playing game set in a post-apocalyptic, transhuman future where Earth has been devastated by a rogue artificial intelligence. Humanity survives scattered throughout the solar system in a variety of political and social factions, using advanced technologies like mind uploading, body-swapping (“resleeving”), and cybernetic enhancements. Player characters are usually agents working for secretive organizations, dealing with existential threats such as hostile AIs, alien intelligences, and dangerous nanotechnology.

The game is known for its strong emphasis on themes like identity, consciousness, and the social impact of radical technology. It uses a percentile (d100) rules system and provides extensive lore on factions, habitats, morphs (bodies), and psychosocial issues of transhumanity. Eclipse Phase is also notable for its Creative Commons licensing, which allows much of its content to be shared and remixed non-commercially.

title: Incremental heuristic search
human_text: Incremental heuristic search algorithms combine both incremental and heuristic search to speed up searches of sequences of similar search problems, which is important in domains that are only incompletely known or change dynamically.S. Koenig, M. Likhachev, Y. Liu and D. Furcy. Incremental Heuristic Search in Artificial Intelligence. Artificial Intelligence Magazine, 25(2), 99-112, 2004. Incremental search has been studied at least since the late 1960s. Incremental search algorithms reuse information from previous searches to speed up the current search and solve search problems potentially much faster than solving them repeatedly from scratch.N. Deo and C. Pang. Shortest-path algorithms: Taxonomy and Annotation. Networks 14, 275–323, 1984. Similarly, heuristic search has also been studied at least since the late 1960s.
gpt_text:
Incremental heuristic search is a family of path-planning algorithms that reuse information from previous searches to speed up solving closely related problems. Instead of planning from scratch every time the environment or start/goal changes slightly, these algorithms update the existing search tree or graph, adjusting costs and priorities based on what has changed. They typically use heuristics (estimates of distance to the goal) much like A*, but add mechanisms to incrementally repair the solution when the world is updated.

Well-known incremental heuristic search methods include algorithms like D*, D* Lite, and Lifelong Planning A*. These are especially useful in robotics and navigation, where an agent moves through a partially known or changing environment: as new obstacles are discovered or removed, the algorithm quickly updates the path rather than recomputing it entirely, offering major efficiency gains.

title: LIDA (cognitive architecture)
human_text: The LIDA (Learning Intelligent Distribution Agent) cognitive architecture is an integrated artificial cognitive system that attempts to model a broad spectrum of cognition in biological systems, from low-level perception/action to high-level reasoning. Developed primarily by Stan Franklin and colleagues at the University of Memphis, the LIDA architecture is empirically grounded in cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience. In addition to providing hypotheses to guide further research, the architecture can support control structures for software agents and robots. Providing plausible explanations for many cognitive processes, the LIDA conceptual model is also intended as a tool with which to think about how minds work.
gpt_text:
LIDA (Learning Intelligent Distribution Agent) is a comprehensive cognitive architecture developed by Stan Franklin and colleagues as an implementation of Global Workspace Theory. It models cognition as a continuous cycle of sensing, understanding, and acting, aiming to explain and simulate human-like cognitive processes such as perception, attention, learning, decision-making, and action selection. LIDA agents operate through repeating “cognitive cycles” in which information is perceived, processed for relevance, broadcast in a global workspace, and then used to guide behavior.

Designed as both a theoretical framework and a practical architecture, LIDA incorporates multiple forms of learning (e.g., perceptual, episodic, procedural) and distinguishes between different kinds of memory systems and processing modules. It has been used to model phenomena like consciousness, task switching, and autonomous decision-making in software agents and robots, making it influential in cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and computational models of consciousness.

title: Evolutionary developmental robotics
human_text: Evolutionary developmental robotics (evo-devo-robo for short) refers to methodologies that systematically integrate evolutionary robotics, epigenetic robotics and morphogenetic robotics to study the evolution, physical and mental development and learning of natural intelligent systems in robotic systems. The field was formally suggested and fully discussed in a published paperY. Jin and Y. Meng, "Morphogenetic robotics: A new emerging field in developmental robotics. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part C: Reviews and Applications, 41(2):145-160, 2011 and further discussed in a published dialogue.Y. Jin and Y. Meng. "Evolutionary Developmental Robotics: The Next Step to Go?" IEEE CIS AMD Newsletter, 8(1):13-14, 2011
gpt_text:
Evolutionary developmental robotics is an interdisciplinary field that combines evolutionary computation, developmental biology principles, and robotics to automatically design both robot bodies and controllers. Instead of hand-engineering a robot’s morphology and brain, researchers use evolutionary algorithms to “evolve” populations of robots over many generations, while developmental processes (inspired by how organisms grow from embryos) shape how simple genetic encodings unfold into complex structures and behaviors.

This approach aims to produce robots that are more adaptive, robust, and versatile than traditionally designed machines. By letting virtual evolution and development explore vast spaces of possible designs—both physical forms and neural control systems—evolutionary developmental robotics seeks to discover novel, often unexpected solutions that can better handle real-world complexity and change.

title: Artificial intelligence, situated approach
human_text: In artificial intelligence research, the situated approach builds agents that are designed to behave effectively successfully in their environment. This requires designing AI "from the bottom-up" by focussing on the basic perceptual and motor skills required to survive. The situated approach gives a much lower priority to abstract reasoning or problem-solving skills.
gpt_text:
The situated approach to artificial intelligence emphasizes that intelligence arises from an agent’s real-time interaction with its environment, rather than from abstract symbol manipulation alone. Instead of focusing on internal reasoning over explicit representations, situated AI systems are embedded in physical or virtual worlds and rely heavily on perception, action, and feedback loops to guide behavior.

This perspective often underpins work in robotics, embodied cognition, and behavior-based AI, where agents learn or adapt by doing—navigating, manipulating objects, or engaging socially—within specific contexts. It contrasts with traditional, purely symbolic AI by arguing that meaningful understanding and robust intelligence depend on the agent’s body, environment, and situational context.

title: Stochastic semantic analysis
human_text: Stochastic semantic analysis is an approach used in computer science as a semantic component of natural language understanding.
gpt_text:
Stochastic semantic analysis is an approach to understanding and interpreting meaning in language using probabilistic models. title: Gödel machine

gpt_text:
A Gödel machine is a theoretical self-improving artificial intelligence proposed by Jürgen Schmidhuber. The name references Kurt Gödel because the system uses formal proofs about its own behavior, akin to reasoning about its own source code.

The Gödel machine contains an initial axiomatic description of itself, its environment, its hardware, and its utility function, plus a proof searcher that looks for beneficial self-modifications. Once the system finds a proof that a certain code change will yield higher expected utility than continuing the current proof search, it halts the search and executes that change. In principle, this yields a provably optimal form of self-improvement under the given axioms, though it remains largely an abstract, idealized framework rather than a practical engineering design.

title: Ensemble averaging (machine learning)

This approach underlies methods like bagging and some forms of stacking, and is commonly used with diverse base learners (e.g., different architectures, hyperparameters, or training subsets). title: Manifold alignment

title: Document mosaicing
human_text: Document mosaicing is a process that stitches multiple, overlapping snapshot images of a document together to produce one large, high resolution composite. The document is slid under a stationary, over-the-desk camera by hand until all parts of the document are snapshotted by the camera’s field of view. As the document slid under the camera, all motion of the document is coarsely tracked by the vision system. The document is periodically snapshotted such that the successive snapshots are overlap by about 50%. The system then finds the overlapped pairs and stitches them together repeatedly until all pairs are stitched together as one piece of document.

The technique typically involves detecting common features in the overlapping regions of the images, computing geometric transformations to align them, and then blending the images to minimize visible seams and differences in lighting. title: Color moments

Typically, the first three moments are used: the mean (average color), the standard deviation (spread or contrast of colors), and the skewness (asymmetry of the color distribution) for each color channel (e.g., R, G, B or another color space like HSV).

Because they compress rich color information into a small set of numbers, color moments are efficient and widely used in image retrieval, classification, and indexing. They are less sensitive to small changes like noise or minor lighting variations compared to raw color histograms, while still being fast to compute and easy to compare between images.

title: Generalized distributive law

title: Hindsight optimization

title: Catastrophic interference
human_text: Catastrophic interference, also known as catastrophic forgetting, is the tendency of an artificial neural network to completely and abruptly forget previously learned information upon learning new information. Neural networks are an important part of the network approach and connectionist approach to cognitive science. With these networks, human capabilities such as memory and learning can be modeled using computer simulations. Catastrophic interference is an important issue to consider when creating connectionist models of memory. It was originally brought to the attention of the scientific community by research from McCloskey and Cohen (1989), and Ratcliff (1990). It is a radical manifestation of the 'sensitivity-stability' dilemma or the 'stability-plasticity' dilemma. Specifically, these problems refer to the challenge of making an artificial neural network that is sensitive to, but not disrupted by, new information. Lookup tables and connectionist networks lie on the opposite sides of the stability plasticity spectrum. The former remains completely stable in the presence of new information but lacks the ability to generalize, i.e. infer general principles, from new inputs. On the other hand, connectionist networks like the standard backpropagation network can generalize to unseen inputs, but they are very sensitive to new information. Backpropagation models can be considered good models of human memory insofar as they mirror the human ability to generalize but these networks often exhibit less stability than human memory. Notably, these backpropagation networks are susceptible to catastrophic interference. This is an issue when modelling human memory, because unlike these networks, humans typically do not show catastrophic forgetting.
gpt_text:

It’s a major obstacle for continual and lifelong learning in AI, where models are expected to accumulate knowledge over time without retraining from scratch. Techniques such as replaying old examples, using separate parameters for different tasks, or regularizing changes to important weights are common strategies to reduce catastrophic interference.
