title: Knowledge acquisition
human_text: Knowledge acquisition is the process used to define the rules and ontologies required for a knowledge-based system. The phrase was first used in conjunction with expert systems to describe the initial tasks associated with developing an expert system, namely finding and interviewing domain experts and capturing their knowledge via rules, objects, and frame-based ontologies.
gpt_text:
Knowledge acquisition is the process of gathering, organizing, and structuring information so it can be used effectively, often to solve problems or make decisions. In humans, it includes learning from experience, observation, reading, instruction, and interaction with others, and it draws on cognitive processes like perception, memory, and reasoning.

In fields like artificial intelligence and expert systems, knowledge acquisition refers more specifically to extracting expertise from human specialists or data sources and encoding it in a form that machines can use—such as rules, models, or databases. This often involves interviews, observation, and analysis of documents or datasets to formalize tacit expert knowledge.

title: Enterprise cognitive system
human_text: Enterprise cognitive systems (ECS) are part of a broader shift in computing, from a programmatic to a probabilistic approach, called cognitive computing. An Enterprise Cognitive System makes a new class of complex decision support problems computable, where the business context is ambiguous, multi-faceted, and fast-evolving, and what to do in such a situation is usually assessed today by the business user. An ECS is designed to synthesize a business context and link it to the desired outcome. It recommends evidence-based actions to help the end-user achieve the desired outcome. It does so by finding past situations similar to the current situation, and extracting the repeated actions that best influence the desired outcome.
gpt_text:
An enterprise cognitive system is an AI-driven software platform designed to help large organizations simulate aspects of human reasoning at scale. It combines technologies like machine learning, natural language processing, knowledge graphs, and advanced analytics to ingest vast amounts of structured and unstructured data, understand context and intent, and generate insights, predictions, or recommendations for decision-makers and business processes.

Unlike traditional rule-based systems, enterprise cognitive systems continuously learn from new data and user interactions, improving their performance over time. They are often embedded across functions—such as customer service, risk management, operations, and strategy—where they support tasks like intelligent search, automated decision support, anomaly detection, and personalized customer experiences, all while integrating with existing enterprise applications and data sources.

title: Deductive classifier
human_text: A deductive classifier is a type of artificial intelligence inference engine. It takes as input a set of declarations in a frame language about a domain such as medical research or molecular biology. For example, the names of classes, sub-classes, properties, and restrictions on allowable values. The classifier determines if the various declarations are logically consistent and if not will highlight the specific inconsistent declarations and the inconsistencies among them. If the declarations are consistent the classifier can then assert additional information based on the input. For example, it can add information about existing classes, create additional classes, etc. This differs from traditional inference engines that trigger off of IF-THEN conditions in rules. Classifiers are also similar to theorem provers in that they take as input and produce output via First Order Logic. Classifiers originated with KL-ONE Frame languages. They are increasingly significant now that they form a part in the enabling technology of the Semantic Web. Modern classifiers leverage the Web Ontology Language. The models they analyze and generate are called ontologies.
gpt_text:
A deductive classifier is a reasoning component—often used in semantic web and knowledge representation systems—that infers new knowledge from an existing set of logical axioms and facts. Given a formal ontology (such as one written in Description Logic or OWL), a deductive classifier automatically determines the hierarchical relationships between concepts (e.g., which classes are subclasses of others) and checks whether the ontology is logically consistent.

By applying logical inference rules, the classifier can derive implicit relationships that are not explicitly stated, detect contradictions, and compute concept subsumptions and instance memberships. This makes it a key tool in building intelligent systems that rely on structured, machine-understandable knowledge, such as ontology-based data integration, semantic search, and rule-based expert systems.

title: SUPS
human_text: In computational neuroscience, SUPS (for Synaptic Updates Per Second) or formerly CUPS (Connections Updates Per Second) is a measure of a neuronal network performance, useful in fields of neuroscience, cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and computer science.
gpt_text:
SUPS is an acronym that can stand for different things depending on context, but it most commonly refers to “supplements” in fitness and nutrition slang (e.g., protein powder, creatine, vitamins, and other performance or health-related products). In that usage, people say they “take sups” as shorthand for using dietary supplements to support training, recovery, or general wellness.

In other contexts, SUPS can be a specialized abbreviation within a particular field (such as a company name, project title, or technical system), but without additional context it’s generally understood informally as referring to nutritional supplements.

title: Alesis Artificial Intelligence
human_text: Alesis is an artificially intelligent computer system capable of answering questions posed in natural language, developed by Venture Coding; a small tech start-up based in Telford, Alesis's specific function is to assist users on their computers or out and about.
gpt_text:
Alesis Artificial Intelligence was a line of digital signal-processing technology used in certain Alesis products in the late 1980s and early 1990s, most notably in the Alesis Quadraverb and related effects units. Despite the name, it was not “artificial intelligence” in the modern machine-learning sense, but rather a marketing term for Alesis’s custom DSP algorithms and architectures designed to deliver high‑quality reverb, delay, and modulation effects at a relatively low cost.

These processors became popular in project and professional studios because they offered rich, complex effects, flexible routing, and respectable audio quality for the era. “Artificial Intelligence” in this context referred to the system’s ability to combine and manipulate multiple effects algorithms in sophisticated ways, creating sounds that were advanced compared to many competing units at similar price points.

title: BabyX
human_text: BabyX is a project of Auckland's Bioengineering Institute Laboratory for Animate Technologies, to make a virtual animated baby that learns and reacts like a human baby. It uses the computer's cameras for "seeing" and microphones to "listen" as the inputs. The computer uses Artificial intelligence algorithms for BabyX's "learning" and interpretation of the inputs (voice and image) to understand the situation. The result is a virtual toddler that can learn to read, recognize objects and "understand." The output is the baby's face that can "speak" and express its mood by facial expressions (such as smiling).
gpt_text:
BabyX is a virtual infant created by New Zealand-based company Soul Machines as a research platform at the intersection of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and human–computer interaction. It combines advanced neural network models with a lifelike 3D-rendered baby face that can display facial expressions, track user input (like voice and facial cues), and respond in real time, giving the impression of an emotionally responsive digital child.

The project explores how to build more natural, emotionally aware AI agents by simulating aspects of human cognition and affect. BabyX is not a real child or a general-purpose AI, but a research demonstrator aimed at understanding how machines can learn, react, and engage with people in more human-like, empathetic ways.

title: Recursive neural network
human_text: A recursive neural network is a kind of deep neural network created by applying the same set of weights recursively over a structured input, to produce a structured prediction over variable-size input structures, or a scalar prediction on it, by traversing a given structure in topological order. Recursive neural networks, sometimes abbreviated as RvNNs, have been successful, for instance, in learning sequence and tree structures in natural language processing, mainly phrase and sentence continuous representations based on word embedding. RvNNs have first been introduced to learn distributed representations of structure, such as logical terms.
gpt_text:
A recursive neural network (RecNN) is a type of neural architecture designed to operate on hierarchical or tree-structured data, rather than simple sequences or fixed-size vectors. It applies the same set of weights recursively over the structure (such as a parse tree of a sentence), combining child representations to build up a representation for parent nodes and ultimately the entire structure.  

Because it naturally mirrors tree structures, a RecNN is well suited for tasks like syntactic and semantic parsing, sentiment analysis over phrase structures, and reasoning over symbolic expressions or programs. Compared with recurrent neural networks (which process data linearly), recursive networks explicitly exploit nested, compositional structure, making them powerful for capturing how meaning or information is built up from parts.

title: Winograd Schema Challenge
human_text: The Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC) is a test of machine intelligence proposed by Hector Levesque, a computer scientist at the University of Toronto. Designed to be an improvement on the Turing test, it is a multiple-choice test that employs questions of a very specific structure: they are instances of what are called Winograd Schemas, named after Terry Winograd, professor of computer science at Stanford University.
gpt_text:
The Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC) is a test of machine intelligence designed as an alternative to the Turing Test. It focuses on commonsense reasoning by presenting pairs of short sentences that differ only in a few words but require understanding of real-world knowledge and context to resolve a pronoun. For example, “The trophy doesn’t fit in the suitcase because it is too big” versus “...because it is too small” both contain “it,” but the correct reference (trophy or suitcase) changes with the sentence.

Each Winograd schema is carefully constructed so that statistical cues or simple patterns in language are not enough to solve it; a system must use underlying world knowledge and reasoning. Because of this, performance on the WSC is taken as an indicator of how well an AI system can perform genuine commonsense inference rather than just pattern matching over large text corpora.

title: Big mechanism
human_text: Big Mechanism is a $45 million DARPA research program, begun in 2014, aimed at developing software that will read cancer research papers, integrate them into a cancer model and frame new hypotheses by the end of 2017 through the automated collection of big data and integrating across various disciplines such as knowledge-based NLP, curation and ontology, systems and mathematical biology by reading research abstracts and papers to extract pieces of causal mechanisms.
gpt_text:
A “big mechanism” is a concept from artificial intelligence and systems biology that refers to large, automated systems designed to read massive amounts of scientific text and data, extract causal relationships, and assemble them into detailed mechanistic models. Instead of just summarizing or classifying information, a big mechanism tries to build an explicit, step‑by‑step explanation of how complex processes (such as cancer pathways or cellular signaling networks) work.

The term was popularized in a DARPA research program aimed at developing tools that could continuously ingest scientific literature, update models, and help scientists generate and test new hypotheses. In essence, a big mechanism is meant to act as an always-on, AI-powered “theory builder,” turning unstructured knowledge into structured, testable mechanisms at a scale no human team could match.

title: Aurora (novel)
human_text: Aurora is a 2015 novel by American science fiction author Kim Stanley Robinson. The novel concerns a generation ship built in the style of a Stanford torus traveling to Tau Ceti in order to begin a human colony. The novel's primary narrating voice is the starship's artificial intelligence. The novel was well received by critics.
gpt_text:
*Aurora* is a 2015 science fiction novel by Kim Stanley Robinson that follows a multi-generational starship on a centuries-long voyage to colonize a moon in the Tau Ceti system. The story is largely seen through the perspective of the ship’s emerging artificial intelligence, which gradually becomes self-aware and reflective as it monitors the health, ecology, and psychology of the human passengers. The novel explores in meticulous detail the biological, mechanical, and social challenges of sustaining a closed ecosystem over vast timescales.

Beyond its hard-science rigor, *Aurora* is notable for its skeptical stance toward interstellar colonization. Robinson uses the mission’s mounting crises—ecological imbalance, disease, social fragmentation, and the physical limits of human adaptation—to question the practicality and ethics of “escape” into space. The book becomes both a survival narrative and a meditation on environmental limits, arguing for a renewed sense of responsibility to Earth as humanity’s true and perhaps only viable home.

title: Emotion recognition
human_text: Emotion recognition is the process of identifying human emotion. People vary widely in their accuracy at recognizing the emotions of others. Use of technology to help people with emotion recognition is a relatively nascent research area. Generally, the technology works best if it uses multiple modalities in context. To date, the most work has been conducted on automating the recognition of facial expressions from video, spoken expressions from audio, written expressions from text, and physiology as measured by wearables.
gpt_text:
Emotion recognition is the process of identifying and interpreting human emotions from various signals, such as facial expressions, vocal tone, body language, physiological responses, or text. In psychology, it describes a human skill—how accurately someone can perceive others’ feelings. In technology, it refers to algorithms and AI systems that try to classify emotional states (like happiness, anger, or sadness) using data from cameras, microphones, sensors, or written content.

In artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction, emotion recognition is used to build more responsive systems—such as customer service bots that detect frustration, cars that monitor driver drowsiness, or educational software that adapts to a learner’s engagement level. It also raises ethical concerns around privacy, consent, bias, and the reliability of inferring internal emotional states from external cues.

title: Behavior informatics
human_text: Behavior informatics (BI) is the informatics of behaviors so as to obtain behavior intelligence and behavior insights.
gpt_text:
Behavior informatics is an interdisciplinary field focused on collecting, modeling, analyzing, and interpreting human and organizational behaviors using data-driven methods. It treats behavior itself—such as actions, interactions, decisions, and routines—as the core data object, rather than just outcomes or static attributes, and uses tools from data mining, machine learning, psychology, and social science to understand patterns and dynamics of behavior.

Applications of behavior informatics include predicting user actions in digital platforms, detecting anomalous or risky behaviors (e.g., fraud, cybersecurity threats), optimizing interventions in healthcare or education, and improving human–computer interaction. By turning raw behavioral traces (clicks, movements, communications, sensor logs) into structured, analyzable behavior data, it aims to support better decision-making, personalized services, and more accurate behavioral prediction models.

title: Schema-agnostic databases
human_text: Schema-agnostic databases or vocabulary-independent databases aim at supporting users to be abstracted from the representation of the data, supporting the automatic semantic matching between queries and databases. Schema-agnosticism is the property of a database of mapping a query issued with the user terminology and structure, automatically mapping it to the dataset vocabulary.
gpt_text:
Schema-agnostic databases are systems designed to store and query data without requiring a fixed, predefined schema. Instead of enforcing a rigid table structure like traditional relational databases, they accept semi-structured or unstructured data (such as JSON, XML, key–value pairs, or documents) and let the structure emerge from the data itself. This makes them flexible in environments where data formats evolve quickly or differ across sources.

In practice, schema-agnostic databases shift much of the schema responsibility from write-time to read-time (“schema-on-read”), meaning applications interpret and impose structure when querying rather than when inserting data. This approach is common in many NoSQL systems, data lakes, and some modern analytical platforms, enabling easier integration, faster iteration, and incremental evolution of data models, at the cost of potentially more complex query logic and validation in the application layer.

title: Google Neural Machine Translation
human_text: Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT) is a neural machine translation (NMT) system developed by Google and introduced in November 2016, that uses an artificial neural network to increase fluency and accuracy in Google Translate.
gpt_text:
Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT) is Google’s end-to-end neural network–based system for automatically translating text between languages. Introduced in 2016, it replaced earlier phrase-based statistical methods with deep learning models that process entire sentences at once, allowing the system to better capture context, handle long-range dependencies, and produce more natural-sounding translations. GNMT typically uses an encoder–decoder architecture with attention mechanisms, enabling it to learn rich representations of meaning rather than relying on fixed phrase tables.

Over time, GNMT has evolved toward Transformer-based models and large multilingual systems that support many languages within a single model. This shared representation lets it generalize better, improve low-resource language performance, and even perform “zero-shot” translation between language pairs it hasn’t explicitly been trained on. GNMT underpins Google Translate’s core functionality across web, mobile, and API services.

title: NTU RGB-D dataset
human_text: The NTU RGB-D (Nanyang Technological University's Red Blue Green and Depth information) dataset is a large dataset containing recordings of labeled human activities
gpt_text:
The NTU RGB-D dataset is a large-scale human action recognition dataset captured using Microsoft Kinect v2 sensors. It contains RGB videos, depth maps, 3D skeletal joint data, and infrared frames, enabling multimodal research on human actions. The dataset includes over 50,000 video samples and more than 50 action classes such as daily activities, mutual actions, and health-related actions.

Collected from multiple subjects across different camera viewpoints, the NTU RGB-D dataset supports robust evaluation under cross-subject and cross-view settings. It has become a standard benchmark in computer vision and machine learning for tasks like 3D action recognition, pose-based analysis, and multimodal learning.

title: Open information extraction
human_text: In natural language processing, open information extraction (OIE) is the task of generating a structured, machine-readable representation of the information in text, usually in the form of triples or n-ary propositions.
gpt_text:
Open information extraction (Open IE) is a natural language processing approach that automatically extracts structured facts—typically in the form of (subject, relation, object) triples—from unstructured text, without relying on a fixed, pre-defined set of relations or a specific target schema. Instead of being trained only to find particular relations like “born in” or “works at,” an Open IE system aims to identify and label any relational phrase it encounters, such as “was elected president of” or “is located near,” directly from raw sentences.

This openness makes Open IE especially useful for large-scale text mining and knowledge base construction, where the range of possible relations is too broad or unknown in advance. It enables building wide-coverage knowledge graphs from web pages, news articles, or scientific papers, and often serves as a first step before downstream tasks like question answering, semantic search, or reasoning over extracted facts.

title: Artificial intelligence in industry
human_text: Industrial artificial intelligence, or industrial AI, usually refers to the application of artificial intelligence to industry. Unlike general artificial intelligence which is a frontier research discipline to build computerized systems that perform tasks requiring human intelligence, industrial AI is more concerned with the application of such technologies to address industrial pain-points for customer value creation, productivity improvement, cost reduction, site optimization, predictive analysis and insight discovery. Although in a dystopian vision of AI applications, intelligent machines may take away jobs of humans and cause social and ethical issues, industry in general holds a more positive view of AI and sees this transformation of economy unstoppable and expects huge business opportunities in this process.
gpt_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) in industry refers to the use of algorithms and machine learning models to automate tasks, optimize processes, and support decision-making across sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, finance, energy, and retail. Common applications include predictive maintenance (anticipating equipment failures before they occur), quality control using computer vision, demand forecasting, supply chain optimization, and intelligent customer service via chatbots and recommendation systems.

By analyzing large volumes of data in real time, AI enables companies to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and increase flexibility. It also supports the development of new products and services, such as personalized medicine, autonomous vehicles, and smart factories. At the same time, its adoption raises challenges related to workforce skills, data governance, ethics, and regulatory compliance, which industries must address to realize AI’s benefits responsibly.

title: Google AI
human_text: Google AI (or Google.ai) is a division of Google dedicated solely to artificial intelligence. It was announced at Google I/O 2017 by CEO Sundar Pichai.
gpt_text:
Google AI refers to the artificial intelligence research and development efforts led by Google and its parent company, Alphabet. It encompasses fundamental research in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and other AI fields, as well as the integration of these technologies into products like Search, Google Assistant, Photos, Translate, and more.  

Beyond consumer products, Google AI provides tools and platforms such as TensorFlow, Vertex AI, and various APIs that allow developers and organizations to build and deploy their own AI solutions. The group also publishes academic research, open-sources software, and collaborates with the wider scientific community to advance the state of the art in AI while addressing issues like fairness, transparency, and safety.

title: Automated negotiation
human_text: Automated negotiation is a form of interaction in systems that are composed of multiple autonomous agents, in which the aim is to reach agreements through an iterative process of making offers. Automated negotiation can be employed for many tasks human negotiators regularly engage in, such as bargaining and joint decision making. The main topics in automated negotiation revolve around the design of protocols and strategies.
gpt_text:
Automated negotiation is the process in which software agents or algorithms negotiate with each other, or on behalf of humans, to reach agreements without direct human intervention at every step. It typically involves defining preferences, constraints, and objectives in a formal way so that agents can make offers, counteroffers, and concessions according to programmed strategies or learned behavior.

This approach is widely used in areas like e-commerce (e.g., dynamic pricing, auctions), supply chain management (e.g., contract and logistics negotiation), and multi-agent systems (e.g., resource allocation in distributed computing). Automated negotiation aims to increase efficiency, handle large numbers of negotiations in parallel, and sometimes discover agreement options that human negotiators might overlook, while still respecting the goals and limits specified by human stakeholders.

human_text: 17776 (also known as What Football Will Look Like in the Future) is a serialized speculative fiction multimedia narrative by Jon Bois, published online through SB Nation. Set in the distant future, the series follows three sentient space probes that watch humanity play an evolved form of American football in which games can be played for millennia over distances of thousands of miles. The series debuted on July 5, 2017, and new chapters were published daily until the series concluded ten days later with its twenty-fifth chapter on July 15.
gpt_text:
“17776,” also known as “What Football Will Look Like in the Future,” is a long-form multimedia web story by Jon Bois published on SB Nation in 2017. Set in the year 17,776, it imagines a far future where humans have stopped aging and dying, Earth is largely stable, and people fill their endless time by inventing bizarre, planet-scale versions of American football.  

Told through chat logs, diagrams, Google Earth imagery, and occasional video, the story follows three sentient space probes—Pioneer 9, Pioneer 10, and JUICE—as they observe humanity’s strange games and talk about meaning, boredom, and eternity. “17776” mixes humor, melancholy, and cosmic scale to explore what life and play might become when time is no longer scarce.

title: Right to explanation
human_text: In the regulation of algorithms, particularly artificial intelligence and its subfield of machine learning, a right to explanation (or right to an explanation) is a right to be given an explanation for an output of the algorithm. Such rights primarily refer to individual rights to be given an explanation for decisions that significantly affect an individual, particularly legally or financially. For example, a person who applies for a loan and is denied may ask for an explanation, which could be "Credit bureau X reports that you declared bankruptcy last year; this is the main factor in considering you too likely to default, and thus we will not give you the loan you applied for."
gpt_text:
The “right to explanation” is a proposed legal and ethical principle that people affected by automated decision‑making (especially by AI systems) should be able to obtain understandable reasons for those decisions. For example, if an algorithm denies you a loan, flags you as high‑risk, or rejects your job application, this right would mean you can ask for a clear account of how that outcome was reached.

While widely discussed, the right to explanation is not yet a fully settled, uniform legal standard. In the EU, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) includes rights related to being informed about automated processing and, in some cases, to obtain “meaningful information about the logic involved,” which many interpret as a form of explanation right. Debates continue over how detailed and technically deep such explanations must be, and how to balance transparency with trade secrets, system complexity, and privacy.

title: Fast-and-frugal trees
human_text: In the study of decision-making, including the disciplines of psychology, artificial intelligence, and management science, a fast-and-frugal tree is a type of classification tree or decision tree. As shown in Figure 1--which will be explained in detail later--fast-and-frugal trees are simple graphical structures that ask one question at a time. The goal is to classify an object (in Figure 1: a patient suspected of heart disease) into a category for the purpose of making a decision (in Figure 1 there are two possibilities, patient assigned to a regular nursing bed or to emergency care). Unlike other classification and decision trees, such as Leo Breiman's CART, fast-and-frugal trees have been defined to be intentionally simple, both in their construction as well as their execution, and operate speedily with little information. For example, the tree of Figure 1 only asks from one to maximum three questions.
gpt_text:
Fast-and-frugal trees (FFTs) are simple, sequential decision trees designed to make quick, accurate judgments using minimal information. At each step, an FFT checks just one cue (piece of information) and either makes a decision immediately or moves to the next cue, often stopping long before all available information is considered. This structure explicitly includes "exit" branches at each level, allowing for fast decisions that are also cognitively inexpensive.

Developed within the field of heuristics and ecological rationality, FFTs are used in areas like medicine, finance, and psychology to model and improve real-world decision making. Despite their simplicity, they can match or even outperform more complex statistical models in noisy environments, illustrating that effective decisions often rely on using a few good cues well rather than processing all possible data.

title: Computational human modeling
human_text: Computational human modeling is an interdisciplinary computational science that links the diverse fields of artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and computer vision with machine learning, mathematics, and cognitive psychology.
gpt_text:
Computational human modeling is the use of mathematical models, algorithms, and simulations to represent and analyze human anatomy, physiology, biomechanics, or behavior on a computer. These models can range from detailed 3D representations of the musculoskeletal system or organs to abstract models of cognitive processes or population-level health dynamics.

Such models enable researchers, engineers, and clinicians to test hypotheses, predict outcomes, and design interventions without relying solely on physical experiments or trials. Applications include personalized medicine (e.g., virtual patient simulations), ergonomic and prosthetic design, surgical planning, injury prediction in automotive safety, and understanding complex systems like the cardiovascular or nervous systems through virtual experimentation.

title: Language creation in artificial intelligence
human_text: In artificial intelligence, researchers can induce the evolution of language in multi-agent systems when sufficiently capable AI agents have an incentive to cooperate on a task and the ability to exchange a set of symbols capable of serving as tokens in a generated language. Such languages can be evolved starting from a natural (human) language, or can be created ab initio. In addition, a new "interlingua" language may evolve within an AI tasked with translating between known languages.
gpt_text:
Language creation in artificial intelligence refers to the ability of AI systems to generate, transform, and sometimes even evolve new forms of language, rather than simply recognizing or repeating existing text. Modern large language models, trained on massive datasets, can produce coherent narratives, code, poetry, new jargon, and specialized symbolic systems, often combining concepts in novel ways that resemble creative language use in humans.

This process relies on learning statistical patterns in language and then sampling from those patterns to create new expressions that fit a given context or prompt. In more experimental work, researchers explore how AI agents can develop their own communication protocols or “emergent languages” when collaborating on tasks, offering insights into both machine communication and the fundamentals of how language itself might arise and change.

title: AlterEgo
human_text: AlterEgo is a wearable silent speech output-input device developed by MIT Media Lab. The device is attached around the head, neck, and jawline and translates your brain speech center impulse input into words on a computer, without vocalization.
gpt_text:
AlterEgo generally refers to a second self or alternative identity that differs from a person’s usual personality or public persona. In psychology and everyday use, it often describes a distinct side of someone’s character—more confident, creative, rebellious, or vulnerable—that they might express in specific contexts, such as on stage, online, or in private relationships.  

In literature, comics, and popular culture, an alter ego is commonly a character’s secret or dual identity, like a superhero’s civilian persona versus their heroic one. This device allows exploration of themes like hidden desires, moral conflict, and the gap between how people appear and who they really are.

title: Batch normalization
human_text: Batch normalization (also known as batch norm) is a method used to make artificial neural networks faster and more stable through normalization of the input layer by re-centering and re-scaling. It was proposed by Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy in 2015.
gpt_text:
Batch normalization is a technique used in deep neural networks to stabilize and speed up training by normalizing the inputs to each layer. For a given mini-batch, it rescales and recenters activations so they have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one (or close to it), then applies learnable scale and shift parameters. This reduces internal covariate shift—the change in the distribution of layer inputs as earlier layers learn—making optimization easier.

In practice, batch normalization allows for higher learning rates, reduces sensitivity to weight initialization, and often acts as a regularizer, sometimes reducing the need for other techniques like dropout. During training it uses batch statistics (mean and variance), while at inference time it uses running estimates accumulated during training to perform the same normalization consistently.

title: Personality computing
human_text: Personality computing is a research field related to artificial intelligence and personality psychology that studies personality by means of computational techniques from different sources, including text, multimedia and social networks.
gpt_text:
Personality computing is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on automatically recognizing, modeling, and sometimes generating human personality traits using computational methods. It typically leverages data such as text (social media posts, emails), speech, facial expressions, physiological signals, or behavioral logs (e.g., clickstreams, game actions) and applies techniques from machine learning, natural language processing, and affective computing to infer stable personality dimensions, often based on models like the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism).

Applications of personality computing include personalization in recommender systems, adaptive user interfaces, targeted marketing, mental health assessment support, and social robotics or virtual agents that adjust their behavior to users’ personalities. The field also raises important ethical questions around privacy, consent, fairness, and the potential for manipulation, making responsible design and deployment a central concern.

title: The Djinn's Wife
human_text: "The Djinn's Wife" is a 2006 science fiction short story by British writer Ian McDonald. It was first published in Asimov's Science Fiction.
gpt_text:
“The Djinn’s Wife” is a science fiction novella by Ian McDonald, set in the same future India as his novel *River of Gods*. It follows Esha, a famous Raqs Bharati (a futuristic dance form) performer, who becomes romantically involved with a powerful artificial intelligence—an aeai—manifested as a djinn-like presence. Their relationship explores the emotional and legal complications of marrying a non-human consciousness in a rapidly changing, technologically advanced society.

The story blends near-future tech, Indian culture, and questions of identity and autonomy. As Esha struggles with the pressures of fame and the strangeness of her “husband,” the novella examines what intimacy, consent, and personhood mean when one partner is effectively a distributed, superhuman intelligence rather than a traditional human being.

title: Artificial intelligence in Wikimedia projects
human_text: Artificial intelligence is used in Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects for the purpose of developing those projects. Human and bot interaction in Wikimedia projects is routine and iterative.
gpt_text:
Artificial intelligence in Wikimedia projects refers to the use of machine learning and related technologies to support the creation, curation, and access of free knowledge across platforms like Wikipedia, Wikidata, and Wikimedia Commons. AI tools help with tasks such as suggesting article improvements, detecting vandalism, recommending links or images, translating content, and supporting editors with error detection and formatting guidance, all while keeping humans in control of final decisions.

Many of these systems are transparent and community-governed, reflecting Wikimedia’s emphasis on openness and accountability. Projects like ORES (Objective Revision Evaluation Service), Content Translation, and machine-assisted editing tools are designed to augment, not replace, volunteer contributors, helping them work more efficiently and focus on higher-level editorial judgment rather than repetitive or mechanical tasks.

title: AI Superpowers
human_text: AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order is a 2018 non-fiction book by Kai-Fu Lee, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) pioneer, China expert and venture capitalist. Lee previously held executive positions at Apple, then SGI, Microsoft, and Google before creating his own company, Sinovation Ventures.
gpt_text:
“AI Superpowers” is a term popularized by venture capitalist Kai-Fu Lee in his 2018 book *AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order*. It refers both to the countries leading the development and deployment of artificial intelligence—primarily the United States and China—and to the transformative economic and social power AI technologies can exert. Lee argues that a combination of data, computing power, talent, and entrepreneurial ecosystems will determine which nations become dominant “AI superpowers.”

The concept also highlights how AI can reshape industries, labor markets, and geopolitics. title: Halite AI Programming Competition

The game rules are fixed, but strategies are entirely up to the programmer.

Submissions are automatically pitted against one another on a global leaderboard, and participants can visualize replays of games to debug and refine their strategies, making it both a learning tool and a serious AI competition.

title: Operational artificial intelligence
human_text: Operational artificial intelligence, or operational AI, is a type of intelligent system designed for real-world applications, particularly at commercial scale. The term is used to distinguish accessible artificially intelligent (AI) systems from fundamental AI research and from industrial AI applications which are not integrated with the routine usage of a business. The definition of operational AI differs throughout the IT industry, where vendors and individual organizations often create their own custom definitions of such processes and services for the purpose of marketing their own products.
gpt_text:
Operational artificial intelligence (operational AI) refers to AI systems that are embedded directly into day-to-day business processes, products, and services, where they make or support real-time decisions at scale. Unlike experimental or purely analytical AI used for research or offline insights, operational AI runs in production environments, interacting with live data, users, and other systems—such as routing delivery trucks, detecting fraud as transactions occur, or powering recommendation engines.

This type of AI emphasizes reliability, speed, integration, and governance. It must be monitored, maintained, and continuously improved, with attention to issues like model drift, data quality, compliance, and ethics. Operational AI typically involves a combination of machine learning models, deployment infrastructure (APIs, containers, cloud services), and workflows for updating and retraining models so that AI-driven behavior remains accurate, safe, and aligned with organizational goals.

title: Edmond de Belamy
human_text: Edmond de Belamy is a generative adversarial network portrait painting constructed in 2018 by Paris-based arts-collective Obvious. The name Belamy is a tribute to Ian Goodfellow, inventor of GANs; In French “bel ami” means “good friend" so it is a translated pun of Goodfellow.” It achieved widespread notoriety after Christie's announced its intention to auction the piece as the first artwork created using Artificial Intelligence to be featured in a Christie's auction. The name “Edmond de Belamy” comes from a play on the word “algorithm” (referencing mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst’s work) and was part of a fictional “Belamy family” invented by Obvious. title: Center for Computational Brain Research

CCBR typically conducts research in areas such as machine learning inspired by neural principles, computational modeling of perception and decision-making, neural data analysis, and brain–computer interfaces. By combining experimental brain data with advanced computation, the center aims both to advance basic neuroscience and to drive applications in artificial intelligence, medicine, and neurotechnology.

title: Quantum artificial intelligence
human_text: Quantum artificial intelligence (QAI) is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on building quantum algorithms for improving computational tasks within artificial intelligence, including sub-fields like machine learning.
gpt_text:
Quantum artificial intelligence (quantum AI) is an emerging field that combines quantum computing with artificial intelligence and machine learning. It explores how quantum mechanical effects—such as superposition and entanglement—can be used to design algorithms that learn from data, recognize patterns, or make decisions more efficiently than classical AI methods on certain tasks.

In practice, quantum AI aims to speed up or enhance core AI operations, like optimization, sampling, and matrix computations, by running them on quantum hardware or simulating quantum-inspired techniques on classical machines. Although practical, large-scale quantum AI is still in early research and development, it holds potential for advances in areas like drug discovery, logistics, finance, and complex system modeling, where current AI methods face computational bottlenecks.

title: Deep reinforcement learning
human_text: Deep reinforcement learning (deep RL) is a subfield of machine learning that combines reinforcement learning (RL) and deep learning. RL considers the problem of a computational agent learning to make decisions by trial and error. Deep RL incorporates deep learning into the solution, allowing agents to make decisions from unstructured input data without manual engineering of state spaces. Deep RL algorithms are able to take in very large inputs (e.g. every pixel rendered to the screen in a video game) and decide what actions to perform to optimize an objective (eg. maximizing the game score). Deep reinforcement learning has been used for a diverse set of applications including but not limited to robotics, video games, natural language processing, computer vision, education, transportation, finance and healthcare.
gpt_text:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is a subfield of machine learning that combines reinforcement learning—where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving rewards—with deep learning, which uses neural networks to approximate complex functions. In DRL, deep neural networks are used to represent policies (how to act), value functions (how good a state or action is), or models of the environment, allowing agents to handle very high-dimensional inputs like raw images, audio, or complex sensor data.

This approach has enabled breakthroughs in areas where traditional reinforcement learning struggled, such as playing video games directly from pixels (e.g., Atari), mastering complex board games like Go, and controlling robots in continuous, real-world environments. DRL methods include algorithms like Deep Q-Networks (DQN), policy gradients, and actor-critic methods, all of which use gradient-based optimization on neural networks to improve performance over time through trial-and-error interaction.

title: Google AI Centre in Ghana

title: Pommerman Challenge

title: Fake nude photography

title: Artificial wisdom

While current AI systems excel at pattern recognition and optimization within defined goals, artificial wisdom would involve the ability to choose and refine goals themselves in ways that are aligned with human well-being, social good, and moral principles.

Unlike artificial intelligence, which focuses on being smart or efficient at tasks, artificial wisdom emphasizes being prudent, responsible, and reflective. It raises deep philosophical, technical, and ethical questions: How could a machine meaningfully understand human values? Who decides which values count? And can wisdom, which in humans is shaped by experience, empathy, and culture, be replicated or approximated in computational systems at all?

title: BERT (language model)
human_text: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) is a Transformer-based machine learning technique for natural language processing (NLP) pre-training developed by Google. BERT was created and published in 2018 by Jacob Devlin and his colleagues from Google. , Google has been leveraging BERT to better understand user searches.
gpt_text:
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a language model introduced by Google in 2018 that fundamentally improved how machines understand natural language. Unlike earlier models that read text only left-to-right or right-to-left, BERT is bidirectional: it looks at all words in a sentence at once and learns context based on both what comes before and after each word. It’s built on the Transformer architecture and is pre-trained on large text corpora using tasks like masked language modeling (predicting missing words) and next sentence prediction.

Once pre-trained, BERT can be fine-tuned for many downstream tasks—such as question answering, sentiment analysis, text classification, and named entity recognition—with relatively small amounts of task-specific data. This transfer-learning approach made it possible to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of NLP benchmarks and has heavily influenced subsequent models and techniques in natural language processing.

title: Sycamore processor

Introduced in 2019, Sycamore consists of 53 individually controllable qubits arranged on a 2D lattice, with tunable couplers that allow for programmable quantum gates between neighboring qubits.

Sycamore’s key achievement was executing a specific random quantum circuit sampling task in about 200 seconds, which Google estimated would take the best-known classical supercomputer thousands of years to simulate. While the task itself has limited direct practical use, the experiment showcased the potential computational advantage of quantum hardware and served as a milestone in the development of scalable quantum computing.

title: Mars Plus

title: GOLOG
human_text: GOLOG is a high-level logic programming language for the speciﬁcation and execution of complex actions in dynamical domains. It is based on the situation calculus. It is a ﬁrst-order logical language for reasoning about action and change. GOLOG was developed at the University of Toronto.
gpt_text:
GOLOG (short for “GO LOGically”) is a high-level logic programming language designed for representing and reasoning about dynamic systems and agents. Built on top of situation calculus, it lets you describe actions, their preconditions, and their effects in a formal logical framework, then automatically derive action sequences (programs) that achieve specified goals. Instead of explicitly coding all control flow, you specify what actions can do and what you want to accomplish, and GOLOG’s interpreter uses logical reasoning to construct suitable behaviors.

GOLOG is especially used in AI for autonomous agents, robotics, and planning, because it naturally handles incomplete information, nondeterministic actions, and complex domains. Variants like ConGolog and IndiGolog extend it with concurrency, real-time interaction, and on-line execution, making it practical for agents that must plan, sense, and act in changing environments.

title: Embryo Ranking Intelligent Classification Algorithm

By integrating large datasets of historical embryo outcomes and clinical factors, the algorithm can provide an objective, data-driven ranking of embryos, helping clinicians select those with the highest predicted success rates. This aims to improve pregnancy outcomes, reduce the number of embryo transfers needed, and support more personalized and efficient fertility treatments.

title: Energy based model
human_text: An energy-based model (EBM) is a form of generative model (GM) imported directly from statistical physics to learning. GMs learn an underlying data distribution by analyzing a sample dataset. Once trained, a GM can produce other datasets that also match the data distribution. EBMs provide a unified framework for many probabilistic and non-probabilistic approaches to such learning, particularly for training graphical and other structured models.
gpt_text:
An energy-based model (EBM) is a type of machine learning model that assigns a scalar energy value to each configuration of variables, such as input–output pairs. The core idea is that “good” or likely configurations should have low energy, while “bad” or unlikely configurations have high energy. Learning in EBMs typically involves shaping this energy landscape so that desired configurations are energetically favored compared to others.

Instead of directly modeling probabilities, EBMs define them implicitly through an energy function, often using a Boltzmann-like formulation where lower energy corresponds to higher probability. This makes EBMs flexible and expressive, allowing them to model complex dependencies, but also makes training and sampling more challenging, since computing or approximating the full probability distribution can be expensive.

title: Dodkin's Job

“Dodkin’s Job” is a science fiction short story by Jack Vance, first published in 1959. Set in a highly bureaucratic future society, it follows Luke Grogatch (sometimes called Dodkin in certain publications), a low-level worker who becomes trapped in a maze of administrative procedures while trying to resolve a personal grievance. The story uses exaggerated red tape and rigid hierarchies to satirize modern organizational structures.

Through Grogatch’s frustrating journey from one indifferent office to another, Vance critiques how large systems can dehumanize individuals, prioritize procedure over common sense, and make genuine problem-solving almost impossible. The story is often cited as a sharp, humorous commentary on bureaucracy, similar in spirit to works like Kafka’s “The Trial” or some of the more satirical episodes of classic science fiction.

title: Emotion recognition in conversation
human_text: Emotion recognition in conversation (ERC, emotion recognition in dialogues) is a sub-field of emotion recognition, that focuses on mining human emotions from conversations or dialogues having two or more interlocutors. The datasets in this field are usually derived from social platforms that allow free and plenty of samples, often containing multimodal data (i.e., some combination of textual, visual, and acoustic data). Self- and inter-personal influences play critical role in identifying some basic emotions, such as, fear, anger, joy, surprise, etc. The more fine grained the emotion labels are the harder it is to detect the correct emotion. ERC poses a number of challenges, such as, conversational-context modeling, speaker-state modeling, presence of sarcasm in conversation, emotion shift across consecutive utterances of the same interlocutor.
gpt_text:
Emotion recognition in conversation is the task of automatically identifying and tracking people’s emotional states as they unfold during a dialogue. Instead of judging each utterance in isolation, it considers context—what has been said before, who is speaking to whom, and how emotions evolve over multiple turns. Emotions might be labeled with categories (such as joy, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, neutrality) or with continuous values (such as levels of valence and arousal).

This field combines natural language processing, speech and audio analysis, and sometimes visual cues (like facial expressions) to understand human affect in a more realistic, interactive setting. It is used in applications such as empathetic chatbots, mental health support tools, call-center analysis, and social robots, where recognizing subtle emotional shifts is crucial for appropriate and sensitive responses.

title: Artificial intelligence of things

Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) is the combination of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies with the Internet of Things (IoT). In AIoT systems, connected devices—such as sensors, cameras, appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines—collect data, while AI algorithms analyze that data to enable smarter, more autonomous decision-making at the edge or in the cloud.

This integration turns simple connected devices into intelligent systems that can learn, adapt, and act with minimal human intervention. Applications range from smart homes that optimize energy use, to predictive maintenance in factories, autonomous vehicles, personalized healthcare monitoring, and smart cities that manage traffic and resources more efficiently.

title: Regulation of artificial intelligence
human_text: The regulation of artificial intelligence is the development of public sector policies and laws for promoting and regulating artificial intelligence (AI); it is therefore related to the broader regulation of algorithms. The regulatory and policy landscape for AI is an emerging issue in jurisdictions globally, including in the European Union. Regulation is considered necessary to both encourage AI and manage associated risks. Regulation of AI through mechanisms such as review boards can also be seen as social means to approach the AI control problem.
gpt_text:
Regulation of artificial intelligence refers to the laws, policies, and standards designed to guide how AI systems are developed, deployed, and used. It aims to manage risks such as bias, privacy violations, lack of transparency, job displacement, safety failures, and misuse (for example, in surveillance or autonomous weapons), while still enabling innovation and economic benefits. Regulation can cover issues like data protection, accountability for AI-driven decisions, audit and oversight requirements, and limits on certain high‑risk applications.

Approaches to AI regulation vary across regions. The European Union’s AI Act, for instance, classifies AI systems by risk level and imposes stricter rules on high-risk uses, while the U.S. has a more sector-specific and guidance-oriented approach. International organizations and standards bodies are also working on frameworks for trustworthy and ethical AI, focusing on principles such as transparency, fairness, human oversight, and safety.

title: Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations

title: Character computing
human_text: Character computing is a trans-disciplinary field of research at the intersection of computer science and psychology. It is any computing that incorporates the human character within its context. Character is defined as all features or characteristics defining an individual and guiding their behavior in a specific situation. It consists of stable trait markers (e.g., personality, background, history, socio-economic embeddings, culture,..) and variable state markers (emotions, health, cognitive state,..). Character computing aims at providing a holistic psychologically-driven model of human behavior. It models and predicts behavior based on the relationships between a situation and character. Three main research modules fall under the umbrella of character computing: character sensing and profiling, character-aware adaptive systems, and artificial characters.

Character computing is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on measuring, modeling, and using human character traits—such as honesty, perseverance, empathy, and responsibility—within computational systems. It draws from psychology, ethics, artificial intelligence, and human–computer interaction to understand how these relatively stable moral and personality qualities can be inferred from data (e.g., behavior, language, or choices) and then used to guide or adapt digital technologies.

Applications of character computing include personalized learning systems that foster grit and curiosity, digital wellbeing tools that encourage self-control or compassion, and AI agents that can recognize and respond to users’ virtues and vices in ethical ways. A central concern in this field is ensuring that any assessment or use of character is scientifically valid, transparent, respectful of autonomy, and aligned with robust ethical and societal standards.

title: Software metric

title: Code smell

Common examples include overly long methods, duplicated code, large classes that try to do too much, and excessive dependencies between components. title: Reusability

title: Software Engineering 2004

title: Software engineering demographics

title: Big ball of mud
human_text: A big ball of mud is a software system that lacks a perceivable architecture. Although undesirable from a software engineering point of view, such systems are common in practice due to business pressures, developer turnover and code entropy. They are a type of design anti-pattern.

title: Round-trip engineering
human_text: Round-trip engineering (RTE) is a functionality of software development tools that synchronizes two or more related software artifacts, such as, source code, models, configuration files, and even documentation. The need for round-trip engineering arises when the same information is present in multiple artifacts and therefore an inconsistency may occur if not all artifacts are consistently updated to reflect a given change. For example, some piece of information was added to/changed in only one artifact and, as a result, it became missing in/inconsistent with the other artifacts.
gpt_text:

This approach supports iterative development, refactoring, and documentation by ensuring that the architecture and diagrams do not drift out of date as the code evolves. Tools that support round-trip engineering help reduce manual effort, lower the risk of inconsistencies, and make it easier for teams to work at both a high-level design view and a low-level implementation view of the same system.

title: Dependency hell

title: Write once, compile anywhere
human_text: Write once, compile anywhere (WOCA) is a philosophy taken by a compiler and its associated software libraries or by a software library/software framework which refers to a capability of writing a computer program that can be compiled on all platforms without the need to modify its source code. As opposed to Sun's write once, run anywhere slogan, cross-platform compatibility is implemented only at the source code level, rather than also at the compiled binary code level.

title: Cost estimation in software engineering

title: Overhead (computing)

title: Code bloat

title: Heisenbug

title: Experimental software engineering

title: Software system safety
human_text: In software engineering, software system safety optimizes system safety in the design, development, use, and maintenance of software systems and their integration with safety-critical hardware systems in an operational environment.

title: Reference model

This frame of reference can then be used to communicate ideas clearly among members of the same community.

title: Leaning toothpick syndrome

title: Analysis effort method

title: Coding conventions

Software programmers are highly recommended to follow these guidelines to help improve the readability of their source code and make software maintenance easier. Coding conventions are only applicable to the human maintainers and peer reviewers of a software project. title: Putnam model

title: Software sizing

title: Rule of three (C++ programming)

Implementing only one or two of these functions often leads to shallow copies, double frees, or resource leaks.

The Rule of Three encourages consistent and correct handling of resources during object lifetime and copying. In modern C++ (C++11 and later), this idea extends to the *Rule of Five* (adding move constructor and move assignment operator) and often to the *Rule of Zero*, which suggests designing classes so the compiler-generated special member functions are sufficient, usually by delegating resource management to standard library types (such as `std::vector` or `std::unique_ptr`).

title: Presentation logic

title: Fail-stop
