title: SQALE
human_text: SQALE (Software Quality Assessment based on Lifecycle Expectations) is a method to support the evaluation of a software application source code. It is a generic method, independent of the language and source code analysis tools, licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0 Unported license. Software editors can freely use and implement the SQALE method.
gpt_text:
SQALE (Software Quality Assessment based on Lifecycle Expectations) is a method and model used to assess and manage technical debt in software systems. It provides a structured way to measure code quality by defining rules, assigning remediation costs, and aggregating these into indicators that show how much effort would be needed to bring the codebase up to a desired quality level.

Often implemented in tools like SonarQube, SQALE organizes issues into characteristics (such as reliability, maintainability, testability) and calculates a “technical debt ratio” or similar metrics. This helps teams prioritize refactoring and quality improvements based on quantified, comparable values rather than subjective judgment.

title: Service virtualization
human_text: In software engineering, service virtualization or service virtualisation is a method to emulate the behavior of specific components in heterogeneous component-based applications such as API-driven applications, cloud-based applications and service-oriented architectures.
gpt_text:
Service virtualization is a technique used in software development and testing to simulate the behavior of dependent systems or services that are unavailable, expensive, slow, or difficult to access. Instead of relying on real external APIs, databases, mainframes, or third-party services, teams create virtual services that mimic their responses and behavior based on predefined scenarios and data.

This allows developers and testers to work in parallel, run automated tests consistently, and avoid bottlenecks caused by dependencies that are incomplete or unstable. By isolating the system under test from real external constraints, service virtualization improves test coverage, speeds up delivery cycles, and reduces environment-related issues.

title: Use case points
human_text: Use case points (UCP or UCPs) is a software estimation technique used to forecast the software size for software development projects. UCP is used when the Unified Modeling Language (UML) and Rational Unified Process (RUP) methodologies are being used for the software design and development. The concept of UCP is based on the requirements for the system being written using use cases, which is part of the UML set of modeling techniques. The software size (UCP) is calculated based on elements of the system use cases with factoring to account for technical and environmental considerations. The UCP for a project can then be used to calculate the estimated effort for a project.
gpt_text:
Use Case Points (UCP) is a software estimation technique used to predict the effort, time, and cost required to develop a system based on its use cases. It evaluates the complexity of actors (users or external systems) and use cases, then adjusts this with technical and environmental factors (such as performance requirements, team experience, tools, and constraints) to produce an overall size measure.

The UCP method is especially useful early in a project, when detailed design is not yet available but use case models are. By providing a structured, relatively objective way to convert functional requirements (use cases) into estimated person-hours or cost, it helps project managers in planning, budgeting, and comparing alternative solutions.

title: Runtime error detection
human_text: Runtime error detection is a software verification method that analyzes a software application as it executes and reports defects that are detected during that execution. It can be applied during unit testing, component testing, integration testing, system testing (automated/scripted or manual), or penetration testing.
gpt_text:
Runtime error detection is the process of identifying bugs and incorrect behavior while a program is running, rather than at compile time. It focuses on problems that only appear with actual data and execution paths, such as null pointer dereferences, out-of-bounds array access, memory leaks, race conditions, and division by zero. Because these errors depend on runtime state, they often escape static analysis and unit tests that don’t cover all scenarios.

Tools and techniques for runtime error detection include dynamic analyzers (like AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, ThreadSanitizer), runtime assertions, exception handling, and built-in runtime checks in languages or frameworks. These mechanisms monitor the program as it executes, detect abnormal or unsafe behavior, and typically log detailed diagnostic information or halt execution to prevent data corruption or security vulnerabilities.

title: Headless software
human_text: Headless software (e.g. "headless Java"Clarification of "headless mode" for Java case or "headless Linux",Clarification of "headless Linux") is software capable of working on a device without a graphical user interface. Such software receives inputs and provides output through other interfaces like network or serial port and is common on servers and embedded devices.
gpt_text:
Headless software is software that runs without a graphical user interface (GUI). Instead of displaying windows, buttons, or visual controls, it operates in the background and is controlled via code, command-line tools, APIs, or configuration files. This makes it ideal for servers, automation, testing, and environments where no screen or user interaction is required.

In web development, “headless” often refers to separating the backend (data and logic) from the frontend (user interface). For example, a headless CMS exposes content via APIs so any frontend—web, mobile, or other devices—can consume it, allowing more flexibility and reuse than traditional, tightly coupled systems.

title: Software map
human_text: A software map represents static, dynamic, and evolutionary information of software systems and their software development processes by means of 2D or 3D map-oriented information visualization. It constitutes a fundamental concept and tool in software visualization, software analytics, and software diagnosis. Its primary applications include risk analysis for and monitoring of code quality, team activity, or software development progress and, generally, improving effectiveness of software engineering with respect to all related artifacts, processes, and stakeholders throughout the software engineering process and software maintenance.
gpt_text:
A software map is a visual representation that shows the structure, components, and relationships within a software system. It can depict modules, services, libraries, data flows, or dependencies, helping people see how parts of the system fit together and interact. Like a geographical map for code, it provides a high-level overview that’s easier to grasp than reading source files or raw documentation alone.

Teams use software maps for understanding legacy systems, planning refactors, onboarding new developers, and identifying complexity or risk hotspots. Depending on the focus, a software map might highlight architecture layers, service boundaries in a microservices setup, dependency graphs between components, or runtime interactions between systems.

title: Software diagnosis
human_text: Software diagnosis (also: software diagnostics) refers to concepts, techniques, and tools that allow for obtaining findings, conclusions, and evaluations about software systems and their implementation, composition, behavior, and evolution. It serves as means to monitor, steer, observe and optimize software development, software maintenance, and software re-engineering in the sense of a business intelligence approach specific to software systems. It is generally based on the automatic extraction, analysis, and visualization of corresponding information sources of the software system. It can also be manually done and not automatic.
gpt_text:
Software diagnosis is the process of detecting, analyzing, and understanding faults, failures, or performance issues within a software system. It involves collecting data (such as logs, traces, metrics, and error reports), identifying symptoms (like crashes, slow responses, or incorrect outputs), and tracing them back to their root causes in the code, configuration, environment, or interactions with other components.

Effective software diagnosis uses techniques such as logging and monitoring, debugging tools, automated testing, anomaly detection, and sometimes AI-based analysis to pinpoint problems quickly and accurately. Its main goal is to reduce downtime, improve reliability and performance, and support maintenance and evolution of the software over time.

title: User onboarding
human_text: User onboarding is the process of improving a person's success with a product or service. This term is often used in reference to software products, and it can be done in a manual or automated way. It is the process through which new software is designed such that new users are provided and acquire the necessary knowledge, skills, and behaviors in order to become “up and running” and effective users of website, app, or software service.
gpt_text:
User onboarding is the process of guiding new users to understand, experience, and receive value from a product or service as quickly and smoothly as possible. It typically includes first-time setup, introductory walkthroughs, helpful prompts or tooltips, and early “wins” that show users the core benefits of the product.  

Effective user onboarding reduces friction and confusion, increases activation and engagement, and helps turn new users into long-term, successful customers. It focuses on what users are trying to achieve, not just on showing features, and often continues beyond the first session through emails, in-app messages, and ongoing education.

title: Design smell
human_text: In computer programming, design smells are "structures in the design that indicate violation of fundamental design principles and negatively impact design quality".Girish Suryanarayana, Ganesh SG, Tushar Sharma (2014). "Refactoring for software design smells: Managing technical debt". Morgan Kaufmann. The origin of the term "design smell" can be traced to the term "code smell" which was featured in the book Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code by Martin Fowler.Fowler, Martin (1999). Refactoring. Improving the Design of Existing Code. Addison-Wesley.
gpt_text:
A design smell is a symptom in the structure of a software system that suggests a potential problem in its design, even if the code still works correctly. It usually signals deeper issues such as poor modularization, unclear responsibilities, tight coupling, or violations of key design principles like SOLID.  

Common examples include God classes (classes that do too much), feature envy (a class overly dependent on another’s data), and shotgun surgery (a change requiring many small edits across the system). While design smells are not bugs themselves, they tend to increase complexity, reduce maintainability, and make future changes more error-prone, so they are often targets for refactoring.

title: ABC Software Metric
human_text: The ABC software metric was introduced by Jerry Fitzpatrick in 1997 to overcome the drawbacks of the LOC.
gpt_text:
The ABC software metric (Assignment Branch Condition) is a code complexity measure that quantifies how much a piece of code “does” by counting three kinds of operations: assignments (A), branches or control flow changes (B), and conditions or logical decisions (C). Each of these is counted in the code, and the metric is then computed as the Euclidean length of the vector (A, B, C): √(A² + B² + C²).  

Unlike traditional metrics like lines of code or cyclomatic complexity, the ABC metric focuses directly on operational complexity, making it useful for assessing how difficult code may be to understand, test, and maintain. Lower ABC values generally correspond to simpler, more readable code.

title: CI/CD
human_text: In software engineering
gpt_text:
CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (or Continuous Deployment). It is a set of practices and tools in software development that automate the process of integrating code changes, testing them, and delivering them to production or staging environments. Continuous Integration focuses on frequently merging small code changes into a shared repository and automatically running tests to catch issues early.  

Continuous Delivery/Deployment extends this by automating the packaging, testing, and release process so that software can be reliably and quickly released at any time. The goal of CI/CD is to reduce integration problems, improve software quality, and increase the speed and reliability of releases.

title: Protocol engineering
human_text: Protocol engineering is the application of systematic methods to the development of communication protocols. It uses many of the principles of software engineering, but it is specific to the development of distributed systems.
gpt_text:
Protocol engineering is the systematic design, specification, implementation, and analysis of communication protocols—rules that govern how data is formatted, transmitted, and interpreted between systems. It covers every layer where structured communication occurs, from low‑level network protocols (like TCP/IP) to application‑level protocols (like HTTP, MQTT, or custom APIs).  

This discipline involves defining message formats, state machines, error handling, timing constraints, security properties, and interoperability requirements, often using formal methods and modeling tools. Protocol engineers focus on reliability, scalability, performance, and security, ensuring that independently developed systems can communicate correctly and efficiently under a wide range of conditions.

title: Software diversity
human_text: Software diversity is a research field about the comprehension and engineering of diversity in the context of software.
gpt_text:
Software diversity is the practice of creating and deploying multiple, functionally equivalent but internally different versions of software components or systems. These differences can be in implementation details, code structure, algorithms, compilation options, or runtime configurations. The goal is to reduce the risk that a single vulnerability, bug, or attack will affect all instances in the same way.

It is often used as a security and reliability strategy: by making systems less uniform, attacks such as malware, exploits, or fault conditions are less likely to succeed consistently across all targets. Techniques include N-version programming, address space layout randomization (ASLR), diversification of binaries, and varying configurations or libraries. This heterogeneity complicates large-scale exploitation and can improve resilience against zero-day vulnerabilities and systemic failures.

title: Software bot
human_text: A software bot is a type of software agent in the service of software project management and software engineering. A software bot has an identity and potentially personified aspects in order to serve their stakeholders
gpt_text:
A software bot is an automated program designed to perform tasks on behalf of a user or system, often repeatedly and at high speed. Bots can operate in many environments—websites, messaging platforms, operating systems, or enterprise applications—and are usually triggered by specific events, schedules, or commands.

They are used for a wide range of purposes, such as customer support (chatbots), system monitoring, data collection and processing, or automating routine workflows (like deploying code or handling tickets). While many bots increase efficiency and reduce manual effort, some can be malicious (e.g., spam bots or bots used in cyberattacks), so systems often include safeguards to detect and manage them.

title: Test design technique
human_text: In software engineering, test design technique is a procedure for determining test conditions, test cases and test data during software testing.
gpt_text:
A test design technique is a systematic method used to identify and create effective test cases from requirements, specifications, or models of a system. Its goal is to ensure that important aspects of the software—such as functionality, workflows, data handling, and edge cases—are tested in a structured and efficient way, rather than relying on ad hoc or random testing.

Common categories of test design techniques include black-box techniques (like equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and decision tables), white-box techniques (such as statement and branch coverage), and experience-based techniques (like exploratory testing and error guessing). Choosing appropriate techniques helps optimize coverage, reduce redundancy, and improve the overall quality and reliability of the software under test.

title: Draft:Software Engineering Education
human_text: Software Engineering Education, in a few obvious words, is the methods and processes of teaching and learning Software Engineering, which may be understood as the study of methods, processes, frameworks and approaches applied to the design, development, operation, and maintenance of software.
gpt_text:
Software engineering education focuses on teaching the principles, methods, and tools needed to design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain software systems in a systematic and reliable way. It combines computer science fundamentals—such as algorithms, data structures, and operating systems—with engineering practices like requirements analysis, architecture, project management, quality assurance, and documentation.

Programs in this field often emphasize both technical proficiency and professional skills, including teamwork, communication, ethics, and lifelong learning. Students typically gain experience through hands-on projects, collaboration using modern development workflows (e.g., version control, continuous integration), and exposure to real-world constraints like scalability, security, and maintainability.

title: ClearType
human_text: ClearType is Microsoft's implementation of subpixel rendering technology in rendering text in a font system. ClearType attempts to improve the appearance of text on certain types of computer display screens by sacrificing color fidelity for additional intensity variation. This trade-off is asserted to work well on LCD flat panel monitors.
gpt_text:
ClearType is a subpixel rendering technology developed by Microsoft to make text on LCD screens (like those in laptops, flat-panel monitors, and some handheld devices) appear smoother and more readable. It takes advantage of the way individual red, green, and blue subpixels are arranged in an LCD pixel, adjusting how text is drawn so that diagonal and curved edges look sharper and less jagged at typical reading sizes.  

Introduced in the early 2000s and integrated into Windows and many Microsoft applications, ClearType significantly improves on traditional anti-aliasing for small fonts, especially on screens with standard resolutions. It is most effective on LCD displays with the expected subpixel layout; on other screen types or unusual subpixel arrangements, the benefits can be reduced or even introduce slight color fringing.

title: Key frame
human_text: A key frame (or keyframe) in animation and filmmaking is a drawing or shot that defines the starting and ending points of any smooth transition. These are called frames because their position in time is measured in frames on a strip of film or on a digital video editing timeline. A sequence of key frames defines which movement the viewer will see, whereas the position of the key frames on the film, video, or animation defines the timing of the movement. Because only two or three key frames over the span of a second do not create the illusion of movement, the remaining frames are filled with "inbetweens".
gpt_text:
A key frame is a specific frame in an animation or video sequence that marks an important point of change, such as a new position, shape, or state of an object. Instead of defining every single frame, animators set key frames at significant moments, and the software (or in traditional animation, in-between artists) fills in the intermediate frames to create smooth motion.

In digital animation, key frames are used to control properties like position, rotation, scale, color, or camera angle over time. By adjusting these key frames on a timeline, creators can precisely choreograph movement and transitions without manually editing each individual frame.

title: Bresenham's line algorithm
human_text: Bresenham's line algorithm is a line drawing algorithm that determines the points of an n-dimensional raster that should be selected in order to form a close approximation to a straight line between two points. It is commonly used to draw line primitives in a bitmap image (e.g. on a computer screen), as it uses only integer addition, subtraction and bit shifting, all of which are very cheap operations in standard computer architectures. It is an incremental error algorithm. It is one of the earliest algorithms developed in the field of computer graphics. An extension to the original algorithm may be used for drawing circles.
gpt_text:
Bresenham's line algorithm is an efficient method for drawing a straight line between two points on a pixel-based display using only integer arithmetic. Instead of computing floating-point slopes, it incrementally decides which pixel is closest to the ideal mathematical line at each step, updating an error term to choose between two candidate pixels (e.g., moving horizontally vs. diagonally).  

Developed by Jack Bresenham at IBM in the 1960s, the algorithm is foundational in computer graphics and is valued for its speed and simplicity, especially on hardware with limited computational power. It produces visually appealing lines with good continuity and is easily adapted for drawing other rasterized shapes such as circles and polygons.

title: Planar (computer graphics)
human_text: In computer graphics, planar is the method of arranging pixel data into several bitplanes of RAM. Each bit in a bitplane is related to one pixel on the screen. Unlike packed, high color, or true color graphics, the whole dataset for an individual pixel isn't in one specific location in RAM, but spread across the bitplanes that make up the display. Planar arrangement determines how pixel data is laid out it memory, not how the data for a pixel is interpreted; pixel data in a planar arrangement could encode either indexed or direct color.
gpt_text:
In computer graphics, “planar” typically refers to a way of organizing and storing image data where the color components (for example, red, green, and blue) are kept in separate memory planes rather than interleaved together. In a planar format, all the red values for every pixel are stored in one continuous block of memory, all the green values in another, and all the blue values in a third, and so on. This contrasts with “packed” (or “chunky”) formats, where each pixel’s full color information is stored together (e.g., RGB or RGBA per pixel).

Planar representations were common in older graphics hardware and some video formats because they can be efficient for certain operations (like manipulating a single color channel or compressing video). They are still used today in many image and video codecs (such as YUV planar formats) because separating channels can simplify processing and improve compression efficiency.

title: Bit blit
human_text: Bit blit (also written BITBLT, BIT BLT, BitBLT, Bit BLT, Bit Blt etc., which stands for bit block transfer) is a data operation commonly used in computer graphics in which several bitmaps are combined into one using a boolean function.
gpt_text:
Bit blit (short for “bit-block transfer”) is a computer graphics operation that copies a block of pixels (bits) from one area of memory to another, often with optional transformations. It was historically central to 2D graphics systems, where moving, masking, or combining images (such as sprites, windows, or icons) efficiently was crucial for performance.

Beyond simple copying, bit blit operations can apply logical operations (like AND, OR, XOR), transparency (using masks), and sometimes scaling or rotation during the transfer. Early graphical user interfaces and games relied heavily on bit blitting for drawing and animation before modern GPUs and compositing window systems became standard.

title: Phong reflection model
human_text: The Phong reflection model (also called Phong illumination or Phong lighting) is an empirical model of the local illumination of points on a surface designed by the computer graphics researcher Bui Tuong Phong. In 3D computer graphics, it is sometimes referred to as "Phong shading", particularly if the model is used with the interpolation method of the same name and in the context of pixel shaders or other places where a lighting calculation can be referred to as “shading”.
gpt_text:
The Phong reflection model is a local illumination model in computer graphics used to approximate how light reflects off a surface. It breaks reflected light into three components: ambient (constant background light), diffuse (matte reflection that depends on the angle between the light and the surface normal), and specular (shiny highlights that depend on the viewer’s position). Each component is scaled by material properties and combined to produce the final color at a point on a surface.

The model’s specular term uses the cosine of the angle between the viewer direction and the ideal reflection direction, raised to a shininess exponent. Higher exponents produce tighter, sharper highlights, mimicking glossier surfaces; lower exponents create broader, duller highlights. While not physically accurate, the Phong model is simple, efficient, and has been widely used in real-time rendering and classic 3D graphics pipelines.

title: Collision detection
human_text: Collision detection is the computational problem of detecting the intersection of two or more objects. Collision detection is a classic issue of computational geometry and has applications in various computing fields, primarily in computer graphics, computer games, computer simulations, robotics and computational physics. Collision detection algorithms can be divided into operating on 2D and 3D objects.
gpt_text:
Collision detection is the computational process of determining when two or more objects in a virtual space intersect, touch, or come sufficiently close to be considered in contact. It is a core component of computer graphics, games, simulations, and robotics, where systems must react realistically when objects bump, overlap, or avoid each other. 

Because checking every object against every other can be expensive, collision detection typically uses optimization techniques such as bounding volumes (spheres, boxes), spatial partitioning (grids, trees like quadtrees or octrees), and multi-phase checks (broad phase to quickly rule out most pairs, then narrow phase for precise tests). Once a collision is detected, a separate process—collision response—handles the physical or logical outcome, such as bouncing, stopping, damage, or triggering events.

title: Color management
human_text: In digital imaging systems, color management (or colour management) is the controlled conversion between the color representations of various devices, such as image scanners, digital cameras, monitors, TV screens, film printers, computer printers, offset presses, and corresponding media.
gpt_text:
Color management is the controlled process of ensuring that colors look as consistent and accurate as possible across different devices and media—such as cameras, monitors, printers, and mobile screens. Because each device reproduces color differently, color management uses standardized profiles and conversions so that a specific color value (like an RGB or CMYK value) appears as intended wherever it is displayed or printed.

This system typically relies on ICC profiles (device-specific descriptions of color behavior) and a color management module (software that translates colors between devices using a reference color space). Effective color management is crucial in photography, graphic design, printing, film, and any workflow where predictable, repeatable color is important.

title: Blitter object
human_text: A Bob (contraction of Blitter object) is a graphical element (GEL) used by the Amiga computer. Bobs are hardware sprite-like objects, movable on the screen with the help of the blitter coprocessor.
gpt_text:
A blitter object is a specialized hardware or software component used for rapidly moving and manipulating blocks of data—typically graphics pixels—in memory. The term comes from "bit-block transfer" (bit blit), and blitter objects are often used in 2D graphics systems to copy, scroll, or animate images on the screen without involving the main CPU for every pixel operation.

In many classic graphics architectures (such as the Amiga or early game consoles), a blitter could perform operations like copying, masking, filling, and combining images (sprites, tiles, backgrounds) directly in video memory. Modern systems generalize this concept into GPU-accelerated textures, sprites, and compositing operations, but the idea remains the same: a blitter object is an efficient engine for bulk pixel or bitmap manipulation.

title: Graphics
human_text: Graphics (from Greek graphikos, "belonging to drawing") are visual images or designs on some surface, such as a wall, canvas, screen, paper, or stone to inform, illustrate, or entertain. In contemporary usage, it includes a pictorial representation of data, as in c manufacture, in typesetting and the graphic arts, and in educational and recreational software. Images that are generated by a computer are called computer graphics.
gpt_text:
Graphics refers to visual elements created, manipulated, or displayed on a surface—such as a screen, paper, or billboard—to convey information, illustrate ideas, or provide aesthetic appeal. This includes images, drawings, diagrams, icons, typography, and complex visual scenes, whether produced by hand or generated digitally.

In computing, graphics specifically involves the use of hardware and software to render visual content, ranging from simple 2D interfaces and charts to detailed 3D models and animations in games, simulations, and design tools. Fields like graphic design, computer graphics, and data visualization all center on using graphics effectively to communicate and enhance user experience.

title: Color histogram
human_text: In image processing and photography, a color histogram is a representation of the distribution of colors in an image. For digital images, a color histogram represents the number of pixels that have colors in each of a fixed list of color ranges, that span the image's color space, the set of all possible colors.
gpt_text:
A color histogram is a graphical representation of the distribution of colors in an image. It counts how many pixels fall into each color value or color range (bin), typically in a specific color space such as RGB, HSV, or Lab, and then plots these counts as a histogram. Each channel (for example, red, green, and blue) can have its own histogram, or they can be combined into a single multidimensional representation.

Color histograms are widely used in computer vision and image processing for tasks like image retrieval, object recognition, and scene analysis. Because they summarize color content regardless of spatial arrangement, they are robust to translation and rotation, but they do not capture where colors appear in the image—only how frequently they occur.

title: Color image
human_text: A (digital) color image is a digital image that includes color information for each pixel.
gpt_text:
A color image is a digital or photographic picture that represents visual information using multiple color channels, typically red, green, and blue (RGB). Each pixel in the image stores intensity values for these channels, which combine to produce the full range of colors perceived by the human eye. This allows color images to capture and display realistic scenes with variations in hue, saturation, and brightness.

Color images are used in photography, television, computer graphics, printing, and virtually all modern visual media. They can be stored and transmitted in various formats (such as JPEG, PNG, or TIFF) and color spaces (like RGB for screens or CMYK for printing), each optimized for specific devices and applications.

title: Scanimate
human_text: Scanimate is an analog computer animation (video synthesizer) system developed from the late 1960s to the 1980s by Computer Image Corporation of Denver, Colorado.
gpt_text:
Scanimate was an early analog video animation system developed in the late 1960s and widely used through the 1970s and early 1980s for creating television graphics, logos, and motion effects. Instead of using digital computers, it relied on analog circuitry and oscilloscopes to manipulate and distort images in real time, allowing artists to “perform” animations live by adjusting knobs and controls.

Because of its fluid, organic motion and distinctive glowing, stretchy look, Scanimate became iconic in broadcast design, especially in TV idents, promos, and title sequences. Many classic retro graphics—flying logos, bending text, and swirling shapes seen in vintage TV—were created with Scanimate before digital animation and computer graphics fully replaced analog systems.

title: Verse protocol
human_text: Verse is a networking protocol allowing real-time communication between computer graphics software. For example, several architects can build a house in the same virtual environment using their own computers, even if they are using different software. If one architect builds a spiral staircase, it instantly appears on the screens of all other users. Verse is designed to use the capacity of one or multiple computers over the Internet: for example, allowing a user with a hand-held computer in Spain to work with the rendering power of a supercomputer in Japan. Its principles are very general, allowing its use in contexts that are advantageous to collaboration such as gaming and visual presentations.
gpt_text:
Verse Protocol is a blockchain-based infrastructure and incentive system designed to support the Bitcoin.com ecosystem and its DeFi products. It centers around the VERSE token, which is used for rewards, liquidity provision, and ecosystem incentives such as cashback, yield farming, and participation in various DeFi services.

Built to be interoperable with multiple chains (notably Ethereum-compatible networks), Verse Protocol aims to make onboarding into crypto and decentralized finance easier for mainstream users. It integrates tightly with Bitcoin.com’s wallet and services to encourage usage, trading, and holding within a unified ecosystem.

title: New York Institute of Technology Computer Graphics Lab
human_text: The Computer Graphics Lab was a computer lab located at the New York Institute of Technology (NYIT) in the late 1970s and 1980s, founded by Dr. Alexander Schure. It was originally located at the "pink building" on the NYIT campus.
gpt_text:
The New York Institute of Technology (NYIT) Computer Graphics Lab was a pioneering research group active mainly in the 1970s and early 1980s, widely regarded as one of the birthplaces of modern computer graphics and animation. Led by Alexander Schure and employing early graphics visionaries such as Edwin Catmull and Alvy Ray Smith, the lab developed groundbreaking techniques in 3D modeling, rendering, animation, and image processing at a time when computer graphics was still a niche experimental field.

Work done at NYIT’s Computer Graphics Lab directly influenced the technologies and methods later used at Lucasfilm’s Computer Division and, ultimately, Pixar. Many foundational concepts in computer animation—such as texture mapping, anti-aliased rendering, and advanced animation tools—were explored or refined there, making the lab an important historical link between early academic research and today’s feature-film computer animation industry.

gpt_text:
A transformation matrix is a mathematical tool, usually represented as a rectangular array of numbers, used to perform linear transformations on vectors and geometric objects. In fields like computer graphics, robotics, and physics, it is used to apply operations such as rotation, scaling, reflection, and translation (the latter via homogeneous coordinates) in a systematic and compact way.

When a vector is multiplied by a transformation matrix, the result is a new vector that has been transformed according to the matrix’s properties. For example, a 2×2 or 3×3 matrix can rotate or scale points in 2D or 3D space, while 3×3 or 4×4 homogeneous matrices can also handle translations and combinations of multiple transformations through matrix multiplication.

title: Texture filtering
human_text: In computer graphics, texture filtering or texture smoothing is the method used to determine the texture color for a texture mapped pixel, using the colors of nearby texels (pixels of the texture). There are two main categories of texture filtering, magnification filtering and minification filtering. Depending on the situation texture filtering is either a type of reconstruction filter where sparse data is interpolated to fill gaps (magnification), or a type of anti-aliasing (AA), where texture samples exist at a higher frequency than required for the sample frequency needed for texture fill (minification). Put simply, filtering describes how a texture is applied at many different shapes, size, angles and scales. Depending on the chosen filter algorithm the result will show varying degrees of blurriness, detail, spatial aliasing, temporal aliasing and blocking. Depending on the circumstances filtering can be performed in software (such as a software rendering package) or in hardware for real time or GPU accelerated rendering or in a mixture of both. For most common interactive graphical applications modern texture filtering is performed by dedicated hardware which optimizes memory access through memory cacheing and pre-fetch and implements a selection of algorithms available to the user and developer.
gpt_text:
Texture filtering is a computer graphics technique used to determine how a texture (an image applied to a 3D surface) is sampled and displayed when its size on screen doesn’t match its original resolution. When a textured object is far away, very close, or viewed at an angle, the graphics hardware must decide how to combine or interpolate texel (texture pixel) values to avoid visual artifacts like blockiness (aliasing) or shimmering.

Common texture filtering methods include nearest-neighbor (choosing the closest texel, fast but blocky), bilinear (smoothly interpolating between nearby texels), trilinear (also blending between mipmap levels to reduce popping), and anisotropic filtering (improving clarity at oblique viewing angles). Higher-quality filters reduce artifacts and improve visual sharpness at the cost of more computation.

title: Bitmap textures
human_text: Bitmap textures are digital images representing a surface, a material, a pattern or even a picture, generated by an artist or designer using a bitmap editor software such as Adobe Photoshop or Gimp or simply by scanning an image and, if necessary, retouching it on a personal computer.
gpt_text:
Bitmap textures are image-based textures used in computer graphics, made up of a grid of pixels (a bitmap) that store explicit color information for each point. Common bitmap formats include PNG, JPEG, BMP, and TGA. These images are mapped onto 3D models or 2D surfaces to provide detailed visual appearance such as colors, patterns, and surface details that would be expensive or complex to generate procedurally.

Because they store fixed-resolution pixel data, bitmap textures can show high detail at their native size but may blur or pixelate when scaled too far. To handle this, graphics pipelines use techniques like mipmapping, filtering, and texture compression. Bitmap textures are widely used in games, film, and real-time rendering for diffuse color maps, normal maps, specular maps, and many other material channels.

title: Himetric
human_text: Himetric is a metric measurement of length similar to twips, used in computing. It is one thousandth of a centimeter or one hundredth of a millimeter (i.e. 10µm or 10−5 m) and is independent of the display or screen resolution.
gpt_text:
Himetric is a logical measurement unit used in Windows and COM-based graphics and printing APIs to provide device-independent sizing. One Himetric unit is defined as 0.01 millimeters, so 100 Himetric units equal 1 millimeter and 2,540 Himetric units equal 1 inch. Because it is based on real-world physical dimensions rather than pixels, Himetric allows applications to maintain consistent object sizes across displays and printers with different resolutions (DPI).

In practice, Himetric units are often used when defining the size and position of controls, images, or drawing surfaces in technologies like OLE/ActiveX, where objects may be embedded and rendered on various devices. Converting between pixels and Himetric typically involves using the device’s DPI to ensure accurate scaling.

title: ROAM
human_text: Real-time optimally adapting mesh (ROAM), is a continuous level of detail algorithm that optimizes terrain meshes. On modern computers, sometimes it is more effective to send a small amount of unneeded polygons to the GPU, rather than burden the CPU with LOD (Level of Detail) calculations—making algorithms like geomipmapping more effective than ROAM. This technique is used by graphics programmers
gpt_text:
ROAM typically refers to a note-taking and knowledge management approach popularized by tools like Roam Research. It emphasizes non-linear, networked thinking, where ideas are captured as individual “nodes” (notes) that are heavily interlinked rather than organized in rigid folders. This creates a personal knowledge graph, making it easier to discover relationships between concepts over time.

In practice, ROAM-style systems rely on daily notes, backlinks (automatic links showing where a page is referenced), and tags to organically build a web of connected information. The goal is to mirror how the brain works—associatively—so that insights emerge from connections between notes rather than from strictly hierarchical organization.

title: Image resolution
human_text: Image resolution is the detail an image holds. The term applies to raster digital images, film images, and other types of images. Higher resolution means more image detail.
gpt_text:
Image resolution refers to the amount of detail an image holds, usually measured by the number of pixels it contains. In digital images, it’s often expressed as width × height in pixels (for example, 1920×1080), or as pixels per inch (PPI) when discussing display quality and sharpness.

In print, resolution is commonly measured in dots per inch (DPI), which indicates how many ink dots a printer can place in a linear inch. Higher resolution generally means a clearer, sharper image with smoother edges and more visible detail, while lower resolution can cause images to look blurry, pixelated, or blocky, especially when enlarged.

title: Film-out
human_text: Film-out is the process in the computer graphics, video production and filmmaking disciplines of transferring images or animation from videotape or digital files to a traditional film print. "Film-out" is a broad term that encompasses the conversion of frame rates, color correction, as well as the actual printing, also called scanning or recording.
gpt_text:
Film-out is the process of transferring digital video or digital intermediate files back onto motion picture film. It’s typically used when a project that was edited and finished digitally needs a film print for theatrical projection, archival preservation, or specific aesthetic qualities associated with film grain and color rendition.

In a film-out workflow, high-resolution digital frames are recorded onto film stock using specialized film recorders, with careful attention to color grading, exposure, and contrast so the film print closely matches the digital master. While digital projection has reduced the need for film-outs, the process remains important for long-term archival storage and for filmmakers seeking the distinctive look and texture of projected celluloid.

title: Physics engine
human_text: A physics engine is computer software that provides an approximate simulation of certain physical systems, such as rigid body dynamics (including collision detection), soft body dynamics, and fluid dynamics, of use in the domains of computer graphics, video games and film (CGI). Their main uses are in video games (typically as middleware), in which case the simulations are in real-time. The term is sometimes used more generally to describe any software system for simulating physical phenomena, such as high-performance scientific simulation.
gpt_text:
A physics engine is a software component that simulates physical laws—such as gravity, collisions, friction, and rigid body dynamics—to create realistic motion and interactions in virtual environments. It calculates how objects move and respond when forces are applied or when they collide, typically using numerical methods to approximate solutions to the equations of motion.

Physics engines are widely used in video games, simulations, animation, robotics, and virtual reality. They allow developers to specify properties like mass, shape, and material, then automatically handle the resulting behavior, so objects fall, bounce, roll, or break in ways that look and feel physically plausible without manually scripting every movement.

title: Texture artist
human_text: A texture artist is an individual who develops textures for digital media, usually for video games, movies, web sites and television shows. These textures can be in the form of 2D or (rarely) 3D art that may be overlaid onto a polygon mesh to create a realistic 3D model.
gpt_text:
A texture artist is a digital art specialist who creates the surface details that make 3D models look realistic or stylistically appropriate in games, films, animation, and visual effects. They paint or design textures—such as skin, fabric, metal, wood, dirt, or damage—and apply them to 3D objects so those objects have color, patterns, and material properties when rendered.  

Using tools like Substance Painter, Photoshop, and 3D software, texture artists work closely with modelers and lighting artists to ensure that materials respond correctly to light and support the project’s visual style, whether that’s photorealistic, stylized, or anything in between.

title: Raster bar
human_text: The raster bar (also referred to as rasterbar or copperbar) is an effect used in demos and older video games that displays animated bars of colour, usually horizontal, which additionally might extend into the border, a.k.a. the otherwise unalterable area (assuming no overscan) of the display. Raster bar-style effects were common on the Atari 2600 and Atari 8-bit family (because they could be easily displayed using the hardware of those systems) and then later in demos for the Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC.
gpt_text:
A raster bar is a horizontal band of color or pattern created by manipulating the video display’s raster beam as it scans across the screen, especially on older systems like the Commodore 64, Amiga, and early arcade machines. Programmers would change color registers or graphics settings at precise scanlines during the display’s refresh, producing eye-catching stripes that appeared to float, bend, or animate independently of the main image.

Raster bars became a hallmark of the demoscene and early game intros, serving as both a visual effect and a demonstration of tight hardware timing and low-level programming skill. Because they rely on syncing code to the screen’s refresh cycle, they’re closely tied to the limitations and behavior of CRT-based video hardware.

title: Procedural surface
human_text: In computer graphics, a procedural surface is a representation of a surface as a mathematical implicit equation, rather than an explicit representation.
gpt_text:
A procedural surface is a geometric surface defined by an algorithm or mathematical procedure rather than by explicitly storing all of its vertices and polygons. Instead of modeling every detail by hand, developers use rules, formulas, or noise functions to generate the surface on the fly, often based on parameters like time, position, or randomness.

This approach is heavily used in computer graphics, games, and simulation to create complex, detailed shapes—such as terrain, waves, or organic forms—while saving memory and enabling easy variation. By adjusting the underlying procedure, artists and engineers can quickly produce different versions of a surface without remodeling it from scratch.

title: Image markup
human_text: Image markup is markup language that attaches annotations to image files. It is a critical technology for many researchers and practitioners, especially in the field of medicine.
gpt_text:
Image markup is the process of adding structured information or annotations to an image to describe its content, structure, or meaning. This can include labels for objects, regions, or people in the image; bounding boxes or polygons outlining features; and metadata such as captions, tags, or descriptions. Image markup is often created manually by humans or semi-automatically with the help of computer vision tools.

It plays a crucial role in training and evaluating machine learning and computer vision systems, enabling tasks such as object detection, image classification, and segmentation. Beyond AI, image markup is also used in design review, medical imaging, education, and documentation to highlight key areas, provide explanations, and improve clarity and accessibility.

title: Cone tracing
human_text: Cone tracing and beam tracing are a derivative of the ray tracing algorithm that replaces rays, which have no thickness, with thick rays.
gpt_text:
Cone tracing is a rendering technique used in computer graphics to approximate how light interacts with surfaces in a scene, especially for effects like soft shadows, reflections, and global illumination. Instead of casting infinitely thin rays (as in traditional ray tracing), cone tracing casts wider, cone-shaped queries through space. As the cone travels, it gathers averaged information over an area rather than a single line, which can efficiently simulate blurry or low-frequency lighting effects.

This method is often combined with voxel representations of the scene (voxel cone tracing), where geometry and lighting are stored in a 3D grid. Cone tracing through this voxel grid allows for fast, approximate indirect lighting and ambient occlusion in real time, making it useful in games and interactive applications, albeit with some loss of fine detail compared to full ray tracing.

title: Space partitioning
human_text: In geometry, space partitioning is the process of dividing a space (usually a Euclidean space) into two or more disjoint subsets (see also partition of a set). In other words, space partitioning divides a space into non-overlapping regions. Any point in the space can then be identified to lie in exactly one of the regions.
gpt_text:
Space partitioning is the process of dividing a space (usually geometric or multidimensional) into smaller, non‑overlapping regions according to certain rules or structures. In computer science and computational geometry, it’s used to organize data points, objects, or volumes so they can be searched, queried, or processed more efficiently. Common examples include BSP trees, k-d trees, quadtrees, and octrees, which recursively split space into subregions.

This technique is fundamental in areas like computer graphics, collision detection, spatial databases, robotics, and game development. By structuring space hierarchically, algorithms can quickly eliminate large regions from consideration, reducing the amount of computation needed for tasks such as finding nearest neighbors, rendering only visible objects, or detecting intersections.

title: Display list
human_text: A display list (or display file) is a series of graphics commands that define an output image. The image is created (rendered) by executing the commands to combine various primitives. This activity is most often performed by specialized display or processing hardware partly or completely independent of the system's CPU for the purpose of freeing the CPU from the overhead of maintaining the display, and may provide output features or speed beyond the CPU's capability.
gpt_text:
A display list is a sequence of preprocessed graphics commands that a program stores and can replay efficiently to draw images or scenes. Instead of issuing individual drawing instructions to the graphics hardware each time, the program records them once in a display list, then executes the list as a single object, which can significantly improve performance and reduce CPU overhead.

Display lists were widely used in older graphics APIs like classic OpenGL and in early game consoles and GPUs. They can encapsulate geometry, transformations, and state changes, making it easier to reuse complex visual content (such as models or UI elements) without rebuilding all the draw calls each frame.

title: Texture synthesis
human_text: Texture synthesis is the process of algorithmically constructing a large digital image from a small digital sample image by taking advantage of its structural content. It is an object of research in computer graphics and is used in many fields, amongst others digital image editing, 3D computer graphics and post-production of films.
gpt_text:
Texture synthesis is the process of automatically generating new images that look like a given example texture, such as wood grain, fabric, stone, or grass. Instead of copying and pasting, the algorithm analyzes the visual patterns, colors, and structures in a small sample and then creates a larger or different-shaped image that appears statistically and visually similar, without obvious seams or repetitions.

It is widely used in computer graphics, gaming, and visual effects to create large, detailed surfaces from small input samples, saving memory and manual design effort. Methods include pixel-based approaches, patch-based copying, and more recent deep learning techniques that capture higher-level structure and style.

title: Joint constraints
human_text: Joint constraints are rotational constraints on the joints of an artificial system. They are used in an inverse kinematics chain, in fields including 3D animation or robotics. Joint constraints can be implemented in a number of ways, but the most common method is to limit rotation about the X, Y and Z axis independently. An elbow, for instance, could be represented by limiting rotation on Y and Z axis to 0 degrees, and constraining the X-axis rotation to 130 degrees.
gpt_text:
Joint constraints are rules or limits applied to how two or more bones, rigid bodies, or components can move relative to each other. They define allowable degrees of freedom—such as how much a joint can rotate, translate, or twist—and prevent unrealistic or unsafe motion, like a knee bending backward or a mechanical arm overextending.  

In fields like biomechanics, robotics, animation, and game physics, joint constraints are used to model real-world behavior: setting ranges of motion for human joints, limiting rotation in robotic arms, or keeping connected objects from penetrating each other. They help ensure stability, realism, and physical plausibility in both simulations and real mechanisms.

title: Steven Anson Coons
human_text: Steven Anson Coons (March 7, 1912 – August 1979) was an early pioneer in the field of computer graphical methods. He was a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the Mechanical Engineering Department. Steven Coons had a vision of interactive computer graphics as a design tool to aid the engineer.
gpt_text:
Steven Anson Coons (1912–1979) was an American engineer, mathematician, and computer graphics pioneer best known for his foundational work on mathematical surface representations used in computer-aided design (CAD). He developed the concept of the “Coons patch,” a method for defining smooth surfaces from boundary curves, which became a cornerstone in geometric modeling and influenced later spline and surface technologies.

Coons worked at MIT, where he contributed to early interactive computer graphics systems and helped shape the emerging field of CAD/CAM for engineering and industrial design. His insights into how computers could represent and manipulate complex shapes laid much of the groundwork for modern 3D modeling, automotive and aerospace surface design, and many contemporary graphics and design tools.

title: Common Image Generator Interface
human_text: The Common Image Generator Interface (CIGI), is an on-the-wire data protocol that allows communication between an Image Generator and its host simulation. The interface is designed to promote a standard way for a host device to communicate with an image generator (IG) within the industry.
gpt_text:
The Common Image Generator Interface (CIGI) is an open, standardized protocol designed to connect image generators (IGs) with host simulation systems, especially in military and aviation training environments. It defines how data such as viewpoint position, sensor settings, environmental conditions, and entity states is exchanged in real time so the IG can render consistent, synchronized visuals for simulators.

By providing a common message format and communication model, CIGI enables interoperability between different vendors’ simulators and image generation systems. This reduces integration effort, promotes reuse of components, and helps ensure that training systems can evolve or be upgraded without completely redesigning the visual subsystem.

title: Image-based modeling and rendering
human_text: In computer graphics and computer vision, image-based modeling and rendering (IBMR) methods rely on a set of two-dimensional images of a scene to generate a three-dimensional model and then render some novel views of this scene.
gpt_text:
Image-based modeling and rendering is a set of techniques in computer graphics that use real photographs or video frames, rather than purely geometric models, as the primary source for creating 3D scenes and generating new views. Instead of carefully modeling every object with polygons and textures, the system captures many images from different viewpoints and uses them to infer scene structure (modeling) and synthesize new images from novel viewpoints (rendering).

These methods often combine computer vision and graphics: algorithms estimate camera positions, depth, and sometimes full 3D geometry from the input images, then reproject and blend the captured pixels to render new perspectives. This approach can achieve highly realistic results because it directly leverages real-world imagery, and it is widely used in applications such as virtual tours, cultural heritage digitization, visual effects, and realistic telepresence.

title: Image tracing
human_text: In computer graphics, image tracing, raster-to-vector conversion or vectorization is the conversion of raster graphics into vector graphics.
gpt_text:
Image tracing is the process of converting a raster image (made of pixels, like a JPEG or PNG) into a vector graphic (made of paths, curves, and shapes). This is commonly done in design software such as Adobe Illustrator or Inkscape, where the software analyzes the image’s colors and edges and generates scalable vector paths that approximate the original artwork.

The main benefit of image tracing is scalability and editability: vector graphics can be resized to any dimension without losing quality and individual elements (shapes, lines, colors) can be easily modified. It’s widely used for turning logos, sketches, or simple graphics into clean, editable vector files suitable for print, web, and large-format outputs.

title: Simple interactive object extraction
human_text: Simple interactive object extraction (SIOX) is an algorithm for extracting foreground objects from color images and videos with very little user interaction. It has been implemented as "foreground selection" tool in the GIMP (since version 2.3.3), as part of the tracer tool in Inkscape (since 0.44pre3), and as function in ImageJ and Fiji (plug-in). Experimental implementations were also reported for Blender and Krita. Although the algorithm was originally designed for videos, virtually all implementations use SIOX primarily for still image segmentation. In fact, it is often said to be the current de facto standard for this task in the open-source world.
gpt_text:
Simple interactive object extraction is a computer vision approach where a user provides minimal input—such as a few clicks, scribbles, or a loose bounding box—and the system automatically isolates (segments) the object of interest from the background. Instead of manually outlining the full object, the user gives rough guidance, and the algorithm refines this into an accurate object mask.

This technique is used in image editing, annotation, and graphics applications to quickly cut out objects, create composites, or generate training data. Modern methods often rely on deep learning to understand object boundaries and semantics, making the extraction robust even when the user input is sparse or imprecise.

title: Viewport
human_text: A viewport is a polygon viewing region in computer graphics.
gpt_text:
In computing and web design, a viewport is the visible area in which content is displayed to a user. On a desktop browser, it’s essentially the part of the web page you can see within the browser window without scrolling; on mobile devices, it’s the portion of a page shown on the screen at any given time. The viewport defines what is immediately visible, while content outside it becomes viewable through scrolling or zooming.

In web development specifically, the viewport is crucial for responsive design. Developers use the `<meta name="viewport">` tag to control how a page scales and fits on different screen sizes, ensuring that text, images, and layout adapt properly on phones, tablets, and desktops.

title: Marching squares
human_text: Marching squares is a computer graphics algorithm that generates contours for a two-dimensional scalar field (rectangular array of individual numerical values). A similar method can be used to contour 2D triangle meshes.
gpt_text:
Marching squares is a computer graphics and computational geometry algorithm used to extract contour lines (isolines) from a 2D scalar field, such as elevation data or intensity values in an image. It works by examining a grid of sample points, looking at each cell of four neighboring samples at a time, and classifying the corners as above or below a chosen threshold. Based on this binary pattern (16 possible configurations), it determines where line segments should be drawn within the cell to approximate the contour.

The algorithm is the 2D analogue of the marching cubes algorithm used in 3D. Marching squares is popular because it is simple, efficient, and produces smooth contour lines suitable for visualization in scientific computing, medical imaging (e.g., outlining regions in scans), and geographic information systems (e.g., drawing elevation contours on maps).

title: Retained mode
human_text: Retained mode in computer graphics is a major pattern of API design in graphics libraries, in which
gpt_text:
Retained mode is a graphics or UI programming model where the system keeps an internal representation (“scene graph” or object tree) of what should be displayed. Instead of drawing everything manually each frame, the programmer creates and updates objects (like shapes, controls, or sprites), and the framework is responsible for rendering them, handling redraws, clipping, and layout automatically.  

This contrasts with immediate mode, where the program issues draw calls directly every frame and the system doesn’t store a persistent model of the scene. Retained mode is common in GUI toolkits and scene-graph-based rendering engines (e.g., WPF, HTML/CSS, many game UI systems), making it easier to manage complex interfaces, animations, and interactions at the cost of less direct, low-level control over each draw operation.

title: Least squares conformal map
human_text: A Least squares conformal map (LSCM) is a 2-D representation of a 3-D shape created using the Least Squares Conformal Mapping Method. By using the map as a guide when creating a new 2-D image, the colors of the 2-D image can be applied to the original 3-D model.
gpt_text:
A Least Squares Conformal Map (LSCM) is a method for parameterizing a 3D surface onto a 2D plane while trying to preserve angles as much as possible. It formulates the conformal (angle-preserving) condition as a least-squares optimization problem, solving a linear system that distributes angular distortion across the surface in an optimal way. This makes it well-suited for tasks like UV unwrapping in computer graphics, where textures must be mapped onto complex shapes.

In practice, LSCM fixes a small number of anchor vertices to remove rigid motion ambiguity, then computes 2D coordinates for all other vertices so that each triangle’s shape in the plane is as close as possible to its shape on the 3D surface. The result is a parameterization that tends to minimize local shear and distortion while remaining computationally efficient and relatively easy to implement.

title: Score bug
human_text: A score bug (or, in an expanded form, a score box or score bar) is a digital on-screen graphic which is displayed at either the top or lower third bottom of the television screen during a broadcast of a sporting event in order to display the current score and other statistics.
gpt_text:
A score bug is a small on-screen graphic used in televised sports broadcasts to show the current score and key game information at all times. Typically positioned in a corner of the screen, it may display team names or logos, the score, game clock, period or inning, and sometimes additional stats like possession indicators or pitch counts.

Score bugs became standard in the late 1990s as networks realized viewers appreciated being able to see the game status instantly without waiting for occasional full-screen updates. Today they are a core part of sports broadcast design, often animated and styled to match a network’s branding and the look of a particular league or event.

title: Newell's algorithm
human_text: Newell's Algorithm is a 3D computer graphics procedure for elimination of polygon cycles in the depth sorting required in hidden surface removal. It was proposed in 1972 by brothers Martin Newell and Dick Newell, and Tom Sancha, while all three were working at CADCentre.
gpt_text:
Newell's algorithm is a classic computer graphics method used to determine which surfaces of 3D objects are visible and which are hidden when rendering a scene. Specifically, it helps resolve visibility among overlapping, possibly non-convex polygons by deciding which polygon lies in front of another from a given viewpoint. It was one of the early practical solutions to the hidden-surface problem before modern z-buffering became standard.

The algorithm works by comparing pairs of polygons using a set of geometric tests (such as checking bounding boxes, depth ranges, and mutual overlap) in order to derive a consistent front-to-back ordering. If a simple ordering is not possible (due to cycles where A appears in front of B, B in front of C, and C in front of A), the algorithm attempts to split polygons to break the cycle. Newell's algorithm was influential in early 3D rendering systems and helped shape later visibility and sorting techniques.

title: Quad-edge
human_text: A quad-edge data structure is a computer representation of the topology of a two-dimensional or three-dimensional map, that is, a graph drawn on a (closed) surface.
gpt_text:
The quad-edge data structure is a flexible way to represent the topology of planar subdivisions and meshes, introduced by Guibas and Stolfi. Instead of separately storing vertices, edges, and faces, each undirected edge is represented by a “quad” of directed edge records (half-edges) that capture all adjacency relationships—between vertices, faces, and neighboring edges—in a unified framework.

This structure makes it easy to traverse and modify complex geometric subdivisions, such as triangulations or polygonal meshes, because local topological updates (like edge flips, splits, and merges) can be done with simple, consistent pointer manipulations. It is widely used in computational geometry for algorithms involving planar graphs, Voronoi diagrams, and Delaunay triangulations.

title: Resel
human_text: A resel, from resolution element, is a concept used in image analysis. It describes the actual spatial resolution in an image or a volume.
gpt_text:
In statistics, a **resel** (short for “resolution element”) is a unit used in random field theory to quantify the amount of *independent* signal present in a continuous data field, such as an image or brain scan. Rather than counting raw pixels or voxels, resels account for the smoothness of the data: many highly correlated neighboring points effectively behave like fewer independent observations.

Resels are crucial in fields like neuroimaging (e.g., fMRI, PET), where researchers test thousands of spatial locations simultaneously. By expressing the search space in resels instead of voxels, one can apply more accurate corrections for multiple comparisons and better control the family-wise error rate when identifying statistically significant activity patterns.

title: Human Race Machine
human_text: The Human Race Machine (HRM) is a computerized console composed of four different programs. The Human Race Machine program allows participants to see themselves with the facial characteristics of six different races: Asian, White, African, Middle Eastern, and Indian, mapped onto their own face. The Age Machine allows viewers see an aged version of his or her face. A version of this methodology has been used for over twenty years by the FBI and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children to help locate kidnap victims and missing children. The Couples Machine combines photographs of two people in different percentages to show the appearance of their child. The Anomaly Machine lets viewers see themselves with facial anomalies. The HRM was created by artist Nancy Burson and David Kramlich; it uses morphing technology. It was shown on Oprah on 2006-02-16.
gpt_text:
The Human Race Machine is an interactive digital tool that allows users to see how their own face might appear if they were of a different race, age, or under other altered conditions. Originally created by artist and inventor Nancy Burson, it uses facial morphing technology to overlay characteristic features associated (often stereotypically) with different racial or demographic groups onto a photograph of the user’s face.

Developed as an educational and artistic project, the Human Race Machine is often used in museums, schools, and diversity-training contexts to spark discussion about race, identity, and bias. By visually transforming users’ faces, it aims to challenge rigid ideas about racial difference and encourage empathy and reflection on how appearance shapes social experience.

title: Intrapixel and Interpixel processing
human_text: CMOS sensor processing is done in pixel level.
gpt_text:
Intrapixel and interpixel processing are concepts from image and signal processing that describe how data from image sensors (like camera CCDs or CMOS arrays) is handled. Intrapixel processing refers to operations performed on the data within a single pixel, treating each pixel independently. Examples include applying a nonlinear tone curve, per-pixel noise reduction, or per-pixel color correction based only on that pixel’s own value and perhaps fixed calibration data.

Interpixel processing involves operations that use information from multiple pixels together, exploiting spatial relationships in the image. This includes tasks like blurring, sharpening, edge detection, demosaicing (reconstructing full color from a color filter array), super‑resolution, and many forms of denoising. Interpixel methods model how neighboring pixels relate to each other to improve visual quality or extract features, while intrapixel methods focus on adjusting each pixel in isolation.

title: Fillrate
human_text: The term pixel fillrate refers to the number of pixels a video card can render to screen and write to video memory in a second or in case of texture fillrate the number of texture map elements (texels) GPU can map to pixels in a second. Pixel fillrates are given in megapixels per second or in gigapixels per second (in the case of newer cards), and they are obtained by multiplying the number of Raster Output Units (ROPs) by the clock frequency of the graphics processor unit (GPU) of a video card and texture fillrate is obtained by multiplying the number of Texture Mapping Units (TMUs) by the clock frequency of the graphics processing unit (GPU). Texture fillrates are given in mega or gigatexels per second. However, there is no full agreement on how to calculate and report fillrates. Other possible method is: to multiply the number of pixel pipelines by the clock frequency.
gpt_text:
Fill rate is a supply chain and inventory management metric that measures the percentage of customer demand that is met directly from available stock, without backorders or lost sales. It’s typically calculated as the number of units (or orders or order lines) fulfilled on time divided by the total units (or orders/lines) requested, expressed as a percentage.

A high fill rate indicates that a company reliably has the right products available when customers want them, improving service levels and customer satisfaction. However, maintaining very high fill rates often requires holding more inventory, which increases costs, so businesses aim to balance fill rate targets with inventory investment and operational efficiency.

title: PDE surface
human_text: PDE surfaces are used in geometric modelling and computer graphics for creating smooth surfaces conforming to a given boundary configuration. PDE surfaces use partial differential equations to generate a surface which usually satisfy a mathematical boundary value problem.
gpt_text:
A PDE surface (Partial Differential Equation surface) is a smooth geometric surface defined as the solution of a partial differential equation subject to boundary conditions. Instead of constructing the surface from patches or control points directly, one specifies how the surface should behave (for example, minimizing curvature or satisfying a physical equilibrium law) and what it must look like along its boundaries, then solves the PDE to obtain the shape in between.

PDE surfaces are widely used in geometric modeling and computer-aided design because they naturally produce smooth, fair shapes that interpolate or approximate given boundary curves. They are especially useful for complex, free-form designs—such as in automotive or aerospace engineering—where controlling global smoothness and aesthetic quality is crucial.

title: OpenGL Architecture Review Board
human_text: The OpenGL Architecture Review Board (ARB) is an industry consortium that governed the OpenGL specification.
gpt_text:
The OpenGL Architecture Review Board (ARB) was the industry consortium responsible for overseeing the development and standardization of the OpenGL graphics API. title: Nonobtuse mesh

Immediate mode in computer graphics is a rendering approach where the application directly issues drawing commands to the graphics API every frame, specifying all the geometry and state needed on the spot. This contrasts with retained mode, where you build and modify a scene graph or object model that the system stores and uses to render frames. Immediate mode is often simpler to reason about and implement, making it popular in debugging tools and “immediate mode GUIs,” but it can be less efficient for complex scenes because it lacks built-in mechanisms for reusing or culling previously defined geometry.

title: Blanking (video)

title: Swizzling (computer graphics)

title: Min/max kd-tree

title: Geomipmapping

title: False radiosity
human_text: False Radiosity is a 3D computer graphics technique used to create texture mapping for objects that emulates patch interaction algorithms in radiosity rendering. Though practiced in some form since the late 90s, this term was coined only around 2002 by architect Andrew Hartness, then head of 3D and real-time design at Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
gpt_text:

Instead of physically simulating how light reflects and scatters between surfaces, it uses tricks like precomputed light maps, ambient occlusion, or screen-space effects to *fake* the appearance of indirect lighting.

Because full radiosity is expensive and often impractical for interactive applications (like games), false radiosity offers a visually convincing compromise. Artists and technical designers can tune the effect by hand—adjusting brightness, color bleeding, and softness—to achieve a more realistic, globally lit look without performing heavy global illumination calculations each frame.

title: Areograph
human_text: Areograph is the commercial name of a photographic technology that assembles photographic components into 3-dimensional environments. Anywhere from 100,000 to several million photographs are stitched by software into a navigable scene, akin to those in a first person shooter. The production of such environments is both faster and cheaper than creating a rendered environment of similar size, as well as being more detailed, given that the source of an Areograph environment is a real-world location.

In historical and conceptual usage, “areograph” can also describe maps or graphical representations of Martian surface features and terrain, analogous to “geography” and “cartography” for Earth. In this sense, an areograph is tied to the study and documentation of Mars’s physical characteristics, including its landscapes, climate patterns, and atmospheric phenomena.

title: Generalized map
human_text: In mathematics, a generalized map is a topological model which allows one to represent and to handle subdivided objects. This model was defined starting from combinatorial maps in order to represent non-orientable and open subdivisions, which is not possible with combinatorial maps. The main advantage of generalized map is the homogeneity of one-to-one mappings in any dimensions, which simplifies definitions and algorithms comparing to combinatorial maps. For this reason, generalized maps are sometimes used instead of combinatorial maps, even to represent orientable closed partitions.
gpt_text:
