Instead of storing just vertices, edges, and faces, a generalized map encodes how these basic elements (called cells) are connected using abstract entities known as darts and a small set of involutive (self-inverse) mappings between them. This allows it to represent complex shapes, including those with holes, non-manifold parts, or higher-dimensional analogues, in a unified and rigorous way.

Because a generalized map cleanly separates topological structure from geometric embedding (the actual coordinates of points), it is widely used in computational geometry, computer graphics, and geometric modeling. It supports efficient algorithms for operations like subdivision, mesh refinement, and topological queries, while remaining flexible enough to handle 2D surfaces, 3D volumes, and higher-dimensional complexes within the same framework.

title: Image-based meshing
human_text: Image-based meshing is the automated process of creating computer models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and finite element analysis (FEA) from 3D image data (such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) or microtomography). Although a wide range of mesh generation techniques are currently available, these were usually developed to generate models from computer-aided design (CAD), and therefore have difficulties meshing from 3D imaging data.

Instead of starting from an idealized CAD model, the workflow segments structures of interest from the images (e.g., organs, bones, porous materials), reconstructs their geometry, and then converts these geometries into surface and volume meshes for simulation or analysis.

This approach is widely used in biomedical engineering, materials science, and geosciences because it captures complex, real-world geometries and internal structures that are difficult or impossible to model analytically. The resulting meshes can be used in finite element, finite volume, or other numerical methods to study mechanical behavior, fluid flow, transport phenomena, or other physical processes in realistic, image-derived domains.

title: Swap chain
human_text: In computer graphics, a swap chain is a series of virtual framebuffers utilized by the graphics card and graphics API for frame rate stabilization and several other functions. The swap chain usually exists in graphics memory, but it can exist in system memory as well. The non-utilization of a swap chain may result in stuttering rendering, but its existence and utilization are required by many graphics APIs. A swap chain with two buffers is a double buffer.

Instead of drawing directly to the display, the application renders each frame into one of these off-screen buffers, and then “swaps” it with the buffer currently being shown. This technique helps avoid flickering and tearing, and allows rendering to proceed smoothly while another image is being displayed.

Most swap chains use double or triple buffering. In double buffering, one buffer is visible while the other is being rendered; when rendering finishes, they are swapped. Triple buffering adds a third buffer to reduce waiting time and better absorb variations in frame rendering time, improving perceived smoothness and responsiveness.

title: Vertex (computer graphics)
human_text: A vertex (plural vertices) in computer graphics is a data structure that describes certain attributes, like the position of a point in 2D or 3D space, or multiple points on a surface.

Beyond position, a vertex often stores additional attributes used in rendering, such as color, surface normal (for lighting calculations), texture coordinates (for mapping images onto surfaces), and sometimes data for animations or special effects. These attributes are processed in the vertex stage of the graphics pipeline (e.g., by vertex shaders) to determine how objects appear on screen.

title: PenTile matrix family
human_text: PenTile matrix is a family of patented subpixel matrix schemes used in electronic device displays. PenTile is a trademark of Samsung. PenTile matrices are used in AMOLED and LCD displays.

The PenTile matrix family is a group of subpixel layouts used in digital displays, especially OLED and some LCD screens, that differ from the traditional RGB stripe arrangement. Instead of giving each pixel its own full set of red, green, and blue subpixels, PenTile designs share subpixels between adjacent pixels, often increasing the number of green subpixels relative to red and blue (for example, RGBG layouts). This exploits the human eye’s higher sensitivity to green and lower sensitivity to fine color detail.

Because of this sharing, PenTile displays can achieve higher apparent resolution or lower manufacturing cost and power usage with fewer total subpixels. However, the non-standard subpixel arrangement can sometimes cause visible artifacts such as color fringing or reduced sharpness in fine text, especially at lower pixel densities. At high resolutions, these artifacts are usually much less noticeable.

title: Polygon soup
human_text: A polygon soup is a set of unorganized polygons, typically triangles, before the application of any structuring operation, such as e.g. octree grouping.
gpt_text:

Each polygon is treated independently, typically just as a list of vertex positions and possibly normals and texture coordinates, with no explicit knowledge of shared edges, adjacency, or topology.

Because of this, polygon soups are simple to store and render but harder to process for tasks like mesh repair, smoothing, collision detection, or physical simulation, which often need consistent connectivity. Many geometry-processing algorithms first convert a polygon soup into a well-structured mesh (with edges, faces, and vertex adjacency) before operating on it.

title: Computer Graphics: Principles and Practice
human_text: Computer Graphics: Principles and Practice is a textbook written by James D. Foley, Andries van Dam, Steven K. Feiner, John Hughes, Morgan McGuire, David F. Sklar, and Kurt Akeley and published by Addison–Wesley. First published in 1982 as Fundamentals of Interactive Computer Graphics, it is widely considered a classic standard reference book on the topic of computer graphics. Balancing theory with implementation details, it is used both as a graduate-level textbook and a professional reference for those designing rendering engines, visualization tools, and interactive graphics applications.

The process of converting continuous visual data into these discrete samples is called sampling.

Sampling plays a key role in rendering quality and performance. title: Device-independent pixel
human_text: A device-independent pixel (also: density-independent pixel, dip, dp) is a unit of length.

This abstraction allows UI elements—such as buttons, text, and icons—to appear roughly the same physical size on phones, tablets, and monitors, even though those devices may have very different resolutions. For example, on Android, 1 dp is defined as 1 physical pixel on a 160 dpi screen, and scales proportionally on higher- or lower-density screens.

title: Hit-testing
human_text: In computer graphics programming, hit-testing (hit detection, picking, or pick correlation ) is the process of determining whether a user-controlled cursor (such as a mouse cursor or touch-point on a touch-screen interface) intersects a given graphical object (such as a shape, line, or curve) drawn on the screen. Hit-testing may be performed on the movement or activation of a mouse or other pointing device.

In graphical user interfaces, games, and drawing applications, the system uses hit-testing to figure out which object should receive input events based on the position of the pointer or touch.

Under the hood, hit-testing often involves checking whether a point lies inside the bounds or shape of visual elements, sometimes using bounding boxes for speed or more precise geometric tests for accuracy. It is a core part of event dispatch, collision detection, and interactive graphics, ensuring that user actions are mapped to the correct visual components.

title: Pose space deformation
human_text: Pose space deformation is a computer animation technique which is used to deform a mesh on skeleton-driven animation. Common use of this technique is to deform the shape of a mesh (for example, an arm) according to the angle of the joint (in this case, the elbow) bent. Although the name is commonly called Pose space deformation on many scholarly articles, 3D animation software rarely uses that name. On Autodesk Maya, it's implemented under the name Pose Deformer, and on Blender, it's implemented as Corrective Shape Keys. The first famous application of this technique was the cloth's movement on the first episode of the animated film The Animatrix.
gpt_text:

Instead of relying solely on joint rotations, PSD uses a “pose space” defined by the character’s joint angles and blends in specially sculpted corrective shapes (often called corrective blendshapes or morph targets) when the character reaches certain poses.

In practice, an artist first rigs a character, then examines problematic poses where the mesh collapses or creases unnaturally. For those poses, they sculpt corrected versions of the mesh and store them as shapes associated with specific joint configurations. During animation, the system detects the current pose in pose space and smoothly interpolates these corrective shapes, producing more natural, volume-preserving deformations around joints and complex areas like shoulders, hips, or faces.

title: SGI algorithm
human_text: The SGI algorithm creates triangle strips from a set of triangles. It was published by K. Akeley, P. Haeberli, and D. Burns as a C program named "tomesh.c" for use with Silicon Graphics' IRIS GL API.

In essence, it takes measured or estimated spectral data, generates a corresponding model of the underlying system or signal, and then inverts this representation to obtain a time-domain or spatial-domain form.

This type of algorithm is valuable when direct measurement in the time domain is difficult or noisy, but reliable frequency-domain data is available. SGI methods often incorporate regularization or constraints to ensure stable inversion, helping to reduce artifacts and noise amplification when transforming from spectrum back to the original domain.

title: Adaptive tile refresh
human_text: Adaptive tile refresh is a computer graphics technique for side-scrolling video games. It was most famously used by id Software's John Carmack in games such as Commander Keen to compensate for the poor graphics performance of PCs in the early 1990s. Its principal innovation is a novel use of several EGA hardware features to perform the scrolling in hardware. The technique is named for its other aspect, the tracking of moved graphical elements in order to minimize the amount of redrawing required in every frame. Together, the combination saves the processing time that would be otherwise required for redrawing the entire screen. Carmack designed the software engine based on a scrolling display for large images from the 1970s.
gpt_text:
Adaptive tile refresh is a display power‑saving technique in which only the parts (“tiles”) of a screen that have changed are updated, rather than refreshing the entire panel at full rate. The display is divided into regions, and the system tracks which regions have new content; unchanged tiles are refreshed less frequently or held using panel self‑refresh or similar mechanisms.

This approach reduces the workload on the display controller and panel, cutting power consumption and sometimes heat, especially for static or mostly static images (e.g., reading, viewing photos, UI with limited motion). It is commonly used in modern mobile devices, laptops, and some TVs as part of broader adaptive or variable refresh technologies aimed at extending battery life while maintaining visual quality.

title: Smoothing group
human_text: In 3D computer graphics, a smoothing group is a group of polygons in a polygon mesh which should appear to form a smooth surface. Smoothing groups are useful for describing shapes where some polygons are connected smoothly to their neighbors, and some are not. For example, in a mesh representing a cylinder, all of the polygons are smoothly connected except along the edges of the end caps. One could make a smoothing group containing all of the polygons in one end cap, another containing the polygons in the other end cap, and a last group containing the polygons in the tube shape between the end caps.
gpt_text:
A smoothing group is a 3D modeling concept used to control how shading appears across adjacent polygons on a mesh. Polygons that share the same smoothing group will have their vertex normals averaged, creating the appearance of a smooth, continuous surface between them. Polygons in different smoothing groups keep a sharp edge between them, as their normals are not blended.

This system is especially important in low- to mid-poly models, where geometry alone cannot define all the desired curvature. By assigning smoothing groups, artists can decide where an object should look rounded (like the side of a cylinder) and where it should look hard-edged (like the corner of a box), without changing the mesh’s topology.

title: Constriction of video
human_text: Constriction (graphics media)
gpt_text:
“Constriction of video” usually refers to reducing a video’s size, either in terms of file size (compression) or visible dimensions (resolution). In compression, video data is encoded more efficiently so it takes up less storage space or bandwidth, often by removing visual details that are less noticeable to the viewer. This lets videos stream more smoothly over the internet or be stored more easily on devices, but excessive compression can cause visible artifacts like blockiness or blurring.

Constriction can also mean lowering a video’s resolution (for example, from 4K down to 1080p or 720p) or frame rate to fit technical limitations, such as slower networks, smaller screens, or hardware constraints. Both forms of constriction aim to make video more manageable and accessible, balancing quality against performance and resource use.

title: Beier–Neely morphing algorithm
human_text: Image morphing is a technique to synthesize a fluid transformation from one image (source image) to another (destination image). Source image can be one or more than one images. There are two parts in the image morphing implementation. The first part is warping and the second part is cross-dissolving.
gpt_text:
The Beier–Neely morphing algorithm is a classic image morphing technique introduced in 1992 that uses pairs of corresponding line segments to control how one image smoothly transforms into another. Instead of relying on just matching points, users draw lines on both the source and target images to indicate how features (like eyes, mouth, or outline) should move and deform during the morph. Each pixel’s new position is calculated from a weighted combination of its relationships to all these line pairs.

This line-based approach gives artists and animators fine-grained, intuitive control over the morph, producing more natural and coherent transformations than simple point-based methods. The algorithm became widely known through its use in film and television effects and remains a foundational technique in image warping and morphing systems.

title: Physically based animation
human_text: Physically based animation is an area of interest within computer graphics concerned with the simulation of physically plausible behaviors at interactive rates. Advances in physically based animation are often motivated by the need to include complex, physically inspired behaviors in video games, interactive simulations, and movies. Although off-line simulation methods exist to solve most all of the problems studied in physically-based animation, these methods are intended for applications that necessitate physical accuracy and slow, detailed computations. In contrast to methods common in offline simulation, techniques in physically based animation are concerned with physical plausibility, numerical stability, and visual appeal over physical accuracy. Physically based animation is often limited to loose approximations of physical behaviors because of the strict time constraints imposed by interactive applications. The target frame rate for interactive applications such as games and simulations is often 25-60 hertz, with only a small fraction of the time allotted to an individual frame remaining for physical simulation. Simplified models of physical behaviors are generally preferred if they are more efficient, easier to accelerate (through pre-computation, clever data structures, or SIMD/GPGPU), or satisfy desirable mathematical properties (such as unconditional stability or volume conservation when a soft body undergoes deformation). Fine details are not important when the overriding goal of a visualization is aesthetic appeal or the maintenance of player immersion since these details are often difficult for humans to notice or are otherwise impossible to distinguish at human scales.
gpt_text:
Physically based animation is an approach in computer graphics where motion is generated by simulating the laws of physics rather than manually specifying every movement. Instead of keyframing all positions and poses, the animator or system defines physical properties—such as mass, forces, constraints, and material behavior—and lets a physics engine compute how objects or characters move over time.

This technique is used for realistic effects like cloth, hair, fluids, rigid bodies, and ragdoll characters, where believable responses to collisions, gravity, and other forces are important. Physically based animation can produce more natural and varied motion, especially in interactive contexts like games, though it can be harder to control precisely than traditional keyframe animation.

title: OpenRL
human_text: PowerVR OpenRL™ is a flexible low level interactive ray tracing API, available for download as an SDK for accelerating ray tracing in both graphics and non-graphics (e.g., physics) applications. OpenRL was developed by the Caustic Professional division of Imagination Technologies. A free perpetual license of OpenRL is available for integration, with either commercial or non-commercial applications.

Such projects aim to lower the barrier to entry for RL research and application by offering reusable components, clear APIs, and integrations with popular environments (e.g., OpenAI Gym–style interfaces). title: Depth peeling
human_text: Depth peeling is a method of order-independent transparency. Depth peeling has the advantage of being able to generate correct results even for complex images containing intersecting transparent objects.

Depth peeling is a multi-pass rendering technique used in computer graphics to correctly display order-independent transparency—that is, scenes with many overlapping transparent surfaces—without needing to sort geometry explicitly. Instead of drawing all transparent objects in a single pass, depth peeling renders the scene multiple times, each time “peeling away” one layer of fragments based on depth, starting from the closest to the camera and moving farther back.

In each pass, the algorithm uses depth tests to discard fragments that are not the next visible layer behind the already-recorded depths from previous passes. The peeled layers are then composited in the correct order to produce an accurate final image, even in complex cases like intersecting or highly overlapping transparent objects. This yields higher visual correctness than simple alpha blending with approximate sorting, at the cost of additional rendering passes and memory.

title: Closest point method
human_text: The closest point method (CPM) is an embedding method for solving partial differential equations on surfaces. The closest point method uses standard numerical approaches such as finite differences, finite element or spectral methods in order to solve the embedding partial differential equation (PDE) which is equal to the original PDE on the surface. The solution is computed in a band surrounding the surface in order to be computationally efficient. In order to extend the data off the surface, the closest point method uses a closest point representation. This representation extends function values to be constant along directions normal to the surface.
gpt_text:
The closest point method is a numerical technique for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) defined on surfaces or curves by embedding them in a higher-dimensional space. Instead of working directly on the complicated geometry, the method extends the surface PDE to a surrounding Cartesian grid by using a “closest point” representation: each point in the embedding space is associated with its nearest point on the surface. This allows standard finite difference or finite element schemes on regular grids to approximate derivatives that are intrinsically defined on the surface.

Practically, the method has two main steps: (1) compute or use a function that maps any point in the embedding space to its closest point on the surface; (2) formulate an extended PDE in the embedding space whose solution, when restricted back to the surface, matches the original surface PDE solution. The closest point method is widely used for problems like diffusion, curvature-driven flows, and other geometric PDEs on complex shapes, taking advantage of the simplicity and efficiency of Cartesian discretizations.

title: K-D-B-tree
human_text: In computer science, a K-D-B-tree (k-dimensional B-tree) is a tree data structure for subdividing a k-dimensional search space. The aim of the K-D-B-tree is to provide the search efficiency of a balanced k-d tree, while providing the block-oriented storage of a B-tree for optimizing external memory accesses.
gpt_text:
A K-D-B-tree (Keyspace Decomposition B-tree) is a multidimensional index structure that combines ideas from k-d trees and B-trees to efficiently handle range and point queries over multiple attributes in large, disk-based datasets. Unlike simple B-trees, which index a single key dimension, a K-D-B-tree partitions space in several dimensions and stores these partitions in a balanced, B-tree-like structure, making it suitable for spatial and multidimensional data such as geographic coordinates or multi-attribute records.

The tree recursively decomposes the data space into rectangular regions (like a k-d tree), but groups these regions into disk pages and manages them with B-tree node logic, supporting efficient insertion, deletion, and search while minimizing disk I/O. This makes K-D-B-trees particularly useful in database systems and spatial indexing where both multidimensional organization and disk efficiency are required.

title: A-buffer
human_text: In computer graphics, A-buffer, also known as anti-aliased, area-averaged or accumulation buffer, is a general hidden surface mechanism suited to medium scale virtual memory computers. It resolves visibility among an arbitrary collection of opaque, transparent, and intersecting objects. Using an easy to compute Fourier window (box filter), it increases the effective image resolution many times over the Z-buffer, with a moderate increase in cost.

Instead of storing just a single color and depth value per pixel, the A-buffer keeps a list of all fragments (surface samples) that affect each pixel, including their colors, depths, and coverage information. This allows the renderer to accurately combine overlapping fragments, produce smooth edges, and handle transparency and complex visibility situations like intersecting or partially transparent objects.

By aggregating all contributing fragments per pixel, the A-buffer can compute anti-aliased pixel colors through area averaging, reducing jagged edges and improving image quality compared with basic Z-buffer approaches. Although more memory-intensive and computationally expensive, it provides higher-quality results and is especially useful for scenes with intricate geometry, transparency, or where high-quality anti-aliasing is required.

title: IMPACT (computer graphics)
human_text: IMPACT (sometimes spelled Impact) is a computer graphics architecture for Silicon Graphics computer workstations. IMPACT Graphics was developed in 1995 and was available as a high-end graphics option on workstations released during the mid-1990s. IMPACT graphics gives the workstation real-time 2D and 3D graphics rendering capability similar to that of even high-end PCs made well after IMPACT's introduction. IMPACT graphics systems consist of either one or two Geometry Engines and one or two Raster Engines in various configurations.

title: Visual computing

Visual computing also includes aspects of pattern recognition, human computer interaction, machine learning and digital libraries. The core challenges are the acquisition, processing, analysis and rendering of visual information (mainly images and video). Application areas include industrial quality control, medical image processing and visualization, surveying, robotics, multimedia systems, virtual heritage, special effects in movies and television, and computer games.

title: Creative visualization (design)
human_text: In design, Creative Visualization refers to the process by which computer generated imagery, digital animation, three-dimensional models, and two-dimensional representations, such as architectural blueprints, engineering drawings, and sewing patterns are created and used in order to visualize a potential product prior to production. Such products include prototypes for vehicles in automotive engineering, apparel in the fashion industry, and buildings in architectural design.

This process helps bridge abstract ideas and concrete outcomes, enabling designers to test aesthetics, functionality, and user experience early on. By repeatedly visualizing and iterating—sometimes supported by tools like 3D modeling, VR, or generative software—creative visualization sharpens concepts, aligns stakeholders around a shared vision, and guides decision-making throughout the design process.

title: Fake nude photography

Several reasons for the creation of these doctored photographs include sexual gratification, stigmatization or embarrassment of the subject, or for commercial gain, such as by selling the photographs on pornography websites. Fakes can be created using image editing software or through machine learning (fake pornographic images created this way are referred to as deepfakes).
