In common architectures like x86, the main modes are user mode and kernel (or supervisor) mode. User mode is where applications run, with limited privileges and controlled access to hardware and memory via system calls. title: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures

title: Improper input validation

title: Lattice-based access control

title: Access Control Matrix

title: Take-grant protection model

title: Non-interference (security)

title: Relay attack

title: Intrusion tolerance

title: Off-site data protection

title: Defensive computing
human_text: Defensive computing is a form of practice for computer users to help reduce the risk of computing problems, by avoiding dangerous computing practices. The primary goal of this method of computing is to be able to anticipate and prepare for potentially problematic situations prior to their occurrence, despite any adverse conditions of a computer system or any mistakes made by other users. This can be achieved through adherence to a variety of general guidelines, as well as the practice of specific computing techniques.
gpt_text:

Instead of assuming that systems, websites, and emails are safe by default, a defensive computing approach assumes things can fail, be misconfigured, or be malicious, and acts accordingly.

It includes habits like keeping backups, using strong and unique passwords, enabling two-factor authentication, being skeptical of links and attachments, keeping software updated, and limiting the data you share. Defensive computing is less about specific tools and more about an attitude: expecting trouble, preparing for it, and minimizing the damage when something goes wrong.

title: Information assurance
human_text: Information assurance (IA) is the practice of assuring information and managing risks related to the use, processing, storage, and transmission of information. Information assurance includes protection of the integrity, availability, authenticity, non-repudiation and confidentiality of user data. IA encompasses not only digital protections but also physical techniques. These protections apply to data in transit, both physical and electronic forms, as well as data at rest. IA is best thought of as a superset of information security (i.e. umbrella term), and as the business outcome of information risk management.
gpt_text:
Information assurance (IA) is the practice of managing and protecting information-related risks to ensure that data and systems remain confidential, accurate, available, and trustworthy. It focuses on safeguarding information throughout its lifecycle—creation, storage, transmission, and disposal—against threats such as unauthorized access, alteration, destruction, or interruption.

IA combines technical controls (like encryption, firewalls, and access controls) with policies, procedures, and training to ensure that people and processes also support security goals. It is closely related to cybersecurity but is broader, emphasizing risk management, compliance, and the resilience of information systems in support of an organization’s mission.

title: Google hacking
human_text: Google hacking, also named Google Dorking,Term Of The Day: Google Dorking - Business InsiderGoogle dork query, techtarget.com is a hacker technique that uses Google Search and other Google applications to find security holes in the configuration and computer code that websites are using.

By combining special search syntax—such as `filetype:`, `intitle:`, `inurl:`, and `site:`—people can uncover exposed files, login pages, configuration data, or other sensitive information that has been inadvertently indexed by Google.

While these techniques can be used legitimately by security professionals to identify and fix vulnerabilities (for example, during penetration testing or security audits), they can also be abused by attackers to discover targets for exploitation. Because of this dual use, organizations are encouraged to secure their systems, configure proper access controls, and prevent sensitive data from being indexed by search engines.

title: High Assurance Guard
human_text: A High Assurance Guard (HAG) is a Multilevel security computer device which is used to communicate between different Security Domains, such as NIPRNet to SIPRNet. A HAG is one example of a Controlled Interface between security levels. HAGs are approved through the Common Criteria process.
gpt_text:
A High Assurance Guard (HAG) is a specialized cybersecurity device or software system designed to securely control and filter information flow between networks of differing security levels, such as between classified and unclassified systems. It enforces strict, formally verified security policies to ensure that only authorized and properly validated data can pass from one domain to another, preventing data leaks, unauthorized disclosure, or injection of malicious content.

High Assurance Guards are typically used in environments with very strong security and compliance requirements—such as defense, intelligence, and critical infrastructure—where traditional firewalls or gateways are not sufficient. They often undergo rigorous evaluation and certification (e.g., under Common Criteria or similar schemes) and may incorporate formal methods, redundancy, and fault-tolerance to achieve high assurance that they behave correctly even under attack or failure conditions.

title: Information technology security assessment
human_text: Information Technology Security Assessment (IT Security Assessment) is an explicit study to locate IT security vulnerabilities and risks.
gpt_text:
Information technology security assessment is a systematic process of evaluating an organization’s IT systems, networks, applications, and processes to identify security weaknesses, vulnerabilities, and noncompliance with policies or standards. It examines how well technical controls (like firewalls, encryption, and access controls) and organizational measures (such as policies, procedures, and training) protect information assets from threats.

These assessments can include activities like vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, configuration reviews, code analysis, and policy audits. The results help organizations understand their current security posture, prioritize risks, and develop remediation plans to reduce the likelihood and impact of security incidents while meeting regulatory and industry requirements.

title: Physical information security
human_text: Physical information security is the intersection, the common ground between physical security and information security. It primarily concerns the protection of tangible information-related assets such as computer systems and storage media against physical, real-world threats such as unauthorized physical access, theft, fire and flood. It typically involves physical controls such as protective barriers and locks, uninterruptible power supplies, and shredders. Information security controls in the physical domain complement those in the logical domain (such as encryption), and procedural or administrative controls (such as information security awareness and compliance with policies and laws).
gpt_text:
Physical information security is the protection of information assets from physical threats such as theft, damage, unauthorized access, or environmental hazards. Instead of focusing on firewalls or encryption, it deals with the real-world safeguards around buildings, rooms, devices, and storage media that hold sensitive data.  

Typical measures include locks and access control systems, surveillance cameras, security guards, visitor logs, secure server rooms, shredding of documents, and proper disposal of hardware like hard drives. Effective physical information security ensures that even if someone is on-site, they still cannot easily see, steal, or destroy important information.

title: Default password
human_text: Where a device needs a username and/or password to log in, a default password is usually provided that allows the device to be accessed during its initial setup, or after resetting to factory defaults.
gpt_text:
A default password is the preconfigured password that comes set on a device, application, or account when it is first installed or shipped from the manufacturer. It’s often something simple and generic, like “admin,” “password,” or a numeric sequence, and is intended to let users access the system the first time so they can configure it.

Default passwords are a major security risk if they are not changed immediately, because they are widely known, easily guessable, and often publicly documented in manuals or online. Attackers routinely scan for systems still using default credentials to gain unauthorized access, making it a basic security best practice to replace any default password with a strong, unique one.

title: Common Criteria Testing Laboratory
human_text: The Common Criteria model provides for the separation of the roles of evaluator and certifier. Product certificates are awarded by national schemes on the basis of evaluations carried by independent testing laboratories.
gpt_text:
A Common Criteria Testing Laboratory (CCTL) is an accredited, independent facility authorized to evaluate information technology products against the Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation (ISO/IEC 15408). These labs assess whether a product’s security functions and assurance measures meet the requirements defined in a specific Security Target at a chosen Evaluation Assurance Level (EAL).  

CCTLs perform activities such as vulnerability analysis, functional and penetration testing, and documentation review, following standardized methodologies and schemes recognized by national or international certification bodies. Their evaluation results form the basis for official Common Criteria certificates, which are widely used by governments and enterprises to select and trust secure IT products.

title: Cryptographic Module Testing Laboratory
human_text: A Cryptographic Module Testing Laboratory (CMTL) is an information technology (IT) computer security testing laboratory that is accredited to conduct cryptographic module evaluations for conformance to the FIPS 140-2 U.S. Government standard.
gpt_text:
A Cryptographic Module Testing Laboratory (CMTL) is an accredited, independent lab that evaluates cryptographic modules—hardware, software, or firmware components that perform encryption, decryption, key management, and related security functions—against established security standards. These labs operate under formal validation programs such as the U.S./Canadian Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), which is based on standards like FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3.

In practice, a CMTL conducts rigorous functional, algorithmic, and security testing to verify that a cryptographic module correctly implements approved algorithms, protects keys, and meets specific requirements for physical and logical security. Successful testing results can lead to official certification or validation, which is often required for use in government systems and other regulated environments.

title: Host protected area
human_text: The host protected area (HPA) is an area of a hard drive or solid-state drive that is not normally visible to an operating system. It was first introduced in the ATA-4 standard CXV (T13) in 2001.
gpt_text:
A Host Protected Area (HPA) is a reserved section on a hard disk or SSD that is hidden from the operating system and standard user-level tools. It’s defined by the ATA (Advanced Technology Attachment) specification and can be configured by system firmware or specialized software so that normal partitioning and file system utilities don’t see or modify it.

Manufacturers and system integrators often use HPAs to store recovery images, diagnostic tools, or proprietary data needed for system management. Because the area is invisible during everyday use, it can also be abused by malware or rootkits to hide data from security software, making it relevant in digital forensics and security analysis.

title: Secure state
human_text: A secure state is an information systems security term to describe where entities in a computer system are divided into subjects and objects, and it can be formally proven that each state transition preserves security by moving from one secure state to another secure state. Thereby it can be inductively proven that the system is secure. As defined in the Bell–LaPadula model, the secure state is built on the concept of a state machine with a set of allowable states in a system. The transition from one state to another state is defined by transition functions.
gpt_text:
A secure state is a condition in which a system, organization, or environment maintains protection of its critical assets—such as data, infrastructure, and operations—against threats, vulnerabilities, and unauthorized access. In this state, security controls are effectively implemented and functioning as intended, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability are preserved.

Achieving a secure state typically involves a combination of technical measures (like encryption, access controls, and monitoring), organizational processes (such as policies, training, and incident response), and continual assessment to adapt to new risks. It’s not a one-time achievement but an ongoing posture that must be maintained and updated as threats evolve.

title: Air Force Cyber Command (Provisional)
human_text: Air Force Cyber Command (Provisional) (AFCYBER (P)) was a proposed United States Air Force Major Command that existed only in provisional status. On 6 October 2008, the Air Force announced that the command would not be brought into permanent activation, and that the cyber mission would be transferred, with the standup of the Twenty-Fourth Air Force, to Air Force Space Command.
gpt_text:
Air Force Cyber Command (Provisional), often written as AFCYBER (P), was an interim organizational entity established by the U.S. Air Force in 2007 to lay the groundwork for a permanent major command focused on cyberspace operations. Its mission was to develop concepts, structures, and capabilities for defending Air Force networks, conducting offensive and defensive cyber operations, and integrating cyber power into broader air and space missions.

Although the Air Force ultimately decided not to stand up a separate major command under this name, the work of Air Force Cyber Command (Provisional) directly contributed to the creation and evolution of what is now Air Forces Cyber (AFCYBER), aligned under Air Combat Command and integrated with U.S. Cyber Command.

title: Defense in depth (computing)
human_text: Defense in depth is a concept used in Information security in which multiple layers of security controls (defense) are placed throughout an information technology (IT) system. Its intent is to provide redundancy in the event a security control fails or a vulnerability is exploited that can cover aspects of personnel, procedural, technical and physical security for the duration of the system's life cycle.
gpt_text:
Defense in depth in computing is a security strategy that uses multiple, layered safeguards to protect systems, data, and networks. Instead of relying on a single control (like a firewall), it combines technical, administrative, and physical measures—such as network segmentation, firewalls, intrusion detection, strong authentication, encryption, access controls, and regular monitoring—so that if one layer fails, others still provide protection.

This approach assumes that breaches and failures are inevitable and focuses on slowing attackers, limiting damage, and increasing the chances of detection and response. It’s commonly applied across all levels of an IT environment: from perimeter defenses and internal networks to endpoints, applications, user accounts, and data storage.

title: Differentiated security
human_text: Differentiated security is a form of computer security that deploys a range of different security policies and mechanisms according to the identity and context of a user or transaction.
gpt_text:
Differentiated security is a security strategy that tailors protections to the specific risks, value, and sensitivity of different systems, data, users, or operations, rather than applying a uniform, one‑size‑fits‑all approach. High-value or high-risk assets (such as financial data, critical infrastructure, or admin accounts) receive stronger controls—like stricter authentication, tighter access permissions, more monitoring, and faster incident response—while lower-risk areas get proportionate, lighter-weight safeguards.  

This approach aims to optimize both security and usability: resources are focused where they matter most, reducing overprotection that can slow operations and underprotection that leaves critical assets exposed. Differentiated security is commonly used in risk-based access control, data classification schemes, and tiered network architectures (e.g., separating public-facing systems from sensitive internal networks).

title: File inclusion vulnerability
human_text: A file inclusion vulnerability is a type of web vulnerability that is most commonly found to affect web applications that rely on a scripting run time. This issue is caused when an application builds a path to executable code using an attacker-controlled variable in a way that allows the attacker to control which file is executed at run time. A file include vulnerability is distinct from a generic directory traversal attack, in that directory traversal is a way of gaining unauthorized file system access, and a file inclusion vulnerability subverts how an application loads code for execution. Successful exploitation of a file inclusion vulnerability will result in remote code execution on the web server that runs the affected web application. An attacker can use remote code execution to create a web shell on the web server, which can be used for website defacement.
gpt_text:
A file inclusion vulnerability is a web security flaw where an application dynamically loads files based on user-controlled input without proper validation. Attackers can exploit this to make the server include unintended files—either local files already on the server (Local File Inclusion, LFI) or remote files from another server (Remote File Inclusion, RFI)—into the application’s execution flow.

Through this, an attacker may read sensitive files (such as configuration files or source code), execute arbitrary code, or gain full control of the server. File inclusion vulnerabilities typically arise in languages and frameworks that support dynamic file loading (for example, using functions like `include` or `require` in PHP) when user input is concatenated directly into file paths without sanitization, validation, or the use of safe whitelisting mechanisms.

title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System
human_text: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is a free and open industry standard for assessing the severity of computer system security vulnerabilities. CVSS attempts to assign severity scores to vulnerabilities, allowing responders to prioritize responses and resources according to threat. Scores are calculated based on a formula that depends on several metrics that approximate ease of exploit and the impact of exploit. Scores range from 0 to 10, with 10 being the most severe. While many utilize only the CVSS Base score for determining severity, temporal and environmental scores also exist, to factor in availability of mitigations and how widespread vulnerable systems are within an organization, respectively.
gpt_text:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is an open, standardized framework used to rate the severity of security vulnerabilities in software and systems. It assigns numerical scores—typically from 0.0 to 10.0—based on factors like how easily a vulnerability can be exploited, what level of access is required, and what impact it has on confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

CVSS is widely used by security teams, vendors, and researchers to prioritize remediation efforts and communicate risk in a consistent way. Organizations often rely on CVSS scores, along with their own context (such as asset importance and exposure), to decide which vulnerabilities to address first.

title: LOMAC
human_text: Low Water-Mark Mandatory Access Control (LOMAC) is a Mandatory Access Control model which protects the integrity of system objects and subjects by means of an information flow policy coupled with the subject demotion via floating labels. In LOMAC, all system subjects and objects are assigned integrity labels, made up of one or more hierarchical grades, depending on their types. Together, these label elements permit all labels to be placed in a partial order, with information flow protections and demotion decisions based on a dominance operator describing the order.
gpt_text:
LOMAC (Low Water-Mark Mandatory Access Control) is a security mechanism for operating systems that aims to limit the damage that can be caused by compromised or untrusted processes. It assigns integrity labels (or levels) to subjects (processes) and objects (files, resources) and enforces rules about how information can flow between them. When a process reads from a lower-integrity object, its own integrity label is “lowered” (the low water-mark), reflecting that it has been influenced by less trustworthy data.

This approach helps prevent high-integrity processes (such as system services) from unintentionally acting on corrupted or malicious data and then affecting other critical parts of the system. LOMAC was notably implemented as an experimental kernel extension for UNIX-like systems (such as FreeBSD) and is related to broader mandatory access control frameworks like those provided by the TrustedBSD project.

title: Q-CERT
human_text: The Qatar Computer Emergency Response Team was created in December 2006 by CERT/CC and ictQATAR. It is Qatar's coordination center in dealing with internet security problems.
gpt_text:
Q-CERT (Qatar Computer Emergency Response Team) is Qatar’s national cybersecurity incident response team, operating under the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. Its core mandate is to enhance the country’s cyber resilience by preventing, detecting, and responding to cybersecurity incidents that affect government entities, critical infrastructure, and, in some cases, private-sector organizations.

Q-CERT’s activities typically include monitoring and analyzing cyber threats, issuing alerts and advisories, coordinating incident response, conducting digital forensics, and promoting best practices and awareness across the country. It also collaborates with international CERTs and security organizations to share threat intelligence and improve Qatar’s overall cybersecurity posture.

title: Ambient authority
human_text: Ambient authority is a term used in the study of access control systems.
gpt_text:
Ambient authority is the implicit permission a program or user has to access resources in its surrounding environment without explicitly being granted that permission for each specific action. It arises from broad, pre-existing privileges—like a user’s file system access, network connectivity, or environment variables—that applications can leverage simply because they are running under that user or system account.  

In security terms, ambient authority is problematic because it blurs the boundary between what a program is *intended* to do and what it *can* do. This makes it harder to enforce the principle of least privilege and easier for bugs or exploits to cause unintended damage. Capability-based security and object-capability systems are often contrasted with ambient authority, as they require explicit, fine-grained delegation of permissions instead of relying on broad, ambient privileges.

title: Intrusion detection system evasion techniques
human_text: Intrusion detection system evasion techniques are modifications made to attacks in order to prevent detection by an intrusion detection system (IDS). Almost all published evasion techniques modify network attacks. The 1998 paper Insertion, Evasion, and Denial of Service: Eluding Network Intrusion Detection popularized IDS evasion, and discussed both evasion techniques and areas where the correct interpretation was ambiguous depending on the targeted computer system. The 'fragroute' and 'fragrouter' programs implement evasion techniques discussed in the paper. Many web vulnerability scanners, such as 'Nikto', 'whisker' and 'Sandcat', also incorporate IDS evasion techniques.
gpt_text:
Intrusion detection system (IDS) evasion techniques are methods attackers use to avoid being detected while probing or compromising networks and hosts. These techniques exploit weaknesses in how IDSs analyze traffic, apply signatures, and correlate events. Common approaches include fragmenting packets or altering protocol fields so that the target system reconstructs traffic differently from the IDS, using encryption or tunneling to hide malicious payloads, and slightly modifying known attack patterns (polymorphism/obfuscation) so they no longer match existing signatures.

Attackers may also slow down or spread out their activities (low-and-slow attacks) to stay below alert thresholds, mimic normal user behavior, or generate large volumes of benign noise to bury malicious events. More advanced techniques target the IDS itself, attempting to overload it, trigger false positives, or exploit configuration gaps between network segments. The goal in all cases is to carry out malicious actions while keeping IDS alerts to a minimum, thereby increasing the chance of a successful, undetected compromise.

title: STRIDE (security)
human_text: STRIDE is a model of threats developed by Praerit Garg and Loren Kohnfelder at Microsoft for identifying computer security threats. It provides a mnemonic for security threats in six categories.
gpt_text:
STRIDE is a threat modeling framework used in computer security to systematically identify and categorize potential threats to a system. The acronym stands for Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege—each representing a different class of attack or security risk. By walking through each STRIDE category for every component or data flow in a system, security analysts can uncover where controls are needed.

In practice, STRIDE helps teams think like an attacker during design and review phases, rather than waiting for vulnerabilities to appear in production. It’s commonly used alongside data flow diagrams to map out how data moves through a system and what could go wrong at each step, guiding the selection of appropriate mitigations such as authentication, integrity checks, logging, access control, and resource limiting.

title: Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol
human_text: Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol (SCEP) is an IETF RFC. This protocol is used by numerous manufacturers of network equipment and software who are developing simplified means of handling certificates for large-scale implementation to everyday users, as well as being referenced in other industry standards.
gpt_text:
The Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol (SCEP) is a network protocol used to automate the process of requesting, issuing, and renewing digital certificates, typically from a certificate authority (CA). It was originally developed by Cisco to simplify certificate deployment for devices such as routers, switches, and other network equipment, and is now commonly used in large-scale environments to manage certificates for many devices with minimal manual intervention.

SCEP works by allowing a client (like a device or application) to generate a key pair, create a certificate signing request (CSR), and securely submit it to a CA over HTTP or HTTPS. The CA then validates the request and returns a signed certificate. While SCEP is widely supported and easy to implement, it is considered less feature-rich and secure compared to newer protocols such as EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport), particularly in areas like strong authentication and modern cryptographic methods.

title: LAIM Working Group
human_text: The LAIM (Log Anonymization and Information Management) Working Group is a NSF and ONR funded research group at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications under the direction of Adam Slagell. Work from this group focuses upon log anonymization and Internet privacy. The LAIM group, established in 2005, has released 3 different log anonymization tools: CANINE, Scrub-PA, and FLAIM. FLAIM is their only tool still under active development.

The LAIM Working Group (Language and AI Model Working Group) typically refers to a collaborative body focused on the development, evaluation, and standardization of language-based AI models and their applications. Such a group usually brings together researchers, engineers, policy experts, and stakeholders to address technical challenges (like benchmarks, safety, robustness, and interpretability) and to define shared best practices or guidelines for working with large language models.

Depending on the specific organization hosting it, a LAIM Working Group may also concentrate on governance issues: data sourcing and documentation, transparency around model capabilities and limitations, alignment with ethical and regulatory frameworks, and ensuring responsible deployment in real-world settings. Its work often results in reports, standards, or open resources that are intended to guide the broader AI community.

title: NOP slide
human_text: In computer security, a NOP slide, NOP sled or NOP ramp is a sequence of NOP (no-operation) instructions meant to "slide" the CPU's instruction execution flow to its final, desired destination whenever the program branches to a memory address anywhere on the slide.
gpt_text:
A NOP slide (or NOP sled) is a sequence of No-Operation (NOP) instructions placed in memory, commonly used in exploit development. Since each NOP does nothing but advance execution to the next instruction, if the processor’s instruction pointer lands anywhere within this sequence, it will “slide” through the NOPs until it reaches the payload (malicious code) at the end.

In classic stack-based buffer overflow attacks, NOP slides help compensate for uncertainty in the exact address of the injected shellcode. By filling a large region with NOPs before the shellcode, attackers increase the chance that an approximate jump address will still lead execution into the slide and eventually into the intended payload.

title: Security breach notification laws
human_text: Security breach notification laws or data breach notification laws are laws that require individuals or entities affected by a data breach, unauthorized access to data,to notify their customers and other parties about the breach, as well as take specific steps to remedy the situation based on state legislature. Data breach notification laws have two main goals. The first goal is to allow individuals a chance to mitigate risks against data breaches. The second goal is to promote company incentive to strengthen data security.Together, these goals work to minimize consumer harm from data breaches, including impersonation, fraud, and identity theft.
gpt_text:
Security breach notification laws require organizations to inform affected individuals and, often, regulators or other authorities when certain types of personal or sensitive data are exposed in a security incident. These laws typically define what constitutes a “breach,” what kinds of data are covered (such as Social Security numbers, financial account details, health information, or login credentials), and the timelines and methods for providing notice. They aim to give people a chance to protect themselves—for example, by changing passwords, monitoring accounts, or freezing credit.

Such laws exist at national, state, and regional levels, and their specific requirements vary widely by jurisdiction. Common elements include obligations to investigate potential breaches, maintain records, notify impacted parties “without unreasonable delay,” and sometimes communicate with regulators, law enforcement, consumer protection agencies, or credit bureaus. Noncompliance can result in fines, enforcement actions, lawsuits, and reputational damage.

title: Operation: Bot Roast
human_text: Operation: Bot Roast is an operation by the FBI to track down bot herders, crackers, or virus coders who install malicious software on computers through the Internet without the owners' knowledge, which turns the computer into a zombie computer that then sends out spam to other computers from the compromised computer, making a botnet or network of bot infected computers. The operation was launched because the vast scale of botnet resources poses a threat to national security.

“Operation: Bot Roast” is a U.S. Department of Justice initiative focused on identifying, exposing, and prosecuting individuals and organizations that use automated social media accounts—“bots”—to spread disinformation, commit fraud, or otherwise manipulate online discourse. The name is often used informally to describe efforts to “smoke out” and dismantle large-scale bot networks that, for example, impersonate real users, amplify propaganda, or run scams. While specific details vary by case, actions under this banner tend to combine technical investigation (such as tracing IP addresses and infrastructure) with traditional law enforcement tools like subpoenas, search warrants, and criminal charges.

title: WS-Trust
human_text: WS-Trust is a WS- specification and OASIS standard that provides extensions to WS-Security, specifically dealing with the issuing, renewing, and validating of security tokens, as well as with ways to establish, assess the presence of, and broker trust relationships between participants in a secure message exchange.
gpt_text:
WS-Trust (Web Services Trust Language) is a specification from the WS-* (Web Services) family that defines how to establish, assess, and broker trust relationships in distributed, service-oriented environments. It extends WS-Security by describing a protocol for issuing, renewing, and validating security tokens, and for exchanging these tokens between clients and services through a specialized web service called a Security Token Service (STS).  

In practice, WS-Trust enables scenarios like single sign-on and federated identity across organizational boundaries, where a client obtains a security token from an STS and presents it to a target service as proof of identity or authorization. It defines standard message formats (e.g., RequestSecurityToken and RequestSecurityTokenResponse) and interaction patterns so that different systems can interoperate securely, even if they use different underlying authentication mechanisms.

title: HTTP tunnel
human_text: HTTP tunneling is used to create a network link between two computers in conditions of restricted network connectivity including firewalls, NATs and ACLs, among other restrictions. The tunnel is created by an intermediary called a proxy server which is usually located in a DMZ.
gpt_text:
An HTTP tunnel is a method of encapsulating network traffic inside HTTP requests and responses so that it can pass through firewalls, proxies, or restrictive networks that normally only allow web traffic (ports 80/443). Instead of communicating directly, one endpoint sends data as the body of an HTTP message to an intermediary (like a proxy), which then forwards the encapsulated data to the intended destination, and vice versa.

This technique is often used to carry non-HTTP protocols (such as SSH or other TCP-based services) over HTTP, making them appear as regular web traffic. While useful for bypassing network restrictions and enabling secure remote access, HTTP tunneling can also be abused to circumvent security policies or exfiltrate data, so it’s a focus of network monitoring and security controls.

title: WS-Federation
human_text: WS-Federation (Web Services Federation) is an Identity Federation specification, developed by a group of companies: BEA Systems, BMC Software, CA Inc. (along with Layer 7 Technologies now a part of CA Inc.), IBM, Microsoft, Novell, HP Enterprise, and VeriSign. Part of the larger Web Services Security framework, WS-Federation defines mechanisms for allowing different security realms to broker information on identities, identity attributes and authentication.
gpt_text:
WS-Federation (Web Services Federation Language) is a specification in the WS-* (Web Services) family that defines how different security realms can share identity and authentication information. It enables single sign-on (SSO) and identity federation between web applications and services, typically across organizational boundaries, by allowing a user authenticated in one security domain to access resources in another without re-authenticating.

Built on top of WS-Trust and other WS-Security standards, WS-Federation uses Security Token Services (STS) to issue, validate, and exchange security tokens (such as SAML tokens). It has been widely used in enterprise environments, for example to integrate on-premises Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) with various web applications, though in many modern scenarios it’s increasingly complemented or replaced by protocols like OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

title: Collaboration-oriented architecture
human_text: Collaboration Oriented Architecture (COA) is a computer system that is designed to collaborate, or use services, from systems that are outside of the operators control. Collaboration Oriented Architecture will often use Service Oriented Architecture to deliver the technical framework.
gpt_text:
Collaboration-oriented architecture is an approach to designing systems, organizations, or software in which the primary goal is to enable effective collaboration among people, teams, or services. Instead of focusing only on individual components or technical efficiency, it emphasizes shared workflows, clear interaction patterns, and communication channels that make it easy for participants to work together toward common goals.

In software and enterprise design, this often means structuring systems around shared data, co-authoring tools, real-time communication, and interoperable services, so that information flows smoothly and responsibilities are clearly distributed. It also tends to incorporate social and organizational factors—such as roles, trust, and governance—directly into the architecture, ensuring that technology and human collaboration practices reinforce each other.

title: WS-SecurityPolicy
human_text: WS-SecurityPolicy is a web services specification, created by IBM and 12 co-authors, that has become an OASIS standard as of version 1.2. It extends the fundamental security protocols specified by the WS-Security, WS-Trust and WS-SecureConversation by offering mechanisms to represent the capabilities and requirements of web services as policies. Security policy assertions are based on the WS-Policy framework.
gpt_text:
WS-SecurityPolicy is an OASIS standard that defines how to express security requirements and capabilities for web services using a machine-readable policy language. It extends the generic WS-Policy framework with specific assertions related to security, such as which authentication mechanisms to use, what kind of encryption or signing is required, and which security tokens (e.g., X.509 certificates, SAML tokens, UsernameTokens) are supported.

title: Clear channel assessment attack

An attacker can periodically transmit short, low-rate or carefully crafted signals that make the channel seem perpetually busy without needing to send large amounts of data.

Because honest devices keep detecting a “busy” medium, they back off repeatedly, which increases latency, reduces throughput, and can effectively starve legitimate traffic. title: National White Collar Crime Center

title: In-session phishing

Because the fraudulent prompt appears to come from the site the user is currently using—like a bank, email provider, or corporate portal—victims are more likely to trust it and enter credentials, payment details, or other confidential data. title: Opal Storage Specification
human_text: The Opal Storage Specification is a set of specifications for features of data storage devices (such as disk drives) that enhance their security. For example, it defines a way of encrypting the stored data so that an unauthorized person who gains possession of the device cannot see the data. That is, it is a specification for self-encrypting drives (SED).

title: Racetrack problem
human_text: A racetrack problem is a specific instance of a type of race condition. A racetrack problem is a flaw in a system or process whereby the output and/or result of the process is unexpectedly and critically dependent on the sequence or timing of other events that run in a circular pattern. This problem is semantically different from a race condition because of the circular nature of the problem.
gpt_text:

The car’s state typically includes its position and velocity, and its actions involve changing acceleration in discrete steps. Because the car has momentum, it can’t stop or turn instantly, making the problem about planning a sequence of moves that respects both the track boundaries and the physics-like motion constraints.

This problem is often modeled as a Markov Decision Process and used to study reinforcement learning, search algorithms, and optimal control strategies. Solutions explore how an agent can learn or compute an optimal policy that balances speed with safety, sometimes under uncertainty (e.g., stochastic movement or noise in actions), making it a useful benchmark for decision-making in dynamic environments.

title: Principal (computer security)
human_text: A principal in computer security is an entity that can be authenticated by a computer system or network. It is referred to as a security principal in Java and Microsoft literature."What Are Security Principals?", docs.microsoft.com, 19 April 2017.

Principals are central to access control: when a principal attempts an action (like reading a file or invoking an API), the system checks that principal’s identity and privileges against security policies. title: DREAD (risk assessment model)

In practice, DREAD is used during threat modeling or vulnerability triage to compare and rank issues so teams can focus first on the most serious risks. Although it was popular in the 2000s, DREAD has since fallen out of favor in some organizations because of concerns about subjectivity and inconsistent scoring between reviewers; many teams now prefer simpler or more prescriptive models such as STRIDE (for classification) and standard risk matrices combining likelihood and impact.

title: Predictable serial number attack
human_text: A predictable serial number attack is a form of security exploit in which the algorithm for generating serial numbers for a particular purpose is guessed, discovered, or reverse engineered, a new serial number is predicted using the algorithm, and the newly generated serial number is then used for a fraudulent purpose, either to obtain an undeserved benefit or to deny service to the legitimate holder of the serial number.

If these values increase sequentially or follow a visible rule (like 1001, 1002, 1003), an attacker can systematically guess other valid values and access data or actions that belong to other users.

This type of vulnerability often leads to unauthorized access to sensitive information (like invoices, tickets, or account details), unauthorized actions (like confirming someone else’s order or resetting another user’s password), or even large-scale data scraping. Secure systems defend against this by using sufficiently long, random, and unguessable identifiers—often cryptographically generated—rather than predictable sequences.

title: Cyber spying

title: TCP reset attack
human_text: TCP reset attack, also known as "forged TCP resets", "spoofed TCP reset packets" or "TCP reset attacks", is a way to tamper and terminate the Internet connection by sending a forged TCP reset packet. This attack exploits how TCP trusts network-layer information and its own sequence number logic. It can be used to forcibly close web sessions, VPN tunnels, BGP sessions between routers, or other long-lived TCP connections. Defenses include using encrypted tunnels that authenticate packets (e.g., IPsec), tighter router/firewall filtering, TCP sequence number randomization, and application-level mechanisms that tolerate or recover from unexpected connection resets.

title: Vanish (computer science)

title: Heap feng shui
human_text: In computer security, heap feng shui (also known as heap grooming) is a technique used in exploits to facilitate arbitrary code execution. title: Return-oriented programming

title: Fail-stop
human_text: A fail-stop subset of a computer language is one that has the same semantics as the original, except in the case where an exceptional condition arises. The fail-stop subset must report an exceptional condition whenever the superset language reports one, but may additionally report an exceptional condition in other cases.

This assumption simplifies fault-tolerant design, because the system never has to deal with subtle or malicious misbehavior—only clean, obvious stoppages. Many algorithms for replication, consensus, and reliable storage are easier to design and reason about under a fail-stop failure model, even though real hardware and software often behave in more complex ways.

title: Trademark (computer security)
human_text: A Trademark in computer security is a contract between code that verifies security properties of an object and code that requires that an object have certain security properties. title: HTTP Strict Transport Security
human_text: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a web security policy mechanism that helps to protect websites against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrade attacks and cookie hijacking. It allows web servers to declare that web browsers (or other complying user agents) should automatically interact with it using only HTTPS connections, which provide Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL), unlike the insecure HTTP used alone. HSTS is an IETF standards track protocol and is specified in RFC 6797.

This protects against attacks like protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking via man‑in‑the‑middle interference, especially on insecure networks. title: FIPS 140-3
human_text: The Federal Information Processing Standard Publication 140-3, (FIPS PUB 140-3), is a U.S. government computer security standard used to approve cryptographic modules. The title is Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules. Initial publication was on March 22, 2019 and it supersedes FIPS 140-2.

title: Linked timestamping
human_text: Linked timestamping is a type of trusted timestamping where issued time-stamps are related to each other.

It works by arranging timestamped data items into a chain or tree structure where each timestamp includes cryptographic information (such as a hash) from previous timestamps, “linking” them together. This makes it computationally infeasible to alter a past record without breaking the entire chain of timestamps that follow.

Because each new timestamp depends on the previous ones, linked timestamping creates a verifiable, tamper-evident history of data over time. Early forms of this idea—using hash chains and hash trees—are foundational to modern blockchain systems, which extend linked timestamping concepts to build decentralized ledgers for cryptocurrencies and other applications.

title: Cloud computing security
human_text: Cloud computing security or, more simply, cloud security refers to a broad set of policies, technologies, applications, and controls utilized to protect virtualized IP, data, applications, services, and the associated infrastructure of cloud computing. title: Cross-application scripting

title: Mayfield's paradox

title: System Service Descriptor Table

title: Length extension attack
human_text: In cryptography and computer security, a length extension attack is a type of attack where an attacker can use Hash(message1) and the length of message1 to calculate Hash(message1 ‖ message2) for an attacker-controlled message2, without needing to know the content of message1. Algorithms like MD5, SHA-1 and most of SHA-2 that are based on the Merkle–Damgård construction are susceptible to this kind of attack. Truncated versions of SHA-2, including SHA-384 and SHA256/512 are not susceptible, nor is the SHA-3 algorithm.

In these schemes, if an attacker knows `hash(message)` and the length of `message`, they can often compute `hash(message || extra_data)` without knowing the original message content or the secret key (if the key is simply prepended), by exploiting how the hash’s internal state and padding work.

This becomes dangerous when a system naively uses `hash(secret || message)` as a message authentication method. An attacker who sees the tag (the hash output) for some message can forge a valid tag for a longer, modified message by “extending” it, effectively bypassing integrity checks. Proper defenses include using HMAC (which is not vulnerable to length extension) or using hash functions/modes not based on Merkle–Damgård, or carefully structuring how secrets and messages are combined.

title: Macro and security

title: Pre-play attack
human_text: In the field of security engineering, a pre-play attack is a cryptographic attack in which an attacker prepares for the attack in advance by carrying out a simulated transaction while pretending to be the device to be attacked, and then repeats the attack a second time with the real device at a time when it is likely to carry out the same series of operations as in the simulation. The technique relies on being able to guess the content of the transaction in advance, something usually made possible by a poor choice of unpredictability within the system. The name is a play on "replay attack". Pre-play attacks are not very effective and chances of success are slim.

When the real protocol run happens, the attacker “plays” these precomputed messages as if they were fresh, tricking the system into accepting them as legitimate. This exploits weak randomness, predictable counters, or any mechanism where future values can be anticipated.

Unlike a replay attack, which reuses previously recorded messages, a pre-play attack doesn’t need prior traffic; it relies on guessing or influencing future protocol data before it is actually used. This kind of vulnerability has appeared in systems like contactless payment cards and authentication protocols where nonces or transaction counters are either predictable, reused, or poorly generated.

title: Malware analysis

title: Buffer over-read
human_text: In computer security and programming, a buffer over-read is an anomaly where a program, while reading data from a buffer, overruns the buffer's boundary and reads (or tries to read) adjacent memory. This is a special case of violation of memory safety.

Unlike a buffer overflow, which writes beyond boundaries, an over-read only reads, but it can still expose sensitive information or cause crashes.

Buffer over-reads are common in low-level languages like C and C++ where memory management is manual and bounds checking is not enforced by default. They can lead to information disclosure (e.g., leaking contents of adjacent memory), undefined behavior, and security vulnerabilities that attackers might exploit to gain insights into program state, cryptographic keys, or other confidential data.

title: Weird machine

title: Security type system
human_text: In computer science, a type system can be described as a syntactic framework which contains a set of rules that are used to assign a type property (int, boolean, char etc.) to various components of a computer program, such as variables or functions. A security type system works in a similar way, only with a main focus on the security of the computer program, through information flow control. Thus, the various components of the program are assigned security types, or labels. The aim of a such system is to ultimately be able to verify that a given program conforms to the type system rules and satisfies non-interference. The type checker then enforces rules—for example, that high-confidentiality data cannot flow into low-confidentiality outputs—so that certain classes of security violations are ruled out at compile time.

This approach allows formal guarantees such as noninterference, meaning that secret inputs cannot influence public outputs as far as the type system can see. Security type systems underlie languages and tools for secure programming, where security policies are encoded into the type discipline itself, making many violations syntactically or statically impossible rather than relying solely on runtime checks or external audits.

title: Language-based security

Examples include type systems that prevent buffer overflows, memory-safe languages that eliminate use-after-free bugs, and information-flow type systems that stop secret data from leaking to public outputs.

By reasoning about code at the language level, these techniques can provide strong, often provable guarantees about program behavior, such as absence of certain classes of vulnerabilities. This can reduce the reliance on ad hoc checks and make security properties easier to analyze, compose, and maintain as software evolves.

title: Project Zero
human_text: Project Zero is a team of security analysts employed by Google tasked with finding zero-day vulnerabilities. It was announced on 15 July 2014.

Project Zero is a security research team created by Google in 2014 to find and report critical software vulnerabilities—especially so-called “zero-day” exploits that are unknown to vendors and actively used by attackers. The team analyzes widely used software, operating systems, browsers, and hardware, then privately discloses bugs to the relevant companies and works with them under a defined disclosure policy and timeline (usually 90 days) to get issues fixed.  

Project Zero has had a major impact on modern cybersecurity, uncovering high-profile vulnerabilities like the Spectre and Meltdown CPU flaws and numerous browser and messaging app exploits. By systematically hunting for bugs and publishing detailed technical write-ups after patches are available, the team helps improve the overall security of the internet ecosystem and pushes vendors to adopt more robust security practices.

title: Adversarial machine learning
human_text: Adversarial machine learning is a machine learning technique that attempts to fool models by supplying deceptive input. The most common reason is to cause a malfunction in a machine learning model.
gpt_text:
Adversarial machine learning is a subfield of AI focused on how machine learning models can be intentionally manipulated or attacked, and how to defend them. It studies “adversarial examples” (inputs that are subtly modified to fool models while appearing normal to humans), data poisoning (corrupting training data), model stealing, and other techniques that degrade model performance or compromise confidentiality and integrity.

Research in this area aims both to understand the vulnerabilities of learning algorithms and to build more robust systems. This includes developing training methods that resist adversarial examples, detection mechanisms for attacks, and evaluation frameworks to measure robustness. Adversarial machine learning is especially important in security-sensitive applications like biometrics, autonomous driving, and content moderation.

title: User activity monitoring
human_text: In the field of information security, user activity monitoring (UAM) is the monitoring and recording of user actions. UAM captures user actions, including the use of applications, windows opened, system commands executed, checkboxes clicked, text entered/edited, URLs visited and nearly every other on-screen event to protect data by ensuring that employees and contractors are staying within their assigned tasks, and posing no risk to the organization.
gpt_text:
User activity monitoring is the process of tracking, recording, and analyzing how users interact with systems, networks, applications, or websites. It can include logging keystrokes, visited URLs, files accessed, applications used, login times, and actions taken within specific software. Organizations use this data to improve security, productivity, compliance, and troubleshooting by detecting unusual or unauthorized behavior.

In cybersecurity and compliance contexts, user activity monitoring helps identify insider threats, data exfiltration, and policy violations, as well as demonstrate adherence to regulations. Because it can involve sensitive personal data and detailed behavioral records, it must be implemented with clear policies, legal compliance, and respect for privacy, often including transparency with users about what is being monitored and why.

title: Hyperjacking
human_text: Hyperjacking is an attack in which a hacker takes malicious control over the hypervisor that creates the virtual environment within a virtual machine (VM) host. The point of the attack is to target the operating system that is below that of the virtual machines so that the attacker's program can run and the applications on the VMs above it will be completely oblivious to its presence.
gpt_text:
Hyperjacking is a type of cyberattack in which an attacker compromises a hypervisor—the software layer that creates and manages virtual machines (VMs)—to gain control over all the virtual environments running on it. Because the hypervisor sits beneath the guest operating systems, a successful hyperjacking attack allows the attacker to monitor, manipulate, or fully control multiple VMs without being easily detected by traditional security tools inside those VMs.

This attack can be carried out by exploiting vulnerabilities in virtualization platforms, installing a malicious hypervisor beneath an existing OS (a “virtual machine based rootkit”), or tampering with management interfaces and APIs used to control virtual infrastructure. Hyperjacking is particularly dangerous in cloud and data center environments, where many critical workloads share the same physical hosts, making the hypervisor a highly valuable target.

title: Army Chief Information Officer/G-6
human_text: The United States Army chief information officer/G-6 (CIO/G-6) was a dual role, reporting both to the secretary of the Army as CIO, and also to the chief of staff of the Army as G-6.LTG Robert Ferrell, USA Army CIO/G-6 overview 15 Feb 2015 The roles were realigned in 2020.

As a headquarters-level staff element, the CIO/G-6 develops policies, standards, and architectures for Army networks and systems, and synchronizes efforts with joint, interagency, and coalition partners. title: US Cyber Challenge
human_text: US Cyber Challenge is a private-public partnership program dedicated to finding high level cybersecurity talent in its endeavor to significantly reduce the shortage in today's cyber workforce. The program identifies, attracts, recruits and trains the next generation of cybersecurity professionals. US Cyber Challenge is currently a program under the Council for CyberSecurity and the Center for Internet Security.

title: Information Sharing and Analysis Center
human_text: An Information Sharing and Analysis Center or (ISAC) is a nonprofit organization that provides a central resource for gathering information on cyber threats to critical infrastructure and providing two-way sharing of information between the private and public sector.
gpt_text:
An Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) is an industry-specific organization that facilitates the collection, analysis, and sharing of cybersecurity and threat information among its members and with relevant government agencies. ISACs help critical infrastructure sectors—such as finance, energy, healthcare, and transportation—quickly disseminate alerts about cyber threats, vulnerabilities, and incidents so members can strengthen their defenses and coordinate responses.

Typically, ISACs operate as trusted, membership-based communities where organizations share sensitive information under agreed rules and protections. They often provide threat intelligence reports, secure communication channels, incident response coordination, and best practices, thereby improving the overall resilience and situational awareness of an entire sector.

title: Software Guard Extensions
human_text: Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) is a set of security-related instruction codes that are built into some modern Intel central processing units (CPUs). They allow user-level as well as operating system code to define private regions of memory, called enclaves, whose contents are protected and unable to be either read or saved by any process outside the enclave itself, including processes running at higher privilege levels.
gpt_text:
Software Guard Extensions (SGX) is an Intel processor technology that provides hardware-based memory encryption to isolate specific application code and data in protected regions of memory called enclaves. Even if an attacker gains full control of the operating system, hypervisor, or physical machine, the contents of these enclaves remain confidential and tamper-resistant.

SGX enables secure execution of sensitive workloads—such as cryptographic operations, key management, or confidential computation—by minimizing the trusted computing base. It also supports remote attestation, allowing a remote party to verify that specific trusted code is running inside a genuine SGX enclave before sharing secrets or data.

title: Bank Verification Number
human_text: The Bank Verification Number commonly called BVN is a biometric identification system implemented by the Central Bank of Nigeria to curb or reduce illegal banking transactions in Nigeria. It is a modern security measure in line with the Central Bank of Nigeria Act 1958 to reduce fraud in the banking system.
gpt_text:
A Bank Verification Number (BVN) is an 11-digit unique identifier assigned to customers of Nigerian banks by the Central Bank of Nigeria. It links all of a customer’s bank accounts across different banks to a single identity, using biometric data such as fingerprints and facial images to verify and protect the customer’s financial profile.

The BVN system is designed to reduce fraud, enhance the security of electronic payments, and improve the overall integrity of the banking system. With a BVN, banks can more accurately confirm a person’s identity, track suspicious activity, and comply with “Know Your Customer” (KYC) and anti–money laundering regulations.

title: ERP security
human_text: ERP Security is a wide range of measures aimed at protecting Enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems from illicit access ensuring accessibility and integrity of system data. ERP system is a computer software that serves to unify the information intended to manage the organization including Production, Supply Chain Management, Financial Management, Human Resource Management, Customer Relationship Management, Enterprise Performance Management. Common ERP systems are SAP, Oracle E-Business Suite, Microsoft Dynamics.

ERP security refers to the practices, technologies, and policies used to protect enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and the sensitive data they handle. Because ERP platforms centralize critical business functions—such as finance, HR, supply chain, and customer data—they are high‑value targets for cyberattacks and insider misuse. Effective ERP security ensures confidentiality, integrity, and availability of this information while supporting regulatory compliance and business continuity.

Key elements of ERP security include strong access controls and role-based permissions, secure configuration and patch management, encryption of data in transit and at rest, continuous monitoring and logging of system activity, and segregation of duties to prevent fraud. It also involves regular security assessments, user training, incident response planning, and integration with broader enterprise security tools (such as identity and access management and SIEM systems).

title: European Information Technologies Certification

EITC programs are typically designed to be modular, accessible, and aligned with European educational and labor market standards, making them suitable for students, professionals, and career changers. title: Exploit kit
human_text: An exploit kit is simply a collection of exploits, which is a simple one-in-all tool for managing a variety of exploits altogether. Exploit kits act as a kind of repository, and make it easy for users without much technical knowledge to use exploits. Users can add their own exploits to it and use them simultaneously apart from the pre-installed ones.
gpt_text:
An exploit kit is a pre-packaged set of malicious tools used by cybercriminals to automatically find and exploit vulnerabilities on a victim’s device, typically when the victim visits a compromised or malicious website. The kit scans the visiting system for known software flaws—often in browsers, plugins, or outdated applications—and, if it finds a match, silently delivers malware such as ransomware, spyware, or banking trojans.

Exploit kits are usually sold or rented on underground markets as “crimeware-as-a-service,” making it easier even for less technically skilled attackers to launch large-scale, automated campaigns. They are frequently updated to incorporate new exploits, and defenders counter them by patching software promptly, using security tools like web filters and intrusion prevention systems, and disabling or removing unnecessary browser plugins.

title: HDIV
human_text: HDIV is a Web Application Security Framework that controls the information flow between the server and the client avoiding many of the most important web risks. HDIV extends web applications behaviour by adding security functionalities, maintaining the API and the framework specification. This implies that HDIV may be used in applications developed in Spring MVC, Grails, JSTL, Struts 1, Struts 2, JavaServer Faces, Symfony in a transparent way to the programmer and without adding any complexity to the application development.
gpt_text:
HDIV (HTTP Data Integrity Validator) is a security framework that focuses on protecting web applications against common vulnerabilities by enforcing data integrity and confidentiality at the server side. It works by automatically validating and securing all data exchanged between the client and the server—such as parameters, hidden fields, and links—so that they cannot be tampered with or manipulated by attackers.

Typically used in Java-based web applications, HDIV integrates into the application’s lifecycle to provide protections against issues like parameter tampering, CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery), and some injection attacks. By maintaining a server-side state and cryptographically validating client-side data, it reduces the need for developers to write extensive manual validation logic, strengthening security while minimizing code changes.

title: KeyRaider
human_text: KeyRaider is computer malware that affects jailbroken Apple iOS devices, specifically iPhones, and allows criminals to steal users' login and password information, as well as to lock the devices and demand a ransom to unlock them. It was discovered by researchers from Palo Alto Networks and WeiPhone in August 2015, and is believed to have led to more than 225,000 people having their login and password information being stolen, making it, according to cybersecurity columnist, Joseph Steinberg, "one of the most damaging pieces of malware ever discovered in the Apple universe." The malware was originally found on a Chinese website, but has spread to 18 countries including the United States. KeyRaider affects only iPhones that have been jailbroken.
gpt_text:
KeyRaider is a piece of iOS malware that specifically targets jailbroken iPhones and iPads. Distributed mainly through unauthorized Cydia repositories, it hooks into system processes to steal Apple ID credentials, device GUIDs, and push notification certificates, and can also intercept iTunes traffic. The stolen information is then uploaded to a remote server controlled by the attackers.

Beyond credential theft, KeyRaider has been used to enable large-scale piracy of App Store purchases by allowing others to download paid apps for free using the compromised accounts. It can also remotely lock infected devices and demand ransom. Discovered around 2015, KeyRaider highlighted the significant security risks associated with jailbreaking and installing untrusted third‑party tweaks.

title: National Cybersecurity FFRDC
human_text: The National Cybersecurity FFRDC (NCF) is a federally funded research and development center operated by MITRE Corporation. It supports the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)'s National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence. NCF is the first and, as of March 2017, only federally funded research and development center dedicated solely to cybersecurity. The National Cybersecurity FFRDC is located at 9700 Great Seneca Hwy in Rockville, Maryland.
