title: Bridging model
human_text: In computer science, a bridging model is an abstract model of a computer which provides a conceptual bridge between the physical implementation of the machine and the abstraction available to a programmer of that machine; in other words, it is intended to provide a common level of understanding between hardware and software engineers.

title: Comparison of instruction set architectures
human_text: An instruction set architecture (ISA) is an abstract model of a computer, also referred to as computer architecture. A realization of an ISA is called an implementation. An ISA permits multiple implementations that may vary in performance, physical size, and monetary cost (among other things); because the ISA serves as the interface between software and hardware. Software that has been written for an ISA can run on different implementations of the same ISA. This has enabled binary compatibility between different generations of computers to be easily achieved, and the development of computer families. Both of these developments have helped to lower the cost of computers and to increase their applicability. For these reasons, the ISA is one of the most important abstractions in computing today.
gpt_text:
Comparison of instruction set architectures (ISAs) examines how different designs define the commands a processor can execute, and how those choices affect performance, power, complexity, and ease of programming or compilation. Key contrasts include RISC vs. CISC (few simple, fixed-length instructions vs. many complex, often variable-length ones), register-based vs. stack-based designs, and differing approaches to addressing modes, data types, and control flow. These differences influence how efficiently code can be generated, how well hardware can be pipelined and parallelized, and how easily the ISA can evolve over time.

In practice, comparing ISAs like x86-64, ARM, RISC-V, and others involves looking at instruction encoding density, backward compatibility, support for specialized extensions (e.g., SIMD, cryptography), and ecosystem maturity (compilers, tools, and software support). Design trade-offs show up in real-world metrics such as performance per watt, silicon area, and how well the architecture scales from tiny embedded systems to large servers.

title: Manycore processor
human_text: Manycore processors are specialist multi-core processors designed for a high degree of parallel processing, containing numerous simpler, independent processor cores (from a few tens of cores to thousands or more). Manycore processors are used extensively in embedded computers and high-performance computing.
gpt_text:

Unlike traditional multicore processors, which focus on a small number of powerful, general-purpose cores, manycore designs emphasize a high degree of parallelism with many simpler, energy-efficient cores working together.

These processors are especially suited to workloads that can be broken into many parallel tasks, such as scientific simulations, graphics rendering, machine learning, and high-performance computing. They often require specialized programming models and tools to efficiently distribute work across all cores, and may include high-speed on-chip networks and memory hierarchies optimized for massive parallelism.

title: Instruction window

title: Load–store architecture
human_text: In computer engineering, a load–store architecture is an instruction set architecture that divides instructions into two categories: memory access (load and store between memory and registers), and ALU operations (which only occur between registers).
gpt_text:
A load–store architecture is a type of CPU design in which only specific instructions can access memory: **load** instructions move data from memory into registers, and **store** instructions move data from registers back to memory. All other operations—such as arithmetic, logic, and comparisons—operate solely on data already held in registers. This contrasts with architectures where arithmetic instructions can directly read from or write to memory.

This approach simplifies the instruction set and hardware control logic, often enabling faster pipelines, more consistent instruction timing, and easier optimization by compilers. Most RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processors—such as classic MIPS, ARM (in its RISC modes), and RISC-V—use a load–store model to achieve high performance and efficiency.

title: Register memory architecture
human_text: In computer engineering, a register–memory architecture is an instruction set architecture that allows operations to be performed on (or from) memory, as well as registers. If the architecture allows all operands to be in memory or in registers, or in combinations, it is called a "register plus memory" architecture.
gpt_text:
Register memory architecture refers to the way a computer’s processor uses small, fast storage locations called registers to hold data and instructions that are being actively processed. Registers sit at the top of the memory hierarchy—much faster but far fewer in number than cache or main memory—and are directly accessed by the CPU’s instruction set. Typical register types include general-purpose registers for arithmetic and logic operations, special-purpose registers like the program counter and stack pointer, and status registers that track conditions such as zero or carry flags.

In many instruction set architectures (ISAs), the design and number of registers strongly influence performance and programming style. For example, load–store architectures (like classic RISC designs) restrict memory access to dedicated load and store instructions, forcing most computation to occur only on register contents. This emphasizes efficient register allocation and minimizes slow memory accesses, which is crucial for high-speed execution.

title: Vectored interrupt
human_text: In computer science, a vectored interrupt is a processing technique in which the interrupting device directs the processor to the appropriate interrupt service routine. This is in contrast to a polled interrupt system, in which a single interrupt service routine must determine the source of the interrupt by checking all potential interrupt sources, a slow and relatively laborious process.
gpt_text:
A vectored interrupt is a hardware interrupt mechanism in which each interrupt source is associated with a specific memory address (an interrupt vector) that directly points to its interrupt service routine (ISR). When an interrupt occurs, the processor automatically fetches the address from a predefined table (the interrupt vector table) and jumps straight to the corresponding handler, rather than having to execute extra code to identify which device caused the interrupt.

This approach speeds up interrupt handling and simplifies software design, because the dispatching of interrupts to their handlers is largely handled by hardware and the vector table. Vectored interrupts are common in microcontrollers, embedded systems, and modern CPUs that support advanced interrupt controllers.

title: Xputer

This flexibility allows applications to either explicitly allocate critical data in high‑bandwidth memory or rely on the hardware to cache frequently used data, improving performance where memory bandwidth is the main bottleneck.

title: Cache control instruction
human_text: In computing, a cache control instruction is a hint embedded in the instruction stream of a processor intended to improve the performance of hardware caches, using foreknowledge of the memory access pattern supplied by the programmer or compiler. They may reduce cache pollution, reduce bandwidth requirement, bypass latencies, by providing better control over the working set. Most cache control instructions do not affect the semantics of a program, although some can.
gpt_text:
A cache control instruction is a directive—usually sent in HTTP headers—that tells browsers and intermediary caches (like CDNs or proxy servers) how to store and reuse a response. These instructions determine whether a resource can be cached, how long it remains valid, when it must be revalidated with the origin server, and under what conditions it should be considered stale.

Common cache-control directives include `max-age` (how many seconds a resource is fresh), `no-cache` (must be revalidated before reuse), `no-store` (must not be saved at all), `public` (cacheable by any cache), and `private` (only by the end user’s browser). By tuning these settings, developers can improve performance and reduce server load while still ensuring that users see up-to-date content.

title: Directory-based cache coherence
human_text: In computer engineering, directory-based cache coherence is a type of cache coherence mechanism, where directories are used to manage caches in place of snoopy methods due to their scalability. Bus snooping methods scale poorly due to the use of broadcasting. These methods can be used to target both performance and scalability of directory systems.
gpt_text:
Directory-based cache coherence is a method used in multiprocessor systems to keep data in multiple caches consistent without relying on a single shared bus for snooping. Instead of having every cache watch all memory transactions, a central (or distributed) directory keeps track of which processors currently hold a copy of each memory block and whether any of them has it in a modified (dirty) state. When a processor wants to read or write a cache line, it consults the directory, which then coordinates invalidations, updates, or data transfers as needed.

This approach scales better than bus-based snooping as the number of processors grows, because it reduces broadcast traffic and contention on a shared bus. However, it requires extra storage for the directory metadata and more complex protocols to manage the states of cache lines and the communication between processors and the directory.

title: Directory-based coherence
human_text: Directory-based coherence is a mechanism to handle Cache coherence problem in Distributed shared memory (DSM) a.k.a. Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA). Another popular way is to use a special type of computer bus between all the nodes as a "shared bus" (a.k.a. System bus). Directory-based coherence uses a special directory to serve instead of the shared bus in the bus-based coherence protocols. Both of these designs use the corresponding medium (i.e. directory or bus) as tool to facilitate the communication between different nodes, and to guarantee that the coherence protocol is working properly along all the communicating nodes. In directory based cache coherence, this is done by using this directory to keep track of the status of all cache blocks, the status of each block includes in which cache coherence "state" that block is, and which nodes are sharing that block at that time, which can be used to eliminate the need to broadcast all the signals to all nodes, and only send it to the nodes that are interested in this single block.
gpt_text:
Directory-based coherence is a cache coherence protocol used in multiprocessor and multicore systems to keep shared memory consistent without relying on broadcast snooping. Instead of having every cache listen to all others’ requests, a central or distributed “directory” keeps track of which cores (or nodes) hold a copy of each memory block and in what state (e.g., shared, modified). When a core wants to read or write a block, it sends a request to the directory, which then coordinates invalidations, updates, or data forwarding among the relevant caches.

This approach scales better than snooping protocols in large systems, because it avoids flooding the interconnect with coherence traffic and limits messages to only those cores that actually share the data. However, it introduces more complex directory structures and potential bottlenecks at the directory controller, so it is often implemented in a distributed manner (e.g., one directory portion per memory controller) to improve scalability and fault tolerance.

title: Branch Queue
human_text: In Computer Architecture, While Branch predictions Branch queue takes place. When Branch Predictor predicts if the branch is taken or not, Branch queue stores the predictions that to be used later.
gpt_text:
A branch queue is a hardware structure used in modern processors to keep track of branch instructions (like if-then-else or loop jumps) as they are fetched and move through the pipeline. It typically stores information such as the branch’s location, predicted outcome (taken or not taken), and the target address, allowing the processor to manage speculative execution and keep the pipeline full.

By maintaining a branch queue, the CPU can handle multiple in-flight branches, resolve them in order, and quickly recover if a branch prediction turns out to be wrong. This helps reduce stalls and misprediction penalties, improving overall instruction throughput and performance in deeply pipelined or superscalar architectures.

title: Andy and Bill's law
human_text: Andy and Bill's law is a statement that new software will always consume any increase in computing power that new hardware can provide. The law originates from a humorous one-liner told in the 1990s during computing conferences: "what Andy giveth, Bill taketh away." The phrase is a riff upon the business strategies of former Intel CEO Andy Grove, and former CEO of Microsoft, Bill Gates. Intel and Microsoft had entered into a lucrative partnership in the 1980s through to the 1990s, and the standard chipsets in Microsoft Windows were Intel brand. Despite the profit Intel gained from the deal, Grove felt that Gates wasn't making full use of the powerful capabilities of Intel chips, and that he was in fact refusing to upgrade his software to achieve optimum hardware performance. Grove's frustration with the dominance of Microsoft software over Intel hardware became public, which spawned the humorous catchphrase; and, later, the law.
gpt_text:
Andy and Bill’s law is an informal observation about the relationship between faster hardware and increasingly demanding software, attributed to Andy Grove (former Intel CEO) and Bill Gates (co-founder of Microsoft). Paraphrased, it says: “What Andy giveth, Bill taketh away” — meaning that the performance gains provided by new processors (Andy/Intel) are quickly consumed by more resource-hungry software (Bill/Microsoft).

The “law” highlights how user-facing software, operating systems, and applications tend to expand in features and complexity as hardware improves, often leaving end users with similar perceived performance despite major underlying hardware advances. It’s frequently cited in discussions of software bloat, efficiency, and why devices don’t always feel faster even as their technical specifications advance rapidly.

title: Scale cube
human_text: The scale cube is a technology model that indicates three methods (or approaches) by which technology platforms may be scaled to meet increasing levels of demand upon the system in question. The three approaches defined by the model include scaling through replication or cloning (the “X axis”), scaling through segmentation along service boundaries or dissimilar components (the “Y axis”) and segmentation or partitioning along similar components (the “Z axis”).
gpt_text:
The *Scale Cube* is a model for thinking about how to scale software systems by visualizing three complementary dimensions of growth. It comes from the book “The Art of Scalability” and labels each axis as follows: X-axis scaling (horizontal cloning of the same application behind load balancers), Y-axis scaling (functional decomposition into separate services or microservices), and Z-axis scaling (data partitioning or sharding, where different subsets of users/data are handled by different instances).

Together, these three axes help architects design systems that can handle higher load, complexity, and data volume. Instead of only adding more powerful servers (vertical scaling), the scale cube encourages spreading work across many machines and services, isolating responsibilities, and splitting data intelligently, which improves performance, fault isolation, and the ability to evolve parts of the system independently.

title: Computation
human_text: A computation is any type of calculationComputation from the Free Merriam-Webster Dictionary that includes both arithmetical and non-arithmetical steps and which follows a well-defined model (e.g. an algorithm).
gpt_text:
Computation is the process of transforming input information into output results by following a well-defined set of rules or operations. It underlies how computers, calculators, and many algorithms work: given data and instructions, a system performs step-by-step procedures to produce an answer or make a decision.

In a broader sense, computation includes everything from simple arithmetic done by hand to complex simulations run on supercomputers. It is central to computer science, mathematics, and many scientific disciplines, enabling tasks like data processing, modeling physical systems, encryption, and automated reasoning.

title: Extractor (mathematics)
human_text: An -extractor is a bipartite graph with nodes on the left and nodes on the right such that each node on the left has neighbors (on the right), which has the added property that
gpt_text:
In mathematics and theoretical computer science, an extractor is a function or algorithm that converts a weakly random source into an output that is close to uniformly random. A “weak” source might be biased or have limited unpredictability (formalized using notions like min-entropy), and an extractor typically uses a small additional input called a “seed” of truly random bits to produce high-quality randomness.

Extractors are fundamental in randomness extraction, derandomization, and cryptography. They allow one to reliably obtain almost-uniform random bits from imperfect physical or computational sources, enabling randomized algorithms and cryptographic protocols to work securely even when only noisy or partially predictable randomness is available.

title: Lambda calculus
human_text: Lambda calculus (also written as λ-calculus) is a formal system in mathematical logic for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application using variable binding and substitution. It is a universal model of computation that can be used to simulate any Turing machine. It was introduced by the mathematician Alonzo Church in the 1930s as part of his research into the foundations of mathematics.
gpt_text:
Lambda calculus is a formal system in mathematical logic and computer science used to define and study computation based on function abstraction and application. Everything in lambda calculus is expressed as functions: you create anonymous functions using λ (lambda) notation, apply them to arguments, and reduce (simplify) the resulting expressions by systematically replacing variables with their values (a process called beta-reduction).

Despite its minimalist design—built only from variables, function definitions, and function applications—lambda calculus is powerful enough to represent any computable function (it is Turing-complete). It forms the theoretical foundation of functional programming languages (such as Haskell and parts of Lisp and ML) and plays a central role in the theory of programming languages, type systems, and formal reasoning about programs.

title: Pseudorandomness
human_text: Pseudorandomness measures the extent to which a sequence of numbers, "though produced by a completely deterministic and repeatable process, appear to be patternless."
gpt_text:
Pseudorandomness refers to sequences of numbers (or bits) that are generated by a deterministic algorithm but appear random according to certain statistical tests. Although they are produced by fixed rules and are fully predictable if you know the algorithm and its initial state (the seed), to an observer without that knowledge they are designed to be indistinguishable from truly random sequences for practical purposes.

In computer science and cryptography, pseudorandomness is crucial because true physical randomness is often hard or slow to obtain. Pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) power simulations, randomized algorithms, games, and many security protocols, with stronger cryptographic PRNGs designed so that even seeing many outputs does not allow an attacker to predict future ones.

title: Quantum computing
human_text: Quantum computing is the use of quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to perform computation. Computers that perform quantum computations are known as quantum computers. Quantum computers are believed to be able to solve certain computational problems, such as integer factorization (which underlies RSA encryption), substantially faster than classical computers. The study of quantum computing is a subfield of quantum information science.
gpt_text:
Quantum computing is a paradigm of computation that uses the principles of quantum mechanics—such as superposition, entanglement, and interference—to process information in ways that classical computers cannot easily replicate. Instead of classical bits that are either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in combinations of 0 and 1 simultaneously. This allows certain computations to explore many possible solutions in parallel.

By exploiting these quantum effects, quantum algorithms can dramatically speed up specific tasks, such as factoring large numbers, searching unstructured databases, simulating quantum systems, and optimizing complex processes. While still in an early, experimental stage—limited by error rates, decoherence, and hardware challenges—quantum computing is seen as a potentially transformative technology for fields like cryptography, materials science, drug discovery, and logistics.

title: Indirect self-reference
human_text: Indirect self-reference describes an object referring to itself indirectly.
gpt_text:
Indirect self-reference is a way for a statement, system, or piece of code to refer to itself without explicitly using direct self-mention (like saying “this sentence” or calling its own name). Instead, the self-reference is achieved through an intermediate structure—such as a code, a description, or another object—that can be decoded or interpreted to point back to the original entity.  

This idea is central in logic, mathematics, and computer science, especially in Gödel’s incompleteness theorems and fixed-point constructions. For example, Gödel encoded mathematical statements as numbers in such a way that a statement could, via its code, assert something about itself. Similarly, in programming, a function might produce or manipulate a representation of its own source through an encoding scheme, achieving self-reference indirectly rather than by naming itself outright.

title: Formal methods
human_text: In computer science, specifically software engineering and hardware engineering, formal methods are a particular kind of mathematically rigorous techniques for the specification, development and verification of software and hardware systems. The use of formal methods for software and hardware design is motivated by the expectation that, as in other engineering disciplines, performing appropriate mathematical analysis can contribute to the reliability and robustness of a design.
gpt_text:
Formal methods are mathematically rigorous techniques used to specify, design, and verify software and hardware systems. They rely on logic and formal languages to describe a system’s behavior precisely, eliminating ambiguity that can occur in natural-language requirements or informal designs. By modeling systems as mathematical objects, formal methods enable developers to reason about correctness properties such as safety, liveness, and security.

These methods include formal specification (writing precise requirements), model checking (automatically exploring system states to find errors), and theorem proving (using logical proof to show that a system satisfies its specification). Formal methods are especially valuable in safety- or security-critical domains—such as aviation, medical devices, cryptographic protocols, and nuclear control systems—where failures are extremely costly or dangerous.

title: Monge array
human_text: In mathematics applied to computer science, Monge arrays, or Monge matrices, are mathematical objects named for their discoverer, the French mathematician Gaspard Monge.
gpt_text:
A Monge array (or Monge matrix) is a matrix of numbers that satisfies a specific inequality capturing a kind of “discrete convexity.” Formally, an array \(A\) is Monge if for all valid indices \(i,j\),
\[
A[i,j] + A[i+1, j+1] \le A[i, j+1] + A[i+1, j].
\]
This means that every \(2 \times 2\) submatrix obeys this inequality, imposing a strong structural pattern on the entries.

Monge arrays arise in optimization and algorithm design, especially in dynamic programming and transportation problems, because their structure allows certain problems (like finding row minima) to be solved much faster than in general matrices. A key property is that the positions of row minima form a nondecreasing sequence across rows, which enables efficient divide-and-conquer or “SMAWK” algorithms.

title: Formal verification
human_text: In the context of hardware and software systems, formal verification is the act of proving or disproving the correctness of intended algorithms underlying a system with respect to a certain formal specification or property, using formal methods of mathematics.
gpt_text:
Formal verification is the use of mathematically rigorous methods to prove or disprove the correctness of a system—such as software, hardware, or protocols—against a formal specification of its desired behavior. Instead of relying on testing or simulation, which can miss rare or complex errors, formal verification uses logic, proofs, and automated tools (like model checkers and theorem provers) to explore all possible behaviors within a given model.

It is widely used in safety- and security-critical domains—such as aerospace, cryptography, and processor design—where subtle bugs can have severe consequences. While powerful, formal verification can be costly and complex to apply, so it is often used on the most critical components or properties (e.g., absence of deadlocks, memory safety, or compliance with security protocols) rather than entire large systems.

title: Correctness (computer science)
human_text: In theoretical computer science, correctness of an algorithm is asserted when it is said that the algorithm is correct with respect to a specification. Functional correctness refers to the input-output behavior of the algorithm (i.e., for each input it produces the expected output).
gpt_text:
In computer science, correctness refers to the property of a program or algorithm that it behaves exactly as specified: for every allowed input, it produces the intended output and exhibits the required behavior (such as terminating, not crashing, and respecting constraints). A system is considered correct if it satisfies its formal specification, often expressed in terms of preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

Correctness is typically studied in two forms: *partial correctness* (the program’s outputs are correct whenever it terminates) and *total correctness* (the program both produces correct outputs and is guaranteed to terminate). Proving correctness can be done through formal methods such as Hoare logic, model checking, and theorem proving, or more informally through testing and code reviews, which provide evidence—but not a formal proof—of correctness.

title: Bio-inspired computing
human_text: Bio-inspired computing, short for biologically inspired computing, is a field of study which seeks to solve computer science problems using models of biology. It relates to connectionism, social behavior, and emergence. Within computer science, bio-inspired computing relates to artificial intelligence and machine learning. Bio-inspired computing is a major subset of natural computation.
gpt_text:
Bio-inspired computing is a field of computer science and engineering that designs algorithms, hardware, and systems modeled on processes found in nature—especially in biology. Instead of relying solely on traditional, deterministic methods, it draws inspiration from phenomena such as evolution, the behavior of swarms, neural processing in brains, immune systems, and even plant growth or gene regulation.

Examples include genetic algorithms that mimic natural selection to optimize solutions, neural networks inspired by the structure and function of the brain for pattern recognition, and swarm intelligence algorithms based on the collective behavior of ants, bees, or birds for routing and coordination tasks. The goal is often to create robust, adaptive, and efficient solutions to complex problems that are difficult to tackle with conventional approaches.

title: Computational learning theory
human_text: In computer science, computational learning theory (or just learning theory) is a subfield of artificial intelligence devoted to studying the design and analysis of machine learning algorithms.
gpt_text:
Computational learning theory is a branch of theoretical computer science and statistics that studies how algorithms can learn from data in a mathematically rigorous way. It focuses on questions like: given a class of functions (or hypotheses), how many examples are needed to learn an accurate one, how much computation is required, and under what assumptions about the data this is possible.  

Key frameworks in computational learning theory include PAC (Probably Approximately Correct) learning, which analyzes when and how quickly a learner can find a hypothesis that is probably close to correct, and models such as online learning, query learning, and VC (Vapnik–Chervonenkis) dimension, which measures the complexity of hypothesis classes. The field provides formal guarantees about generalization, sample complexity, and learnability, forming the theoretical foundation for many modern machine learning methods.

title: Simulation preorder
human_text: In theoretical computer science a simulation preorder is a relation between state transition systems associating systems that behave in the same way in the sense that one system simulates the other.
gpt_text:
Simulation preorder is a binary relation between states (or processes) in labelled transition systems that formalizes the idea of one system being able to “mimic” another’s behavior step by step. A state p is said to simulate a state q if, whenever q can make a transition labeled with some action to a new state q′, then p can make a transition with the same action to some state p′ that again simulates q′. This condition is required to hold for all possible actions and successor states of q.

Because simulation is reflexive and transitive, it forms a preorder (hence the name). Intuitively, if p simulates q (often written q ⊑ p), then p is at least as capable or as informative as q in terms of observable behaviors. Simulation preorder is weaker than bisimulation (which requires mutual simulation), and is widely used in process algebra, model checking, and refinement to express that an implementation safely refines or preserves the behaviors of a specification.

title: Bisimulation
human_text: In theoretical computer science a bisimulation is a binary relation between state transition systems, associating systems that behave in the same way in the sense that one system simulates the other and vice versa.
gpt_text:
Bisimulation is a mathematical relation used in logic and computer science to formalize when two systems behave in the same way, step by step. Given two state-transition systems (like labeled graphs or automata), a bisimulation pairs states from one system with states from the other such that each possible move from a state in one system can be matched by a corresponding move from its paired state in the other system, with the resulting states again related by the same pairing.

This notion is central in concurrency theory, process calculi (like CCS and the π-calculus), and modal logic. If two processes are bisimilar, they are considered behaviorally indistinguishable: no external observer, limited to watching their possible actions and reactions, can tell them apart.

title: Quantum algorithm
human_text: In quantum computing, a quantum algorithm is an algorithm which runs on a realistic model of quantum computation, the most commonly used model being the quantum circuit model of computation. A classical (or non-quantum) algorithm is a finite sequence of instructions, or a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, where each step or instruction can be performed on a classical computer. Similarly, a quantum algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, where each of the steps can be performed on a quantum computer. Although all classical algorithms can also be performed on a quantum computer, the term quantum algorithm is usually used for those algorithms which seem inherently quantum, or use some essential feature of quantum computation such as quantum superposition or quantum entanglement.
gpt_text:
A quantum algorithm is a step-by-step computational procedure designed to run on a quantum computer, exploiting quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition, entanglement, and interference. Unlike classical algorithms, which operate on bits that are either 0 or 1, quantum algorithms operate on qubits that can represent 0 and 1 simultaneously, enabling fundamentally different ways of processing information.

This allows certain problems to be solved more efficiently than is known to be possible classically. Famous examples include Shor’s algorithm for factoring large numbers in polynomial time (threatening many current cryptographic systems) and Grover’s algorithm, which provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Quantum algorithms are a central research area in quantum computing, aiming to identify tasks where quantum computers can offer a clear advantage over classical ones.

title: Interactive computation
human_text: In computer science, interactive computation is a mathematical model for computation that involves input/output communication with the external world during computation. This is in contrast to the traditional understanding of computation which assumes reading input only before computation and writing output only after computation, thus defining a kind of "closed" computation.
gpt_text:
Interactive computation is a model of computation in which a system continually exchanges information with its environment—receiving inputs and producing outputs over time—rather than computing a final result from a fixed input and then halting. Unlike classical Turing machine computation, which assumes all input is given at the start and all output is produced at the end, interactive computation focuses on ongoing, step-by-step interaction.

This perspective is fundamental for understanding modern computing systems such as operating systems, network servers, web applications, and user interfaces, which are designed to run indefinitely and respond dynamically to external events. The theory of interactive computation extends traditional computability and complexity theory to better capture these real-world, concurrent, and reactive behaviors.

title: Granular computing
human_text: Granular computing (GrC) is an emerging computing paradigm of information processing that concerns the processing of complex information entities called "information granules", which arise in the process of data abstraction and derivation of knowledge from information or data. Generally speaking, information granules are collections of entities that usually originate at the numeric level and are arranged together due to their similarity, functional or physical adjacency, indistinguishability, coherency, or the like.
gpt_text:
Granular computing is a computational paradigm that models and processes information using “granules” — clusters of elements grouped together based on similarity, indistinguishability, proximity, or functionality. Instead of working directly with individual, fine-grained data points, granular computing organizes data into higher-level units (granules) such as intervals, clusters, or abstract concepts, making complex problems easier to understand and solve.

This approach is especially useful for dealing with uncertainty, vagueness, and large-scale data. It underlies and connects methods like fuzzy sets, rough sets, clustering, and hierarchical modeling, providing a framework for multi-level, human-like reasoning where problems can be viewed and solved at different levels of detail.

title: Semigroup action
human_text: In algebra and theoretical computer science, an action or act of a semigroup on a set is a rule which associates to each element of the semigroup a transformation of the set in such a way that the product of two elements of the semigroup (using the semigroup operation) is associated with the composite of the two corresponding transformations. The terminology conveys the idea that the elements of the semigroup are acting as transformations of the set. From an algebraic perspective, a semigroup action is a generalization of the notion of a group action in group theory. From the computer science point of view, semigroup actions are closely related to automata: the set models the state of the automaton and the action models transformations of that state in response to inputs.
gpt_text:
A semigroup action is a way for a semigroup to act as transformations on a set, generalizing the idea of a group action but without requiring inverses. Formally, if \(S\) is a semigroup (a set with an associative binary operation) and \(X\) is a set, an action of \(S\) on \(X\) is a function \(S \times X \to X\), written \((s, x) \mapsto s \cdot x\), such that \((st) \cdot x = s \cdot (t \cdot x)\) for all \(s, t \in S\) and \(x \in X\).

This captures the idea that each element of \(S\) acts as a rule for moving points of \(X\), and composing elements of \(S\) corresponds to applying the associated transformations in sequence. Unlike group actions, there is no requirement for an identity element or inverses in the semigroup, so one typically gets a one-sided “dynamics” on \(X\) that can’t necessarily be undone.

title: Corecursion
human_text: In computer science, corecursion is a type of operation that is dual to recursion. Whereas recursion works analytically, starting on data further from a base case and breaking it down into smaller data and repeating until one reaches a base case, corecursion works synthetically, starting from a base case and building it up, iteratively producing data further removed from a base case. Put simply, corecursive algorithms use the data that they themselves produce, bit by bit, as they become available, and needed, to produce further bits of data. A similar but distinct concept is generative recursion which may lack a definite "direction" inherent in corecursion and recursion.
gpt_text:
Corecursion is a way of defining potentially infinite data structures or processes by describing how to *produce* their next piece, rather than how to *consume* or reduce them to a final result. Where recursion typically breaks a problem down until it reaches a base case and then combines results (e.g., summing a list), corecursion instead specifies how to keep generating more output step by step (e.g., generating an infinite stream of numbers), often without requiring a traditional base case.

In functional programming and type theory, corecursion is dual to recursion: recursion operates over inductive types (finite structures like finite lists or trees), while corecursion works with coinductive types (possibly infinite streams or processes). Correct corecursive definitions must be *productive*: each step must yield a new observable part of the result in finite time, ensuring the definition meaningfully describes an ongoing, potentially unending computation.

title: Rough set
human_text: In computer science, a rough set, first described by Polish computer scientist Zdzisław I. Pawlak, is a formal approximation of a crisp set (i.e., conventional set) in terms of a pair of sets which give the lower and the upper approximation of the original set. In the standard version of rough set theory (Pawlak 1991), the lower- and upper-approximation sets are crisp sets, but in other variations, the approximating sets may be fuzzy sets.
gpt_text:
A rough set is a mathematical model for dealing with vagueness and uncertainty in data, introduced by Zdzisław Pawlak. Instead of representing a concept as a crisp set of objects that either belong or do not belong, a rough set uses two approximations: a lower approximation (objects that definitely belong) and an upper approximation (objects that possibly belong). The boundary region between these two captures the uncertainty about membership.

Rough set theory works directly from the data and the indiscernibility relation between objects—if two objects have the same values for all considered attributes, they are indiscernible. Using these relations, rough sets help discover patterns, reduce attributes (feature selection), and extract decision rules without requiring any additional probability or membership functions, making them useful in data mining, machine learning, and knowledge discovery.

title: PEPA
human_text: Performance Evaluation Process Algebra (PEPA) is a stochastic process algebra designed for modelling computer and communication systems introduced by Jane Hillston in the 1990s. The language extends classical process algebras such as Milner's CCS and Hoare's CSP by introducing probabilistic branching and timing of transitions.
gpt_text:
PEPA (Performance Evaluation Process Algebra) is a formal language used to model and analyze the performance of concurrent and distributed systems. It extends traditional process algebras by attaching exponentially distributed activity durations (rates) to actions, allowing both qualitative (behavioral) and quantitative (performance) analysis within a single framework.

Using PEPA, systems are described as interacting components that perform actions at given rates, which can be composed through operators for choice, parallel composition, and synchronization. These models can be automatically translated into continuous-time Markov chains or other analyzable structures, enabling the study of metrics like throughput, utilization, and response times for complex software, hardware, or communication systems.

title: Exact cover
human_text: In mathematics, given a collection of subsets of a set X, an exact cover is a subcollection of such that each element in X is contained in exactly one subset in.
gpt_text:
An exact cover is a collection of subsets from a given family of sets such that every element of the underlying universe appears in **exactly one** of the chosen subsets. Formally, given a finite set \(X\) and a family of subsets \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)\), an exact cover is a subfamily \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\) where each element of \(X\) belongs to one and only one set in \(\mathcal{C}\).

The exact cover problem asks whether such a subfamily exists for a given \(X\) and \(\mathcal{S}\), and it is a classic NP-complete problem in computer science and combinatorics. It can model puzzles and tasks like Sudoku, tiling problems, and scheduling. Donald Knuth’s Algorithm X with the “dancing links” technique is a well-known method for solving exact cover instances efficiently in practice.

title: Automated reasoning
human_text: Automated reasoning is an area of computer science (involves knowledge representation and reasoning) and metalogic dedicated to understanding different aspects of reasoning. The study of automated reasoning helps produce computer programs that allow computers to reason completely, or nearly completely, automatically. Although automated reasoning is considered a sub-field of artificial intelligence, it also has connections with theoretical computer science and philosophy.
gpt_text:
Automated reasoning is a branch of artificial intelligence and mathematical logic focused on enabling computers to reason logically and prove or disprove statements automatically. It involves designing algorithms and systems that can manipulate formal representations of knowledge—such as logical formulas—to derive conclusions, verify correctness, or find counterexamples without human intervention.

This field underpins many practical tools, including theorem provers, SAT/SMT solvers, and model checkers, which are used to verify hardware and software, assist in mathematical proof discovery, optimize systems, and ensure safety-critical properties. By formalizing reasoning steps that humans typically perform informally, automated reasoning helps make reasoning processes more reliable, repeatable, and scalable to complex problems.

title: Bigraph
human_text: A bigraph (often used in the plural bigraphs) can be modelled as the superposition of a graph (the link graph) and a set of trees (the place graph).A Brief Introduction To Bigraphs, IT University of Copenhagen, Denmark.Milner, Robin. The Bigraphical Model, University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory, UK.
gpt_text:
A bigraph (short for “bidirectional graph” or “bipartite graph,” depending on context) is a mathematical structure used to model systems with two types of relationships at once. In its more specialized sense, introduced by Robin Milner, a bigraph represents both the spatial arrangement of components (who is inside what) and their connectivity (who is linked to whom) in a single formalism. This makes bigraphs useful for describing complex, mobile, and distributed systems where both location and interaction matter, such as ubiquitous computing or biological networks.

More informally, a bigraph can be seen as a pair of graphs sharing the same set of nodes: one captures a “place” structure (a tree-like nesting of components), and the other captures a “link” structure (the communication or connection network). This dual view allows researchers and engineers to reason rigorously about how systems change over time, move in space, and interact through communication links.

title: ACM SIGACT
human_text: ACM SIGACT or SIGACT is the Association for Computing Machinery Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computation Theory, whose purpose is support of research in theoretical computer science. It was founded in 1968 by Patrick C. Fischer.
gpt_text:

It serves researchers, educators, and practitioners interested in areas such as algorithms, complexity theory, cryptography, computational geometry, and related mathematical foundations of computing.

SIGACT sponsors major conferences like STOC (Symposium on Theory of Computing), publishes newsletters and bulletins, supports awards recognizing outstanding theoretical work, and promotes the exchange of ideas within the theory community. It plays a central role in shaping and disseminating research in the foundations of computer science worldwide.

title: Motion planning
human_text: Motion planning, also path planning (also known as the navigation problem or the piano mover's problem) is a computational problem to find a sequence of valid configurations that moves the object from the source to destination. The term is used in computational geometry, computer animation, robotics and computer games.
gpt_text:
Motion planning is the process of computing a feasible path or sequence of movements for a robot or agent to move from a start state to a goal state without collisions and while respecting constraints (like joint limits, dynamics, or obstacles). It is a core problem in robotics, autonomous vehicles, animation, and computer games, where an entity must navigate through an environment safely and efficiently.  

Techniques for motion planning range from classical geometric methods (like visibility graphs and configuration space representations) to sampling-based algorithms such as PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) and RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree), as well as optimization-based approaches that treat planning as a constrained optimization problem. Advanced motion planners also consider uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, and real-time re-planning to operate robustly in complex, changing environments.

title: Computational problem
human_text: In theoretical computer science, a computational problem is a problem that a computer might be able to solve or a question that a computer may be able to answer. For example, the problem of factoring
gpt_text:
A computational problem is a task or question that can be precisely described and solved by an algorithm executed on a computational device (like a computer). It specifies what input is given and what output is required, without necessarily prescribing how to obtain that output. For example, “Given a list of numbers, determine whether any two of them add up to 10” is a computational problem.

In theoretical computer science, computational problems are classified by their difficulty and resource requirements, such as time and memory, leading to complexity classes like P, NP, and others. This abstraction helps researchers understand which problems can be solved efficiently, which are intractable, and how changes in algorithms or computing models affect what can be feasibly computed.

title: Bird–Meertens formalism
human_text: The Bird–Meertens formalism (BMF) is a calculus for deriving programs from specifications (in a functional-programming setting) by a process of equational reasoning. It was devised by Richard Bird and Lambert Meertens as part of their work within IFIP Working Group 2.1.
gpt_text:

Its main value lies in enabling systematic program transformation: starting from a clear but inefficient specification, you apply algebraic rules to gradually obtain an efficient implementation while preserving correctness by construction. This approach is closely related to functional programming (notably Haskell), program derivation, and calculational proofs.

title: Notation for theoretic scheduling problems
human_text: A convenient notation for theoretic scheduling problems was introduced by Ronald Graham, Eugene Lawler, Jan Karel Lenstra and Alexander Rinnooy Kan in. It consists of three fields: α, β and γ.
gpt_text:
In theoretical scheduling, problems are described using a compact three-field notation α | β | γ (Graham’s notation).  
- α (machine environment) specifies the type and number of machines, e.g., 1 (single machine), Pm (m identical parallel machines), Qm (uniform machines with different speeds), Rm (unrelated machines), or more specialized settings like flow shops (Fm) and job shops (Jm).  
- β (job characteristics/constraints) captures details such as release dates (rj), precedence constraints (prec), preemption allowed (pmtn), setup times, batching, or other structural restrictions.  
- γ (objective function) states what is being optimized, such as minimizing the makespan (Cmax), total completion time (∑Cj), maximum lateness (Lmax), total tardiness (∑Tj), or weighted versions (e.g., ∑wjCj).

This notation provides a standardized, concise way to classify and compare scheduling problems, express complexity results, and refer to known algorithms or hardness results across the scheduling literature.

title: Full employment theorem
human_text: In computer science and mathematics, a full employment theorem is a term used, often humorously, to refer to a theorem which states that no algorithm can optimally perform a particular task done by some class of professionals. The name arises because such a theorem ensures that there is endless scope to keep discovering new techniques to improve the way at least some specific task is done.
gpt_text:
The “full employment theorem” is an informal name often given to arguments showing that certain kinds of complex work can never be completely automated away. In computer science and AI, it usually refers to the idea that as long as we keep creating new software, systems, or models, there will always be unsolved problems—like debugging, verification, specifying goals correctly, handling edge cases, and adapting systems to new contexts—that require human (or at least non-automated) effort. This is sometimes linked to results like Rice’s theorem or the halting problem, which prove there is no general algorithm that can decide all interesting properties of programs.

Because of these fundamental limitations, each time we build more sophisticated automated systems, we also create new layers of tasks: interpreting outputs, integrating tools, maintaining infrastructure, defining requirements, and dealing with failures in novel environments. The “full employment” label is tongue‑in‑cheek, but it captures the core point: automation doesn’t eliminate all work; it often shifts and transforms it, and some categories of high-level or meta-level work are provably impossible to fully automate in a general way.

In practice, an API calculus typically focuses on how services interact, how requests and responses flow, and how contracts or types ensure correctness when APIs are combined. This can help in reasoning about compatibility between services, ensuring safe evolution of APIs, and verifying properties such as reliability, security, or deadlock-freedom in distributed systems.

title: Chemical computer
human_text: A chemical computer, also called a reaction-diffusion computer, Belousov–Zhabotinsky (BZ) computer, or gooware computer, is an unconventional computer based on a semi-solid chemical "soup" where data are represented by varying concentrations of chemicals. The computations are performed by naturally occurring chemical reactions.
gpt_text:

In these systems, information can be encoded in concentrations of molecules, reaction rates, or spatial patterns of chemicals, and computation occurs as reactions proceed according to well-defined rules (analogous to logic gates or algorithms).

Examples include reaction–diffusion systems, DNA computing, and other forms of molecular computing, where carefully designed chemical networks solve problems such as pattern formation, logic operations, or optimization tasks. Chemical computers are of interest for their potential to operate in environments where electronics fail, to interface directly with biological systems, and to perform massively parallel computations at very small scales.

title: Expander mixing lemma
human_text: The expander mixing lemma intuitively states that the edges of certain -regular graphs are evenly distributed throughout the graph. In particular, the number of edges between two vertex subsets and is always close to the expected number of edges between them in a random -regular graph, namely.
gpt_text:
The expander mixing lemma is a fundamental result in graph theory that quantifies how “random-like” a good expander graph is. For a regular graph with good expansion (i.e., with all nontrivial eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix bounded in magnitude by a small number), the lemma states that the number of edges between any two vertex sets is very close to what you would expect in a truly random graph of the same edge density. The deviation from this expected value is tightly controlled by the second-largest eigenvalue of the graph.

Formally, in a \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices with adjacency eigenvalues \(d = \lambda_1 \ge |\lambda_2| \ge \dots\), the lemma asserts that for any two vertex sets \(S,T\),
\[
\left| e(S,T) - \frac{d}{n}|S||T| \right| \le \lambda \sqrt{|S||T|(1 - |S|/n)(1 - |T|/n)},
\]
where \(e(S,T)\) is the number of edges between \(S\) and \(T\), and \(\lambda = \max_{i\ge 2}|\lambda_i|\). This shows that small \(\lambda\) implies strong pseudorandomness: every cut behaves almost like in a random graph.

title: British Colloquium for Theoretical Computer Science
human_text: The British Colloquium for Theoretical Computer Science (BCTCS) is an organisation, founded in 1985, that represents the interests of Theoretical Computer Science in the UK, e.g. through representation on academic boards and providing commentary and evidence in response to consultations from public bodies. The BCTCS operates under the direction of an Organising Committee, with an Executive consisting of a President, Secretary and Treasurer. The current President is Barnaby Martin.

Founded in the 1980s, BCTCS typically features invited talks by leading international researchers, contributed talks by participants (often including PhD students and early-career academics), and sessions aimed at fostering interaction across different subareas of theory.
