human_text: In mathematics, logic and computer science, a formal language is called recursively enumerable (also recognizable, partially decidable, semidecidable, Turing-acceptable or Turing-recognizable) if it is a recursively enumerable subset in the set of all possible words over the alphabet of the language, i.e., if there exists a Turing machine which will enumerate all valid strings of the language.
gpt_text:
A recursively enumerable (r.e.) language is a set of strings for which there exists a Turing machine that will list (or “enumerate”) all and only the strings in the set, or equivalently, a Turing machine that halts and accepts exactly those strings in the language. If a string is in the language, the machine will eventually accept it; if a string is not in the language, the machine may either reject it or run forever without halting.

R.e. languages capture the notion of partial computability: membership can be semi-decided (you can recognize when something is in the language by eventual acceptance), but you may not be able to always determine non-membership in finite time. Every decidable (recursive) language is recursively enumerable, but not every recursively enumerable language is decidable.

title: Post correspondence problem
human_text: The Post correspondence problem is an undecidable decision problem that was introduced by Emil Post in 1946. Because it is simpler than the halting problem and the Entscheidungsproblem it is often used in proofs of undecidability.
gpt_text:
The Post correspondence problem (PCP) is a classic decision problem in theoretical computer science and computability theory, introduced by Emil Post in 1946. You are given a finite set of domino-like tiles, each with a string on the top and a string on the bottom, over some alphabet. The question is whether there exists a sequence of these tiles (allowing repetition) such that, when you concatenate the top strings of the chosen tiles and the bottom strings of those tiles in the same order, the two resulting strings are exactly the same.

PCP is famous because it is undecidable in general: there is no algorithm that can always determine, for every possible instance, whether a matching sequence exists. It is one of the fundamental problems used to prove the undecidability of other problems and to demonstrate the limits of algorithmic computation.

title: Hypercomputation
human_text: Hypercomputation or super-Turing computation refers to models of computation that can provide outputs that are not Turing-computable. For example, a machine that could solve the halting problem would be a hypercomputer; so too would one that can correctly evaluate every statement in Peano arithmetic.
gpt_text:
Hypercomputation refers to hypothetical models of computation that can solve problems or perform tasks beyond the capabilities of a standard Turing machine. In classical computer science, Turing machines define the upper limit of what is algorithmically computable; hypercomputational models challenge this boundary by allowing, for example, infinitely many computational steps in finite time (as in “supertasks”), access to oracles that instantly solve undecidable problems, or the exploitation of exotic physical processes.

These ideas are mostly theoretical and often controversial, as no known physical system has been conclusively shown to implement genuine hypercomputation. Nonetheless, the study of hypercomputation is important for clarifying the limits of algorithms, exploring the relationship between physics and computation, and examining whether the Church–Turing thesis—informally, that all effectively calculable functions are Turing-computable—might have exceptions in certain physical or conceptual frameworks.

title: Markov algorithm
human_text: In theoretical computer science, a Markov algorithm is a string rewriting system that uses grammar-like rules to operate on strings of symbols. Markov algorithms have been shown to be Turing-complete, which means that they are suitable as a general model of computation and can represent any mathematical expression from its simple notation. Markov algorithms are named after the Soviet mathematician Andrey Markov, Jr.A New Kind of Science
gpt_text:
A Markov algorithm (or Markov normal algorithm) is a formal model of computation based on string rewriting. It operates on an initial string using a finite, ordered list of rules of the form “pattern → replacement.” The algorithm scans the current string to find the first rule whose pattern appears as a substring; it then replaces that occurrence with the rule’s replacement string. Some rules are marked as terminal; applying a terminal rule causes the algorithm to halt.

Markov algorithms are important in theoretical computer science because they are Turing-complete: anything computable by a Turing machine can also be computed by a Markov algorithm. They provide an alternative, more syntactic view of computation focused on manipulating symbols according to simple rewriting rules, and they have influenced later formalisms like string-rewriting systems and term-rewriting languages.

title: Gödel numbering
human_text: In mathematical logic, a Gödel numbering is a function that assigns to each symbol and well-formed formula of some formal language a unique natural number, called its Gödel number. The concept was used by Kurt Gödel for the proof of his incompleteness theorems. ()
gpt_text:
Gödel numbering is a technique, introduced by Kurt Gödel, for encoding mathematical objects (like symbols, formulas, and proofs) as natural numbers in a precise and systematic way. The basic idea is to assign each basic symbol of a formal language a unique natural number, then use an encoding scheme—often based on prime factorization—to translate entire sequences of symbols into single numbers. For example, a formula can be turned into a unique “Gödel number,” and conversely, that number can be decoded back into the original formula.

This construction lets statements in a formal system talk about other statements and proofs inside the same system, because properties of formulas (such as “this formula is provable”) can be rephrased as properties of their corresponding numbers. Gödel used this method in his incompleteness theorems to create self-referential mathematical statements, such as a statement that effectively says, “This statement is not provable,” all within arithmetic itself.

title: Typed lambda calculus
human_text: A typed lambda calculus is a typed formalism that uses the lambda-symbol () to denote anonymous function abstraction. In this context, types are usually objects of a syntactic nature that are assigned to lambda terms; the exact nature of a type depends on the calculus considered (see kinds below). From a certain point of view, typed lambda calculi can be seen as refinements of the untyped lambda calculus, but from another point of view, they can also be considered the more fundamental theory and untyped lambda calculus a special case with only one type.
gpt_text:
Typed lambda calculus is a formal system that extends the untyped lambda calculus by assigning types to expressions (terms) and enforcing rules about how they can be combined. Each variable and function has a type (such as `Bool`, `Nat`, or more complex function types like `A → B`), and the type system prevents ill-formed operations—for example, applying a boolean as if it were a function. This makes programs more predictable and many errors detectable at the level of types rather than during evaluation.

Typed lambda calculi come in many variants (simply typed, polymorphic/System F, dependent type theories, etc.), each increasing the expressiveness of the type system. They form a foundational framework for understanding and designing programming languages, especially functional ones, and provide a basis for reasoning about programs, proving properties about them, and ensuring certain kinds of correctness by construction.

title: Computational semiotics
human_text: Computational semiotics is an interdisciplinary field that applies, conducts, and draws on research in logic, mathematics, the theory and practice of computation, formal and natural language studies, the cognitive sciences generally, and semiotics proper. The term encompasses both the application of semiotics to computer hardware and software design and, conversely, the use of computation for performing semiotic analysis. The former focuses on what semiotics can bring to computation; the latter on what computation can bring to semiotics.
gpt_text:
Computational semiotics is the study and modeling of signs, symbols, and meaning-making processes using computational methods. It combines semiotics (the theory of signs and sign systems) with computer science, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science to understand how meaning can be represented, processed, and generated by machines.  

In practice, computational semiotics informs areas like natural language processing, human–computer interaction, multimedia analysis, and intelligent interfaces. By treating texts, images, gestures, and other forms of communication as structured sign systems, it aims to improve how computers interpret human input, produce meaningful output, and engage in more “semantically aware” interaction.

title: Interactive computation
human_text: In computer science, interactive computation is a mathematical model for computation that involves input/output communication with the external world during computation. This is in contrast to the traditional understanding of computation which assumes reading input only before computation and writing output only after computation, thus defining a kind of "closed" computation.
gpt_text:
Interactive computation is a model of computation where a system continuously interacts with its environment—receiving inputs and producing outputs over time—rather than taking a single input, computing, and then halting with a single output (as in the classical Turing machine model). In interactive systems, computation is ongoing and dialog-like: the behavior at any moment can depend on a sequence of past interactions, not just an initial input.

This concept is crucial for understanding modern computing systems such as operating systems, web servers, distributed systems, and interactive applications, all of which are designed to respond to a changing environment and user actions. Interactive computation broadens the traditional notion of what it means to compute, emphasizing processes, communication, and responsiveness rather than just function evaluation.

title: Church–Turing–Deutsch principle
human_text: In computer science and quantum physics, the Church–Turing–Deutsch principle (CTD principle) is a stronger, physical form of the Church–Turing thesis formulated by David Deutsch in 1985. The principle states that a universal computing device can simulate every physical process.
gpt_text:
The Church–Turing–Deutsch principle is a strengthened version of the Church–Turing thesis proposed by David Deutsch. It states, roughly, that every physically realizable process can be simulated by a universal computing device, such as a universal Turing machine or, more specifically in Deutsch’s formulation, a universal quantum computer. Where the original Church–Turing thesis concerns what is mathematically computable, the Church–Turing–Deutsch principle links computation to the laws of physics.

This principle suggests that the limits of what can be computed are exactly the limits imposed by physical law: if a process can happen in our universe, then in principle it can be simulated by a suitable universal computer obeying the same physical laws. It underpins the idea that computation is not merely a mathematical abstraction but a fundamental aspect of physical reality, and it motivates the study of quantum computation as capturing the full power of physically possible information processing.

title: Turing degree
human_text: In computer science and mathematical logic the Turing degree (named after Alan Turing) or degree of unsolvability of a set of natural numbers measures the level of algorithmic unsolvability of the set.
gpt_text:
A Turing degree is a way of classifying sets of natural numbers (or decision problems) according to their level of algorithmic unsolvability. Two sets have the same Turing degree if each can be computed from the other using a Turing machine equipped with an oracle for that set; in other words, they are mutually Turing reducible and thus share the same “computational power.”

These degrees form a partially ordered structure: one degree is less than or equal to another if every problem in the first can be solved using an oracle for any problem in the second. The least Turing degree corresponds to all computable (decidable) sets, while higher degrees capture increasingly complex non-computable problems, such as the halting problem. This framework underpins much of classical computability theory and the study of relative computability.

title: Blockhead (thought experiment)
human_text: Blockhead is the name of a theoretical computer system invented as part of a thought experiment by philosopher Ned Block, which appeared in a paper titled "Psychologism and Behaviorism". Block did not name the computer in the paper.
gpt_text:
The Blockhead thought experiment, introduced by philosopher Ned Block, is designed to challenge behaviorist and purely functionalist accounts of intelligence and understanding. It imagines a machine (the “Blockhead”) that appears to carry on an intelligent conversation—passing something like the Turing Test—by consulting a gigantic lookup table of all possible input–output pairs, rather than by genuinely processing or understanding what is being said. For any sentence you speak to it, the machine simply looks up a pre-written, appropriate response and outputs it.

Block uses this scenario to argue that merely exhibiting the right behavioral patterns or input–output relations is not sufficient for genuine mentality, understanding, or consciousness. If the Blockhead passes the Turing Test yet intuitively has no mind at all—just a vast database—then behavioral criteria alone cannot capture what it is to think or understand, highlighting a gap between observable behavior and inner mental states.

title: X-machine
human_text: The X-machine (XM) is a theoretical model of computation introduced by Samuel Eilenberg in 1974.<ref
gpt_text:
An X-machine is a theoretical model of computation that extends finite state machines by adding a separate data memory and processing functions. Formally, it consists of a finite set of states, an input/output alphabet, a memory structure, and a set of processing functions that transform both the input and the memory. Transitions between states are not triggered directly by input symbols, but by these processing functions, which consume input, update memory, and produce output.

Because the memory and functions can be arbitrarily complex, X-machines can describe a much wider range of systems than simple automata, while still having a clear, mathematically rigorous structure. They are often used in formal methods, especially for specifying and testing software systems, since they can model both control flow (via states) and data transformations (via memory and functions) in a unified framework.

title: Simply typed lambda calculus
human_text: The simply typed lambda calculus (), a form
gpt_text:
Simply typed lambda calculus (STLC) is a typed version of the lambda calculus, a formal system for expressing computation using function abstraction and application. In STLC, every term has a type (such as basic types like `Bool` or `Nat`, or function types like `A → B`), and operations are only allowed when the types match correctly. This typing discipline rules out many nonsensical expressions and guarantees properties like the absence of certain runtime errors.

Formally, STLC consists of variables, lambda abstractions (functions), and applications, together with a typing system that assigns types to terms via inference rules. One key property of STLC is strong normalization: every well-typed term reduces to a normal form (computation always terminates). STLC is foundational in logic and computer science, underpinning type systems of many programming languages and corresponding, via the Curry–Howard correspondence, to a fragment of intuitionistic logic.

title: Parallel terraced scan
human_text: The parallel terraced scan is a multi-agent based search technique that is basic to cognitive architectures, such as Copycat, Letter-string, the Examiner, Tabletop, and others. It was developed by John Rehling and Douglas Hofstadter at the Center for Research on Concepts and Cognition at Indiana University, Bloomington.
gpt_text:
Parallel Terraced Scan is a computational strategy introduced by cognitive scientist Douglas Hofstadter to model human-like thinking, especially in tasks involving analogy, perception, and creativity. Instead of following a single rigid path, it explores many small, partial solution paths in parallel, allocating more attention and resources to those that appear promising while still keeping alternative possibilities alive at lower intensity.

The “terraced” aspect refers to different levels of processing: some processes operate quickly and shallowly, others more slowly and deeply, all running concurrently and influencing each other. This architecture is designed to capture the fluid, context-sensitive, and non-linear nature of human thought, where ideas compete and cooperate dynamically until a coherent solution or interpretation emerges.

title: Numbering (computability theory)
human_text: In computability theory a numbering is the assignment of natural numbers to a set of objects such as functions, rational numbers, graphs, or words in some language. A numbering can be used to transfer the idea of computability and related concepts, which are originally defined on the natural numbers using computable functions, to these different types of objects.
gpt_text:
In computability theory, a *numbering* is a systematic way of assigning natural numbers to mathematical objects so that each object can be effectively identified and manipulated by algorithms. Formally, a numbering of a set \(S\) is a surjective total function \(\nu : \mathbb{N} \to S\); the number \(n\) is then called the *index* (or code) of the object \(\nu(n)\). This lets us talk about “the \(n\)-th partial computable function,” “the \(n\)-th Turing machine,” or “the \(n\)-th recursively enumerable set” by fixing an appropriate numbering of those objects.

Numberings are central because computability is defined on natural numbers, so representing more complex objects via indices allows them to be studied algorithmically. Special classes such as *effective* or *acceptable* numberings preserve key computability properties and are unique up to computable transformations, which underlies many standard results in recursion theory (like the s-m-n theorem and the recursion theorem).

title: Admissible numbering
human_text: In computability theory, admissible numberings are enumerations (numberings) of the set of partial computable functions that can be converted to and from the standard numbering. These numberings are also called acceptable numberings and acceptable programming systems.
gpt_text:
An admissible numbering is a way of assigning natural numbers to partial computable functions so that this indexing behaves “well” from the standpoint of computability theory. Formally, it is a surjective mapping from ℕ onto the set of partial computable functions (often on ℕ or finite strings) that is effective enough to allow simulation and comparison of programs within the model.

The key property of an admissible numbering is that it is universal up to effective translation: any other “reasonable” numbering of the same class of functions can be transformed into it by a total computable function on indices. This captures the idea that different programming systems or description methods for algorithms are essentially equivalent, as long as they are computably intertranslatable.

title: Semi-Thue system
human_text: In theoretical computer science and mathematical logic a string rewriting system (SRS), historically called a semi-Thue system, is a rewriting system over strings from a (usually finite) alphabet. Given a binary relation between fixed strings over the alphabet, called rewrite rules, denoted by , an SRS extends the rewriting relation to all strings in which the left- and right-hand side of the rules appear as substrings, that is , where , , , and are strings.
gpt_text:
A Semi-Thue system is a formal rewriting system used in theoretical computer science and mathematical logic to study string transformations. It consists of an alphabet (a set of symbols) and a set of production rules, where each rule allows one string over that alphabet to be replaced by another. Unlike some more restricted systems, these rules can be applied anywhere within a string, not just at the beginning or end.

Semi-Thue systems are closely related to formal grammars and are powerful enough to describe general computation. They play a key role in understanding decision problems (such as the word problem), since questions like “Can string A be transformed into string B using these rules?” can encode complex computational tasks.

title: Cylindrification
human_text: In computability theory a cylindrification is a construction that associates a cylindric numbering to each numbering. The concept was first introduced by Yuri L. Ershov in 1973.
gpt_text:
Cylindrification is a process or transformation that produces a “cylinder-like” object from a given mathematical or geometric structure. In topology and geometry, it often refers to taking a space and forming its product with an interval (typically [0,1]), creating a cylinder over that space; for example, turning a curve into a surface that looks like a tube. This construction is used to study continuous deformations (homotopies) and to build or analyze more complex spaces.

In other contexts, such as logic and algebra (notably in cylindric algebras), cylindrification is an operation that corresponds to adding or “projecting over” an extra dimension or variable, somewhat analogous to taking a Cartesian product with a line or interval. Across these uses, the core idea is extending an object into a higher-dimensional, cylinder-like form while preserving much of its original structure.

title: Cylindric numbering
human_text: In computability theory a cylindric numbering is a special kind of numbering first introduced by Yuri L. Ershov in 1973.
gpt_text:
Cylindric numbering is a concept from computability theory and logic that generalizes the notion of Gödel-style numberings of syntactic objects (like formulas or programs) by imposing an additional “cylindric” structure on them. In such a numbering, the domain (often a set of tuples or sequences) is encoded into natural numbers in a way that respects certain coordinatewise or projection properties, reminiscent of cylindric algebras in logic, where one can “forget” or “fix” components.

Intuitively, a cylindric numbering lets you encode multidimensional data (such as tuples of objects, or formulas with free variables) into single numbers while preserving a kind of modular control over each coordinate or variable position. This makes cylindric numberings useful in studying fine-grained relationships between effective encodings, degrees of unsolvability, and the interaction between syntax (variables, parameters) and computability-theoretic properties.

title: Tarski–Kuratowski algorithm
human_text: In computability theory and mathematical logic the Tarski–Kuratowski algorithm is a non-deterministic algorithm which produces an upper bound for the complexity of a given formula in the arithmetical hierarchy and analytical hierarchy.
gpt_text:
The Tarski–Kuratowski algorithm is a classical decision procedure for the first-order theory of real closed fields, such as the real numbers with addition, multiplication, and order. It is based on quantifier elimination: given a formula with quantifiers over the reals, the algorithm systematically transforms it into an equivalent quantifier-free formula. This implies that questions about the truth of statements involving polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals are, in principle, mechanically decidable.

Developed from work by Alfred Tarski and Kazimierz Kuratowski in the mid-20th century, the algorithm is of primarily theoretical importance, as it establishes decidability rather than providing a practical tool—its worst-case complexity is extremely high. Nonetheless, it laid the foundations for later, more efficient quantifier-elimination methods (such as cylindrical algebraic decomposition) used in real algebraic geometry, formal verification, and symbolic computation.

title: Limits of computation
human_text: The limits of computation are governed by a number of different factors. In particular, there are several physical and practical limits to the amount of computation or data storage that can be performed with a given amount of mass, volume, or energy.
gpt_text:
The limits of computation are the fundamental boundaries on what problems can be solved—or how efficiently they can be solved—by any algorithmic process, regardless of hardware or programming language. Some tasks are *undecidable*, meaning no algorithm can exist that always produces a correct yes/no answer in finite time; the classic example is the Halting Problem, which asks whether a given program will eventually stop or run forever. This shows that there are well-defined questions about computations themselves that no computer can fully answer.

Even for problems that *are* solvable in principle, resource limits impose further constraints. Computational complexity theory studies how time and memory requirements grow with input size, and it classifies problems into categories like P, NP, and EXP. Many practically important tasks (e.g., certain optimization or combinatorial problems) appear to require resources that grow exponentially, making them infeasible for large inputs. Together, undecidability and complexity bounds define the theoretical ceiling on what computation can achieve, regardless of technological advances.

title: Parallel computation thesis
human_text: In computational complexity theory, the parallel computation thesis is a hypothesis which states that the time used by a (reasonable) parallel machine is polynomially related to the space used by a sequential machine. The parallel computation thesis was set forth by Chandra and Stockmeyer in 1976.
gpt_text:
The parallel computation thesis is an informal principle in theoretical computer science stating that parallel computational models (like PRAMs or other parallel machines with multiple processors) do not provide fundamentally more computational power than standard sequential models (like Turing machines); they mainly offer speedups by exploiting parallelism. In other words, anything a reasonable parallel model can compute, a standard sequential model can also compute, with at most a polynomial slowdown in time.

This thesis parallels the Church–Turing thesis, but focuses on parallel rather than general computation. It underlies much of complexity theory involving parallel classes such as NC (problems efficiently solvable in parallel) and supports the idea that parallelism changes resource trade-offs (time vs. processors) rather than expanding what is computable in principle.

title: Omega language
human_text: An ω-language is a set of infinite-length sequences of symbols.
gpt_text:
In theoretical computer science and logic, an *omega language* is a set of infinite sequences (or words) over a given alphabet. Unlike ordinary formal languages, which consist of finite strings of symbols, omega languages deal with strings of countably infinite length, often written as \( \omega \)-words. They are fundamental in the study of non-terminating systems, such as operating systems, communication protocols, or reactive programs that are intended to run forever.

Omega languages are commonly specified and analyzed using automata that read infinite inputs (like Büchi, Rabin, or Streett automata) or temporal logics (such as LTL). They provide a rigorous way to express and verify properties like “something good happens infinitely often” or “a certain error never occurs,” making them central in formal verification and model checking.

title: Scale factor (computer science)
human_text: In computer science, a scale factor is a number used as a multiplier to represent a number on a different scale, functioning similarly to an exponent in mathematics. A scale factor is used when a real-world set of numbers needs to be represented on a different scale in order to fit a specific number format. Although using a scale factor extends the range of representable values, it also decreases the precision, resulting in rounding error for certain calculations.
gpt_text:
In computer science, a **scale factor** is a constant that describes how resource usage (time, memory, bandwidth, etc.) grows as the size of a problem or dataset changes. When analyzing algorithms or systems, it often refers to the proportional change in input size or workload and how that affects performance—for example, doubling the input might double the running time if the algorithm is linear, meaning the time complexity has a scale factor of 2 for that change.

More concretely, scale factors show up in performance modeling, benchmarking, and simulations, where they can be used to generate larger or smaller synthetic workloads from a base case. For instance, a database benchmark might define a scale factor of 10 to mean “10 times the base dataset size,” allowing engineers to study how well a system scales as usage grows.

title: Turing machine equivalents
human_text: A Turing machine is a hypothetical computing device, first conceived by Alan Turing in 1936. Turing machines manipulate symbols on a potentially infinite strip of tape according to a finite table of rules, and they provide the theoretical underpinnings for the notion of a computer algorithm.
gpt_text:
Turing machine equivalents are models of computation that can simulate any Turing machine and thus compute exactly the same class of functions (the Turing-computable or recursive functions). Despite differing in structure or intuition, they are all equally powerful in terms of what they can compute, even if they differ in efficiency or convenience.

Common Turing-equivalent models include the λ-calculus, register machines, Post systems, μ-recursive functions, cellular automata like Rule 110, and modern programming languages (under idealized assumptions such as unbounded memory). The existence of many equivalent models underpins the Church–Turing thesis: the informal notion of “effectively computable” coincides with what can be computed by any of these formal systems.

title: Computation history
human_text: In computer science, a computation history is a sequence of steps taken by an abstract machine in the process of computing its result. Computation histories are frequently used in proofs about the capabilities of certain machines, and particularly about the undecidability of various formal languages.
gpt_text:
A computation history is a step-by-step record of how a computation progresses from its initial state to its final result. In theoretical computer science, especially in the study of Turing machines and formal languages, it typically lists each configuration (machine state, tape contents, and head position) at every step of the machine’s execution.  

Computation histories are used to reason about what a machine does, to prove properties like correctness or decidability, and to encode computations into other formal systems (for example, turning the question “Does this machine accept this input?” into a question about whether there exists a valid sequence of configurations obeying the machine’s transition rules).

title: Description number
human_text: Description numbers are numbers that arise in the theory of Turing machines. They are very similar to Gödel numbers, and are also occasionally called "Gödel numbers" in the literature. Given some universal Turing machine, every Turing machine can, given its encoding on that machine, be assigned a number. This is the machine's description number. These numbers play a key role in Alan Turing's proof of the undecidability of the halting problem, and are very useful in reasoning about Turing machines as well.
gpt_text:
A **description number** is a natural number used to encode a formal description, typically of a Turing machine, program, or mathematical object, into a purely numerical form. This idea comes from mathematical logic and computability theory, where syntactic objects (like strings, formulas, or algorithms) are systematically assigned unique numbers so that questions about those objects can be turned into questions about numbers.

Alan Turing introduced description numbers to formalize the notion of computability: each Turing machine can be represented by a finite description, which can in turn be encoded as a single integer. This allows us to talk about “the machine with description number n” and to construct universal machines and undecidability proofs (such as for the halting problem) purely in arithmetic terms.

title: Stream X-Machine
human_text: The Stream X-machine (SXM) is a model of computation introduced by Gilbert Laycock in his 1993 PhD thesis, The Theory and Practice of Specification Based Software Testing.Gilbert Laycock (1993)
gpt_text:
A Stream X-Machine (SXM) is a formal computational model that extends the classical finite state machine by combining it with a structured memory (data states) and well-defined processing functions. Unlike basic automata that operate only on input symbols and control states, an SXM processes streams of inputs using a separate data component and transition functions that can transform both the control state and the data, and can also produce outputs. This makes it a powerful model for specifying and reasoning about complex, data-rich systems.

In software engineering, Stream X-Machines are often used as a basis for formal specification and model-based testing. Because the model separates control flow (states and transitions) from data manipulation (memory and processing functions), it supports rigorous test generation with proven coverage properties. SXMs are particularly useful in designing and verifying reactive or interactive systems, where inputs and outputs occur as continuous streams over time.

title: History of the Church–Turing thesis
human_text: The history of the Church–Turing thesis ("thesis") involves the history of the development of the study of the nature of functions whose values are effectively calculable; or, in more modern terms, functions whose values are algorithmically computable. It is an important topic in modern mathematical theory and computer science, particularly associated with the work of Alonzo Church and Alan Turing.
gpt_text:
The Church–Turing thesis emerged independently in the 1930s from the work of Alonzo Church and Alan Turing, who were each trying to formalize the intuitive notion of an “effective procedure” or “mechanical computation.” Church introduced the λ‑calculus (1932–36) as a formal system for defining computable functions, and proved that various notions of calculability coincided with λ‑definability. Around the same time, Turing (1936) analyzed what a human “computer” could do step-by-step and proposed the Turing machine as a precise model of mechanical calculation; he then showed that his notion of computability matched Church’s. This convergence, along with similar results by Emil Post and others, led to the informal thesis that these formalisms capture all effectively computable functions.

Historically, the thesis was not presented as a mathematical theorem but as a methodological and philosophical claim about the limits of computation: anything that can be computed by any effective means can be computed by a Turing machine (or any equivalent formalism). Over time it was strengthened and generalized, influencing the foundations of computability theory, the development of modern computer science, and later the “physical Church–Turing thesis,” which asserts that any physically realizable computing device can be efficiently simulated by a Turing machine. Debates about hypercomputation, quantum computing, and physical limits of computation have kept the status and scope of the thesis an active topic in logic, philosophy, and theoretical computer science.

title: Super-recursive algorithm
human_text: In computability theory, super-recursive algorithms are a generalization of ordinary algorithms that are more powerful, that is, compute more than Turing machines. The term was introduced by Mark Burgin, whose book "Super-recursive algorithms" develops their theory and presents several mathematical models. Turing machines and other mathematical models of conventional algorithms allow researchers to find properties of recursive algorithms and their computations. In a similar way, mathematical models of super-recursive algorithms, such as inductive Turing machines, allow researchers to find properties of super-recursive algorithms and their computations.
gpt_text:
A super-recursive algorithm is a theoretical model of computation that is claimed to go beyond the power of classical Turing machines in some sense—typically by producing progressively better approximations to a result or by operating over infinite time or data streams. Unlike standard (recursive) algorithms, which must halt with a final output, super-recursive algorithms may generate outputs in a limit process, refine answers indefinitely, or rely on more powerful computational paradigms such as inductive Turing machines or trial-and-error machines.

The concept arises mainly in the study of hypercomputation, which explores whether there are meaningful models of computation that can solve problems unsolvable by ordinary Turing machines (like the halting problem) under idealized assumptions. While these models are mathematically interesting and can illuminate aspects of learning, approximation, and ongoing computation, their physical realizability remains speculative and controversial.

title: Communicating X-Machine
human_text: The Communicating (Stream) X-Machine is a model of computation introduced by various researchers in the 1990s to model systems composed of communicating agents. The model exists in several variants, which are either based directly on Samuel Eilenberg's X-machineS. Eilenberg (1974)
gpt_text:
A Communicating X-Machine (CXM) is a formal modeling framework that extends the classic X-Machine by allowing multiple machines to interact via communication channels. Each X-Machine combines finite control (states and transitions) with an internal memory and processing functions, and in a CXM model, several such machines exchange messages, enabling the description of distributed or concurrent systems.

This approach is particularly useful in software engineering and formal verification, as it provides a mathematically precise way to specify complex, interacting components while keeping each component’s logic relatively simple. CXMs support rigorous analysis, test generation, and verification of system properties such as correctness of communication protocols and overall system behavior.

title: Introduction to the Theory of Computation
human_text: Introduction to the Theory of Computation () is a standard textbook in theoretical computer science, written by Michael Sipser and first published by PWS Publishing in 1997.
gpt_text:
“Introduction to the Theory of Computation” usually refers to the field (and often the well-known textbook by Michael Sipser) that studies the fundamental limits of what can be computed, how efficiently it can be done, and how we formally describe computational processes. It provides mathematical models of computation—such as finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines—to rigorously define what an algorithm is and what problems are solvable by machines.

The subject is typically divided into three main areas: automata and formal languages (how machines recognize patterns and languages), computability theory (which problems can or cannot be solved algorithmically, including undecidability results like the Halting Problem), and complexity theory (how much time or memory is needed to solve problems, and classes like P, NP, and NP-complete). Together, these ideas form the theoretical foundation underlying computer science, independent of any particular programming language or hardware.

title: Recursive language
human_text: In mathematics, logic and computer science, a formal language (a set of finite sequences of symbols taken from a fixed alphabet) is called recursive if it is a recursive subset of the set of all possible finite sequences over the alphabet of the language. Equivalently, a formal language is recursive if there exists a total Turing machine (a Turing machine that halts for every given input) that, when given a finite sequence of symbols as input, accepts it if it belongs to the language and rejects it otherwise. Recursive languages are also called decidable.
gpt_text:
A recursive language (also called a decidable language) is a set of strings over some alphabet for which there exists a Turing machine that always halts and correctly decides membership: it accepts every string in the language and rejects every string not in the language, never looping indefinitely. In other words, there is an algorithm that, given any input string, will eventually answer “yes” if the string is in the language and “no” if it is not.

Recursive languages are important in computability theory because they capture precisely those decision problems that are fully solvable by an algorithm. They are a subset of the recursively enumerable languages, which only require that the machine halts on strings in the language (it may loop forever on strings not in the language).

title: Circuit (computer science)
human_text: In theoretical computer science, a circuit is a model of computation in which input values proceed through a sequence of gates, each of which computes a function. Circuits of this kind provide a generalization of Boolean circuits and a mathematical model for digital logic circuits. Circuits are defined by the gates they contain and the values the gates can produce. For example, the values in a Boolean circuit are boolean values, and the circuit includes conjunction, disjunction, and negation gates. The values in an integer circuit are sets of integers and the gates compute set union, set intersection, and set complement, as well as the arithmetic operations addition and multiplication.
gpt_text:
In computer science, a circuit usually refers to a *Boolean circuit*: a network of logical gates (like AND, OR, NOT) connected by wires to compute a function on binary inputs. Each gate takes one or more input bits, performs a simple logical operation, and produces an output bit; by wiring many gates together in layers, a circuit can implement complex computations such as arithmetic operations, comparison, or even entire algorithms.

Boolean circuits are a key model in computational complexity theory. Researchers study how many gates (size) and how many layers (depth) are needed to compute particular functions, using circuits to classify problems by their resource requirements. This abstract model corresponds closely to real digital hardware, where physical electronic circuits implement the logic that runs computer processors and other digital systems.

title: Primitive recursive set function
human_text: In mathematics, primitive recursive set functions or primitive recursive ordinal functions are analogs of primitive recursive functions, defined for sets or ordinals rather than natural numbers. They were introduced by.
gpt_text:
A primitive recursive set function is the set-theoretic analogue of a primitive recursive function on the natural numbers. Instead of operating on numbers, it operates on sets (often within a foundational system like ZF), and is built up from very basic initial set functions—such as projection functions, constant functions, pairing, union, and similar operations—using a restricted collection of defining schemes like composition and recursion.  

These functions are designed so that their computation process is always finite and explicitly determined, ensuring that they are “effectively computable” in a strong, highly structured sense. Primitive recursive set functions play a role in proof theory and constructive set theory, where one studies which set operations and constructions can be carried out in a strictly controlled, recursion-based framework.

title: Enumerator (computer science)
human_text: An enumerator is a Turing machine that lists, possibly with repetitions, elements of some set S, which it is said to enumerate. A set enumerated by some enumerator is said to be recursively enumerable.
gpt_text:
In computer science, an enumerator is an abstraction that systematically lists elements of a collection or a set, typically in a defined sequence. It provides a way to traverse data structures (like arrays, lists, trees, or hash tables) one element at a time without exposing or depending on the underlying representation. Many programming languages offer built‑in enumerator or iterator constructs (e.g., `IEnumerator` in C#, iterators in C++/Java/Python) that let you loop over elements with simple syntax (such as `foreach` or `for-each` loops).

In a more theoretical sense, an enumerator can also refer to a computational process (often modeled as a Turing machine with an output device) that generates all elements of a set, possibly with repetition and in no particular order, but such that every member of the set eventually appears. This concept is central in computability theory, where a set is called recursively enumerable if there exists such a procedure that enumerates its elements.

title: Reachability analysis
human_text: Reachability analysis is a solution to the reachability problem in the particular context of distributed systems. It is used to determine which global states can be reached by a distributed system which consists of a certain number of local entities that communicated by the exchange of messages.
gpt_text:
Reachability analysis is a formal method used to determine which states of a system can be reached from a given initial state, following the system’s rules or dynamics. It is widely used in control theory, formal verification, and safety-critical system design to check whether “bad” or unsafe states are possible and to ensure that desired states are attainable. 

In practice, reachability analysis systematically explores the state space of models such as automata, hybrid systems, or differential equations. By computing or over-approximating all reachable states, engineers and researchers can verify properties like safety, liveness, and stability, detect design flaws, and synthesize controllers that keep the system within safe operating conditions.

title: ESP game
human_text: The ESP game is a human-based computation game developed to address the problem of creating difficult metadata. The idea behind the game is to use the computational power of humans to perform a task that computers cannot (originally, image recognition) by packaging the task as a game. It was originally conceived by Luis von Ahn of Carnegie Mellon University. Google bought a licence to create its own version of the game (Google Image Labeler) in 2006 in order to return better search results for its online images. The licence of the data acquired by Ahn's ESP game, or the Google version, is not clear. Google's version was shut down on September 16, 2011 as part of the Google Labs closure in September 2011.
gpt_text:
The ESP game is a human computation game developed by Luis von Ahn and colleagues to harness human intelligence for labeling images. In the game, two anonymous players are shown the same image and asked to type words describing it; when both independently enter the same word, it’s considered a “match” and they earn points. Because the players don’t communicate and are incentivized to agree on obvious descriptors, the matched words are typically accurate and relevant labels for the image.

These labels can then be used to improve image search, accessibility tools, and computer vision systems. The ESP game is a classic example of turning a tedious task (manual annotation) into a fun activity, illustrating how “games with a purpose” can solve computational problems that are difficult for machines but easy for humans.

title: Human-based computation
human_text: Human-based computation (HBC), human-assisted computation,Shahaf, 2007 ubiquitous human computing or distributed thinking (by analogy to distributed computing) is a computer science technique in which a machine performs its function by outsourcing certain steps to humans, usually as microwork. This approach uses differences in abilities and alternative costs between humans and computer agents to achieve symbiotic human–computer interaction. For computationally difficult tasks such as image recognition, human-based computation plays a central role in training Deep Learning-based Artificial Intelligence systems. In this case, human-based computation has been referred to as human-aided artificial intelligence.
gpt_text:
Human-based computation is a problem-solving approach that integrates human intelligence directly into computational processes, typically for tasks that computers alone struggle with, such as image recognition, natural language understanding, subjective judgment, or creativity. Instead of fully automating a task, it distributes small units of work to many people—often over the internet—who perform these micro-tasks, with their outputs aggregated by software into a final result.

This concept underlies systems like crowdsourcing platforms (e.g., Amazon Mechanical Turk), online games with a purpose (like reCAPTCHA and the ESP Game), and citizen science projects. By combining human perceptual and cognitive strengths with the speed and scalability of computers, human-based computation enables the solution of large, complex problems that would be too difficult, expensive, or time-consuming for either humans or machines to tackle alone.

title: Collaborative innovation network
human_text: Collaborative innovation is a process in which multiple players contribute towards creating new products with customers and suppliers.
gpt_text:
A collaborative innovation network (COIN) is a group of self-motivated people who share a common vision and work together—often virtually—to create new ideas, products, or solutions. Members contribute voluntarily, share knowledge openly, and build on each other’s work, usually across organizational, geographic, or disciplinary boundaries. These networks are driven more by shared purpose and trust than by formal hierarchy or rigid structures.

COINs often rely on digital communication tools and social media, making it easy for participants to connect, coordinate, and rapidly iterate on ideas. Well-known examples include open-source software communities and online scientific collaborations, where innovation emerges from continuous interaction, peer review, and collective problem-solving.

title: Human search engine
human_text: A human search engine is a search engine that uses human participation to filter the search results and assist users in clarifying their search request. The goal is to provide users with a limited number of relevant results, as opposed to traditional search engines that often return many results that may or may not be relevant.
gpt_text:
A human search engine is a service or system in which people—not algorithms alone—play a central role in finding, filtering, and organizing information. Instead of relying purely on automated web crawlers and ranking formulas like traditional search engines, human search engines use human judgment to interpret questions, evaluate sources, and present relevant, high-quality answers.

These can take the form of Q&A platforms, expert networks, or curated search services where human editors or community members review and refine results. Human search engines are especially useful for nuanced, subjective, or complex queries where context and critical thinking matter more than sheer data volume.

title: 3form
human_text: 3form Free Knowledge Exchange is one of the earliest examples of human-based computation and human-based genetic algorithm (Kosorukoff, 1998). It uses both human-based selection and three types of human-based innovation (contributing new content, mutation, and recombination), in order to implement collaborative problem-solving between humans. However, on May 8 2016 3 form was down due to technical issue.
gpt_text:
3form is a materials and design company known for its translucent architectural panels and sustainable surface materials used in interior and exterior design. Their products often incorporate resin, glass, and other composites that can be customized with colors, textures, and embedded materials to achieve specific aesthetic and functional effects.

Widely used in commercial spaces, hospitality, healthcare, and offices, 3form panels are commonly applied as room dividers, wall features, doors, ceilings, and lighting elements. The company emphasizes environmental responsibility, offering materials with recycled content and options designed to meet green building standards such as LEED.

title: Ontogame
human_text: OntoGame is a project and series of games that aim at weaving the Semantic Web. It was initiated by Katharina Siorpaes and Martin Hepp at the University of Innsbruck. The core idea is that, despite significant advancement in technology and tools, building ontologies, annotating data, and aligning multiple ontologies remain tasks that highly depend on human intelligence, both as a source of domain expertise and for making conceptual choices. This means that people need to contribute time, and sometimes other resources, to this endeavor.
gpt_text:
OntoGame is a series of online “games with a purpose” designed to help build and refine formal ontologies—structured representations of knowledge—by harnessing human intelligence through playful tasks. Players perform simple game activities such as classifying, relating, or annotating concepts, and their collective input is translated into semantic data that can improve the quality of knowledge bases used in areas like the Semantic Web.

Developed in the mid-2000s by researchers at the University of Vienna, OntoGame adapts ideas from human computation and crowdsourcing: instead of requiring experts to manually encode large ontologies, it distributes small, intuitive micro-tasks to many non-expert players. By comparing and aggregating players’ answers, the system can detect consensus, filter out noise, and incrementally construct or refine logically structured concept hierarchies and relations.

title: FamilySearch Indexing
human_text: FamilySearch Indexing is a volunteer project established and run by FamilySearch, a genealogy organization of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The project aims to create searchable digital indexes of scanned images of historical documents that are relevant to genealogy. The documents include census records, birth and death certificates, marriage licenses, military and property records, and other vital records maintained by local, state, and national governments. However, to access the billions of names that appear on these images, indexes are needed to be able to search them efficiently.
gpt_text:
FamilySearch Indexing is a volunteer-driven program run by FamilySearch, a nonprofit genealogy organization sponsored by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Volunteers around the world help convert digitized historical records—such as birth, marriage, death, census, and immigration documents—into searchable, typed indexes.

By transcribing key information from old handwritten or printed records, indexers make it possible for anyone to easily search for ancestors by name, date, and place on FamilySearch.org. This crowdsourced effort greatly speeds up genealogical research and preserves access to important historical documents that might otherwise remain difficult to find or interpret.

title: Page Hunt
human_text: Page Hunt is a game developed by Bing for investigating human research behavior. It is a so-called "game with a purpose", as it pursues additional goals: not only to provide entertainment but also to harness human computation for some specific research task.
gpt_text:
Page Hunt was an experimental game developed by Microsoft Research that turned web search evaluation into a fun, crowd-powered activity. Players were shown a web page and asked to guess which search queries would make that page appear in the top results for Bing. By entering queries they thought matched the page’s content, users effectively helped identify how well the search engine was ranking pages and which queries were missing or underperforming.

The collected data from Page Hunt was used to improve search relevance, discover new query–page associations, and diagnose gaps where good pages were not being retrieved for appropriate queries. It is often cited as an example of “games with a purpose,” where a game’s mechanics produce useful data for machine learning and information retrieval research.

title: EteRNA
human_text: Eterna is a browser-based "game with a purpose", developed by scientists at Carnegie Mellon University and Stanford University, that engages users to solve puzzles related to the folding of RNA molecules."RNA Game Lets Players Help Find a Biological Prize", John Markoff, New York Times, January 10, 2011 The project is supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, Stanford University, and the National Institutes of Health. Prior funders include the National Science Foundation."Rebooting science outreach", Alan Chen, American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, June 2011
gpt_text:
EteRNA is an online citizen science game in which players design RNA molecules that are then tested in real-world laboratory experiments. Created through a collaboration between scientists and game designers, it turns RNA folding—an important problem in biology and medicine—into interactive puzzles that anyone can attempt to solve, regardless of scientific background.

Players propose RNA sequences that should fold into target shapes; the most promising designs are synthesized and evaluated in labs, and the results are fed back into the game. These crowdsourced solutions help researchers improve computational models of RNA structure and can inform real-world applications such as RNA-based therapeutics, biosensors, and synthetic biology tools.

title: Participatory sensing
human_text: Participatory sensing is the concept of communities (or other groups of people) contributing sensory information to form a body of knowledge.wilsoncenter.org
gpt_text:
Participatory sensing is a data collection approach in which individuals use their personal devices—typically smartphones with sensors like GPS, cameras, and accelerometers—to gather and share information about their environment or experiences. Instead of relying solely on dedicated instruments or experts, participatory sensing distributes sensing tasks across many voluntary participants, often at large scale and in real time.

This model is used in areas such as environmental monitoring (e.g., air quality, noise levels), urban planning (e.g., reporting potholes or traffic conditions), and public health (e.g., tracking symptoms or physical activity). It leverages the ubiquity of mobile technology to create rich, fine-grained datasets, while also raising important questions about privacy, data quality, and participant motivation.

title: SETILive
human_text: SETILive was an online project of Zooniverse that utilized live participants to analyze radio telescope data in real time to recognize patterns to find extraterrestrial intelligences (ETI's). The project ceased live operations on 12 October 2014, but still allows archival analysis.
gpt_text:
SETILive was a citizen science project launched by the SETI Institute in collaboration with Zooniverse, designed to involve the public directly in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Participants examined real-time data from radio telescopes—particularly the Allen Telescope Array—looking for unusual radio signals that automated algorithms might miss, such as patterns that stood out from background noise or human-made interference.

By turning signal-spotting into an online, game-like activity, SETILive aimed to harness human pattern-recognition abilities at scale. Although the project is no longer active, it served as a notable experiment in crowdsourcing complex scientific analysis and engaging the public in the scientific process behind SETI research.

title: Codd's 12 rules
human_text: Codd's twelve rules are a set of thirteen rules (numbered zero to twelve) proposed by Edgar F. Codd, a pioneer of the relational model for databases, designed to define what is required from a database management system in order for it to be considered relational, i.e., a relational database management system (RDBMS).. They are sometimes jokingly referred to as "Codd's Twelve Commandments".
gpt_text:
Codd’s 12 rules are a set of guidelines proposed by Edgar F. Codd to define what it means for a database system to be truly relational. They were introduced to distinguish genuine relational database management systems (RDBMS) from products that only partially implemented relational concepts. Each “rule” describes a property or capability that a system should have, such as representing all data as values in tables, supporting a comprehensive high-level query language, and ensuring logical data independence so applications are insulated from changes in physical storage.

The rules cover aspects like guaranteed access to all data (via table name, primary key, and column name), systematic treatment of null values, a single logical data model (the relational model), views that are logically updatable, and the integrity of data being definable in the schema rather than in application code. While no commercial system perfectly satisfies all 12 rules, they remain a foundational reference for understanding the principles and goals of relational databases.

title: Database theory
human_text: Database theory encapsulates a broad range of topics related to the study and research of the theoretical realm of databases and database management systems.
gpt_text:
Database theory is the branch of computer science that studies the formal principles behind the design, operation, and optimization of databases. It provides mathematical models—such as the relational model, set theory, and logic—to describe data, queries, and constraints in a precise way. Core topics include relational algebra and calculus, query languages like SQL, normalization and schema design, integrity constraints, and the theory of transactions and concurrency.

By focusing on correctness, efficiency, and expressiveness, database theory guides how practical database management systems are built and improved. It helps answer questions like what can be expressed in a query language, how to optimize queries, how to avoid redundancy and anomalies in data, and how to guarantee consistency and reliability even in the presence of failures or concurrent access.

title: Data cube
human_text: In computer programming contexts, a data cube (or datacube) is a multi-dimensional ("n-D") array of values. Typically, the term datacube is applied in contexts where these arrays are massively larger than the hosting computer's main memory; examples include multi-terabyte/petabyte data warehouses and time series of image data.
gpt_text:
A data cube is a multidimensional data structure used in data warehousing and online analytical processing (OLAP) to organize and analyze data across multiple dimensions, such as time, location, and product. Instead of viewing data only in two dimensions (rows and columns), a data cube lets users explore metrics (like sales or revenue) along several axes at once, enabling complex aggregations and summaries.

Each cell in a data cube contains aggregated values (for example, total sales for a given product in a specific region during a particular time period). This structure supports fast querying and slicing/dicing of data, making it easier for analysts and decision-makers to discover trends, patterns, and insights from large datasets.

title: Attribute domain
human_text: In computing, the attribute domain is the set of values allowed in an attribute.
gpt_text:
In database design, an attribute domain is the set of all possible valid values that a particular attribute (column) can take. It defines the type, format, and constraints of the data—for example, an attribute “Age” might have the domain of all integers between 0 and 120, and an attribute “Email” might have the domain of character strings matching an email pattern.

Defining clear attribute domains helps enforce data integrity and consistency: the database system can reject values that fall outside the specified domain, preventing invalid or nonsensical data from being stored.

title: Transitive dependency
human_text: A transitive dependency is a functional dependency which holds by virtue of transitivity among various software components.
gpt_text:
A transitive dependency occurs in a relational database when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, rather than depending directly on the table’s primary key. In other words, attribute A depends on attribute B, and attribute B depends on the primary key, so A is transitively dependent on the primary key through B.

Transitive dependencies are important in normalization, especially when moving from Second Normal Form (2NF) to Third Normal Form (3NF). To achieve 3NF, transitive dependencies are removed by placing the indirectly dependent attributes into a separate table, which reduces redundancy and update anomalies.

title: Entity–attribute–value model
human_text: Entity–attribute–value model (EAV) is a data model to encode, in a space-efficient manner, entities where the number of attributes (properties, parameters) that can be used to describe them is potentially vast, but the number that will actually apply to a given entity is relatively modest. Such entities correspond to the mathematical notion of a sparse matrix.
gpt_text:
The entity–attribute–value (EAV) model is a data modeling pattern used to store highly variable or sparsely populated attributes in a compact, flexible way. Instead of having a wide table with many columns (one per attribute), EAV stores data in three main columns: the entity (what the data is about, such as a patient or product), the attribute (the type of data, such as “height” or “color”), and the value (the actual data point). This allows new attributes to be added without altering the database schema.

EAV is commonly used in domains like biomedical databases, product catalogs, and content management systems, where different entities may have many possible attributes but only a few are actually used per instance. Its main trade-offs are that it can complicate queries, indexing, and validation, and may reduce performance compared to traditional relational designs, especially for analytic or reporting workloads.

title: Recursive join
human_text: The recursive join is an operation used in relational databases, also sometimes called a "fixed-point join". It is a compound operation that involves repeating the join operation, typically accumulating more records each time, until a repetition makes no change to the results (as compared to the results of the previous iteration).
gpt_text:
A recursive join is a database operation used to repeatedly join a table to itself (or through a hierarchy of related rows) to traverse multi-level relationships, such as organizational charts, folder trees, or bill-of-materials structures. Instead of a single self-join, a recursive join iteratively follows parent–child links until all connected levels are retrieved.

In SQL, this is typically implemented with a recursive common table expression (CTE), where an anchor query selects the base level (e.g., root nodes), and a recursive query repeatedly joins the CTE back to the underlying table using a parent/child key. The database engine executes this loop-like process until no new rows are produced, effectively walking the hierarchy.

title: Database storage structures
human_text: Database tables and indexes may be stored on disk in one of a number of forms, including ordered/unordered flat files, ISAM, heap files, hash buckets, or B+ trees. Each form has its own particular advantages and disadvantages. The most commonly used forms are B+ trees and ISAM. Such forms or structures are one aspect of the overall schema used by a database engine to store information.
gpt_text:
Database storage structures are the low-level ways in which a database physically organizes and stores data on disk or in memory so it can be retrieved, updated, and managed efficiently. They provide the foundation for higher-level database concepts like tables, indexes, and transactions, directly influencing performance, scalability, and reliability.

Common storage structures include heap files (unsorted collections of records), B+ tree indexes (balanced tree structures optimized for range queries and ordered access), and hash indexes (using hash functions for fast equality lookups). Databases also use pages or blocks as fixed-size units of storage, record formats to pack rows into pages, and specialized structures like log files for write-ahead logging, plus columnar storage layouts in analytical systems to speed up aggregation and compression.

title: V-optimal histograms
human_text: Histograms are most commonly used as visual representations of data. However, Database systems use histograms to summarize data internally and provide size estimates for queries. These histograms are not presented to users or displayed visually, so a wider range of options are available for their construction. Simple or exotic histograms are defined by four parameters, Sort Value, Source Value, Partition Class and Partition Rule. The most basic histogram is the equi-width histogram, where each bucket represents the same range of values. That histogram would be defined as having a Sort Value of Value, a Source Value of Frequency, be in the Serial Partition Class and have a Partition Rule stating that all buckets have the same range.
gpt_text:
V-optimal histograms are a type of histogram used in databases and data analysis that aim to minimize the total approximation error between the true data distribution and the histogram’s summarized representation. Instead of simply dividing the data range into equally sized buckets or allocating equal numbers of values per bucket, V-optimal histograms choose bucket boundaries so that the variance (or squared error) within each bucket is as small as possible, leading to a lower overall error across all buckets.

They are particularly useful for query optimization, where the database system needs accurate estimates of value distributions (e.g., for selectivity estimation in SQL queries) while storing only a compact summary. Computing an exactly optimal V-optimal histogram is computationally expensive, so practical systems use dynamic programming or approximation algorithms to construct them efficiently while still achieving near-minimal error.

title: Conjunctive query
human_text: In database theory, a conjunctive query is a restricted form of first-order queries using the logical conjunction operator. Many first-order queries can be written as conjunctive queries. In particular, a large part of queries issued on relational databases can be expressed in this way. Conjunctive queries also have a number of desirable theoretical properties that larger classes of queries (e.g., the relational algebra queries) do not share.
gpt_text:
A conjunctive query is a foundational type of database query that selects data using only conjunctions (AND), existential quantification, and atomic predicates (like table relations and equality), without disjunction (OR) or negation. In relational databases, it corresponds closely to a SELECT-FROM-WHERE query that uses only joins, selections, and projections, with conditions combined by AND.

Formally, a conjunctive query can be written as an existentially quantified conjunction of relational atoms, such as  
∃x₁,…,xₙ (R₁(…) ∧ R₂(…) ∧ … ∧ Rₖ(…)),  
often with some variables designated as the output. Conjunctive queries are important in database theory because they are expressive enough for many practical queries, yet simple enough to allow deep analysis of properties like containment, equivalence, and optimization.

title: Nested set model
human_text: The nested set model is a technique for representing nested sets (also known as trees or hierarchies) in relational databases.
gpt_text:
The nested set model is a way of representing hierarchical (tree-like) data in a relational database using two numeric boundaries, typically called `left` and `right` (or `lft` and `rgt`), instead of parent-child pointers. Each node in the tree is assigned a pair of numbers such that a node’s `left` value is set when you “enter” it in a depth-first traversal, and its `right` value is set when you “leave” it. A node’s descendants are all the nodes whose `left` and `right` values fall strictly between that node’s `left` and `right`.

This structure makes it very efficient to query entire subtrees or find all descendants/ancestors with a single range-based query, which can be an advantage over adjacency lists in read-heavy systems. However, inserting, moving, or deleting nodes can be expensive, because it often requires updating many `left`/`right` values in the table to keep the numeric intervals consistent.

title: Single Table Inheritance
human_text: Single table inheritance is a way to emulate object-oriented inheritance in a relational database. When mapping from a database table to an object in an object-oriented language, a field in the database identifies what class in the hierarchy the object belongs to. All fields of all the classes are stored in the same table, hence the name "Single Table Inheritance". In Ruby on Rails the field in the table called 'type' identifies the name of the class. In Hibernate (Java) and Entity Framework this pattern is called Table-Per-Class-Hierarchy and Table-Per-Hierarchy (TPH) respectively., and the column containing the class name is called the Discriminator column.
gpt_text:
Single Table Inheritance (STI) is an object‑relational mapping pattern where multiple classes in an inheritance hierarchy are stored in a single database table. The table contains all possible columns needed by any subclass, plus a “type” (or similar) discriminator column that indicates which subclass a given row represents. Each subclass then maps to the same table but filters rows by that discriminator value.

This approach simplifies schema design and querying, since all related records live in one table, but it can lead to sparsely populated columns (many NULLs for fields only used by certain subclasses) and increasingly unwieldy tables as the hierarchy grows. STI is common in frameworks like Ruby on Rails, which provide built‑in support for it.

title: Principle of orthogonal design
human_text: The principle of orthogonal design (abbreviated POOD) was developed by database researchers David McGoveran and Christopher J. Date in the early 1990s, and first published "A New Database Design Principle" in the July 1994 issue of Database Programming and Design and reprinted several times. It is the second of the two principles of database design, which seek to prevent databases from being too complicated or redundant, the first principle being the principle of full normalization (POFN).
gpt_text:
The *Principle of Orthogonal Design* (POD) is a database design guideline stating that each distinct fact should be represented in one and only one place in a schema. In other words, no two base relations (tables) should represent the same information, and each relation should have a clear, non-overlapping responsibility. This reduces redundancy, ambiguity, and the risk of inconsistent data updates across the system.

POD goes beyond normal forms by focusing on the logical independence of relations: if two tables can be seen as different "views" or decompositions of the same underlying relationship, they violate orthogonality. By enforcing orthogonal design, database schemas become easier to understand, maintain, and evolve, because each concept has a unique, well-defined home.

title: Chase (algorithm)
human_text: The chase is a simple fixed-point algorithm testing and enforcing implication of data dependencies in database systems. It plays important roles in database theory as well as in practice.
gpt_text:
The **chase** is an algorithm used in database theory to enforce and reason about constraints—especially dependencies like functional, inclusion, and tuple-generating dependencies—on relational data or logical theories. Given a database instance and a set of constraints, the chase repeatedly applies those constraints to “repair” or extend the instance so that it satisfies all of them, often by adding new tuples or equating values as required by the rules.

The chase is fundamental in areas such as query optimization, data exchange, data integration, and ontology-based data access. It underlies many proofs of decidability and complexity, and is used to test implication of constraints, check query containment under constraints, and construct universal solutions in data exchange. Variants of the algorithm (e.g., standard chase, oblivious chase, core chase) differ mainly in how aggressively they apply rules and handle redundancy and termination.

title: Dependency theory (database theory)
human_text: Dependency theory is a subfield of database theory which studies implication and optimization problems related to logical constraints, commonly called dependencies, on databases.
gpt_text:
In database theory, dependency theory studies formal constraints on data—primarily *dependencies*—that describe how values in one part of a database determine or restrict values in another. The most common examples are functional dependencies (FDs), multivalued dependencies (MVDs), and inclusion dependencies (INDs). These constraints are used to reason about the correctness, consistency, and structure of relational schemas, and form the mathematical foundation behind many design techniques.

Dependency theory underlies the process of normalization: decomposing relations into well-structured forms (like 3NF, BCNF) that avoid redundancy and update anomalies while preserving dependencies and enabling efficient querying.
