It provides inference rules (such as Armstrong’s axioms for FDs), algorithms for testing implication and equivalence of dependencies, and criteria for lossless-join decomposition and dependency preservation, making it a core theoretical area in relational database design.

title: Probabilistic database
human_text: Most real databases contain data whose correctness is uncertain. In order to work with such data, there is a need to quantify the integrity of the data. This is achieved by using probabilistic databases.
gpt_text:
A probabilistic database is a database system in which data items can have associated probabilities, representing uncertainty about their values, presence, or relationships. Instead of assuming every record and attribute is definitely correct and present, the system explicitly models “maybe” data, such as a tuple being in the table with 70% likelihood or an attribute having multiple possible values with different probabilities.

These systems are designed to answer queries while correctly propagating and combining these uncertainties, often returning not just results but also the probability that each result is correct. Probabilistic databases are especially useful in domains like information extraction, sensor data management, data integration, and scientific data, where imperfect, noisy, or conflicting information is common.

title: Data item
human_text: A data item describes an atomic state of a particular object concerning a specific property at a certain time point. A collection of data items for the same object at the same time forms an object instance (or table row). Any type of complex information can be broken down to elementary data items (atomic state). Data items are identified by object (o), property (p) and time (t), while the value (v) is a function of o, p and t: v = F(o,p,t).
gpt_text:
A data item is a single, distinct piece of data that can be stored, processed, or transmitted by a computer system. It typically represents one value or fact, such as a person’s age (e.g., 32), a product ID (e.g., “P-1045”), or a temperature reading (e.g., 21.5°C). 

In databases and information systems, a data item is often the smallest unit of information that still has meaning in a given context, corresponding to a field or attribute within a record (for example, the “Name” field in a customer record). Multiple data items are combined to form more complex structures like records, tables, or files.

title: Data event
human_text: A data event is a relevant state transition defined in an event schema. Typically, event schemata are described by pre- and post condition for a single or a set of data items. In contrast to ECA (Event condition action), which considers an event to be a signal, the data event not only refers to the change (signal), but describes specific state transitions, which are referred to in ECA as conditions.
gpt_text:
A data event is a specific occurrence or change involving data that is captured and recorded by a system, application, or process. It typically represents something that happened at a particular time—such as a user clicking a button, a transaction being completed, a sensor reading being generated, or a record being created, updated, or deleted in a database.

In data-driven and event-driven architectures, data events are fundamental units of information used for tracking behavior, triggering automated workflows, real-time analytics, monitoring, and auditing. Each data event usually includes details like a timestamp, the type of event, the entity involved, and relevant contextual attributes.

title: Bidirectionalization
human_text: In computer science, bidirectionalization refers to the process of given a source-to-view transformation (automatically) finding a mapping from the original source and an updated view to an updated source.
gpt_text:
Bidirectionalization is the process of turning a one-way transformation (a function that maps inputs to outputs) into a two-way, or bidirectional, transformation that can also update the original input when the output changes. This is especially important in areas like lenses in functional programming, model-view synchronization in user interfaces, and data synchronization between different representations or formats.

The core idea is that instead of only computing a result from some source data, a bidirectionalized program can also interpret edits to the result and translate them back into corresponding edits to the source. Designing such transformations is challenging, because they must maintain consistency between source and view while respecting constraints like information loss and ambiguity.

title: Persistent Object Identifier
human_text: In database design, a Persistent Object Identifier (POID) is a unique identifier of a record on a table, used as the primary key. Important characteristics of a POID are that it does not carry business information and are not generally exported or otherwise made visible to data users; as such a POID has many of the characteristics of a surrogate key. The only purpose of the POID is to act as the primary key on the table where it is defined and to be referenced as the foreign key by other tables. Because POIDs, like surrogate keys, do not carry business information, they are immune to changes in the form or meaning of business data.
gpt_text:
A Persistent Object Identifier (POI) is a long-lasting, unique reference assigned to a digital or physical object so it can always be reliably located and cited, even if its actual storage location or metadata changes over time. Unlike ordinary URLs, which can break when content moves or systems change, a POI is designed to remain stable and resolvable, typically through an intermediary service that maps the identifier to the object’s current location.

Systems such as DOIs (Digital Object Identifiers), Handles, ARKs, and URNs are common implementations of persistent identifiers. They are widely used in scholarly publishing, data repositories, and digital libraries to ensure that articles, datasets, software, and other resources can be consistently referenced, discovered, and linked across systems and over long periods.

title: Full table scan
human_text: A full table scan (also known as a sequential scan) is a scan made on a database where each row of the table is read in a sequential (serial) order and the columns encountered are checked for the validity of a condition. Full table scans are usually the slowest method of scanning a table due to the heavy amount of I/O reads required from the disk which consists of multiple seeks as well as costly disk to memory transfers.
gpt_text:
A full table scan is a database operation where the query engine reads every row of a table to find the data that matches the query condition. Instead of using an index to jump directly to relevant rows, the database starts at the first row and sequentially checks each one until it reaches the end of the table.

Full table scans are simple and sometimes efficient for small tables or queries that need most of the data anyway (e.g., reporting, aggregations over the whole table). However, on large tables they can be expensive and slow, consuming significant I/O and CPU. In performance tuning, frequent full table scans on large tables are a sign you may need indexes, query rewrites, or schema changes.

title: Analytical base table
human_text: In database theory, the Analytical Base Table (ABT) is a flat table that is used for building analytical models and scoring (predicting) the future behavior of a subject.
gpt_text:
An analytical base table (ABT) is a structured dataset specifically prepared for analytics and modeling, typically in data mining or machine learning projects. It is usually organized at a clearly defined “grain” (for example, one row per customer, account, or transaction) and contains all relevant predictor variables (features) and, when supervised learning is involved, one or more target variables (outcomes to be predicted).  

The ABT consolidates data from multiple source systems—such as transactional databases, CRM systems, and logs—into a clean, consistent format optimized for analysis rather than for operational use. It often includes engineered features (aggregations, ratios, flags, time-window summaries) that capture meaningful patterns and behaviors, making it the primary input for building, training, and evaluating predictive models and other advanced analytics.

title: Canonical cover
human_text: A canonical cover for F (a set of functional dependencies on a relation scheme) is a set of dependencies such that F logically implies all dependencies in , and logically implies all dependencies in F.
gpt_text:
A **canonical cover** (also called a minimal cover) of a set of functional dependencies in a relational database schema is a simplified, equivalent set of dependencies that has no redundancy. It preserves exactly the same implication power as the original set—meaning it determines the same keys and integrity constraints—but is stripped of all unnecessary attributes and duplicate or implied dependencies.

Formally, a canonical cover typically has these properties: (1) every functional dependency has a single attribute on the right-hand side; (2) no functional dependency can be removed without changing the closure of the set; and (3) no attribute in any left-hand side can be removed without changing the closure. Canonical covers are crucial in normalization, helping to design efficient and consistent database schemas by making the dependency structure as clear and compact as possible.

title: Hyperview (computing)
human_text: A hyperview in computing is a hypertextual view of the content of a database or set of data on a group of activities. As with a hyperdiagram multiple views are linked to form a hyperview.James Martin Rapid Application Development 1991 - Page 58 "Many views may be logically linked to form a hyperview, just as many diagrams are logically linked to form a hyperdiagram. A hyperview is a collection of knowledge about a given activity or group of activities and the data these activities use."
gpt_text:
In computing, a *hyperview* generally refers to an interface or visualization that presents multiple related views of data, documents, or application states in a single, integrated space, allowing users to navigate between them non‑linearly. It extends the idea of a “view” (a particular representation of information) into something more like a web or graph of views, often enriched with hyperlinks, context links, or dynamic transitions.

Hyperviews are used in systems where users need to explore complex, interlinked information—such as hypermedia systems, advanced IDEs, data visualization tools, and knowledge management applications. Rather than following a strict sequence of screens or pages, users can jump among connected views based on relationships (such as references, dependencies, or semantic links), supporting exploratory browsing and more flexible understanding of the underlying data or code.

title: PACELC theorem
human_text: In theoretical computer science, the PACELC theorem is an extension to the CAP theorem. It states that in case of network partitioning (P) in a distributed computer system, one has to choose between availability (A) and consistency (C) (as per the CAP theorem), but else (E), even when the system is running normally in the absence of partitions, one has to choose between latency (L) and consistency (C).
gpt_text:
The PACELC theorem is an extension of the CAP theorem that more fully describes the trade-offs in distributed databases. While CAP focuses on what happens *during a network partition* (you must choose between Availability and Consistency), PACELC adds that *Else* (when there is no partition), systems still face a trade-off between Latency and Consistency. Formally: “If there is a Partition (P), choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).”

This means every distributed system can be characterized as something like “PA/EL” (prioritizes Availability on partition, and low Latency otherwise) or “PC/EC” (prioritizes Consistency both during and outside partitions), and so on. PACELC highlights that even in normal operation, achieving strong consistency often requires higher latency, while systems that favor low latency frequently relax consistency guarantees (e.g., eventual consistency).

title: Range reporting
human_text: In computational geometry and database theory, a range reporting query asks for a list of the points that match the query. The query is often specified by a geometric shape, containing all the points that should match, and is called a range. Range reporting is a special case of range searching, in which queries may return other kinds of aggregate information about points in a range.
gpt_text:
Range reporting is a type of query in computational geometry and data structures where, given a set of points (often in 1D, 2D, or higher dimensions), you preprocess them so that you can quickly list all points that lie inside a specified query range. The “range” can be an interval on a line, an axis-aligned rectangle in the plane, a box in higher dimensions, or more complex shapes, depending on the problem variant.

The focus in range reporting is on both efficiency and completeness: the data structure should use reasonable space, answer queries quickly, and return all points in the range, typically in time proportional to the number of reported points plus some small overhead (e.g., O(log n + k), where n is the number of stored points and k is the number of points found). Classic structures used for range reporting include range trees, segment trees, k-d trees, and related spatial indexes.

title: Imieliński–Lipski algebra
human_text: An Imieliński–Lipski algebras is an extension of relational algebra onto tables with different types of null values. It is used to operate on relations with incomplete information.
gpt_text:
Imieliński–Lipski algebra is a formal framework for representing and manipulating **incomplete or uncertain information in relational databases**. Introduced by Tomasz Imieliński and Witold Lipski in the early 1980s, it extends classical relational algebra so that queries can be evaluated even when some attribute values are missing, unknown, or partially specified. Instead of treating nulls informally, it gives a precise semantic basis for how such incomplete data should behave under operations like selection, projection, and join.

The key idea is to model a database not as a single, fully known instance, but as a **set of possible worlds** (all the complete databases consistent with the incomplete information). The Imieliński–Lipski algebra then defines the result of a query as those tuples that appear in all or some of these possible worlds, depending on the intended semantics (e.g., certain vs. possible answers). This laid important theoretical foundations for later work on incomplete information, uncertain databases, and knowledge representation in data management.

title: Database repair
human_text: The problem of database repair is a question about relational databases which has been studied in database theory, and which is a particular kind of data cleansing. The problem asks about how we can "repair" an input relational database in order to make it satisfy integrity constraints. The goal of the problem is to be able to work with data that is "dirty", i.e., does not satisfy the right integrity constraints, by reasoning about all possible repairs of the data, i.e., all possible ways to change the data to make it satisfy the integrity constraints, without committing to a specific choice.
gpt_text:
Database repair is the process of detecting, correcting, and recovering from errors, corruption, or inconsistencies in a database so that it can return to a valid, usable state. Problems may stem from hardware failures, software bugs, crashes, faulty transactions, or user mistakes, and can manifest as missing records, invalid references, unreadable pages, or broken indexes.  

Repair techniques range from using built-in database tools (such as consistency checks, integrity constraint enforcement, and index rebuilding) to restoring from backups and applying transaction logs to recover lost or corrupted data. In more advanced settings, database repair can also involve automated reasoning to minimally modify data so that it satisfies all constraints again while preserving as much original information as possible.

title: Discrete optimization
human_text: Discrete optimization is a branch of optimization in applied mathematics and computer science.
gpt_text:
Discrete optimization is the study of mathematical methods for finding the best solution from a finite or countably infinite set of possibilities, where some or all decision variables can take only discrete (often integer or binary) values. Unlike continuous optimization, which works over real-valued variables and smooth spaces, discrete optimization problems often involve combinatorial structures such as graphs, sets, or sequences and are frequently NP-hard.

Typical examples include integer programming, traveling salesman and vehicle routing problems, scheduling, network design, and resource allocation with indivisible items. Techniques used range from exact methods (like branch-and-bound, cutting planes, and dynamic programming) to heuristics and metaheuristics (such as greedy algorithms, local search, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms) that trade optimality guarantees for speed and scalability on large, complex problems.

title: Continuous optimization
human_text: Continuous optimization is a branch of optimization in applied mathematics.
gpt_text:
Continuous optimization is the branch of optimization that deals with problems where some or all decision variables can take any value from a continuous range (such as all real numbers in an interval), rather than being restricted to discrete sets. The goal is to find the best value(s) of these variables that minimize or maximize an objective function, possibly under a set of equality and inequality constraints.

It underpins many areas of science, engineering, machine learning, and economics—examples include training neural networks, designing structures, or calibrating financial models. Methods for continuous optimization include gradient-based techniques (like gradient descent and Newton’s method), interior-point methods, and derivative-free approaches when gradients are unavailable or unreliable.

title: Multidisciplinary design optimization
human_text: Multi-disciplinary design optimization (MDO) is a field of engineering that uses optimization methods to solve design problems incorporating a number of disciplines. It is also known as multidisciplinary system design optimization (MSDO).
gpt_text:
Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO) is a methodology for designing complex systems by simultaneously considering multiple interacting disciplines—such as aerodynamics, structures, controls, and manufacturing—within a single optimization framework. Instead of optimizing each discipline separately and then trying to reconcile conflicts, MDO integrates them so that trade-offs and couplings are captured explicitly during the design process.

This approach is widely used in fields like aerospace, automotive, and energy systems, where performance, cost, weight, reliability, and environmental impact must all be balanced. MDO typically employs advanced numerical optimization, high-fidelity simulations, and clever problem decompositions to manage computational cost while finding designs that outperform those produced by traditional, discipline-by-discipline methods.

title: Minimax theorem
human_text: In the mathematical area of game theory, a minimax theorem is a theorem providing conditions that guarantee that the max–min inequality is also an equality.
gpt_text:
The minimax theorem is a fundamental result in game theory, originally proved by John von Neumann, which states that in any finite two‑player zero-sum game with mixed strategies, there exists a value of the game such that each player can guarantee at least (or at most) this value, regardless of the opponent’s actions. More concretely, the player trying to maximize the payoff has an optimal mixed strategy and the player trying to minimize the payoff has an optimal mixed strategy, and the maximum over all minimizing responses equals the minimum over all maximizing responses.

Formally, if the payoff function is \(f(x, y)\), where \(x\) is a mixed strategy of player 1 and \(y\) is a mixed strategy of player 2, the theorem states:
\[
\max_x \min_y f(x, y) = \min_y \max_x f(x, y).
\]
This equality underpins equilibrium analysis in competitive situations, justifying the use of mixed strategies and forming the basis for many results in economics, optimization, and statistical decision theory.

title: Utility maximization problem
human_text: In microeconomics, the utility maximization problem is the problem consumers face: "how should I spend my money in order to maximize my utility?" It is a type of optimal decision problem. It consists of choosing how much of each available good or service to consume, taking into account a constraint on total spending as well as the prices of the goods.
gpt_text:
A utility maximization problem is a core concept in microeconomics where an individual or household chooses a combination of goods and services that yields the highest possible satisfaction (utility) subject to a constraint, usually a budget. Formally, it involves maximizing a utility function—representing preferences—over all affordable bundles of goods given prices and income.

The solution to this problem predicts how demand for each good depends on prices and income. Under standard assumptions (like more is better and diminishing marginal utility), the optimal choice equalizes the marginal utility per dollar spent across goods, and the resulting demand functions form the basis for consumer theory and market demand analysis.

title: Topology optimization
human_text: Topology optimization (TO) is a mathematical method that optimizes material layout within a given design space, for a given set of loads, boundary conditions and constraints with the goal of maximizing the performance of the system. TO is different from shape optimization and sizing optimization in the sense that the design can attain any shape within the design space, instead of dealing with predefined configurations.
gpt_text:
Topology optimization is a computational design method that determines the best material layout within a given design space, for a given set of loads, boundary conditions, and performance targets. Instead of just adjusting dimensions of a fixed shape, it allows the shape itself—and even the connectivity of material—to change, effectively “carving out” or “growing” structures to meet objectives like minimum weight, maximum stiffness, or specific frequency behavior.

Commonly used in mechanical, aerospace, civil, and product design, topology optimization often produces organic-looking, lattice-like structures that are difficult to reach with traditional design intuition but are well-suited to advanced manufacturing methods such as 3D printing. The process typically involves iterative finite element analysis and mathematical optimization techniques to remove inefficient material while satisfying constraints on strength, stiffness, manufacturability, or other performance criteria.

title: Shape optimization
human_text: Shape optimization is part of the field of optimal control theory. The typical problem is to find the shape which is optimal in that it minimizes a certain cost functional while satisfying given constraints. In many cases, the functional being solved depends on the solution of a given partial differential equation defined on the variable domain.
gpt_text:
Shape optimization is a field in applied mathematics and engineering focused on finding the best possible shape of an object or domain to optimize a given performance measure, subject to constraints. The “shape” can refer to anything from the cross-section of an airplane wing to the layout of a mechanical part, and the performance measure might be drag, stress, weight, heat transfer, or acoustic properties.

Mathematically, shape optimization problems are often formulated as minimizing (or maximizing) an objective function that depends on a domain, such as an integral over that domain or its boundary, under physical laws described by partial differential equations (PDEs). Techniques include gradient-based methods using shape derivatives, level-set methods, and topology optimization, and the field is widely used in aerospace, automotive design, structural mechanics, and fluid dynamics.

title: Linear complementarity problem
human_text: In mathematical optimization theory, the linear complementarity problem (LCP) arises frequently in computational mechanics and encompasses the well-known quadratic programming as a special case. It was proposed by Cottle and Dantzig
gpt_text:
A linear complementarity problem (LCP) is a type of mathematical optimization problem where one seeks a vector \(x\) that satisfies a system of linear inequalities together with complementarity conditions. Given a matrix \(M\) and a vector \(q\), the LCP is to find \(x \ge 0\) such that
\[
Mx + q \ge 0,\quad \text{and} \quad x^\top (Mx + q) = 0,
\]
which means that for each component \(i\), at least one of \(x_i\) or \((Mx+q)_i\) must be zero. This captures the idea that certain pairs of variables cannot both be strictly positive at the same time.

LCPs arise in many areas, including game theory (e.g., computing Nash equilibria), mechanics (contact and friction problems), and economics (equilibrium models and market clearing). They generalize linear programming and can be solved by specialized algorithms such as pivoting methods (similar to the simplex method), interior-point methods, or iterative schemes, depending on properties of the matrix \(M\).

title: Descent direction
human_text: In optimization, a descent direction is a vector that, in the sense below, moves us closer towards a local minimum of our objective function.
gpt_text:
In optimization, a descent direction is any direction in which a function’s value decreases locally from a given point. Formally, for a differentiable function \(f(x)\), a vector \(d\) is a descent direction at point \(x\) if the directional derivative along \(d\) is negative, i.e., \(\nabla f(x)^\top d < 0\). This means that moving a small step from \(x\) in the direction \(d\) will reduce the value of \(f\).

Descent directions are central to iterative optimization algorithms such as gradient descent. The negative gradient \(-\nabla f(x)\) is the canonical descent direction because it points in the direction of steepest local decrease in function value, but many other directions can also qualify as descent directions as long as they yield a negative directional derivative.

title: Shekel function
human_text: Shekel function is a multidimensional, multimodal, continuous, deterministic function commonly used as a test function for testing optimization techniques.
gpt_text:
The shekel function (often “Shekel’s foxholes” function) is a standard benchmark function used in optimization and evolutionary computation to test and compare global optimization algorithms. It is defined as a multimodal function in several dimensions with many local minima (“foxholes”) and typically one or a few global minima, making it challenging for algorithms to avoid getting trapped in suboptimal regions.

Mathematically, it is usually expressed as a sum of terms involving inverse quadratic forms centered at fixed points, with different weight parameters. Because of its highly irregular landscape and sharp peaks and valleys, the Shekel function is particularly useful for evaluating the robustness and exploration capabilities of optimization methods such as genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, and other metaheuristics.

title: Backtracking line search
human_text: In (unconstrained) minimization, a backtracking line search, a search scheme based on the Armijo–Goldstein condition, is a line search method to determine the amount to move along a given search direction. It involves starting with a relatively large estimate of the step size for movement along the search direction, and iteratively shrinking the step size (i.e., "backtracking") until a decrease of the objective function is observed that adequately corresponds to the decrease that is expected, based on the local gradient of the objective function.
gpt_text:
Backtracking line search is an algorithm used in optimization to automatically choose how far to move along a descent direction when minimizing a function. Starting from a candidate step size (often 1), it repeatedly shrinks the step by a constant factor (like 0.5) until a sufficient decrease in the objective function is observed according to a condition such as the Armijo rule.  

This method balances progress and stability: it avoids steps that are too large (which might increase the function or cause divergence) while also not being overly conservative. It is widely used in gradient-based methods, including gradient descent and quasi-Newton methods, because it requires only function and gradient evaluations and is simple to implement.

title: Wolfe conditions
human_text: In the unconstrained minimization problem, the Wolfe conditions are a set of inequalities for performing inexact line search, especially in quasi-Newton methods, first published by Philip Wolfe in 1969.
gpt_text:
The Wolfe conditions are criteria used in line search methods for optimization to choose a suitable step size along a search direction. They ensure that each step both sufficiently reduces the objective function and has an appropriate slope behavior, helping gradient-based methods (like quasi-Newton or conjugate gradient) converge reliably.

There are two main Wolfe conditions. The **Armijo (sufficient decrease) condition** requires that the function value at the new point be reduced enough relative to a linear prediction from the current gradient. The **curvature condition** requires that the directional derivative (slope along the search direction) at the new point not be too steep, ensuring the step is not overly short. The **strong Wolfe conditions** tighten the curvature condition by bounding the absolute value of the new directional derivative, balancing progress with stability.

title: Paper bag problem
human_text: In geometry, the paper bag problem or teabag problem is to calculate the maximum possible inflated volume of an initially flat sealed rectangular bag which has the same shape as a cushion or pillow, made out of two pieces of material which can bend but not stretch.
gpt_text:
The “paper bag problem” usually refers to a brainteaser about identifying what’s in a bag when your senses are limited or when information is incomplete. A classic version: you have several identical paper bags, each containing different items (e.g., coins of different weights, or balls of different colors), but you can only sample or weigh a few items and must deduce which bag is which using logic and minimal tests.  

These problems are used in math, logic, and computer science to teach reasoning under uncertainty, optimization (using the fewest tests or samples), and systematic problem‑solving. They highlight how much information can be extracted from very limited observations if you design your strategy carefully.

title: Corner solution
human_text: A corner solution is a special solution to an agent's maximization problem in which the quantity of one of the arguments in the maximized function is zero. In non-technical terms, a corner solution is when the chooser is either unwilling or unable to make a tradeoff.
gpt_text:
A corner solution is an outcome in an optimization problem where the optimal choice lies at the boundary (or “corner”) of the feasible set rather than at an interior point. In economics, this often occurs in consumer choice when the best affordable bundle involves consuming zero units of one good—for instance, spending all income on good X and none on good Y—so the usual condition that the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio does not hold.

Corner solutions typically arise when preferences or technologies make it optimal to specialize completely in one option, or when constraints are binding in such a way that the optimum is forced to the edge of what is possible. They contrast with interior solutions, where all chosen variables are strictly positive and first-order optimality conditions (like setting derivatives equal to zero) fully characterize the optimum.

title: Highly optimized tolerance
human_text: In applied mathematics, highly optimized tolerance (HOT) is a method of generating power law behavior in systems by including a global optimization principle. It was developed by Jean M. Carlson in the early 2000s. For some systems that display a characteristic scale, a global optimization term could potentially be added that would then yield power law behavior. It has been used to generate and describe internet-like graphs, forest fire models and may also apply to biological systems.
gpt_text:
Highly optimized tolerance (HOT) is a concept from complex systems theory describing how systems that are carefully tuned for high performance under expected conditions become extremely fragile to unexpected disturbances. In other words, when a system (natural, engineered, or social) is optimized to handle the most common stresses very efficiently, it often does so by sacrificing robustness to rare or unusual events.

This idea helps explain why tightly optimized systems—like global supply chains, financial markets, or certain biological networks—can function very efficiently most of the time but suffer catastrophic failures when hit by surprises outside their design assumptions. HOT emphasizes the trade-off between efficiency and resilience: optimization narrows the range of tolerated disturbances, making rare shocks disproportionately damaging.

title: Guess value
human_text: In mathematical modeling, a guess value is more commonly called a starting value or initial value. These are necessary for most optimization problems which use search algorithms, because those algorithms are mainly deterministic and iterative, and they need to start somewhere. One common type of application is nonlinear regression.
gpt_text:
“Guess value” typically refers to an initial estimate used as a starting point in calculations or algorithms that refine the result iteratively. It’s common in numerical methods such as Newton-Raphson for solving equations, where the method begins with a guess value for the solution and improves it step by step until it reaches an acceptable accuracy.

In practical settings like spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel’s Goal Seek or IRR functions), a guess value can be provided to help the program converge more quickly or to the correct solution when multiple solutions are possible. While not always strictly required, a good guess value can significantly improve the speed and reliability of convergence.

title: Walrasian auction
human_text: A Walrasian auction, introduced by Léon Walras, is a type of simultaneous auction where each agent calculates its demand for the good at every possible price and submits this to an auctioneer. The price is then set so that the total demand across all agents equals the total amount of the good. Thus, a Walrasian auction perfectly matches the supply and the demand.
gpt_text:
A Walrasian auction, also known as a Walrasian tâtonnement process, is a theoretical market mechanism used in economics to determine equilibrium prices for multiple goods simultaneously. In this framework, an auctioneer announces a vector of prices, and all buyers and sellers respond by stating how much they want to buy or sell at those prices. No trades occur until prices adjust to a point where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply for every good.

The process iteratively adjusts prices: if demand exceeds supply for a good, its price is raised; if supply exceeds demand, its price is lowered. Under certain idealized conditions (perfect competition, complete markets, rational agents, no transaction costs), this procedure converges to a Walrasian (competitive) equilibrium, where markets clear and no participant can improve their outcome by trading at different prices.

title: Process optimization
human_text: Process optimization is the discipline of adjusting a process so as to optimize (make the best or most effective use of) some specified set of parameters without violating some constraint. The most common goals are minimizing cost and maximizing throughput and/or efficiency. This is one of the major quantitative tools in industrial decision making.
gpt_text:
Process optimization is the systematic improvement of business or technical processes to achieve better performance, typically by reducing costs, increasing speed, improving quality, or using fewer resources. It involves analyzing how work is currently done, identifying bottlenecks or waste, and then redesigning steps, inputs, or tools to make the process more efficient and effective.

Methods used in process optimization include techniques like Lean, Six Sigma, and statistical process control, as well as data analysis, automation, and simulation. It is applied across industries—manufacturing, logistics, software development, healthcare, and services—to deliver more value with the same or fewer inputs while maintaining or enhancing reliability and customer satisfaction.

title: Cake number
human_text: In mathematics, the cake number, denoted by Cn, is the maximum number of regions into which a 3-dimensional cube can be partitioned by exactly n planes. The cake number is so-called because one may imagine each partition of the cube by a plane as a slice made by a knife through a cube-shaped cake.
gpt_text:
The *cake number* of a polyhedron (or other solid) is the smallest number of pieces into which it can be cut so that those pieces can be rearranged to form its mirror image, using only rigid motions (translations and rotations, but no reflections through a plane). It measures how “far” a 3D shape is from being directly superimposable on its mirror image without flipping it over like a reflection in a mirror.

For example, a perfectly symmetric sphere has cake number 1, because it is already congruent to its mirror image. More irregular or chiral solids, such as certain knot-like shapes or “handed” objects, can require multiple pieces; their cake number reflects the minimal complexity of such a dissection.

title: Distributed constraint optimization
human_text: Distributed constraint optimization (DCOP or DisCOP) is the distributed analogue to constraint optimization. A DCOP is a problem in which a group of agents must distributedly choose values for a set of variables such that the cost
gpt_text:
Distributed constraint optimization (DCOP) is a framework for coordinating multiple autonomous agents to make joint decisions that satisfy constraints while optimizing a global objective (such as minimizing cost or maximizing utility). Each agent controls one or more variables, constraints can span multiple agents, and communication is typically limited to neighbors in a constraint graph. The goal is to find assignments to all variables that respect constraints and optimize the total objective, despite decentralized control and partial information.

DCOP is widely used in multi-agent systems for problems like sensor network coordination, distributed scheduling, and resource allocation. Algorithms for DCOP (e.g., DPOP, ADOPT, Max-Sum) trade off solution quality, communication overhead, and computation, making the framework suitable for settings where centralization is infeasible due to privacy, scalability, or robustness concerns.

title: Demand optimization
human_text: Demand optimization is the application of processes and tools to maximize return on sales. This usually involves the application of mathematical modeling techniques using computer software.
gpt_text:
Demand optimization is the process of strategically managing and influencing customer demand to better align with a company’s capacity, inventory, and financial goals. Instead of simply reacting to demand, organizations use data, forecasting, and pricing or promotion tactics to shape when, where, and how much customers buy. This helps reduce stockouts and overstock, improve service levels, and maximize revenue or profit.

Common techniques in demand optimization include dynamic pricing, promotion planning, product assortment decisions, and demand shaping (such as steering customers toward certain products or time windows). It typically relies on advanced analytics, including machine learning, to analyze historical sales, seasonality, market trends, and customer behavior to make more accurate and profitable decisions.

title: Dead-end elimination
human_text: The dead-end elimination algorithm (DEE) is a method for minimizing a function over a discrete set of independent variables. The basic idea is to identify "dead ends", i.e., combinations of variables that are not necessary to define a global minimum because there is always a way of replacing such combination by a better or equivalent one. Then we can refrain from searching such combinations further. Hence, dead-end elimination is a mirror image of dynamic programming, in which "good" combinations are identified and explored further. Although the method itself is general, it has been developed and applied mainly to the problems of predicting and designing the structures of proteins. It closely related to the notion of dominance in optimization also known as substitutability in a Constraint Satisfaction Problem. The original description and proof of the dead-end elimination theorem can be found in.
gpt_text:
Dead-end elimination (DEE) is an algorithmic technique used in computational protein design to efficiently search through the enormous space of possible side-chain conformations (rotamers) on a protein backbone. Its key idea is to provably discard (“eliminate”) rotamers that cannot be part of any global minimum-energy conformation, based on pairwise energy comparisons, without having to evaluate all combinations explicitly.

By iteratively removing such “dead-end” choices, DEE dramatically reduces the combinatorial complexity of the problem, making it feasible to find or approximate the lowest-energy arrangement of side chains for a given protein sequence or backbone. It provides mathematical guarantees: once a rotamer is eliminated by DEE criteria, it is certain not to appear in any optimal solution under the assumed energy model.

title: Mathematical Optimization Society
human_text: The Mathematical Optimization Society (MOS), known as the Mathematical Programming Society until 2010,The Mathematical Optimization Society was known as the Mathematical Programming Society (MPS) until 2010. is an international association of researchers active in optimization. The MOS encourages the research, development, and use of optimization—including mathematical theory, software implementation, and practical applications (operations research).
gpt_text:
The Mathematical Optimization Society (MOS) is an international professional organization devoted to the theory, algorithms, and applications of mathematical optimization. It brings together researchers and practitioners working in areas such as linear, nonlinear, integer, combinatorial, and stochastic optimization, as well as related fields in operations research and applied mathematics.

MOS supports the optimization community by sponsoring major journals (including *Mathematics of Operations Research*), organizing conferences such as the triennial International Symposium on Mathematical Programming (ISMP), and promoting the exchange of ideas between academia, industry, and government. It plays a key role in advancing both the theoretical foundations and practical impact of optimization worldwide.

title: Central composite design
human_text: In statistics, a central composite design is an experimental design, useful in response surface methodology, for building a second order (quadratic) model for the response variable without needing to use a complete three-level factorial experiment.
gpt_text:
Central composite design (CCD) is an experimental design used in response surface methodology to build a quadratic (curved) model for a response variable efficiently. It extends a factorial or fractional factorial design by adding center points (to estimate pure error and check curvature) and “axial” or “star” points (to capture curvature in each factor direction). This allows estimation of linear, interaction, and squared terms for multiple factors with relatively few experimental runs.

CCD is widely used in process optimization, formulation studies, and engineering because it balances statistical efficiency with practical run size. By fitting a second-order (quadratic) model, it helps identify optimal settings of input factors, visualize response surfaces and contour plots, and understand how variables jointly influence performance or quality outcomes.

title: Relaxation (approximation)
human_text: In mathematical optimization and related fields, relaxation is a modeling strategy. A relaxation is an approximation of a difficult problem by a nearby problem that is easier to solve. A solution of the relaxed problem provides information about the original problem.
gpt_text:
In optimization and computational complexity, a *relaxation* (or approximation via relaxation) is the process of simplifying a hard problem by loosening some of its constraints, so that the new “relaxed” problem is easier to solve. A typical example is turning an integer programming problem into a linear program by allowing variables that were required to be integers to take any real values. The solution to the relaxed problem can usually be found efficiently and provides a bound or guide for the original problem.

Relaxations are central to approximation algorithms: the relaxed problem is solved exactly (or nearly so), and then its solution is “rounded” or otherwise converted into a feasible solution for the original, harder problem. The quality of the resulting approximation can often be quantified, giving provable guarantees on how close the relaxed solution is to optimal for the original problem.

title: Mixed complementarity problem

title: Faustmann's formula

Basis pursuit is an optimization technique used to find the sparsest solution to an underdetermined linear system. Given a system \(Ax = b\) with many more unknowns than equations, basis pursuit seeks the solution \(x\) that has the fewest nonzero entries, typically by replacing the intractable \(\ell_0\)-minimization with \(\ell_1\)-minimization:  
\[
\min_x \|x\|_1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad Ax = b.
\]

It is central in compressed sensing, signal processing, and sparse representation, where the underlying assumption is that the true signal can be expressed using only a small number of basis elements. Under certain conditions on the matrix \(A\) (such as the Restricted Isometry Property), basis pursuit can exactly recover the sparsest solution, making it a powerful tool for reconstruction from limited or noisy measurements.

This is typically formulated as minimizing the \(\ell_1\)-norm of \(x\) (promoting sparsity) subject to a constraint on the \(\ell_2\)-norm of the residual \( \|Ax - y\|_2 \leq \epsilon \), where \(\epsilon\) reflects the noise magnitude.

The \(\ell_1\) penalty makes the optimization convex and computationally tractable, while still favoring solutions with many zero or near-zero components, making it effective for recovering signals from undersampled or corrupted measurements.

This connection to SDP makes SOS a powerful, computationally tractable tool for solving or bounding difficult optimization problems involving polynomials, such as in control theory, robust optimization, and verification. title: Multicriteria classification
human_text: In multiple criteria decision aiding (MCDA), multicriteria classification (or sorting) involves problems where a finite set of alternative actions should be assigned into a predefined set of preferentially ordered categories (classes). This method typically uses models or rules that aggregate information from all criteria, sometimes incorporating weights that reflect their relative importance. Techniques can range from simple scoring and threshold rules to more advanced methods like outranking, machine learning classifiers with multicriteria inputs, or fuzzy logic systems, all designed to handle trade-offs and support more balanced, realistic classification decisions.

title: Berth allocation problem
human_text: The berth allocation problem (also known as the berth scheduling problem) is a NP-complete problem in operations research, regarding the allocation of berth space for vessels in container terminals. Vessels arrive over time and the terminal operator needs to assign them to berths to be served (loading and unloading containers) as soon as possible. Different factors affect the berth and time assignment of each vessel.

Because ships vary in size, priority, and handling requirements, and ports may have multiple quays and operational rules, the BAP is complex and often modeled using mathematical programming or heuristics. Variants include discrete and continuous berth allocation, dynamic (ships arrive over time) and static (all information known in advance) versions, and integrated models that combine berth allocation with quay crane assignment or yard planning.

The max–min inequality is a basic result in optimization and game theory that relates the maximum of minimum values to the minimum of maximum values. For a real-valued function \(f(x, y)\) defined on product sets \(X \times Y\), it states
\[
\max_{x \in X} \min_{y \in Y} f(x, y) \;\le\; \min_{y \in Y} \max_{x \in X} f(x, y).
\]
Intuitively, if one player chooses \(x\) to maximize their guaranteed payoff (assuming the opponent chooses \(y\) to hurt them as much as possible), that guaranteed payoff can never exceed the payoff that the opponent can ensure by first choosing \(y\) to minimize the worst-case payoff over all \(x\).

This inequality underpins the distinction between max–min and min–max strategies in zero-sum games and optimization problems. Under additional conditions (like convexity/concavity and compactness), the inequality can become an equality—this is the content of various min–max theorems (such as von Neumann’s minimax theorem), which guarantee the existence of saddle points and equilibrium strategies.

title: Vector optimization
human_text: Vector optimization is a subarea of mathematical optimization where optimization problems with a vector-valued objective functions are optimized with respect to a given partial ordering and subject to certain constraints. A multi-objective optimization problem is a special case of a vector optimization problem: The objective space is the finite dimensional Euclidean space partially ordered by the component-wise "less than or equal to" ordering.

Instead of minimizing or maximizing one function, you deal with several functions at once, often representing conflicting goals such as cost vs. quality or speed vs. safety. Because these objectives usually cannot all be improved at the same time, solutions are compared using a partial order (e.g., componentwise comparisons).

A central concept in vector optimization is Pareto optimality (or efficiency): a solution is Pareto optimal if there is no other feasible solution that improves at least one objective without worsening another. Rather than yielding a single “best” solution, vector optimization typically produces a set of trade-off solutions (the Pareto front), from which a decision-maker can choose based on preferences or additional information.

title: Low-rank approximation

In applications, often there are other constraints on the approximating matrix apart from the rank constraint, e.g., non-negativity and Hankel structure.

This idea underlies many practical methods in data science and signal processing, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and matrix factorization techniques. By using a low-rank approximation, one can compress data, denoise signals, and uncover latent factors in large datasets, making computations more efficient and often improving generalization in machine learning tasks.

title: TOPSIS
human_text: The Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) is a multi-criteria decision analysis method, which was originally developed by Ching-Lai Hwang and Yoon in 1981 with further developments by Yoon in 1987, and Hwang, Lai and Liu in 1993.

TOPSIS (Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution) is a multi-criteria decision-making method used to rank a set of alternatives based on how close they are to an ideal solution. The ideal solution is a hypothetical alternative that maximizes all beneficial criteria and minimizes all cost criteria, while the negative-ideal solution does the opposite. Each real alternative is evaluated on multiple criteria, normalized, weighted, and then its distance to both the ideal and negative-ideal solutions is calculated.

The core idea is that the best choice should be as close as possible to the ideal solution and as far as possible from the negative-ideal solution. A “closeness coefficient” is computed for each alternative, and alternatives are ranked accordingly. TOPSIS is widely used in engineering, management, supply chain, and other fields where decisions must account for multiple, often conflicting criteria.

title: Mean field annealing
human_text: Mean field annealing is a deterministic approximation to the simulated annealing technique of solving optimization problems. This method uses mean field theory and is based on Peierls' inequality.

The system’s energy (or cost) is then minimized iteratively by updating these mean field values while gradually lowering a temperature parameter that controls how strongly the system is allowed to fluctuate.

Because it uses deterministic updates and continuous approximations, mean field annealing is typically faster and more scalable than standard simulated annealing, though it may be more prone to getting trapped in local minima. It has been applied to problems such as image restoration, pattern recognition, and combinatorial optimization, where large, complex energy landscapes make exact optimization infeasible.

title: Weber problem
human_text: In geometry, the Weber problem, named after Alfred Weber, is one of the most famous problems in location theory. It requires finding a point in the plane that minimizes the sum of the transportation costs from this point to n destination points, where different destination points are associated with different costs per unit distance.
gpt_text:
The Weber problem (also called the Fermat–Weber problem) is a classic optimization problem in location theory: given a set of points in the plane (often representing customers, cities, or demand locations) and possibly weights for each point, find the location of a facility that minimizes the sum of weighted distances to all those points. Unlike the simpler “center of mass” problem, which minimizes the sum of squared distances, the Weber problem focuses on minimizing the sum of actual distances (usually Euclidean), making it more realistic for many geographic and logistical applications.

Because there is generally no closed-form solution for more than a few points, the Weber problem is typically solved using iterative numerical methods, such as Weiszfeld’s algorithm. It underpins many models in operations research, urban planning, and transportation, where deciding where to place warehouses, service centers, or hubs is crucial for reducing total travel cost or time.

title: Reverse logistics network modelling

Using mathematical and computational tools (such as optimization models, simulation, and multi-criteria decision-making), reverse logistics network modelling helps companies choose the number, type, and placement of facilities, allocate product flows, and estimate costs, service levels, and environmental impacts. title: Unit commitment problem in electrical power production
human_text: The unit commitment problem (UC) in electrical power production is a large family of mathematical optimization problems where the production of a set of electrical generators is coordinated in order to achieve some common target, usually either match the energy demand at minimum cost or maximize revenues from energy production. This is necessary because it is difficult to store electrical energy on a scale comparable with normal consumption; hence, each (substantial) variation in the consumption must be matched by a corresponding variation of the production.
gpt_text:

The goal is to meet forecasted electricity demand and reserve requirements at minimum total cost while satisfying operational constraints such as generator capacity limits, minimum up/down times, ramp rates, and startup/shutdown costs.

Because it involves binary on/off decisions combined with continuous power output levels and numerous technical constraints, the unit commitment problem is typically formulated as a mixed-integer optimization problem. It is central to day-ahead and intra-day scheduling in power systems and becomes more complex with high shares of renewables, uncertainty in demand and generation, and the need to ensure system reliability and stability.

title: Stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis
human_text: Stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA) is a multiple-criteria decision analysis method for problems with missing or incomplete information.

Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA) is a family of decision-support methods used when choices must be made among alternatives based on multiple criteria, but there is uncertainty or imprecision in the data, criteria weights, or decision maker preferences. Instead of requiring exact weights or scores, SMAA treats them as uncertain (often with probability distributions) and uses simulation to explore a wide range of possible preference scenarios.

The outcome of SMAA is typically expressed as rank acceptability indices: for each alternative, the method estimates the probability that it would achieve a given rank (e.g., be the best, second best, etc.) across all simulated scenarios. This helps decision makers understand how robust each option is under uncertainty and incomplete preference information, supporting more transparent and defensible choices in complex, real-world decision problems.

title: Deterministic global optimization
human_text: Deterministic global optimization is a branch of numerical optimization which focuses on finding the global solutions of an optimization problem whilst providing theoretical guarantees that the reported solution is indeed the global one, within some predefined tolerance. The term "deterministic global optimization" typically refers to complete or rigorous (see below) optimization methods. Rigorous methods converge to the global optimum in finite time. Deterministic global optimization methods are typically used when locating the global solution is a necessity (i.e. when the only naturally occurring state described by a mathematical model is the global minimum of an optimization problem), when it is extremely difficult to find a feasible solution, or simply when the user desires to locate the best possible solution to a problem.
gpt_text:
Deterministic global optimization is a branch of mathematical optimization focused on finding the true global minimum or maximum of a function under given constraints, with guarantees that the solution is not just locally optimal. Unlike local optimization methods that can get trapped in nearby optima depending on starting points, deterministic global methods use systematic strategies—such as branch-and-bound, interval analysis, or convex relaxations—to explore the search space in a way that can rigorously prove optimality or bound the global optimum.

These methods do not rely on randomness (in contrast to stochastic or metaheuristic approaches) and instead provide mathematically certified results, often with explicit error bounds. Deterministic global optimization is especially important in fields like chemical engineering, design under uncertainty, control, and mixed-integer nonlinear programming, where missing the true global solution can lead to significantly inferior designs or unsafe decisions.

title: Simulation-based optimization
human_text: Simulation-based optimization (also known as simply simulation optimization) integrates optimization techniques into simulation modeling and analysis. Because of the complexity of the simulation, the objective function may become difficult and expensive to evaluate. Usually, the underlying simulation model is stochastic, so that that the objective function must be estimated using statistical estimation techniques (called output analysis in simulation methodology).
gpt_text:
Simulation-based optimization is a methodology for finding good or optimal decisions in systems that are too complex, uncertain, or analytically intractable to model with simple equations. Instead of using closed-form formulas, it couples an optimization algorithm (such as search, heuristics, or metaheuristics) with a simulation model that mimics the real system’s behavior under different decision settings. The optimization engine proposes candidate solutions, the simulation evaluates their performance (e.g., cost, time, reliability), and the process iterates to improve the solutions.

This approach is widely used in areas like manufacturing, logistics, finance, and healthcare, where randomness, complex interactions, or detailed operational rules make traditional optimization difficult. It is especially valuable when decisions must be tested under realistic conditions—such as variable demand, machine failures, or random arrival times—and where understanding performance distributions and risk is as important as finding point estimates of optimal performance.

title: Online optimization
human_text: Online optimization is a field of optimization theory, more popular in computer science and operations research, that deals with optimization problems having no or incomplete knowledge of the future (online). These kind of problems are denoted as online problems and are seen as opposed to the classical optimization problems where complete information is assumed (offline). The research on online optimization can be distinguished into online problems where multiple decisions are made sequentially based on a piece-by-piece input and those where a decision is made only once. A famous online problem where a decision is made only once is the Ski rental problem. In general, the output of an online algorithm is compared to the solution of a corresponding offline algorithm which is necessarily always optimal and knows the entire input in advance (competitive analysis).
gpt_text:
Online optimization is a framework in which decisions must be made sequentially over time without knowing future inputs in advance. At each step, the algorithm observes some information (like a new request, data point, or cost function), chooses an action immediately, and then incurs a cost or receives a reward based on that action. Unlike traditional “offline” optimization, which assumes full knowledge of all data beforehand, online optimization models settings where information arrives gradually and irreversibly, such as online advertising, routing, or portfolio selection.

A central goal in online optimization is to design algorithms whose performance is competitive with the best fixed decision in hindsight, measured via notions like regret or competitive ratio. This has led to a rich theory and practical methods such as online gradient descent, multiplicative weights, and other adaptive algorithms that update decisions based on past feedback while remaining robust to uncertainty and change.

The proximal operator is a mathematical tool used to handle non-smooth or complex functions in optimization problems. For a given function \( f \) and parameter \( \lambda > 0 \), the proximal operator of \( f \) at a point \( x \) is defined as  
\[
\text{prox}_{\lambda f}(x) = \arg\min_{u} \left( f(u) + \frac{1}{2\lambda}\|u - x\|^2 \right).
\]
Intuitively, it finds a point \( u \) that balances being close to \( x \) while also having a low value of \( f(u) \).

Proximal operators generalize the notion of projection onto a set and are central in modern optimization algorithms, especially for problems with regularizers like the \( \ell_1 \)-norm or indicator functions of constraints. They enable splitting methods such as proximal gradient and ADMM, allowing complex objectives to be minimized via simple, often closed-form, iterative steps.

Clarke's generalized Jacobian is a set-valued extension of the classical Jacobian matrix used for nonsmooth analysis. For a locally Lipschitz function \( f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m \), which may fail to be differentiable on some points, Clarke's generalized Jacobian at a point \( x \) is defined as the convex hull of all limit points of ordinary Jacobians \( Df(x_k) \) at nearby differentiable points \( x_k \to x \). \[
\partial f(x) = \text{conv} \left\{ \lim_{k \to \infty} Df(x_k) : x_k \to x,\ f \text{ differentiable at } x_k \right\}.
\]

This construction yields a nonempty, compact, convex set of matrices that behaves much like a derivative in optimization and control theory, even when \( f \) is not differentiable. It underpins generalized gradient methods, provides optimality conditions for nonsmooth optimization, and supports chain rules and calculus similar to that of smooth functions, but adapted to the nonsmooth setting.

title: AL procedure
human_text: The AL procedure is a procedure for fair item assignment between two people. It finds an envy-free item assignment of a subset of the items. Moreover, the resulting allocation is Pareto efficient in the following sense: there is no other envy-free allocation which is better for one person and not worse for the other person.

This procedure is especially useful when unlabeled data are plentiful but labeling is expensive or time-consuming, such as in medical imaging or legal document review. Key concepts include influence of variables (how much each input bit affects the output), noise stability and noise sensitivity (how random perturbations of inputs affect the output), Fourier expansion of Boolean functions (expressing them as sums of parity functions), and threshold phenomena. The Keynes–Ramsey rule (often called the Ramsey–Euler condition) is a fundamental result in intertemporal economics that characterizes optimal consumption over time. In its common continuous-time form, it states that the optimal growth rate of consumption equals the difference between the interest rate and the rate of time preference, scaled by the inverse of the intertemporal elasticity of substitution:  
\[
\frac{\dot{c}}{c} = \frac{1}{\theta}(r - \rho),

Intuitively, the rule balances the benefit of consuming more today against the benefit of saving and consuming more tomorrow. If the return on saving \(r\) exceeds the impatience rate \(\rho\), optimal consumption should grow over time; if it is lower, consumption should fall. The Keynes–Ramsey rule underpins many models in macroeconomics and growth theory, such as the Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model, by describing how a forward-looking representative household chooses its consumption path.

title: Superiorization
human_text: Superiorization is an iterative method for constrained optimization. It is used for improving the efficacy of an iterative method whose convergence is resilient to certain kinds of perturbations. Such perturbations are designed to "force" the perturbed algorithm to produce more useful results for the intended application than the ones that are produced by the original iterative algorithm. The perturbed algorithm is called the superiorized version of the original unperturbed algorithm. If the original algorithm is computationally efficient and useful in terms of the target application and if the perturbations are inexpensive to calculate, the method may be used to steer iterates without additional computation cost.

Instead of replacing a given algorithm, superiorization perturbs its iterations in small, carefully chosen ways so that, while it still converges to a feasible or acceptable solution, the resulting solution is “better” according to some secondary criterion (often a cost function or quality measure). The key idea is to exploit the algorithm’s robustness to certain perturbations.

This approach is especially useful in applications like image reconstruction (e.g., in medical imaging), where one must first satisfy a system of constraints (data fidelity, physical limits) but would also like to reduce noise, artifacts, or other undesirable properties. Superiorization keeps the computational cost close to that of the original feasibility algorithm while systematically steering its output toward higher-quality solutions without needing to solve a full, often more expensive, optimization problem.
