It incorporated basic AI and learning features for its time, allowing it to gradually adapt to a user’s writing style and vocabulary. Ultra Hal also supported text-to-speech and speech recognition, making it usable as a talking desktop companion as well as a simple productivity helper.

title: Cognitive infocommunications
human_text: Cognitive infocommunications (CogInfoCom)Cognitive infocommunications investigates the link between the research areas of infocommunications and the cognitive sciences, as well as the various engineering applications which have emerged as the synergic combination of these sciences.
gpt_text:
Cognitive infocommunications (CogInfoCom) is an interdisciplinary field that studies and designs communication systems connecting human and artificial cognitive entities. Its aim is to enable these different cognitive systems—such as people, robots, AI agents, and smart devices—to share information in ways that extend or enhance human cognitive capabilities. This can involve translating information into more accessible forms (e.g., visual to auditory), creating new channels for interaction, or tightly integrating human thinking with machine processing.

In practice, CogInfoCom covers technologies and methods for human–computer interaction, augmented and virtual reality, assistive systems, and intelligent environments. It examines how information should be represented, transmitted, and transformed so that both humans and machines can understand, learn from, and act on it effectively, ultimately supporting more natural, efficient, and adaptive collaboration between human and artificial cognition.

title: Interactive machine translation
human_text: Interactive machine translation (IMT), is a specific sub-field of computer-aided translation. Under this translation paradigm, the computer software that assists the human translator attempts to predict the text the user is going to input by taking into account all the information it has available. Whenever such prediction is wrong and the user provides feedback to the system, a new prediction is performed considering the new information available. Such process is repeated until the translation provided matches the user's expectations.
gpt_text:
Interactive machine translation (IMT) is a computer-assisted translation approach where a human translator and a machine translation system work together in real time. Instead of the system producing a full translation that the human later edits, IMT continuously updates its suggestions as the translator types, corrects, or accepts parts of the output. The system uses these human inputs to predict and propose the best continuation of the translation, often at the word or phrase level.

This collaboration aims to combine the speed and consistency of machine translation with the accuracy and nuance of human expertise. IMT can significantly reduce the time and effort required for high-quality translations by minimizing repetitive corrections and leveraging the translator’s choices to refine further suggestions on the fly.

title: Law of conservation of complexity
human_text: The law of conservation of complexity is an adage in human–computer interaction stating that every application has an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be removed or hidden. Instead, it must be dealt with, either in product development or in user interaction.
gpt_text:
The “law of conservation of complexity” (often attributed informally to Larry Tesler) is the idea that in any non‑trivial system, total complexity cannot be eliminated—only shifted around. If you simplify the user’s experience, you typically increase complexity in the underlying implementation, documentation, or maintenance; if you simplify the implementation, you may push more complexity onto users or other parts of the system.

In software and product design, this “law” is used to explain why seemingly simple interfaces often require very sophisticated back‑end logic, and why attempts to oversimplify development can make products harder to use. It’s a reminder that design choices are about where complexity should reside, not whether it can be made to disappear.

title: User virtualization
human_text: User virtualization refers to the independent management of all aspects of the user on the desktop environment. User virtualization decouples a user's profile, settings and data from the operating system and stores this information into a centralized data share either in the data center or cloud. User virtualization solutions provide consistent and seamless working environments across a range of application delivery mechanisms. Although user virtualization is most closely associated with desktop virtualization, in fact, this technology can be used to manage user profiles on physical desktops as well. As the range of currently used operating systems expands, and the use of multiple devices by workers to perform their jobs escalates, user virtualization can support the creation of a "follow-me" identity that will allow access to a workspace without being tied into only a single device or a single location.
gpt_text:
User virtualization is a technology approach that separates a user’s personal environment—such as settings, profiles, applications, and data—from the underlying physical device or operating system. Instead of being tied to a single PC, a user’s desktop experience is stored and managed centrally (often in the data center or cloud) and delivered dynamically to any compatible device they log into.  

This allows users to have a consistent, personalized workspace across multiple endpoints (laptops, thin clients, virtual desktops, etc.), while IT gains easier management, improved security, and more flexible deployment. It’s commonly used in virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), remote desktop services, and enterprise environments needing roaming profiles or non-persistent desktops.

title: Interruption science
human_text: Interruption science is the interdisciplinary scientific study concerned with how interruptions affect human performance, and the development interventions to ameliorate the disruption caused by interruptions. Interruption science is branch of human factors psychology and emerged from human–computer interaction and cognitive psychology.
gpt_text:
Interruption science is the study of how interruptions affect human attention, performance, cognition, and well‑being, particularly in work and digital environments. It draws on psychology, human–computer interaction, and organizational behavior to understand what happens when tasks are broken by phone calls, messages, notifications, or colleagues, and how people resume their work afterward.  

Researchers in interruption science examine factors like timing, task complexity, context, and individual differences to determine when interruptions are most disruptive or occasionally helpful. The field also explores strategies and system designs (such as batching notifications, “do not disturb” modes, and workflow redesign) to reduce the negative impacts of interruptions on productivity, error rates, stress, and satisfaction.

title: Thanatosensitivity
human_text: Thanatosensitivity describes an epistemological-methodological approach into technological research and design that actively seeks to integrate the facts of mortality, dying, and death into traditional user-centered design. First coined by Michael Massimi and Andrea Charise from the University of Toronto in a joint paper presented at CHI 2009, thanatosensitivity refers to a humanistically grounded approach to human–computer interaction (HCI) research and design that recognizes and engages with the conceptual and practical issues surrounding death in the creation of interactive systems.
gpt_text:
Thanatosensitivity is a design perspective that explicitly considers death, dying, and mortality in the creation of technologies and systems. Coined in human–computer interaction (HCI), it encourages designers to think about what happens to digital data, accounts, and interactions when users become seriously ill, pass away, or are bereaved, and to build features that handle these situations with care and respect.

This approach can involve planning for digital legacies, creating options for memorialization, supporting grieving processes, and ensuring that systems accommodate sensitive transitions (like closing or handing over accounts). Thanatosensitive design aims to reduce distress and confusion around death-related issues in digital environments by making them an intentional, thoughtful part of the design process rather than an afterthought.

title: Flexibility–usability tradeoff
human_text: The flexibility–usability tradeoff is a design principle maintaining that, as the flexibility of a system increases, its usability decreases. The tradeoff exists because accommodating flexibility requires satisfying a larger set of requirements, which results in complexity and usability compromises.
gpt_text:
The flexibility–usability tradeoff is a design principle stating that as a system becomes more flexible—able to handle a wider variety of tasks or user needs—it often becomes less usable for any single, specific purpose. Highly flexible tools (like feature-rich software or multi-purpose devices) tend to be more complex, harder to learn, and may require more steps or configuration to accomplish basic tasks.

Conversely, systems designed to do fewer things can be streamlined and optimized, making them faster, more intuitive, and easier for users to master. Designers use this principle to balance the breadth of functionality with simplicity, deciding whether a product should serve many use cases moderately well or a few use cases extremely well.

title: Stimulus–response compatibility
human_text: Stimulus–response (S–R) compatibility is the degree to which a person's perception of the world is compatible with the required action. S–R compatibility has been described as the "naturalness" of the association between a stimulus and its response, such as a left-oriented stimulus requiring a response from the left side of the body. A high level of S–R compatibility is typically associated with a shorter reaction time, whereas a low level of S-R compatibility tends to result in a longer reaction time, a phenomenon known as the Simon effect.
gpt_text:
Stimulus–response compatibility (SRC) refers to how naturally a response matches the stimulus that triggers it. When a stimulus and the required response are well aligned with our expectations or habitual actions (for example, pressing a button on the right when a light appears on the right), reactions are faster and more accurate. This is known as high or compatible SRC.

When the mapping is less intuitive—such as pressing a left key for a right-side light—reaction times slow and errors increase, reflecting low or incompatible SRC. SRC is an important concept in cognitive psychology, human factors, and interface design, because arranging controls and displays to maximize compatibility can reduce mental workload and improve performance and safety.

title: Human Media Lab
human_text: The Human Media Lab (HML) is a research laboratory in Human-Computer Interaction at Queen's University's School of Computing in Kingston, Ontario. Its goals are to advance user interface design by creating and empirically evaluating disruptive new user interface technologies, and educate graduate students in this process. The Human Media Lab was founded in 2000 by Prof. Roel Vertegaal and employs an average of 12 graduate students.
gpt_text:
The Human Media Lab is a research laboratory, originally based at Queen’s University in Kingston, Canada, that explores the future of human–computer interaction (HCI). It focuses on developing novel interfaces that make computing more organic, intuitive, and seamlessly integrated into everyday life—often by rethinking screens, devices, and interaction methods beyond conventional flat displays and keyboards.

Notable projects from the lab include flexible and shape-changing displays, ambient and ubiquitous computing environments, and interfaces that use context-awareness, touch, gesture, and even eye input. By merging design, engineering, and cognitive science, the Human Media Lab aims to create technologies that feel more like natural extensions of human capabilities rather than separate, rigid tools.

title: J.F. Schouten School for User System Interaction
human_text: J.F. Schouten School for User System Interaction is a research institute of the Eindhoven University of Technology dedicated to user interaction with man-made systems, including Human Computer Interaction.
gpt_text:
The J.F. Schouten School for User System Interaction was a graduate research school in the Netherlands focused on human-computer interaction, user-centered design, and related areas where people and technology meet. It was a joint initiative of Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) and Tilburg University, named after the Dutch psychologist Jan Frederik Schouten, a pioneer in experimental and applied psychology.

The school coordinated PhD education, research training, and collaboration across disciplines such as psychology, computer science, industrial design, and communication studies. Its work addressed topics like usability, user experience, cognitive ergonomics, and the design of interactive systems, aiming to improve how people use and experience technological products and services.

title: Interaction Design Foundation
human_text: The Interaction Design Foundation is an educational organization which produces open access educational materials online with the stated goal of "democratizing education by making world-class educational materials free for anyone, anywhere." The platform also offers courses taught by industry experts and professors in psychology, computer science, cognitive science, and more.
gpt_text:
The Interaction Design Foundation (IDF) is an online education platform focused on user experience (UX) and interaction design. Founded in Denmark in 2002, it offers self-paced courses, literature, and community resources aimed at designers, developers, product managers, and others working in digital product design. Its mission is to make high-quality design education affordable and accessible worldwide.

IDF collaborates with academics and industry experts to create course content that covers topics such as usability, human-computer interaction, design thinking, information architecture, and user research. In addition to courses, it provides local chapters, events, and forums where members can network, share knowledge, and build their professional portfolios.

title: Smart shoe
human_text: Smart shoes is a smart footwear technology. It adopts smartphone applications to support tasks cannot be done with standard footwear. The uses shows vibrating of the smart phone to tell users when and where to turn to reach their destination via Google Maps or self-lacing.
gpt_text:
A smart shoe is a footwear product embedded with sensors, electronics, and connectivity features that track and analyze data about the wearer’s movement and environment. Common capabilities include counting steps, measuring distance, monitoring gait, detecting impact forces, and sometimes even tracking posture or balance. These shoes typically sync with a smartphone or other device via Bluetooth to provide real-time feedback and long-term activity logs.

Beyond fitness tracking, smart shoes can support specialized uses, such as assisting runners with performance optimization, helping patients in rehabilitation monitor recovery, or enabling navigation assistance for visually impaired users through haptic feedback. Some models also offer features like automatic lacing, pressure-based controls, or integration with gaming and virtual reality experiences.

title: Brain painting
human_text: Brain painting is a non-invasive P300-based brain-computer interface (BCI) that allows painting without the use of muscular activity. The technology combines electroencephalography, signal processing algorithms and visual stimulation on a monitor to detect where the user focuses his attention, allowing him to voluntarily trigger commands to a painting software. The research project aims at assisting people afflicted with the Locked-in syndrome due to neurological or neuromuscular disease (e.g. amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ALS), who are severely restricted in communication with their environment, and therefore cut off from the possibility of creative expression.
gpt_text:
Brain painting is an art-making technique that uses brain–computer interface (BCI) technology to let people create images using only their brain activity, often measured via EEG (electroencephalography). Instead of physically moving a brush or stylus, the artist focuses attention or performs mental tasks that the system translates into commands for selecting colors, shapes, or brush strokes on a digital canvas.

This method is especially important for people with severe motor impairments (such as advanced ALS or high-level spinal cord injury), as it provides a way to express creativity and communicate visually without requiring muscle control. Beyond assistive use, brain painting is also explored in media art and neuroscience research as a way to study creativity, perception, and human–machine interaction.

title: Human sensing
human_text: Human sensing (also called human detection or human presence detection) encompasses a range of technologies for detecting the presence of a human body in an area of space, typically without the intentional participation of the detected person. Common applications include search and rescue, surveillance, and customer analytics (for example, people counters).
gpt_text:
Human sensing is the field of techniques and technologies used to detect, measure, and interpret human presence, behavior, states, and activities. It encompasses sensors and algorithms that can capture physical signals (like movement, posture, heart rate, or voice) and contextual cues (such as location or interactions with devices) in order to understand what people are doing or experiencing.  

This can involve cameras and computer vision, wearable sensors, microphones, radar, pressure sensors, smartphones, or ambient devices embedded in homes, cars, and public spaces. Human sensing underpins applications such as activity recognition, health and wellbeing monitoring, smart environments, human–computer interaction, security and surveillance, and assistive technologies that adapt to users’ needs and conditions.

title: PACT (interaction design)
human_text: In interaction design, PACT (an acronym for People, Activities, Contexts, Technologies) is a structure used to analyse with whom, what and where a user interact with a user interface. Interaction is considered, in this framework, as a relationship between people, activities, contexts, and technologies.
gpt_text:
PACT in interaction design is a framework used to analyze and design user experiences by focusing on four key elements: People, Activities, Contexts, and Technologies. It helps designers systematically consider who the users are (their abilities, goals, preferences), what they are trying to do (tasks and workflows), where and under what circumstances they do it (physical, social, organizational context), and with what tools or systems (devices, interfaces, platforms).

By exploring variations within each PACT element—different user groups, task complexities, usage environments, and technology types—designers can identify requirements, constraints, and opportunities for better interaction. This structured thinking supports more inclusive, effective, and context-appropriate design solutions.

title: Example-centric programming
human_text: Example-centric programming is an approach to software development that helps the user to create software by locating and modifying small examples into a larger whole. That approach can be helped by tools that allow an integrated development environment (IDE) to show code examples or API documentation related to coding behaviors occurring in the IDE. “Borrow” tactics are often employed from online sources, by programmers leaving the IDE to troubleshoot.
gpt_text:
Example-centric programming is a style of software development in which programmers rely heavily on concrete examples—such as code snippets, sample inputs/outputs, tests, or usage scenarios—to understand, design, and implement functionality. Instead of starting from abstract specifications alone, developers work from illustrative cases that show how a feature should behave, often drawing from documentation, online forums, or existing codebases.

This approach can speed up learning new libraries or APIs, help clarify ambiguous requirements, and make complex behaviors more tangible. It overlaps with practices like test-driven development (where tests are executable examples), literate programming (where examples explain concepts), and “programming by example” tools that infer code from demonstrations.

title: Blended space
human_text: A blended space is a space in which a physical environment and a virtual environment are deliberately integrated in a close knit way. The aim of blended space design is to provide people with the experience of feeling a sense of presence in the blended space, acting directly on the content of the blended space. Examples of blended spaces include augmented reality devices such as the Microsoft Hololens and games such as Pokemon GO in addition to many smartphone tourism apps, smart meeting rooms and applications such as bus tracker systems.
gpt_text:
In cognitive linguistics and conceptual integration theory, a *blended space* is a mental space where elements from two or more input spaces are selectively projected and combined to create new meaning. This blend is not just a simple mixture; it develops its own emergent structure—ideas, relationships, or inferences that are not present in any single input alone.

Blended spaces help explain how people understand metaphors, analogies, jokes, and creative thinking in general. For example, when we talk about “the desktop” on a computer, we blend elements of a physical office desk (papers, folders, trash can) with elements of a digital interface, creating a new conceptual space that guides how we interact with software.

title: Empathy in online communities
human_text: Empathy has been studied in the context of online communities as it pertains to enablers of interpersonal communication, anonymity, as well as barriers to online relationships, such as ambiguity, cyberbullying and Internet trolling.
gpt_text:
Empathy in online communities is the ability and practice of understanding, validating, and constructively responding to others’ feelings and perspectives through digital communication. It shows up in actions like offering supportive replies, using inclusive language, acknowledging others’ struggles, and being mindful of how tone can be misread without facial expressions or vocal cues.  

Because online spaces often lack physical presence and immediate feedback, empathy has to be expressed more deliberately—through careful wording, active listening (reading), asking clarifying questions, and avoiding impulsive or hostile reactions. When present, it improves trust, reduces conflict and harassment, encourages honest sharing, and helps diverse groups coexist more respectfully in forums, social media, gaming platforms, and other digital communities.

title: Video game rehabilitation
human_text: Video game rehabilitation is a process of using common video game consoles and methodology to target and improve physical and mental weaknesses through therapeutic processes. Video games are becoming an integral part of occupational therapy practice in acute, rehabilitation, and community settings. The design for video games in rehabilitation is focused on a number of fundamental principles, such as reward, goals, challenge, and meaningful play. ‘Meaningful play’ emerges from the relationship between player action and system outcome, apparent to the player through, visual, physical and aural feedback. Platforms that feature motion control, notably the Nintendo Wii, Microsoft's Xbox Kinect, Sony's Eye Toy, and virtual reality have all been effective in this field of research. Methodologies have been applied to all age groups, from toddlers to the elderly. It has been used in a variety of cases ranging from stroke rehabilitation, cerebral palsy and other neurological impairments, to tendinitis and multiple sclerosis. Researchers have promoted such technology based on the personalization of gaming systems to patients, allowing for further engagement and interaction. Additionally, gaming consoles have the ability to capture real-time data and provide instant feedback to the patients using the systems. Currently, several researchers have performed case studies to demonstrate the benefits of this technology. Repeat trials and experiments have shown that outcomes are easily replicated among various groups worldwide. Additionally, the outcomes have increased interest in the field, growing experiments beyond simple case studies to experiments with a larger participant base.
gpt_text:
Video game rehabilitation refers to the use of video games and game-like technologies (often called “serious games”) to support physical, cognitive, or emotional recovery in medical and therapeutic settings. These games are designed or adapted to help patients practice specific movements, improve balance, rebuild strength, enhance attention or memory, and increase motivation to participate in therapy. Motion sensors, VR headsets, and custom controllers can track a patient’s performance, giving real-time feedback and enabling therapists to adjust difficulty and goals.

Because many traditional rehabilitation exercises are repetitive and can be demotivating, incorporating game elements—such as scores, levels, and rewards—helps keep patients engaged and more likely to stick with their therapy programs. Video game rehabilitation is used in areas such as stroke recovery, orthopedic rehab, Parkinson’s disease, pediatric therapy, and mental health, and is often combined with conventional treatments rather than replacing them.

title: Holus
human_text: Holus is a holographic product under development by H+Technology. The concept was first developed in 2013, before funding via Kickstarter meant the product could be taken to market. The purpose of Holus is to simulate holographic experiences and is technically different from typical hologram stickers found on credit cards and currency notes.
gpt_text:
“Holus” isn’t a widely established technical or historical term on its own, but it commonly appears as part of the English expression “holus-bolus.” That phrase means “all at once,” “in one go,” or “entirely,” and is often used to describe doing or accepting something in a single, sweeping action rather than in parts (e.g., “They swallowed the plan holus-bolus”). Its origins are likely playful or dialectal, emerging in English by the 19th century.

In some contexts, “Holus” may also appear as a proper name—for a company, brand, product, or fictional character. In those cases, its meaning depends entirely on the specific usage or universe where it appears, since there is no dominant, universally recognized definition of “Holus” on its own.

title: Stent-electrode recording array
human_text: Stentrode (Stent-electrode recording array) is a small stent-mounted electrode array that is permanently implanted into a blood vessel in the brain without the need for open brain surgery. It is being developed to hopefully function as a brain–computer interface (BCI) for people with paralyzed or missing limbs, who will use their neural signals or thoughts to control powered exoskeletons, robotic prosthesis, computers or other devices.
gpt_text:
A stent-electrode recording array is a neural interface device that combines a vascular stent with embedded electrodes to record brain activity from within blood vessels rather than directly on or inside brain tissue. Delivered via a catheter into a cerebral blood vessel (often a vein adjacent to motor cortex), it expands to press its electrodes against the vessel wall, where they can pick up local field potentials and other neural signals.

This “endovascular” approach aims to reduce the invasiveness and surgical risks associated with traditional brain implants, since it avoids open-skull procedures and direct penetration of brain tissue. Stent-electrode arrays are being explored for brain–computer interfaces, such as enabling communication or control of external devices in people with severe paralysis.

title: Aesthetic–usability effect
human_text: The aesthetic–usability effect describes a paradox that people perceive more aesthetic designs as much more intuitive than those considered to be less aesthetically pleasing. The effect has been observed in several experiments and has significant implications regarding the acceptance, use, and performance of a design. Usability and aesthetics are the two most important factors in assessing the overall user experience for an application. Usability and aesthetics are judged by a user's reuse expectations, and then their post-use, or experienced, final judgement. A user's cognitive style can influence how they interact with and perceive an application, which in turn can influence their judgement of said application.
gpt_text:
The aesthetic–usability effect is a cognitive bias where people perceive more attractive products, interfaces, or designs as easier to use, even when their actual usability is no better (or is worse) than less attractive alternatives. In other words, visual appeal positively colors a user’s judgment of how usable or effective something is.

This effect matters in design because users are more tolerant of minor usability issues in aesthetically pleasing products, and they’re more likely to engage with them, explore features, and persist through difficulties. As a result, good visual design can enhance both first impressions and overall satisfaction, but it should complement—never replace—solid usability and accessibility.

title: Center for Humane Technology
human_text: The Center for Humane Technology (formerly known as Time Well Spent) is a nonprofit organization focused on the ethics of consumer technology. The Center advocates for regulators and technology companies to avoid social media features and profit incentives that it sees as contributing to internet addiction, political extremism, political polarization, and misinformation.
gpt_text:
The Center for Humane Technology (CHT) is a nonprofit organization focused on realigning technology with humanity’s best interests. Founded by former tech insiders, including ex-Google design ethicist Tristan Harris, it critiques the ways platforms and devices are designed to capture attention, exploit psychological vulnerabilities, spread misinformation, and deepen polarization. CHT works to shift the tech industry away from ad-driven, engagement-maximizing business models toward systems that prioritize well-being, democracy, and shared truth.

The organization conducts research, produces educational resources (such as the “Social Dilemma” documentary and the “Your Undivided Attention” podcast), and collaborates with policymakers, technologists, educators, and the public. Its initiatives aim to raise awareness of the systemic harms caused by current tech design practices and to promote alternative design principles and regulations that support mental health, healthy relationships, and a more resilient society.

title: Post-tech
human_text: Post-tech, (or post-technology, post-digital-technology) is type of technology that is more concerned about being human than about technology. It advocates a design that is not merely focused on efficiency and exploiting users by increasing their time spent with digital devices and technology itself but to support the user's focus and intent, well-being, and independence (from technology). With this interstitial spaces could also be created, similar to what Michel Foucault describes as Heterotopia (space).
gpt_text:
Post-tech generally refers to cultural, economic, or design movements that come after—or push beyond—the current technology-centered paradigm. Instead of celebrating constant innovation for its own sake, post-tech thinking questions the dominance of digital tools, automation, and hyper-connectivity, and asks how technology can better serve human values, ecological limits, and social well-being.

In practice, post-tech ideas may show up as a renewed interest in low-tech or appropriate technology, deliberate disconnection from digital platforms, or designs that prioritize durability, repair, and human scale over speed and novelty. It’s less about abandoning technology entirely and more about rebalancing our relationship with it, treating it as a constrained, thoughtful tool rather than an unquestioned driver of progress.

title: Barrier pointing
human_text: Barrier pointing (also "edge pointing") is a term used in human–computer interaction to describe a design technique in which targets are placed on the peripheral borders of touchscreen interfaces to help increase motor articulation. Barrier pointing is part of a broader category of research on the ways interaction changes on the design of the physical edges of GUI touchscreens in surface computing. The ways in which barrier pointing are multifarious and include the use of barrier targets (or barrier widgets), buttons.
gpt_text:
Barrier pointing is a pointing technique used in diving (and sometimes in gymnastics) where the arms are fully extended and locked straight overhead, forming a rigid “barrier” line from the hands through the shoulders to the torso. The fingers are held tightly together and pointed, and the shoulders are lifted to create the longest, straightest possible line.

This position improves body alignment and reduces drag during rotations and entries into the water. In diving, barrier pointing helps the diver maintain a tight, streamlined shape, especially in straight and pike positions, contributing to cleaner lines and more precise, vertical entries.

title: Feminist HCI
human_text: Feminist HCI is a subfield of human-computer interaction (commonly called HCI) that focuses on helping the field of HCI build interactions that pay attention to gender, equity, and social justice in research and in the design process.
gpt_text:
Feminist HCI (Human–Computer Interaction) is an approach to designing and evaluating interactive systems that draws on feminist theories and values—such as equity, empowerment, inclusivity, and respect for diversity. Rather than treating users as neutral or homogeneous, it highlights how technologies can reinforce or challenge power imbalances related to gender, race, class, and other identities, and aims to make those dynamics visible and address them in the design process.

In practice, feminist HCI encourages participatory and care-centered methods, long-term engagement with communities, and sensitivity to lived experience, emotion, and embodiment. It questions whose perspectives shape technologies, whose needs are prioritized, and who is excluded. By foregrounding marginalized voices and experiences, feminist HCI seeks to create more just, reflective, and humane digital systems and interactions.

title: Time travel debugging
human_text: Time travel debugging or time traveling debugging is the process of stepping back in time through source code to understand what is happening during execution of a computer program. Typically, debugging and debuggers, tools that assist a user with the process of debugging, allow users to pause the execution of running software and inspect the current state of the program. Users can then step forward in time, stepping into or over statements and proceeding in a forward direction. Interactive debuggers include the ability to modify code and step forward based on updated information. Reverse debugging tools allow users to step backwards in time through the steps that resulted in reaching a particular point in the program. Time traveling debuggers provide these features and also allow users to interact with the program, changing the history if desired, and watch how the program responds.
gpt_text:
Time travel debugging is a software debugging technique that lets developers move both forward and backward in a program’s execution, as if replaying a recording. Instead of only stepping line-by-line from the current point onward, you can “rewind” to earlier states, inspect variables, and see exactly how the program reached a certain condition or bug.

This approach is especially powerful for diagnosing intermittent, hard-to-reproduce issues. By capturing and replaying execution, time travel debugging removes the need to guess past states or re-run the program repeatedly, allowing developers to deterministically reproduce and analyze complex bugs with greater precision and less trial-and-error.

title: Human presence detection
human_text: Human presence detection is a range of technologies and methods for detecting the presence of a human body in an area of interest (AOI), or verification that computer, smartphone (or other device controlled by software) is operated by human.
gpt_text:
Human presence detection is the capability of a system—often using sensors like radar, cameras, infrared, ultrasonic, or pressure—to determine whether a person is physically present in a given area. It goes beyond simple motion detection by identifying a human specifically, sometimes even when they are relatively still, and can estimate distance, position, or occupancy status.

This technology is widely used in applications such as smart lighting and HVAC control (turning systems on or off based on room occupancy), automotive safety (detecting occupants in seats or people around a vehicle), security systems (identifying intruders), and consumer electronics (waking devices when a user approaches). Advanced implementations may use AI and signal processing to distinguish humans from pets, objects, or background motion, improving accuracy and reducing false alarms.

title: Responsive computer-aided design
human_text: Responsive computer-aided design (also simplified to responsive design) is an approach to computer-aided design (CAD) that utilizes real-world sensors and data to modify a three-dimensional (3D) computer model. The concept is related to cyber-physical systems through blurring of the virtual and physical worlds, however, applies specifically to the initial digital design of an object prior to production.
gpt_text:
Responsive computer-aided design (responsive CAD) refers to CAD systems and workflows that automatically adapt design geometry to changes in parameters, context, or usage conditions. Instead of creating static drawings or models, designers define relationships, constraints, and rules—such as dimensions, material properties, or environmental factors—so the design can adjust itself dynamically when those inputs change. This often relies on parametric modeling, constraint-based design, and sometimes scripting or computational design tools.

In practice, responsive CAD is used to quickly explore design variations, optimize performance, and customize products or structures. For example, a building façade might automatically reconfigure its shading elements based on sun angles, or a mechanical component might resize and reinforce itself when different load requirements are entered. This approach speeds up iteration, reduces manual rework, and supports more adaptive, performance-driven design processes.

title: Human-robot collaboration
human_text: Human-Robot Collaboration is the study of collaborative processes in human and robot agents work together to achieve shared goals. Many new applications for robots require them to work alongside people as capable members of human-robot teams. These include robots for homes, hospitals, and offices, space exploration and manufacturing. Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) is an interdisciplinary research area comprising classical robotics, human-computer interaction, artificial intelligence, design, cognitive sciences and psychology.
gpt_text:
Human-robot collaboration (HRC) refers to people and robots working together in a shared space or on shared tasks, often in real time. Unlike traditional industrial robots that are isolated behind safety fences, collaborative robots (“cobots”) are designed to operate safely near humans, reacting to their actions and sometimes even learning from demonstration or guidance.

HRC combines the strengths of both: humans provide creativity, problem-solving, and adaptability, while robots contribute precision, strength, and consistency. It is increasingly used in manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, and service industries to improve productivity, reduce physical strain on workers, and enable more flexible, responsive production processes.

title: Human-agent team
human_text: A human-agent team is a system composed of multiple interacting humans and artificial intelligence systems. The artificial intelligence system may be a robotic system, a decision support system, or a virtual agent. Human agent teaming provides an interaction paradigm that differs from traditional approaches such as supervisory control, or user interface design, by enabling the computer to have a certain degree of autonomy. The paradigm draws from various scientific research fields, being strongly inspired by the way humans work together in teams, and constituting a special type of multi-agent system.
gpt_text:
A human-agent team is a collaborative group composed of people and artificial agents (such as AI systems, robots, or software assistants) working together toward shared goals. In these teams, each partner contributes complementary strengths: humans provide judgment, creativity, and contextual understanding, while agents offer speed, data processing, consistency, and the ability to operate in environments or at scales that are challenging for humans.

Effective human-agent teaming focuses on coordination, communication, and trust between humans and agents. This includes designing interfaces and behaviors so that agents can explain their reasoning, understand human intent, adapt to human preferences, and support human decision-making without overwhelming or misleading users. Human-agent teams are used in domains such as healthcare, defense, transportation, customer service, and complex data analysis.

title: Neural dust
human_text: Neural dust is a term used to refer to millimeter-sized devices operated as wirelessly powered nerve sensors; it is a type of brain–computer interface. The sensors may be used to study, monitor, or control the nerves and muscles and to remotely monitor neural activity. In practice, a medical treatment could introduce thousands of neural dust devices into human brains. The term is derived from "smart dust", as the sensors used as neural dust may also be defined by this concept.
gpt_text:
Neural dust refers to ultra-miniaturized, wireless sensor nodes—often imagined as tiny chips or particles—that can be implanted in or near nerve tissue to record and potentially stimulate neural activity. These devices are designed to operate without batteries, typically powered and read out via ultrasound or electromagnetic fields, enabling long-term monitoring of the nervous system with minimal invasiveness.

In concept, neural dust could enable high-resolution brain–computer interfaces, chronic health monitoring, or precise neuromodulation by scattering many small sensors throughout the body or brain. While still largely experimental and facing significant engineering and biocompatibility challenges, it represents a frontier in merging electronics with the nervous system at very small scales.

title: Notification LED
human_text: A Notification LED is a small RGB or monochrome LED light usually present on the front-facing screen bezel (display side) of smartphones and feature phones whose purpose is to blink or pulse to notify the phone user of missed calls, incoming SMS messages, notifications from other messaging apps etc. Versus: For and against LED notification lights in phones It usually pulses in a continuous way to draw the attention of the user. It is a part of the device's notification system that uses a cloud-powered push notification service to relay remote notification messages to the user, or local notifications. Similar to audio notifications, a notification LED is a very battery-efficient way to inform the user of new notifications without turning on the screen at all.
gpt_text:
A notification LED is a small light on electronic devices (like smartphones, laptops, or routers) that signals alerts or status information without turning on the main display. It typically use different colors or blink patterns to indicate things like new messages, missed calls, charging status, low battery, or connectivity issues.

Because it consumes very little power, a notification LED lets users see important updates at a glance, even when the device is otherwise in standby or sleep mode. Some devices and apps allow users to customize the LED’s behavior—for example, assigning specific colors or blink rates to different types of notifications.

title: Algorithmics
human_text: Algorithmics is the systematic study of the design and analysis of algorithms. It is fundamental and one of the oldest fields of computer science. It includes algorithm design, the art of building a procedure which can solve efficiently a specific problem or a class of problem, algorithmic complexity theory, the study of estimating the hardness of problems by studying the properties of the algorithm that solves them, or algorithm analysis, the science of studying the properties of a problem, such as quantifying resources in time and memory space needed by this algorithm to solve this problem.
gpt_text:
Algorithmics is the area of computer science that focuses on designing, analyzing, and optimizing algorithms—step‑by‑step procedures for solving computational problems. It studies how to transform a problem into a precise sequence of operations that a computer can perform, and how efficiently this can be done in terms of time, memory, and other resources.

The field covers topics such as algorithm design techniques (like divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy methods), complexity analysis (Big-O notation, time and space complexity), data structures, and correctness proofs. Algorithmics provides the theoretical foundation that underpins efficient software, cryptography, artificial intelligence, networking, and many other domains in computing.

title: Proof of space
human_text: Proof of space (PoSpace), also called Proof-of-capacity (PoC) or Proof-of-storage, is a means of showing that one has a legitimate interest in a service (such as sending an email) by allocating a non-trivial amount of memory or disk space to solve a challenge presented by the service provider.
gpt_text:
Proof of space is a consensus mechanism used in some cryptocurrencies and distributed systems where participants prove they have allocated a certain amount of disk storage rather than expending computational power (as in proof of work). A miner (or farmer) precomputes and stores large data structures (plots) on their hard drive; when a new block needs to be produced, the network issues a challenge, and participants respond by showing that, within their stored data, they have a value that closely matches the challenge.

Because it relies on storage instead of intensive computation, proof of space is designed to be more energy-efficient and accessible, leveraging unused disk space rather than powerful specialized hardware. It is often combined with other mechanisms (e.g., proof of time) to improve security, prevent grinding attacks, and ensure fair block production.

title: Join-based tree algorithms
human_text: In computer science, join-based tree algorithms are a class of algorithms for self-balancing binary search trees. This framework aims at designing highly-parallelized algorithms for various balanced binary search trees.
gpt_text:
Join-based tree algorithms are a family of algorithms for balanced binary search trees (such as AVL trees, red–black trees, and treaps) that use a small set of primitive operations—most importantly a “join” operation—to implement all higher-level updates. The central idea is that, given two trees where all keys in the first are smaller than all keys in the second (plus an optional separating key), a join operation can efficiently merge them into a single balanced tree. Using this primitive, operations like insert, delete, split, and union can be expressed in a uniform, often simpler way.

This approach separates concerns: the rebalancing logic is localized inside the join (and sometimes split) routines, while the rest of the algorithms become structurally simple and easier to reason about or parallelize. Join-based designs can lead to cleaner implementations, facilitate proving correctness and complexity bounds, and in some cases improve performance or scalability compared to more ad hoc, operation-specific tree algorithms.

title: Creative computing
human_text: Creative computing covers the interdisciplinary area at the cross-over of the creative arts and computing. Issues of creativity include knowledge discovery, for example.
gpt_text:
Creative computing is the use of computers and digital technologies as tools for artistic expression, invention, and imaginative problem-solving. It blends programming, design, art, and often storytelling to create interactive media, digital art, games, generative graphics, music, and other expressive works. Rather than focusing only on efficiency or utility, creative computing emphasizes experimentation, play, and exploration.

This field encourages people—often including beginners and non-technical users—to think creatively about technology: writing code to draw visuals, building interactive installations, training AI to produce images or music, or designing playful apps and experiences. It sits at the intersection of computer science and the arts, and is central to areas like creative coding, digital media arts, and computational design.

title: Animal-computer interaction
human_text: Animal-computer interaction (ACI) is a field of research for the design and use of technology with, for and by animals. It emerged from, and is heavily influenced by, the discipline of human-computer interaction (HCI).
gpt_text:
Animal-computer interaction (ACI) is an interdisciplinary field that studies how animals interact with digital technologies and designs systems specifically for their needs, abilities, and welfare. It combines insights from animal behavior, computer science, interaction design, and ethics to create interfaces and devices that animals can understand and use—such as touchscreens for primates, sensor-based toys for dogs, or wearable trackers for wildlife.

ACI aims both to enrich animals’ lives and to enable better communication between humans and animals. Applications range from improving the welfare of companion and working animals (for example, service dogs signaling handlers through digital devices) to supporting conservation and research (such as tracking and monitoring wild animals in non-invasive ways).

title: Dining philosophers problem
human_text: In computer science, the dining philosophers problem is an example problem often used in concurrent algorithm design to illustrate synchronization issues and techniques for resolving them.
gpt_text:
The dining philosophers problem is a classic concurrency and synchronization problem in computer science, introduced by Edsger Dijkstra. It describes a scenario in which a number of philosophers sit around a circular table, each with a plate of food and a chopstick (or fork) between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs to pick up both chopsticks adjacent to them. The challenge is to design a protocol for picking up and putting down chopsticks so that no philosopher starves and the system avoids deadlock (where everyone is waiting indefinitely) and livelock (where progress is continually attempted but never made).

This problem models resource allocation in concurrent systems, where multiple processes compete for limited shared resources. Solutions typically involve imposing ordering constraints, introducing asymmetry (e.g., some philosophers pick up left then right, others right then left), using resource hierarchies, or employing mechanisms like semaphores or mutexes to ensure mutual exclusion and prevent circular wait conditions.

title: Sleeping barber problem
human_text: In computer science, the sleeping barber problem is a classic inter-process communication and synchronization problem between multiple operating system processes. The problem is analogous to that of keeping a barber working when there are customers, resting when there are none, and doing so in an orderly manner.

When a customer arrives, they either wake the barber if he’s sleeping, sit in a waiting chair if available, or leave if all waiting chairs are occupied.

The problem focuses on how to coordinate the actions of the barber and multiple customers so that no race conditions, lost wakeups, or deadlocks occur. It’s typically solved using semaphores, mutexes, or other synchronization primitives to ensure mutual exclusion in critical sections and proper ordering of events (barber sleeping, customers arriving, haircuts being performed).

title: Starvation (computer science)
human_text: In computer science, resource starvation is a problem encountered in concurrent computing where a process is perpetually denied necessary resources to process its work. Starvation may be caused by errors in a scheduling or mutual exclusion algorithm, but can also be caused by resource leaks, and can be intentionally caused via a denial-of-service attack such as a fork bomb.
gpt_text:
In computer science, starvation is a situation where one or more threads or processes are perpetually denied the resources they need to make progress, even though those resources are available in the system. This typically happens in concurrent or multitasking environments when scheduling or synchronization policies repeatedly favor other tasks, so the starved task waits indefinitely without ever completing.

Starvation can occur due to priority-based scheduling (low-priority tasks never getting CPU time), unfair locking or synchronization mechanisms (some threads always winning access to a lock), or resource allocation strategies that don’t guarantee fairness. It differs from deadlock in that the starved task *could* proceed if it were given resources, whereas in deadlock a cycle of dependencies prevents progress for all involved tasks. Prevention techniques focus on fairness, such as aging (gradually increasing a task’s priority) and using fair locks or schedulers.

title: Concurrency pattern
human_text: In software engineering, concurrency patterns are those types of design patterns that deal with the multi-threaded programming paradigm.
gpt_text:
A concurrency pattern is a reusable design solution for managing multiple tasks that execute at the same time within a software system. Instead of inventing ad hoc ways to handle threads, processes, or asynchronous operations, developers use well-known patterns that clarify how work is split, coordinated, and synchronized while avoiding common pitfalls like race conditions and deadlocks.

Examples include patterns such as Producer–Consumer (one part of the system generates data while another consumes it), Futures/Promises (representing results of computations that complete later), Actor Model (isolated entities communicate via messages), and Read–Write Locks (optimizing access to shared data). These patterns help structure concurrent code so it is safer, more scalable, and easier to reason about.

title: Temporal logic of actions
human_text: Temporal logic of actions (TLA) is a logic developed by Leslie Lamport, which combines temporal logic with a logic of actions.

The Temporal Logic of Actions (TLA) is a formalism introduced by Leslie Lamport for specifying and reasoning about concurrent and distributed systems. It combines classical logic with temporal operators (like “always” and “eventually”) and explicit *actions* that describe how a system’s state can change from one step to the next. A system in TLA is modeled as a set of variables and actions that relate old and new values of these variables, together with temporal formulas that state what must hold over all possible execution traces.

TLA is especially useful for specifying high‑level system properties such as safety (“nothing bad ever happens”) and liveness (“something good eventually happens”) in a mathematically precise way. It underlies the TLA+ specification language and the TLC model checker, which allow engineers to write, explore, and automatically check specifications of complex algorithms and protocols before implementing them.

title: Concurrency semantics
human_text: In computer science, concurrency semantics is a way to give meaning to concurrent systems in a mathematically rigorous way. Concurrency semantics is often based on mathematical theories of concurrency such as various process calculi, the actor model, or Petri nets.
gpt_text:

It defines what outcomes are allowed or forbidden when threads or processes interact through shared memory, messages, or other resources—answering questions like “Is this reordering of operations legal?” or “Can this data race produce that result?”

Different models of concurrency semantics (such as sequential consistency, linearizability, or the Java/C/C++ memory models) specify what programmers can safely assume about visibility of writes, ordering of operations, and atomicity. These semantics are crucial for reasoning about correctness, detecting bugs like data races and deadlocks, and designing concurrent algorithms and synchronization mechanisms.

title: Cigarette smokers problem
human_text: The cigarette smokers problem is a concurrency problem in computer science, originally described in 1971 by Suhas Patil.

It involves three smoker processes, each having an infinite supply of one of three ingredients needed to roll a cigarette (tobacco, paper, or matches), and an agent process that repeatedly places two of the three ingredients on a table. Only the smoker who has the third, missing ingredient can proceed to roll and smoke a cigarette.

The problem is used to design and analyze solutions that prevent race conditions, deadlocks, and starvation when multiple processes compete for resources. It is commonly solved using synchronization primitives like semaphores, monitors, or condition variables, and serves as an educational example for understanding interprocess communication and proper resource allocation in concurrent systems.

title: Synchronization (computer science)
human_text: In computer science, synchronization refers to one of two distinct but related concepts: synchronization of processes, and synchronization of data. Process synchronization refers to the idea that multiple processes are to join up or handshake at a certain point, in order to reach an agreement or commit to a certain sequence of action. Data synchronization refers to the idea of keeping multiple copies of a dataset in coherence with one another, or to maintain data integrity. Process synchronization primitives are commonly used to implement data synchronization.
gpt_text:
In computer science, synchronization refers to the coordination of concurrent processes or threads so they can safely access shared resources without interfering with each other. Without synchronization, operations that appear simple—like incrementing a counter or writing to a shared data structure—can lead to race conditions, data corruption, or unpredictable behavior when executed by multiple threads or processes at the same time.

Synchronization is typically achieved using mechanisms such as locks (mutexes), semaphores, monitors, condition variables, barriers, and atomic operations. These tools ensure properties like mutual exclusion (only one thread can access a critical section at a time) and ordering (operations happen in a defined sequence), which are essential for building correct and reliable concurrent and parallel programs.

title: Active object
human_text: The active object design pattern decouples method execution from method invocation for objects that each reside in their own thread of control. The goal is to introduce concurrency, by using asynchronous method invocation and a scheduler for handling requests.Bass, L., Clements, P., Kazman, R. Software Architecture in Practice. Addison Wesley, 2003

An active object is a design pattern in concurrent and distributed systems where an object owns its own thread of control and processes requests asynchronously. Instead of callers invoking methods directly and blocking until completion, they send requests (often as messages or method calls wrapped in futures) to the active object, which queues and executes them in its dedicated thread.

This pattern decouples method invocation from execution, making it easier to structure concurrent behavior, avoid explicit locking, and prevent race conditions. Active objects are common in systems that need responsive user interfaces, background processing, or message-driven architectures, and underpin many actor-model frameworks and event-driven systems.

title: Memory ordering
human_text: Memory ordering describes the order of accesses to computer memory by a CPU. The term can refer either to the memory ordering generated by the compiler during compile time, or to the memory ordering generated by a CPU during runtime.

Memory ordering refers to the rules that determine the order in which reads and writes to memory appear to occur across different threads or processors. On modern CPUs and in concurrent programming, operations may be reordered by hardware or compilers for performance, as long as they preserve certain guarantees. Memory ordering models (like sequential consistency, acquire-release, or relaxed ordering) specify what behaviors are allowed and what constraints must be enforced so that multithreaded programs behave predictably.

In practice, developers use synchronization primitives (locks, atomics, barriers, fences) to impose specific orderings between memory operations. For example, a “release” store followed by an “acquire” load on another thread can ensure that all writes before the release become visible before any reads after the acquire. Correct use of memory ordering is crucial to avoid subtle concurrency bugs such as data races and visibility issues.

title: Producer–consumer problem
human_text: In computing, the producer–consumer problem (also known as the bounded-buffer problem) is a classic example of a multi-process synchronization problem, the first version of which was proposed by Edsger W. Dijkstra in 1965 in his unpublished manuscript,

The producer–consumer problem is a classic example in concurrent programming and operating systems that illustrates synchronization challenges when multiple processes (or threads) share a common resource. In this problem, one or more producers generate data items and place them into a shared buffer, while one or more consumers remove items from that buffer for processing. The key constraints are that producers must not add items to a full buffer, and consumers must not remove items from an empty buffer.

Solving the producer–consumer problem typically involves using synchronization mechanisms like semaphores, mutexes, monitors, or condition variables to coordinate access to the buffer and avoid race conditions. Correct solutions ensure mutual exclusion (only one thread manipulates the buffer at a time) and proper signaling so that producers and consumers wait when necessary and proceed safely when the buffer state allows.

title: Parallel I/O
human_text: Parallel I/O, in the context of a computer, means the performance of multiple input/output operations at the same time, for instance simultaneously outputs to storage devices and display devices. It is a fundamental feature of operating systems.

It is widely used in high-performance computing, large-scale databases, and data-intensive applications where many processes or threads need to read and write large volumes of data at the same time.

In practice, parallel I/O often involves specialized file systems (like parallel file systems), libraries (such as MPI-IO or HDF5), and hardware architectures (multiple disks, RAID arrays, or distributed storage) that coordinate concurrent access to shared data. By overlapping and distributing I/O operations, parallel I/O helps applications scale more efficiently as they use more compute nodes or cores.

title: History monoid
human_text: In mathematics and computer science, a history monoid is a way of representing the histories of concurrently running computer processes as a collection of strings, each string representing the individual history of a process. The history monoid provides a set of synchronization primitives (such as locks, mutexes or thread joins) for providing rendezvous points between a set of independently executing processes or threads.
gpt_text:
A history monoid is an algebraic structure used to model concurrent or partially ordered sequences of events, especially in theoretical computer science. It extends the idea of a free monoid (all finite words over an alphabet) by incorporating an independence relation between letters/events. Instead of treating every sequence as totally ordered, a history monoid identifies sequences that differ only by swapping adjacent, independent events, so they represent the same “history” of what happened.

Formally, given an alphabet \(A\) and an independence relation \(I \subseteq A \times A\) (symmetric and irreflexive), the history monoid is the quotient of the free monoid \(A^*\) by the smallest congruence that allows commuting of independent letters: \(ab \equiv ba\) whenever \((a,b) \in I\). This captures the idea that independent actions can occur in any order without changing the overall behavior, making history monoids useful in concurrency theory and the study of trace languages.

title: Hennessy–Milner logic
human_text: In computer science, Hennessy–Milner logic (HML) is a dynamic logic used to specify properties of a labeled transition system (LTS), a structure similar to an automaton. It was introduced in 1980 by Matthew Hennessy and Robin Milner in their paper "On observing nondeterminism and concurrency" (ICALP).

Its formulas are built from propositional connectives together with modal operators that talk about the possible actions a process can perform and what must hold afterward (e.g., “[a]φ” meaning “after every a-transition, φ holds,” and “⟨a⟩φ” meaning “there exists an a-transition after which φ holds”).  

A central result, the Hennessy–Milner theorem, states that over certain classes of systems (notably image-finite ones), two processes are bisimilar if and only if they satisfy exactly the same HML formulas. This makes HML a powerful tool for characterizing behavioral equivalence and for specifying and verifying properties of processes in concurrency theory.

title: ABA problem
human_text: In multithreaded computing, the ABA problem occurs during synchronization, when a location is read twice, has the same value for both reads, and "value is the same" is used to indicate "nothing has changed". However, another thread can execute between the two reads and change the value, do other work, then change the value back, thus fooling the first thread into thinking "nothing has changed" even though the second thread did work that violates that assumption.
gpt_text:
The ABA problem is a concurrency issue that arises in multithreaded or lock-free algorithms when a shared value is read, changed to something else, and then changed back to its original value between two reads. A thread that uses compare-and-swap (CAS) or similar atomic operations may see the same value “A” before and after its operation and incorrectly conclude that nothing has changed, even though the value was temporarily changed to “B” and then restored to “A.”

This can lead to subtle and hard-to-detect bugs, such as operating on freed or repurposed memory, breaking data structure invariants, or losing updates. Common strategies to prevent the ABA problem include tagging values with version counters, using larger atomic primitives (like double-width CAS to store both a value and a version), or employing memory reclamation schemes such as hazard pointers.

title: Memory model (programming)
human_text: In computing, a memory model describes the interactions of threads through memory and their shared use of the data.

It describes what values a read can legally observe, how writes become visible to other threads, and which reorderings of instructions are allowed by the compiler and hardware while still preserving “correct” program behavior.

Memory models are crucial in concurrent programming because modern processors and compilers perform optimizations that can change the apparent order of operations. Languages like C++ and Java define their own memory models to give programmers a clear contract for writing thread-safe code using primitives such as locks, atomics, and volatile variables. A well-defined memory model enables both safe reasoning about concurrent code and efficient implementation on different hardware architectures.

title: Racetrack problem
human_text: A racetrack problem is a specific instance of a type of race condition. A racetrack problem is a flaw in a system or process whereby the output and/or result of the process is unexpectedly and critically dependent on the sequence or timing of other events that run in a circular pattern. This problem is semantically different from a race condition because of the circular nature of the problem.

It is often used in artificial intelligence and reinforcement learning as a benchmark for planning and control under constraints. The problem highlights issues like state representation (position and velocity), search in large discrete state spaces, and trade-offs between speed and safety when navigating complex environments.

title: Stochastic Petri net
human_text: Stochastic Petri nets are a form of Petri net where the transitions fire after a probabilistic delay determined by a random variable.

In addition to places, transitions, and tokens, each transition in an SPN is associated with a firing rate or probability distribution, typically exponential, which governs the stochastic timing of its occurrence. This allows the model to capture both the logical structure of a system and the uncertainty in when events happen.

SPNs are widely used in performance and reliability analysis of concurrent, distributed, and fault-tolerant systems—such as computer networks, manufacturing systems, and communication protocols. By translating an SPN into an underlying continuous-time Markov chain, analysts can compute performance metrics like throughput, response time, and failure probabilities.

title: Nets within Nets

Nets within Nets (NwN) is an extension of Petri nets in which tokens themselves can be Petri nets. This creates a hierarchical or object-oriented modeling style where a “system net” coordinates the interactions of many “token nets,” each representing complex entities such as processes, agents, or components.

This formalism is particularly useful for modeling systems with dynamic structure and rich internal states, such as workflow systems, multi-agent systems, biological processes, and distributed or adaptive software. By letting tokens carry their own logic and state transitions, Nets within Nets provide a powerful way to represent both the global coordination and the local behavior of system components in a unified, mathematically precise framework.

title: Channel system (computer science)
human_text: In computer science, a channel system is a finite state machine similar to communicating finite-state machine in which there is a single system communicating with itself instead of many systems communicating with each other. A channel system is similar to a pushdown automaton where a queue is used instead of a stack. Those queues are called channels. Intuitively, each channel represents a sequence a message to be sent, and to be read in the order in which they are sent.

In computer science, a **channel system** is a formal model of computation where processes communicate by sending and receiving messages through channels—abstract, usually unbounded FIFO (first-in, first-out) queues. Each process executes a sequence of operations (like `send` and `receive`) on named channels, and the system’s state is defined by the control location of each process plus the contents of all channels.

Channel systems are widely used to model and analyze concurrent and distributed systems, such as communication protocols, networked services, and message-passing programs. Because channels may be unbounded, reachability and verification questions (e.g., “can this error state be reached?”) often become undecidable in the general case, making channel systems a central object of study in formal verification and automata theory.
